paragraphs: The paper develops a self-organizing Hopfield-type network for television image compression using vector quantization. In this setting, a codebook supplies representative patterns for encoding image information. The proposed approach makes the organization of the neural network part of how an image-specific codebook is generated.

A distinctive feature is the use of metastable network states as an additional storage resource. These states offer further representational possibilities within the spin-glass-like network. The method therefore connects the collection of states available to the network with the collection of representatives available for compression.

The authors use the Minimal Overlap learning rule to optimize the organization of attractors, the states toward which the network's dynamics tend. Their self-organizing scheme produces an adaptive codebook for a given television image. The contribution lies in linking attractor organization, extra storage through metastable states, and codebook adaptation within one approach. This makes the network's internal dynamics directly relevant to the representation used for image compression.
summary.tldr: A self-organizing Hopfield network uses metastable states and organized attractors to generate adaptive codebooks for television image compression.

title: Neural Approach for TV Image Compression Using a Hopfield Type Network

paragraphs: This paper develops a faster way to train recurrent neural networks online, as their activity unfolds. It identifies a tradeoff in existing methods: backward propagation through time requires a backward pass for accumulating errors, while forward learning can operate online but incurs substantial computation when updating a large sensitivity matrix.

The proposed method replaces direct integration of the high-dimensional sensitivity dynamics with a forward calculation of their Green’s function. This reformulation avoids redundant computations, after which weights can be updated when an error needs correction. The authors describe the resulting algorithm as one order faster per time step than the sensitivity-matrix approach.

A numerical example classifies state trajectories with a recurrent network and supports the claimed speed advantage over the Williams–Zipser algorithm. The significance is that online operation and computational efficiency are addressed together. The method retains a forward-in-time learning procedure while changing the calculation needed to connect network errors to weight updates, targeting a specific computational bottleneck in recurrent learning.
summary.tldr: A Green’s-function formulation reduces redundant sensitivity calculations to accelerate online recurrent-network learning.

title: Green's Function Method for Fast On-Line Learning Algorithm of Recurrent Neural Networks

paragraphs: This paper analyzes how expected training error relates to expected error on new data for nonlinear learning systems. It considers models such as multilayer perceptrons and radial-basis-function networks. The central question is how to account for model complexity when interpreting the fit achieved on a training sample.

The authors derive a second-order relationship involving sample size, effective noise variance, regularization strength, and an effective number of parameters. This effective count generally differs from the literal number of model parameters for nonlinear or regularized systems. Monte Carlo experiments support that theoretical conclusion, showing why simply counting adjustable parameters can misrepresent the complexity relevant to prediction.

The paper also proposes generalized prediction error as an estimate of the relationship. It extends established prediction-risk estimates to the nonlinear setting. The significance is a framework that links generalization to the model's effective flexibility under regularization, allowing complexity to be treated as more than a fixed property of the network's parameter count.
summary.tldr: Generalization depends on an effective parameter count that can differ from the literal count in nonlinear or regularized models.

title: The Effective Number of Parameters: An Analysis of Generalization and Regularization in Nonlinear Learning Systems

paragraphs: The paper presents an implemented neural model of recognizing familiar objects in scenes containing multiple, potentially overlapping objects. It brings together selective attention, perceptual organization, and transformations supporting invariant recognition. The central question is how these processes cooperate to separate objects, choose what to process, and identify what is present.

Spatially organized feature maps feed two main routes: one represents location, and the other processes object shape and attributes. An early attention mechanism favors a contiguous region of the visual field. That location-based selection also controls normalization within the recognition route, linking where the model attends to how it prepares an object for recognition.

Segmentation separates the scene into entities, while an oscillatory binding mechanism allows multiple segmented entities to be represented at once. Connections between the location and recognition routes coordinate the functional subsystems. The authors report overall behavior consistent with several psychophysical findings. The contribution is an integrated computational account in which attention, grouping, and recognition actively support one another.
summary.tldr: An oscillator network coordinates attention, segmentation, and normalization to recognize objects within complex visual scenes.

title: Perceiving Complex Visual Scenes: An Oscillator Neural Network Model that Integrates Selective Attention, Perceptual Organisation, and Invariant Recognition

We present an MS-TDNN for recognizing continuously spelled letters, a task characterized by a small but highly confusable vocabulary. Our MS-TDNN achieves 98.5/92.0% word accuracy on speaker dependent/independent tasks, outper(cid:173) forming previously reported results on the same databases. We pro(cid:173) pose training techniques aimed at improving sentence level perfor(cid:173) mance, including free alignment across word boundaries, word du(cid:173) ration modeling and error backpropagation on the sentence rather than the word level. Architectures integrating submodules special(cid:173) ized on a subset of speakers achieved further improvements.

paragraphs: This paper recognizes letters spoken continuously, a task with relatively few possible labels but substantial confusion between them. Its Multi-State Time Delay Neural Network combines a time-delay network's ability to identify speech sounds with dynamic time warping. The alignment procedure accommodates timing differences while the complete system performs word-level classification and learns through backpropagation.

The reported word accuracies are 98.5% for speaker-dependent recognition and 92.0% for speaker-independent recognition. These results exceed previously reported performance on the same databases. The distinction matters because recognizing a familiar speaker and handling speakers independently are different recognition settings, and the paper reports them separately.

The authors also propose training changes aimed at whole-sentence performance. These include allowing alignment across word boundaries, modeling word duration, and propagating errors from the sentence level rather than only individual words. Architectures with submodules specialized for subsets of speakers yield further improvements. Together, these directions connect local sound recognition, sequence alignment, and speaker variation within one trainable recognition architecture.
summary.tldr: An MS-TDNN combines learned speech features and flexible alignment to recognize continuously spoken letters with strong reported accuracy.

title: Connected Letter Recognition with a Multi-State Time Delay Neural Network

paragraphs: The paper compares feed-forward networks with fixed hidden units against networks whose hidden units can vary. It asks how these choices affect the resources required to represent functions on a finite set of points. Two resources are distinguished: the number of synaptic weights and the number of hidden units.

For approximation, the task is to represent every function in an open subset of functions defined on that finite domain. The authors find that both network categories require the same minimum number of synaptic weights. In this setting, allowing hidden units to vary does not lower the stated minimum weight requirement.

The second task is to represent every binary labeling of the domain. When the points are in general position, networks with variable threshold hidden units can require substantially fewer hidden units than any fixed-hidden-unit network. The results therefore depend on both the task and the resource being counted. Equal requirements for weights in function approximation coexist with a hidden-unit advantage in representing arbitrary dichotomies.
summary.tldr: Fixed and variable hidden-unit networks share one approximation weight bound, but variable units can reduce the hidden-unit count for binary labelings.

title: Some Estimates of Necessary Number of Connections and Hidden Units for Feed-Forward Networks

abstract: In this paper we propose recurrent neural networks with feedback into the input units for handling two types of data analysis problems. On the one hand, this scheme can be used for static data when some of the input variables are missing. On the other hand, it can also be used for sequential data, when some of the input variables are missing or are available at different frequencies. Unlike in the case of probabilistic models (e.g. Gaussian) of the missing variables, the network does not attempt to model the distribution of the missmg variables given the observed variables. Instead it is a more "discriminant" approach that fills in the missing variables for the sole purpose of minimizing a learning criterion (e.g., to minimize an output error).

paragraphs: This paper proposes recurrent neural networks that feed information back into their input units to handle incomplete observations. The approach covers static records with missing variables and sequential data in which variables are missing or observed at different frequencies. These cases share a practical issue: the network cannot always receive a complete set of fresh inputs.

The feedback mechanism allows missing inputs to be filled in as part of the learning system. The objective is discriminative: the filled values are chosen to help minimize a learning criterion, such as error at the output. Their role is therefore defined by the task the network is trained to perform.

This differs from estimating a conditional probability distribution for missing variables given observed ones. The paper's approach centers the quality of the eventual prediction or other learning objective. That distinction matters because it connects completion directly to task performance. The same recurrent arrangement provides a proposed framework for both gaps in static data and unequal observation schedules in sequences.
summary.tldr: Input-feedback recurrent networks fill missing or asynchronous inputs according to the learning task's objective.

title: Recurrent Neural Networks for Missing or Asynchronous Data

abstract: We present a new approach to reinforcement learning in which the poli(cid:173) cies considered by the learning process are constrained by hierarchies of partially specified machines. This allows for the use of prior knowledge to reduce the search space and provides a framework in which knowledge can be transferred across problems and in which component solutions can be recombined to solve larger and more complicated problems. Our approach can be seen as providing a link between reinforcement learn(cid:173) ing and "behavior-based" or "teleo-reactive" approaches to control. We present provably convergent algorithms for problem-solving and learn(cid:173) ing with hierarchical machines and demonstrate their effectiveness on a problem with several thousand states.

This allows for the use of prior knowledge to reduce the search space and provides a framework in which knowledge can be transferred across problems and in which component solutions can be recombined to solve larger and more complicated problems. Our approach can be seen as providing a link between reinforcement learn(cid:173) ing and "behavior-based" or "teleo-reactive" approaches to control. paragraphs: Reinforcement learning can face a large search space when it must discover an entire policy without structural guidance. This paper constrains the policies under consideration using hierarchies of partially specified machines. The machines encode some organization of behavior while leaving choices open for the learning process to resolve.

This arrangement gives prior knowledge a direct role in determining which solutions the learner explores. The hierarchy also provides a framework for transferring knowledge across problems and recombining component solutions into behavior for larger tasks. The approach connects reinforcement learning with behavior-based and teleo-reactive control by bringing structured descriptions of behavior into policy learning.

The authors present algorithms for both problem-solving and learning with hierarchical machines and prove their convergence. They also demonstrate effectiveness on a problem with several thousand states. The central tradeoff is inherent in the method: the hierarchy reduces the search space by constraining available policies. Its benefit is a way to retain learnable decisions while supplying reusable structure that helps organize a complicated control problem.
summary.tldr: Partially specified hierarchical machines constrain reinforcement learning, enabling structured search and reusable component solutions with convergent algorithms.

title: Reinforcement Learning with Hierarchies of Machines

abstract: Motivated by the findings of modular structure in the association cortex, we study a multi-modular model of associative memory that can successfully store memory patterns with different levels of ac(cid:173) tivity. We show that the segregation of synaptic conductances into intra-modular linear and inter-modular nonlinear ones considerably enhances the network's memory retrieval performance. Compared with the conventional, single-module associative memory network, the multi-modular network has two main advantages: It is less sus(cid:173) ceptible to damage to columnar input, and its response is consistent with the cognitive data pertaining to category specific impairment.

paragraphs: The paper investigates an associative-memory network organized into multiple modules, motivated by modular structure in association cortex. The model can store memory patterns with different levels of activity. This makes the organization of the network relevant to both the kinds of patterns it retains and its ability to retrieve them.

A central design choice separates connections within modules from connections between modules. Within-module synaptic conductances are linear, while between-module conductances are nonlinear. The authors report that this division considerably improves retrieval performance. The benefit therefore depends on assigning different interaction rules to the two levels of organization, as well as having multiple modules.

Compared with a conventional single-module associative memory, the model is less vulnerable to damage to columnar input. Its responses also agree with cognitive observations of category-specific impairment. These results connect memory performance and damage response within one architecture, suggesting that modular organization can help explain both successful retrieval and selective patterns of impairment.
summary.tldr: A modular associative memory with different within-module and between-module interactions improves retrieval and robustness to input damage.

title: Multi-modular Associative Memory

abstract: We discuss the problem of catastrophic fusion in multimodal recog(cid:173) nition systems. This problem arises in systems that need to fuse different channels in non-stationary environments. Practice shows that when recognition modules within each modality are tested in contexts inconsistent with their assumptions, their influence on the fused product tends to increase, with catastrophic results. We ex(cid:173) plore a principled solution to this problem based upon Bayesian ideas of competitive models and inference robustification: each sensory channel is provided with simple white-noise context mod(cid:173) els, and the perceptual hypothesis and context are jointly esti(cid:173) mated. Consequently, context deviations are interpreted as changes in white noise contamination strength, automatically adjusting the influence of the module. The approach is tested on a fixed lexicon automatic audiovisual speech recognition problem with very good results.

paragraphs: Combining sensory channels can fail when the environment changes in ways their recognition modules do not expect. The abstract describes a particularly damaging behavior: a module operating outside its assumptions can gain influence over the combined result. The paper calls this catastrophic fusion and seeks a principled way to control it.

The proposed Bayesian approach gives each sensory channel simple context models based on white noise. It estimates the perceptual interpretation and the context together. When a channel deviates from its expected conditions, the model interprets that deviation through the strength of noise contamination. This allows the channel's influence to adjust automatically as part of inference.

The authors test the method on audiovisual speech recognition with a fixed vocabulary and report very good results. The central contribution is to make channel reliability part of the recognition model itself. Audio and visual evidence are combined while simultaneously assessing the conditions under which each was obtained, addressing the source of the fusion failure.
summary.tldr: Jointly estimating sensory interpretations and noise conditions helps prevent unreliable channels from dominating audiovisual recognition.

title: Bayesian Robustification for Audio Visual Fusion

abstract: Singular value decomposition (SVD) can be viewed as a method for unsupervised training of a network that associates two classes of events reciprocally by linear connections through a single hidden layer. SVD was used to learn and represent relations among very large numbers of words (20k-60k) and very large numbers of natural text passages (lk- 70k) in which they occurred. The result was 100-350 dimensional "semantic spaces" in which any trained or newly aibl word or passage could be represented as a vector, and similarities were measured by the cosine of the contained angle between vectors. Good accmacy in simulating human judgments and behaviors has been demonstrated by performance on multiple-choice vocabulary and domain knowledge tests, emulation of expert essay evaluations, and in several other ways. Examples are also given of how the kind of knowledge extracted by this method can be applied.

paragraphs: The paper investigates how relationships between words and text passages can support the learning of human-like knowledge. It uses singular value decomposition to learn from large collections of word occurrences. The method is interpreted as unsupervised training of a network that associates words and passages through a single hidden layer with linear connections.

The learned representation places words and passages in semantic spaces with 100 to 350 dimensions. Similarity is measured by the angle between their vectors, using cosine similarity. This gives the system one common representation for comparing language items, with the structure learned from the passages in which words occur rather than from separately supplied judgments of their meanings.

The abstract reports good agreement with human judgments and behavior on multiple-choice vocabulary and domain-knowledge tests, expert essay evaluations, and other tasks. These findings show that the learned relationships can support more than a single text-comparison exercise. The paper also presents examples of applications for the knowledge extracted by this method.
summary.tldr: SVD learns semantic spaces from word–passage relationships that reproduce aspects of human vocabulary knowledge and text judgments.

title: Learning Human-like Knowledge by Singular Value Decomposition: A Progress Report

abstract: Everybody "knows" that neural networks need more than a single layer of nonlinear units to compute interesting functions. We show that this is false if one employs winner-take-all as nonlinear unit: • Any boolean function can be computed by a single k-winner-take(cid:173) all unit applied to weighted sums of the input variables. • Any continuous function can be approximated arbitrarily well by a single soft winner-take-all unit applied to weighted sums of the input variables. • Only positive weights are needed in these (linear) weighted sums. This may be of interest from the point of view of neurophysiology, since only 15% of the synapses in the cortex are inhibitory. In addi(cid:173) tion it is widely believed that there are special microcircuits in the cortex that compute winner-take-all. • Our results support the view that winner-take-all is a very useful basic computational unit in Neural VLS!: o it is wellknown that winner-take-all of n input variables can be computed very efficiently with 2n transistors (and a to(cid:173) tal wire length and area that is linear in n) in analog VLSI [Lazzaro et at., 1989] o we show that winner-take-all is not just useful for special pur(cid:173) pose computations, but may serve as the only nonlinear unit for neural circuits with universal computational power o we show that any multi-layer perceptron needs quadratically in n many gates to compute winner-take-all for n input variables, hence winner-take-all provides a substantially more powerful computational unit than a perceptron (at about the same cost of implementation in analog VLSI). In addi(cid:173) tion it is widely believed that there are special microcircuits in the cortex that compute winner-take-all. • Our results support the view that winner-take-all is a very useful basic computational unit in Neural VLS!: o it is wellknown that winner-take-all of n input variables can be computed very efficiently with 2n transistors (and a to(cid:173) tal wire length and area that is linear in n) in analog VLSI [Lazzaro et at., 1989] o we show that winner-take-all is not just useful for special pur(cid:173) pose computations, but may serve as the only nonlinear unit for neural circuits with universal computational power o we show that any multi-layer perceptron needs quadratically in n many gates to compute winner-take-all for n input variables, hence winner-take-all provides a substantially more powerful computational unit than a perceptron (at about the same cost of implementation in analog VLSI). Complete proofs and further details to these results can be found in [Maass, 2000]. 294

paragraphs: This paper challenges the idea that interesting neural computation necessarily requires several layers of nonlinear units. It proves that a single k-winner-take-all operation applied to weighted input sums can compute any Boolean function. A single soft winner-take-all operation applied to such sums can also approximate any continuous function arbitrarily closely.

The weighted sums require only positive weights. The authors connect this property to biological interest in predominantly excitatory cortical connections and proposed winner-take-all microcircuits. The mathematical point is that selecting among competing linear responses provides enough nonlinearity for universal computational power, even when the preceding weighted sums are restricted in this way.

The paper also argues for winner-take-all as a hardware building block. It cites efficient analog implementations and proves that multilayer perceptrons need a number of gates growing quadratically with the number of inputs to compute winner-take-all. This comparison highlights how choosing the basic computational unit changes circuit complexity: an operation that is compact as a dedicated circuit can be expensive to reproduce using perceptron gates.
summary.tldr: Winner-take-all can supply the only nonlinear operation needed for universal neural computation, with positive weights in the preceding linear sums.

title: Neural Computation with Winner-Take-All as the Only Nonlinear Operation

abstract: In this paper we define a probabilistic computational model which generalizes many noisy neural network models, including the recent work of Maass and Sontag [5]. We identify weak ergodicjty as the mechanism responsible for restriction of the computational power of probabilistic models to definite languages, independent of the characteristics of the noise: whether it is discrete or analog, or if it depends on the input or not, and independent of whether the variables are discrete or continuous. We give examples of weakly ergodic models including noisy computational systems with noise depending on the current state and inputs, aggregate models, and computational systems which update in continuous time.

We give examples of weakly ergodic models including noisy computational systems with noise depending on the current state and inputs, aggregate models, and computational systems which update in continuous time.

paragraphs: This paper introduces a probabilistic computational model that encompasses many models of noisy neural networks. Its question is theoretical: what property of a noisy system limits the kinds of languages it can recognize? A common framework allows the authors to study that restriction across systems with different kinds of randomness and state variables.

They identify weak ergodicity as the mechanism that restricts computational power to the class of definite languages. The result does not depend on noise being discrete rather than analog, or on whether it depends on the input. It also applies without requiring the system's variables to be either exclusively discrete or exclusively continuous.

The authors give examples of weakly ergodic systems with noise depending on both current state and input, aggregate models, and systems evolving in continuous time. These examples illustrate the reach of the framework across different implementations. The key qualification is the weak-ergodicity property: the paper locates the computational restriction in that property, rather than asserting that every system containing noise has the same limitation.
summary.tldr: Weak ergodicity explains a restriction to definite languages across a broad family of noisy computational models.

title: Noisy Neural Networks and Generalizations

abstract: In recent years variational methods have become a popular tool for approximate inference and learning in a wide variety of proba- bilistic models. For each new application, however, it is currently necessary (cid:12)rst to derive the variational update equations, and then to implement them in application-speci(cid:12)c code. Each of these steps is both time consuming and error prone. In this paper we describe a general purpose inference engine called VIBES (‘Variational Infer- ence for Bayesian Networks’) which allows a wide variety of proba- bilistic models to be implemented and solved variationally without recourse to coding. New models are speci(cid:12)ed either through a simple script or via a graphical interface analogous to a drawing package. VIBES then automatically generates and solves the vari- ational equations. We illustrate the power and (cid:13)exibility of VIBES using examples from Bayesian mixture modelling.

paragraphs: Variational methods support approximate inference and learning in probabilistic models, but applying them often requires substantial manual work. For each application, researchers must derive update equations and implement specialized code. This paper introduces VIBES, an inference engine intended to automate both steps and reduce their time cost and susceptibility to errors.

Users specify a model through a simple script or a graphical interface resembling a drawing tool. VIBES then generates the corresponding variational equations and solves them automatically. This separates describing a probabilistic model from writing the mathematical updates and application-specific implementation needed to perform inference.

The authors illustrate the system's flexibility with examples from Bayesian mixture modeling. The contribution is a general-purpose route to variational solutions for a wide variety of models, making model specification the main user-facing task. Its scope remains variational inference: automating the equations provides an approximate-inference workflow, rather than changing those approximations into exact Bayesian calculations.
summary.tldr: VIBES automatically derives and solves variational inference equations from scripted or graphical Bayesian-network specifications.

title: VIBES: A Variational Inference Engine for Bayesian Networks

abstract: The design of cooperative multi-robot systems is a highly active research area in robotics. Two lines of research in particular have generated inter- est: the solution of large, weakly coupled MDPs, and the design and im- plementation of market architectures. We propose a new algorithm which joins together these two lines of research. For a class of coupled MDPs, our algorithm automatically designs a market architecture which causes a decentralized multi-robot system to converge to a consistent policy. We can show that this policy is the same as the one which would be produced by a particular centralized planning algorithm. We demonstrate the new algorithm on three simulation examples: multi-robot towing, multi-robot path planning with a limited fuel resource, and coordinating behaviors in a game of paint ball.

Two lines of research in particular have generated inter- est: the solution of large, weakly coupled MDPs, and the design and im- plementation of market architectures. paragraphs: Coordinating several robots requires accounting for how their decisions affect one another. This paper connects two approaches to that problem: planning with large, weakly coupled Markov decision processes and coordinating robots through market architectures. Its contribution is an algorithm that automatically designs a market architecture for a specified class of coupled decision processes.

The resulting market causes the decentralized robot system to converge to a consistent policy. The authors also establish that this policy matches the one produced by a particular centralized planning algorithm. This gives the distributed coordination process a precise connection to a centralized planning procedure, rather than leaving their relationship only as an empirical question.

The guarantee applies to the stated class of coupled decision processes and the particular centralized algorithm used in the comparison. The paper demonstrates the method in simulations of cooperative towing, path planning under a limited fuel resource, and behavior coordination in paintball. Together, these examples illustrate the approach across different coordination tasks without extending the guarantee to every multi-robot problem.
summary.tldr: For a class of coupled MDPs, an automatically designed market makes decentralized robots converge to the policy of a particular centralized planner.

title: Auction Mechanism Design for Multi-Robot Coordination

abstract: We propose a probabilistic model based on Independent Component Analysis for learning multiple related tasks. In our model the task parameters are assumed to be generated from independent sources which account for the relatedness of the tasks. We use Laplace distributions to model hidden sources which makes it possible to identify the hidden, independent components instead of just modeling correlations. Furthermore, our model enjoys a sparsity property which makes it both parsimonious and robust. We also propose efficient algorithms for both empirical Bayes method and point estimation. Our experimental results on two multi-label text classification data sets show that the proposed approach is promising.

Furthermore, our model enjoys a sparsity property which makes it both parsimonious and robust. We also propose efficient algorithms for both empirical Bayes method and point estimation. paragraphs: The paper proposes a probabilistic approach to learning several related tasks together. Its central assumption is that the parameters for those tasks arise from hidden independent sources. Shared sources provide an explanation for why tasks are related, making the structure behind their parameters part of the model rather than treating every task in isolation.

The approach builds on independent component analysis and assigns Laplace distributions to the hidden sources. The authors state that this allows identification of the independent components, going beyond a description of correlations among tasks. The model also has a sparsity property, which they associate with a compact representation and robustness.

The authors develop efficient algorithms for empirical Bayes learning and for point estimation. Experiments on two multi-label text classification datasets give promising results. The contribution therefore includes both a model of task relationships and ways to fit it. Its interpretation depends on the independent-source assumption: the hidden components are the proposed mechanism through which information about related tasks is organized and shared.
summary.tldr: A sparse probabilistic model explains related tasks through independent Laplace-distributed sources and shows promising results on two text classification datasets.

title: Learning Multiple Related Tasks using Latent Independent Component Analysis

abstract: We consider criteria for variational representations of non-Gaussian latent variables, and derive variational EM algorithms in general form. We establish a general equivalence among convex bounding methods, evidence based methods, and ensemble learning/Variational Bayes methods, which has previously been demonstrated only for particular cases.
originalAbstract: We consider criteria for variational representations of non-Gaussian latent variables, and derive variational EM algorithms in general form. We establish a general equivalence among convex bounding methods, evidence based methods, and ensemble learning/Variational Bayes methods, which has previously been demonstrated only for particular cases.

paragraphs: This paper studies models containing hidden variables whose distributions are non-Gaussian. Its focus is on criteria for representing those variables variationally and on deriving expectation-maximization algorithms in a general form. The aim is to describe a broad approach to this class of models rather than derive a procedure only for one particular example.

The central theoretical result establishes a general equivalence among convex bounding methods, evidence-based methods, and ensemble learning or Variational Bayes methods. These are different formulations for handling the latent-variable problem. Showing an equivalence connects their mathematical roles and provides a common account of methods that might otherwise be considered separately.

According to the abstract, such equivalences had previously been demonstrated only in particular cases. Extending the connection to a general formulation is therefore the main advance, alongside the variational EM derivations. Its significance is a unified understanding of these approaches to non-Gaussian latent-variable models, rather than an empirical claim that one named method outperforms the others.
summary.tldr: The paper derives general variational EM algorithms and establishes an equivalence among convex bounding, evidence-based, and Variational Bayes approaches.

title: Variational EM Algorithms for Non-Gaussian Latent Variable Models

abstract: Most algorithms for solving Markov decision processes rely on a discount factor, which ensures their convergence. In fact, it is often used in problems with is no intrinsic motivation. In this paper, we show that when used in approximate dynamic programming, an artificially low discount factor may significantly improve the performance on some problems, such as Tetris. We propose two explanations for this phenomenon. Our first justification follows directly from the standard approximation error bounds: using a lower discount factor may decrease the approximation error bounds. However, we also show that these bounds are loose, a thus their decrease does not entirely justify a better practical performance. We thus propose another justification: when the rewards are received only sporadically (as it is the case in Tetris), we can derive tighter bounds, which support a significant performance increase with a decrease in the discount factor.

paragraphs: A discount factor controls how strongly a decision-making algorithm values later rewards. It also helps ensure convergence in many methods for Markov decision processes, even when discounting has no intrinsic motivation in the task. This paper studies an intriguing consequence: deliberately lowering the discount factor can substantially improve approximate dynamic programming on some problems, including Tetris.

The authors first examine the usual bounds on approximation error. Those bounds can become smaller when the discount factor decreases, providing one explanation for the improvement. However, the paper also shows that these bounds are loose. A reduction in a loose bound does not by itself fully explain the observed practical benefit.

A second analysis focuses on problems in which rewards arrive only occasionally. For this setting, the authors derive tighter bounds that support substantial improvement from lower discounting. The resulting argument is conditional on the reward structure and approximation setting. It explains why changing the effective planning horizon can help on some tasks without claiming that lower discount factors always improve decisions.
summary.tldr: Lower discount factors can improve approximate dynamic programming on some tasks, with tighter error bounds explaining benefits when rewards are sporadic.

title: Biasing Approximate Dynamic Programming with a Lower Discount Factor

abstract: Metric learning algorithms can provide useful distance functions for a variety of domains, and recent work has shown good accuracy for problems where the learner can access all distance constraints at once. However, in many real applications, constraints are only available incrementally, thus necessitating methods that can perform online updates to the learned metric. Existing online algorithms offer bounds on worst-case performance, but typically do not perform well in practice as compared to their offline counterparts. We present a new online metric learning algorithm that updates a learned Mahalanobis metric based on LogDet regularization and gradient descent. We prove theoretical worst-case performance bounds, and empirically compare the proposed method against existing online metric learning algorithms. To further boost the practicality of our approach, we develop an online locality-sensitive hashing scheme which leads to efficient updates for approximate similarity search data structures. We demonstrate our algorithm on multiple datasets and show that it outperforms relevant baselines.

We prove theoretical worst-case performance bounds, and empirically compare the proposed method against existing online metric learning algorithms. We demonstrate our algorithm on multiple datasets and show that it outperforms relevant baselines.

paragraphs: Metric learning adapts a distance function to the relationships a task needs to capture. This paper addresses applications where distance constraints arrive incrementally, requiring updates as new information becomes available. The authors identify a practical gap: existing online methods have worst-case guarantees but often perform poorly compared with methods that receive all constraints at once.

Their algorithm updates a Mahalanobis metric through gradient descent with LogDet regularization. They prove worst-case performance bounds and empirically compare the method with existing online metric learners. This combines theoretical analysis with evaluation of whether the online updates work well on observed data.

The paper also develops an online locality-sensitive hashing scheme so that approximate similarity-search data structures can be updated efficiently. This addresses the practical connection between changing a distance function and maintaining a search system that uses it. Experiments on multiple datasets show performance exceeding relevant baselines. Together, the learning and hashing components make the contribution about both adapting similarity judgments and supporting efficient search as those judgments change.
summary.tldr: An online Mahalanobis metric learner combines worst-case guarantees with an updatable hashing scheme for efficient approximate similarity search.

title: Online Metric Learning and Fast Similarity Search

abstract: Little work has been done to directly combine the outputs of multiple supervised and unsupervised models. However, it can increase the accuracy and applicability of ensemble methods. First, we can boost the diversity of classification ensemble by incorporating multiple clustering outputs, each of which provides grouping constraints for the joint label predictions of a set of related objects. Secondly, ensemble of supervised models is limited in applications which have no access to raw data but to the meta-level model outputs. In this paper, we aim at calculating a consolidated classification solution for a set of objects by maximizing the consensus among both supervised predictions and unsupervised grouping constraints. We seek a global optimal label assignment for the target objects, which is different from the result of traditional majority voting and model combination approaches. We cast the problem into an optimization problem on a bipartite graph, where the objective function favors smoothness in the conditional probability estimates over the graph, as well as penalizes deviation from initial labeling of supervised models. We solve the problem through iterative propagation of conditional probability estimates among neighboring nodes, and interpret the method as conducting a constrained embedding in a transformed space, as well as a ranking on the graph. Experimental results on three real applications demonstrate the benefits of the proposed method over existing alternatives.

paragraphs: This paper combines information from classifiers and clustering methods to assign labels jointly to a collection of objects. Classifiers provide predicted labels, while clustering outputs provide constraints about which objects belong together. Combining both can broaden an ensemble’s information sources, including situations where only model outputs are available and the underlying raw data cannot be accessed.

The authors formulate consensus as an optimization problem on a bipartite graph. The objective encourages neighboring nodes to have smooth conditional probability estimates while penalizing departures from the initial supervised labels. Iterative propagation passes these estimates among neighboring nodes, seeking a globally coordinated assignment rather than deciding every object’s label through a separate majority vote.

The method also admits interpretations as constrained embedding in a transformed space and as ranking on a graph. These viewpoints connect the label-combination procedure to the structure of its optimization. Experiments on three real applications demonstrate benefits over existing alternatives. The contribution is a concrete way to make supervised predictions and unsupervised grouping information jointly influence classification through a shared consensus objective.
summary.tldr: A graph-based optimization combines classifier predictions and clustering constraints into joint labels, with reported benefits on three real applications.

title: Graph-based Consensus Maximization among Multiple Supervised and Unsupervised Models

abstract: We propose a novel information theoretic approach for semi-supervised learning of conditional random fields. Our approach defines a training objective that combines the conditional likelihood on labeled data and the mutual information on unlabeled data. Different from previous minimum conditional entropy semi-supervised discriminative learning methods, our approach can be naturally cast into the rate distortion theory framework in information theory. We analyze the tractability of the framework for structured prediction and present a convergent variational training algorithm to defy the combinatorial explosion of terms in the sum over label configurations. Our experimental results show that the rate distortion approach outperforms standard $l_2$ regularization and minimum conditional entropy regularization on both multi-class classification and sequence labeling problems.
originalAbstract: We propose a novel information theoretic approach for semi-supervised learning of conditional random fields. Our approach defines a training objective that combines the conditional likelihood on labeled data and the mutual information on unlabeled data. Different from previous minimum conditional entropy semi-supervised discriminative learning methods, our approach can be naturally cast into the rate distortion theory framework in information theory. We analyze the tractability of the framework for structured prediction and present a convergent variational training algorithm to defy the combinatorial explosion of terms in the sum over label configurations. Our experimental results show that the rate distortion approach outperforms standard $l_2$ regularization and minimum conditional entropy regularization on both multi-class classification and sequence labeling problems.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to train conditional random fields using both labeled and unlabeled examples. Its objective combines conditional likelihood on labeled data with mutual information on unlabeled data. This gives the unlabeled examples a role in training through an information-based criterion, alongside the direct supervision supplied by known labels.

The authors connect this objective to rate distortion theory, providing an information-theoretic framework for the learning problem. They distinguish it from approaches that minimize conditional entropy. For structured predictions, the computational challenge is that summing over possible label configurations can involve a combinatorial number of terms. The paper analyzes tractability and develops a convergent variational training algorithm to address that difficulty.

Experiments cover both multiclass classification and sequence labeling. In those experiments, the proposed approach outperforms standard l2 regularization and minimum conditional entropy regularization. These findings support the usefulness of the information-based objective across the two evaluated prediction settings, while the variational algorithm makes the structured training problem computationally manageable.
summary.tldr: An information-theoretic training objective helps conditional random fields use unlabeled data and improves results on classification and sequence labeling experiments.

title: A Rate Distortion Approach for Semi-Supervised Conditional Random Fields

abstract: In standard Gaussian Process regression input locations are assumed to be noise free. We present a simple yet effective GP model for training on input points corrupted by i.i.d. Gaussian noise. To make computations tractable we use a local linear expansion about each input point. This allows the input noise to be recast as output noise proportional to the squared gradient of the GP posterior mean. The input noise variances are inferred from the data as extra hyperparameters. They are trained alongside other hyperparameters by the usual method of maximisation of the marginal likelihood. Training uses an iterative scheme, which alternates between optimising the hyperparameters and calculating the posterior gradient. Analytic predictive moments can then be found for Gaussian distributed test points. We compare our model to others over a range of different regression problems and show that it improves over current methods.
originalAbstract: In standard Gaussian Process regression input locations are assumed to be noise free. We present a simple yet effective GP model for training on input points corrupted by i.i.d. Gaussian noise. To make computations tractable we use a local linear expansion about each input point. This allows the input noise to be recast as output noise proportional to the squared gradient of the GP posterior mean. The input noise variances are inferred from the data as extra hyperparameters. They are trained alongside other hyperparameters by the usual method of maximisation of the marginal likelihood. Training uses an iterative scheme, which alternates between optimising the hyperparameters and calculating the posterior gradient. Analytic predictive moments can then be found for Gaussian distributed test points. We compare our model to others over a range of different regression problems and show that it improves over current methods.

paragraphs: The paper addresses Gaussian process regression when training inputs themselves are uncertain. Standard regression treats input locations as exact, but this model assumes they are corrupted by independent, identically distributed Gaussian noise. Accounting for that uncertainty changes how the model interprets discrepancies between its predictions and the observed outputs.

To keep computation tractable, the authors locally linearize the function around each input. This converts input uncertainty into an output-noise contribution proportional to the squared gradient of the posterior mean. The interpretation is that an input perturbation matters more where the predicted function changes rapidly. Where it changes slowly, the same input uncertainty has a smaller effect on the output.

Input-noise variances become additional hyperparameters learned by maximizing marginal likelihood. Training alternates between optimizing these parameters and recalculating the posterior gradient. The method also provides analytic predictive moments for Gaussian-distributed test inputs. Comparisons across several regression problems show improvements over the methods considered, supporting the usefulness of this local approximation for the evaluated noisy-input settings.
summary.tldr: A local linear approximation lets Gaussian process regression learn input uncertainty as a gradient-dependent contribution to output noise.

title: Gaussian Process Training with Input Noise

abstract: In this paper we present an algorithm to learn a multi-label classifier which attempts at directly optimising the F-score. The key novelty of our formulation is that we explicitly allow for assortative (submodular) pairwise label interactions, i.e., we can leverage the co-ocurrence of pairs of labels in order to improve the quality of prediction. Prediction in this model consists of minimising a particular submodular set function, what can be accomplished exactly and efficiently via graph-cuts. Learning however is substantially more involved and requires the solution of an intractable combinatorial optimisation problem. We present an approximate algorithm for this problem and prove that it is sound in the sense that it never predicts incorrect labels. We also present a nontrivial test of a sufficient condition for our algorithm to have found an optimal solution. We present experiments on benchmark multi-label datasets, which attest the value of our proposed technique. We also make available source code that enables the reproduction of our experiments.

The key novelty of our formulation is that we explicitly allow for assortative (submodular) pairwise label interactions, i.e., we can leverage the co-ocurrence of pairs of labels in order to improve the quality of prediction. Prediction in this model consists of minimising a particular submodular set function, what can be accomplished exactly and efficiently via graph-cuts. Learning however is substantially more involved and requires the solution of an intractable combinatorial optimisation problem. We present an approximate algorithm for this problem and prove that it is sound in the sense that it never predicts incorrect labels. We also present a nontrivial test of a sufficient condition for our algorithm to have found an optimal solution. We present experiments on benchmark multi-label datasets, which attest the value of our proposed technique. We also make available source code that enables the reproduction of our experiments.

paragraphs: The paper develops a classifier for examples that can have several labels at once, with a learning objective that attempts to optimize the F-score directly. Its model includes pairwise interactions favoring labels that occur together. These assortative interactions let predictions incorporate label co-occurrence instead of treating every label as an unrelated decision.

For a fitted model, prediction reduces to minimizing a submodular set function, which can be solved exactly and efficiently using graph cuts. Training presents a different computational challenge: it requires an intractable combinatorial optimization. The authors therefore introduce an approximate algorithm for that learning problem, separating tractable prediction from the harder process of fitting the model.

They prove a soundness property for the approximate procedure, described as never predicting incorrect labels, and provide a test of a sufficient condition for having reached an optimal solution. That optimality test is conditional, rather than a guarantee that every run finds the optimum. Benchmark experiments support the technique’s value, and the authors supply source code for reproducing their experiments.
summary.tldr: A multi-label model uses label co-occurrence for exact graph-cut prediction, with approximate training and a sufficient-condition test for optimality.

title: Submodular Multi-Label Learning

abstract: We study the problem of estimating a manifold from random samples. In particular, we consider piecewise constant and piecewise linear estimators induced by k-means and k-ﬂats, and analyze their performance. We extend previous results for k-means in two separate directions. First, we provide new results for k-means reconstruction on manifolds and, secondly, we prove reconstruction bounds for higher-order approximation (k-ﬂats), for which no known results were previously available. While the results for k-means are novel, some of the technical tools are well-established in the literature. In the case of k-ﬂats, both the results and the mathematical tools are new.
originalAbstract: We study the problem of estimating a manifold from random samples. In particular, we consider piecewise constant and piecewise linear estimators induced by k-means and k-ﬂats, and analyze their performance. We extend previous results for k-means in two separate directions. First, we provide new results for k-means reconstruction on manifolds and, secondly, we prove reconstruction bounds for higher-order approximation (k-ﬂats), for which no known results were previously available. While the results for k-means are novel, some of the technical tools are well-established in the literature. In the case of k-ﬂats, both the results and the mathematical tools are new.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to estimate a manifold from randomly sampled points. It examines two ways of building an approximation from simpler pieces: k-means produces a piecewise constant representation, while k-flats produces a piecewise linear one. The question is how well these representations reconstruct the underlying manifold.

The authors extend the theory of k-means reconstruction on manifolds and establish reconstruction bounds for k-flats. The latter addresses a higher-order approximation: local linear pieces can represent structure differently from isolated representative points. The analysis gives mathematical bounds for these estimators, providing a basis for assessing reconstruction quality beyond their use as computational procedures.

The paper distinguishes the novelty of its two contributions. Its k-means results are new but use some established analytical tools. For k-flats, it reports both new reconstruction results, where none were previously known, and new mathematical techniques. The contribution is therefore principally theoretical, expanding what can be established about manifold approximation from random samples.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes new manifold-reconstruction bounds for k-means and k-flats, including new analytical tools for piecewise linear approximation.

title: Learning Manifolds with K-Means and K-Flats

abstract: We introduce kernel nonparametric tests for Lancaster three-variable interaction and for total independence, using embeddings of signed measures into a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. The resulting test statistics are straightforward to compute, and are used in powerful three-variable interaction tests, which are consistent against all alternatives for a large family of reproducing kernels. We show the Lancaster test to be sensitive to cases where two independent causes individually have weak influence on a third dependent variable, but their combined effect has a strong influence. This makes the Lancaster test especially suited to finding structure in directed graphical models, where it outperforms competing nonparametric tests in detecting such V-structures.

The resulting test statistics are straightforward to compute, and are used in powerful three-variable interaction tests, which are consistent against all alternatives for a large family of reproducing kernels. We show the Lancaster test to be sensitive to cases where two independent causes individually have weak influence on a third dependent variable, but their combined effect has a strong influence. This makes the Lancaster test especially suited to finding structure in directed graphical models, where it outperforms competing nonparametric tests in detecting such V-structures.

paragraphs: Some relationships among three variables are especially apparent when their combined behavior is examined. This paper introduces nonparametric kernel tests for Lancaster three-variable interaction and for total independence. These address related but distinct questions about joint structure, using a framework that represents signed measures in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space.

That representation produces test statistics that are straightforward to compute. For a large family of kernels, the interaction tests are consistent against all alternatives: with increasing data, they can detect departures covered by the testing problem. The result supplies a theoretical foundation for detecting interaction without choosing a fixed parametric form for the variables' relationship.

The Lancaster test is particularly sensitive when two independent causes each have a weak effect on a third variable but exert a strong combined effect. This pattern is relevant to V-shaped structures in directed graphical models. The authors report that their test outperforms competing nonparametric tests at detecting these structures, linking the interaction measure to a concrete structure-discovery task.
summary.tldr: Kernel tests detect three-variable interactions, including strong combined effects that help reveal V-structures in directed graphical models.

title: A Kernel Test for Three-Variable Interactions

abstract: The receptive field (RF) of a sensory neuron describes how the neuron integrates sensory stimuli over time and space. In typical experiments with naturalistic or flickering spatiotemporal stimuli, RFs are very high-dimensional, due to the large number of coefficients needed to specify an integration profile across time and space. Estimating these coefficients from small amounts of data poses a variety of challenging statistical and computational problems. Here we address these challenges by developing Bayesian reduced rank regression methods for RF estimation. This corresponds to modeling the RF as a sum of several space-time separable (i.e., rank-1) filters, which proves accurate even for neurons with strongly oriented space-time RFs. This approach substantially reduces the number of parameters needed to specify the RF, from 1K-100K down to mere 100s in the examples we consider, and confers substantial benefits in statistical power and computational efficiency. In particular, we introduce a novel prior over low-rank RFs using the restriction of a matrix normal prior to the manifold of low-rank matrices. We then use a localized'' prior over row and column covariances to obtain sparse, smooth, localized estimates of the spatial and temporal RF components. We develop two methods for inference in the resulting hierarchical model: (1) a fully Bayesian method using blocked-Gibbs sampling; and (2) a fast, approximate method that employs alternating coordinate ascent of the conditional marginal likelihood. We develop these methods under Gaussian and Poisson noise models, and show that low-rank estimates substantially outperform full rank estimates in accuracy and speed using neural data from retina and V1."

title: Bayesian inference for low rank spatiotemporal neural receptive fields

abstract: We develop a new exponential family probabilistic model for permutations that can capture hierarchical structure, and that has the well known Mallows and generalized Mallows models as subclasses. We describe how one can do parameter estimation and propose an approach to structure search for this class of models. We provide experimental evidence that this added flexibility both improves predictive performance and enables a deeper understanding of collections of permutations.

We describe how one can do parameter estimation and propose an approach to structure search for this class of models. We provide experimental evidence that this added flexibility both improves predictive performance and enables a deeper understanding of collections of permutations.

paragraphs: The paper develops a probabilistic model for permutations, or orderings of a set of items. Its purpose is to capture hierarchical structure in collections of orderings. Such a model assigns probabilities to different permutations while allowing the organization of the model itself to express structure in the data.

The proposed family is an exponential family and includes both Mallows and generalized Mallows models as special cases. This makes it an extension of established permutation models, with additional flexibility for hierarchy. The authors describe parameter estimation and propose a structure-search procedure, addressing both how to fit a chosen model and how to look for its structural organization.

Experiments provide evidence that the extra flexibility improves predictive performance and helps explain collections of permutations more deeply. These are complementary benefits: better prediction concerns which orderings the model expects, while structural understanding concerns how the observed collection is organized. The contribution therefore combines a broader modeling family with fitting tools and empirical support for the usefulness of its hierarchy.
summary.tldr: A hierarchical probabilistic family extends Mallows permutation models and improves prediction and interpretability in experiments.

title: Recursive Inversion Models for Permutations

abstract: We introduce Embed to Control (E2C), a method for model learning and control of non-linear dynamical systems from raw pixel images. E2C consists of a deep generative model, belonging to the family of variational autoencoders, that learns to generate image trajectories from a latent space in which the dynamics is constrained to be locally linear. Our model is derived directly from an optimal control formulation in latent space, supports long-term prediction of image sequences and exhibits strong performance on a variety of complex control problems.

paragraphs: Embed to Control addresses learning and controlling nonlinear dynamical systems directly from pixel images. Its central task is to learn a latent representation that supports both image generation and control. The method places this representation inside a deep generative model belonging to the variational-autoencoder family.

The key structural requirement concerns how the latent state changes over time: its dynamics must be locally linear. This makes local evolution in the learned space compatible with a simpler dynamical description while the overall task involves nonlinear systems and image observations. The model learns to generate image trajectories, so the representation concerns sequences and their evolution rather than only isolated images.

The authors derive the model directly from an optimal-control formulation in latent space, making control part of the model's construction. They report support for long-term image-sequence prediction and strong performance across several complex control problems. These findings position E2C as a way to connect visual representation learning with dynamical modeling and action selection through one structured latent space.
summary.tldr: Embed to Control learns locally linear latent dynamics from raw images to support sequence prediction and nonlinear-system control.

title: Embed to Control: A Locally Linear Latent Dynamics Model for Control from Raw Images

abstract: Computing the MAP assignment in graphical models is generally intractable. As a result, for discrete graphical models, the MAP problem is often approximated using linear programming relaxations. Much research has focused on characterizing when these LP relaxations are tight, and while they are relatively well-understood in the discrete case, only a few results are known for their continuous analog. In this work, we use graph covers to provide necessary and sufficient conditions for continuous MAP relaxations to be tight. We use this characterization to give simple proofs that the relaxation is tight for log-concave decomposable and log-supermodular decomposable models. We conclude by exploring the relationship between these two seemingly distinct classes of functions and providing specific conditions under which the MAP relaxation can and cannot be tight.

paragraphs: Maximum a posteriori inference seeks the most probable assignment in a graphical model, but computing it is generally intractable. Linear programming relaxations replace the original problem with a more manageable one. The key theoretical question is when this replacement is tight, meaning that the relaxation accurately captures the original optimization problem.

While tightness is relatively well understood for discrete models, the paper addresses the less developed continuous case. It uses graph covers to characterize exactly when continuous MAP relaxations are tight. The characterization supplies both necessary and sufficient conditions, making it a criterion for exactness rather than only a collection of favorable examples.

The authors then use the characterization to give simple proofs of tightness for log-concave decomposable and log-supermodular decomposable models. They also examine relationships between these two classes and identify specific circumstances in which tightness can or cannot hold. The contribution clarifies when an approximate inference formulation can deliver an exact answer for the continuous models under consideration.
summary.tldr: Graph covers yield necessary and sufficient conditions for continuous MAP relaxations to be exact.

title: Exactness of Approximate MAP Inference in Continuous MRFs

abstract: In multi-step learning, where a final learning task is accomplished via a sequence of intermediate learning tasks, the intuition is that successive steps or levels transform the initial data into representations more and more ``suited" to the final learning task. A related principle arises in transfer-learning where Baxter (2000) proposed a theoretical framework to study how learning multiple tasks transforms the inductive bias of a learner. The most widespread multi-step learning approach is semi-supervised learning with two steps: unsupervised, then supervised. Several authors (Castelli-Cover, 1996; Balcan-Blum, 2005; Niyogi, 2008; Ben-David et al, 2008; Urner et al, 2011) have analyzed SSL, with Balcan-Blum (2005) proposing a version of the PAC learning framework augmented by a ``compatibility function" to link concept class and unlabeled data distribution. We propose to analyze SSL and other multi-step learning approaches, much in the spirit of Baxter's framework, by defining a learning problem generatively as a joint statistical model on $X \times Y$. This determines in a natural way the class of conditional distributions that are possible with each marginal, and amounts to an abstract form of compatibility function. It also allows to analyze both discrete and non-discrete settings. As tool for our analysis, we define a notion of $\gamma$-uniform shattering for statistical models. We use this to give conditions on the marginal and conditional models which imply an advantage for multi-step learning approaches. In particular, we recover a more general version of a result of Poggio et al (2012): under mild hypotheses a multi-step approach which learns features invariant under successive factors of a finite group of invariances has sample complexity requirements that are additive rather than multiplicative in the size of the subgroups.

It includes semi-supervised learning, where an unsupervised step precedes supervised learning, within a broader generative description of learning problems.

The authors define a joint statistical model over inputs and outputs. For each input marginal, this specifies compatible conditional distributions, giving an abstract compatibility relation between unlabeled data and the prediction task. They introduce gamma-uniform shattering as a tool for analyzing both discrete and nondiscrete statistical models.

These gains depend on model structure and assumptions, rather than holding for arbitrary preprocessing sequences.
summary.tldr: A statistical framework identifies conditions under which intermediate learning steps reduce sample needs.

title: Multi-step learning and underlying structure in statistical models

abstract: We propose a deep generative model for learning to distill the hidden factors of variation within a set of labeled observations into two complementary codes. One code describes the factors of variation relevant to solving a specified task. The other code describes the remaining factors of variation that are irrelevant to solving this task. The only available source of supervision during the training process comes from our ability to distinguish among different observations belonging to the same category. Concrete examples include multiple images of the same object from different viewpoints, or multiple speech samples from the same speaker. In both of these instances, the factors of variation irrelevant to classification are implicitly expressed by intra-class variabilities, such as the relative position of an object in an image, or the linguistic content of an utterance. Most existing approaches for solving this problem rely heavily on having access to pairs of observations only sharing a single factor of variation, e.g. different objects observed in the exact same conditions. This assumption is often not encountered in realistic settings where data acquisition is not controlled and labels for the uninformative components are not available. In this work, we propose to overcome this limitation by augmenting deep convolutional autoencoders with a form of adversarial training. Both factors of variation are implicitly captured in the organization of the learned embedding space, and can be used for solving single-image analogies. Experimental results on synthetic and real datasets show that the proposed method is capable of disentangling the influences of style and content factors using a flexible representation, as well as generalizing to unseen styles or content classes.

paragraphs: The paper learns two complementary representations of an observation: one for variation relevant to a chosen task and another for the remaining variation. The method augments a deep convolutional autoencoder with adversarial training. The result supports disentangling useful representations under the stated category-based supervision. summary.tldr: Adversarial autoencoder training separates task-relevant and irrelevant variation using category-based supervision, with demonstrated generalization to unseen styles or content.

title: Disentangling factors of variation in deep representation using adversarial training

abstract: Suppose, we are given a set of $n$ elements to be clustered into $k$ (unknown) clusters, and an oracle/expert labeler that can interactively answer pair-wise queries of the form, ``do two elements $u$ and $v$ belong to the same cluster?''. The goal is to recover the optimum clustering by asking the minimum number of queries. In this paper, we provide a rigorous theoretical study of this basic problem of query complexity of interactive clustering, and give strong information theoretic lower bounds, as well as nearly matching upper bounds. Most clustering problems come with a similarity matrix, which is used by an automated process to cluster similar points together. To improve accuracy of clustering, a fruitful approach in recent years has been to ask a domain expert or crowd to obtain labeled data interactively. Many heuristics have been proposed, and all of these use a similarity function to come up with a querying strategy. Even so, there is a lack systematic theoretical study. Our main contribution in this paper is to show the dramatic power of side information aka similarity matrix on reducing the query complexity of clustering. A similarity matrix represents noisy pair-wise relationships such as one computed by some function on attributes of the elements. A natural noisy model is where similarity values are drawn independently from some arbitrary probability distribution $f_+$ when the underlying pair of elements belong to the same cluster, and from some $f_-$ otherwise. We show that given such a similarity matrix, the query complexity reduces drastically from $\Theta(nk)$ (no similarity matrix) to $O(\frac{k^2\log{n}}{\cH^2(f_+\|f_-)})$ where $\cH^2$ denotes the squared Hellinger divergence. Moreover, this is also information-theoretic optimal within an $O(\log{n})$ factor. Our algorithms are all efficient, and parameter free, i.e., they work without any knowledge of $k, f_+$ and $f_-$, and only depend logarithmically with $n$.

These results quantify how informative noisy similarities can sharply reduce expert queries under the stated independent-draw model.
summary.tldr: Under an independent similarity model, noisy pairwise side information sharply reduces the expert queries needed for clustering, with nearly matching theoretical bounds.

title: Query Complexity of Clustering with Side Information

abstract: We develop a novel computationally efficient and general framework for robust hypothesis testing. The new framework features a new way to construct uncertainty sets under the null and the alternative distributions, which are sets centered around the empirical distribution defined via Wasserstein metric, thus our approach is data-driven and free of distributional assumptions. We develop a convex safe approximation of the minimax formulation and show that such approximation renders a nearly-optimal detector among the family of all possible tests. By exploiting the structure of the least favorable distribution, we also develop a tractable reformulation of such approximation, with complexity independent of the dimension of observation space and can be nearly sample-size-independent in general. Real-data example using human activity data demonstrated the excellent performance of the new robust detector.

The new framework features a new way to construct uncertainty sets under the null and the alternative distributions, which are sets centered around the empirical distribution defined via Wasserstein metric, thus our approach is data-driven and free of distributional assumptions. We develop a convex safe approximation of the minimax formulation and show that such approximation renders a nearly-optimal detector among the family of all possible tests.
