paragraphs: Hypothesis testing chooses between competing explanations for observations, but the distributions associated with those explanations may be uncertain. This paper represents that uncertainty using sets centered on empirical distributions. Wasserstein distance determines which nearby distributions belong to each set, providing a data-driven construction without assuming a particular distributional family.

The authors formulate robust testing as a minimax problem and develop a safe convex approximation. They show that the approximation yields a nearly optimal detector within the family of all possible tests. This turns protection against unfavorable distributions into an optimization problem with a more manageable computational form.

By exploiting the structure of a least favorable distribution, they further derive a tractable reformulation. Its complexity is independent of observation dimension and can be nearly independent of sample size in general. A real-data example involving human activity demonstrates strong detector performance. The contribution combines distributional robustness with computational accessibility, addressing both uncertainty about the hypotheses and the practical cost of constructing a test.
summary.tldr: Wasserstein uncertainty sets yield a data-driven robust testing framework with a tractable approximation and near-optimality guarantees.

title: Robust Hypothesis Testing Using Wasserstein Uncertainty Sets

abstract: Deep convolutional neural networks have demonstrated their powerfulness in a variety of applications. However, the storage and computational requirements have largely restricted their further extensions on mobile devices. Recently, pruning of unimportant parameters has been used for both network compression and acceleration. Considering that there are spatial redundancy within most filters in a CNN, we propose a frequency-domain dynamic pruning scheme to exploit the spatial correlations. The frequency-domain coefficients are pruned dynamically in each iteration and different frequency bands are pruned discriminatively, given their different importance on accuracy. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed scheme can outperform previous spatial-domain counterparts by a large margin. Specifically, it can achieve a compression ratio of 8.4x and a theoretical inference speed-up of 9.2x for ResNet-110, while the accuracy is even better than the reference model on CIFAR-110.

paragraphs: Convolutional networks can demand too much storage and computation for mobile devices. Pruning addresses this by removing parameters that contribute little to performance. This paper focuses on spatial redundancy within convolutional filters: correlations among filter values suggest that the frequency domain may offer a useful place to identify and remove redundant information.

The proposed scheme dynamically prunes frequency-domain coefficients at each iteration. It treats frequency bands differently because they differ in their importance to accuracy. The method therefore combines a change in representation with an adaptive pruning process, using spatial correlations to guide compression rather than treating all frequency components alike.

summary.tldr: Dynamic frequency-domain pruning exploits filter correlations, reporting 8.4-fold compression and a theoretical 9.2-fold speedup for ResNet-110.

title: Frequency-Domain Dynamic Pruning for Convolutional Neural Networks

abstract: We describe Bayesian Layers, a module designed for fast experimentation with neural network uncertainty. It extends neural network libraries with drop-in replacements for common layers. This enables composition via a unified abstraction over deterministic and stochastic functions and allows for scalability via the underlying system. These layers capture uncertainty over weights (Bayesian neural nets), pre-activation units (dropout), activations ( stochastic output layers''), or the function itself (Gaussian processes). They can also be reversible to propagate uncertainty from input to output. We include code examples for common architectures such as Bayesian LSTMs, deep GPs, and flow-based models. As demonstration, we fit a 5-billion parameter Bayesian Transformer'' on 512 TPUv2 cores for uncertainty in machine translation and a Bayesian dynamics model for model-based planning. Finally, we show how Bayesian Layers can be used within the Edward2 language for probabilistic programming with stochastic processes.

paragraphs: Bayesian Layers makes uncertainty modeling available through replacements for familiar neural network layers. The module treats deterministic and stochastic functions within one interface, so researchers can compose them into larger architectures. Its design aims to speed up experimentation while using the underlying neural network system to support computation at scale.

The abstraction covers several places where uncertainty can enter a model: weights in Bayesian neural networks, pre-activation units through dropout, activations through stochastic output layers, and entire functions through Gaussian processes. Reversible layers can also propagate uncertainty from inputs to outputs. Code examples illustrate architectures including Bayesian recurrent networks, deep Gaussian processes, and flow-based models.

Together, these examples illustrate the module’s range and scalability, with the central contribution being a shared software abstraction for building uncertainty-aware models.
summary.tldr: Bayesian Layers provides composable neural network components for experimenting with uncertainty across multiple model families.

title: Bayesian Layers: A Module for Neural Network Uncertainty

abstract: A new approach to explainable AI, denoted {\it deliberative explanations,\/} is proposed. Deliberative explanations are a visualization technique that aims to go beyond the simple visualization of the image regions (or, more generally, input variables) responsible for a network prediction. Instead, they aim to expose the deliberations carried by the network to arrive at that prediction, by uncovering the insecurities of the network about the latter. The explanation consists of a list of insecurities, each composed of 1) an image region (more generally, a set of input variables), and 2) an ambiguity formed by the pair of classes responsible for the network uncertainty about the region. Since insecurity detection requires quantifying the difficulty of network predictions, deliberative explanations combine ideas from the literatures on visual explanations and assessment of classification difficulty. More specifically, the proposed implementation combines attributions with respect to both class predictions and a difficulty score. An evaluation protocol that leverages object recognition (CUB200) and scene classification (ADE20K) datasets that combine part and attribute annotations is also introduced to evaluate the accuracy of deliberative explanations. Finally, an experimental evaluation shows that the most accurate explanations are achieved by combining non self-referential difficulty scores and second-order attributions. The resulting insecurities are shown to correlate with regions of attributes that are shared by different classes. Since these regions are also ambiguous for humans, deliberative explanations are intuitive, suggesting that the deliberative process of modern networks correlates with human reasoning.
originalAbstract: A new approach to explainable AI, denoted {\it deliberative explanations,\/} is proposed. Deliberative explanations are a visualization technique that aims to go beyond the simple visualization of the image regions (or, more generally, input variables) responsible for a network prediction. Instead, they aim to expose the deliberations carried by the network to arrive at that prediction, by uncovering the insecurities of the network about the latter. The explanation consists of a list of insecurities, each composed of 1) an image region (more generally, a set of input variables), and 2) an ambiguity formed by the pair of classes responsible for the network uncertainty about the region. Since insecurity detection requires quantifying the difficulty of network predictions, deliberative explanations combine ideas from the literatures on visual explanations and assessment of classification difficulty. More specifically, the proposed implementation combines attributions with respect to both class predictions and a difficulty score. An evaluation protocol that leverages object recognition (CUB200) and scene classification (ADE20K) datasets that combine part and attribute annotations is also introduced to evaluate the accuracy of deliberative explanations. Finally, an experimental evaluation shows that the most accurate explanations are achieved by combining non self-referential difficulty scores and second-order attributions. The resulting insecurities are shown to correlate with regions of attributes that are shared by different classes. Since these regions are also ambiguous for humans, deliberative explanations are intuitive, suggesting that the deliberative process of modern networks correlates with human reasoning.

paragraphs: A visual explanation often highlights the image regions that support a prediction. Deliberative explanations add another question: where does the network encounter ambiguity between competing classes? Each reported insecurity contains a region and a pair of classes associated with uncertainty about that region, giving the explanation a more specific structure.

The proposed implementation combines attributions for class predictions with attributions for a score measuring prediction difficulty. This links evidence about what the network predicts with evidence about where making that prediction is difficult. The authors also introduce an evaluation protocol using part and attribute annotations from CUB200 object recognition and ADE20K scene classification.

In the experiments, the most accurate explanations combine non-self-referential difficulty scores with second-order attributions. The resulting insecurities correlate with regions containing attributes shared across classes. Such shared attributes can also be ambiguous to people, making the visualizations intuitive. This correspondence suggests a connection with human reasoning, rather than establishing that networks deliberate in the same way humans do.
summary.tldr: Deliberative explanations visualize image regions where a network is uncertain between specific pairs of classes.

title: Deliberative Explanations: visualizing network insecurities

abstract: We give the first polynomial-time algorithm for robust regression in the list-decodable setting where an adversary can corrupt a greater than 1/2 fraction of examples. For any \alpha < 1, our algorithm takes as input a sample {(x i,y i)} {i \leq n} of n linear equations where \alpha n of the equations satisfy y i = \langle x_i,\ell^ \rangle +\zeta for some small noise \zeta and (1-\alpha) n of the equations are {\em arbitrarily} chosen. It outputs a list L of size O(1/\alpha) - a fixed constant - that contains an \ell that is close to \ell^ . Our algorithm succeeds whenever the inliers are chosen from a certifiably anti-concentrated distribution D. In particular, this gives a (d/\alpha)^{O(1/\alpha^8)} time algorithm to find a O(1/\alpha) size list when the inlier distribution is a standard Gaussian. For discrete product distributions that are anti-concentrated only in regular directions, we give an algorithm that achieves similar guarantee under the promise that \ell^* has all coordinates of the same magnitude. To complement our result, we prove that the anti-concentration assumption on the inliers is information-theoretically necessary. To solve the problem we introduce a new framework for list-decodable learning that strengthens the ``identifiability to algorithms'' paradigm based on the sum-of-squares method.

paragraphs: Robust regression becomes especially difficult when an adversary controls most examples. This paper studies a setting where only an α fraction of equations follow the intended linear relationship with small noise, while the rest are arbitrary. It seeks a short list of candidate regressors containing a good answer, rather than requiring one uniquely determined output.

The authors give the first polynomial-time algorithm for this list-decodable setting, producing O(1/α) candidates. Success requires the genuine examples to come from a certifiably anti-concentrated distribution. For standard Gaussian inliers, the running time is (d/α) raised to O(1/α⁸), making its dependence on the genuine-data fraction explicit.

For certain discrete product distributions, a similar guarantee requires the true coefficient vector to have coordinates of equal magnitude. The authors also prove that anti-concentration is information-theoretically necessary, so this condition addresses recoverability itself. Their algorithmic framework strengthens the connection between identifiability and computation using the sum-of-squares method, explaining how a recoverable candidate can be found despite majority corruption.
summary.tldr: Under anti-concentration conditions, list-decodable regression efficiently returns a short candidate list containing an accurate regressor despite majority corruption.

title: List-decodable Linear Regression

abstract: Humans are able to perform a myriad of sophisticated tasks by drawing upon skills acquired through prior experience. For autonomous agents to have this capability, they must be able to extract reusable skills from past experience that can be recombined in new ways for subsequent tasks. Furthermore, when controlling complex high-dimensional morphologies, such as humanoid bodies, tasks often require coordination of multiple skills simultaneously. Learning discrete primitives for every combination of skills quickly becomes prohibitive. Composable primitives that can be recombined to create a large variety of behaviors can be more suitable for modeling this combinatorial explosion. In this work, we propose multiplicative compositional policies (MCP), a method for learning reusable motor skills that can be composed to produce a range of complex behaviors. Our method factorizes an agent's skills into a collection of primitives, where multiple primitives can be activated simultaneously via multiplicative composition. This flexibility allows the primitives to be transferred and recombined to elicit new behaviors as necessary for novel tasks. We demonstrate that MCP is able to extract composable skills for highly complex simulated characters from pre-training tasks, such as motion imitation, and then reuse these skills to solve challenging continuous control tasks, such as dribbling a soccer ball to a goal, and picking up an object and transporting it to a target location.

This paper proposes multiplicative compositional policies, or MCP, to learn reusable motor skills that can be combined for subsequent tasks.

MCP organizes an agent's skills into a collection of primitives and permits multiple primitives to be active simultaneously through multiplicative composition. The resulting flexibility allows learned components to be transferred and recombined when a new task demands a different behavior. This directly addresses the need for coordinated skills in high-dimensional characters such as humanoid bodies.

Those skills are then reused for continuous-control tasks such as moving a soccer ball toward a goal and carrying an object to a target. The results show that the learned primitives support useful recombination in the evaluated tasks, giving hierarchical control a way to reuse experience across coordinated behaviors.
summary.tldr: MCP learns motor primitives that can act together through multiplicative composition and transfer to new simulated control tasks.

title: MCP: Learning Composable Hierarchical Control with Multiplicative Compositional Policies

abstract: Jaccard similarity is widely used as a distance measure in many machine learning and search applications. Typically, hashing methods are essential for the use of Jaccard similarity to be practical in large-scale settings. For hashing binary (0/1) data, the idea of one permutation hashing (OPH) with densification significantly accelerates traditional minwise hashing algorithms while providing unbiased and accurate estimates. In this paper, we propose a strategy named “re-randomization” in the process of densification that could achieve the smallest variance among all densification schemes. The success of this idea naturally inspires us to generalize one permutation hashing to weighted (non-binary) data, which results in the socalled “bin-wise consistent weighted sampling (BCWS)” algorithm. We analyze the behavior of BCWS and compare it with a recent alternative. Extensive experiments on various datasets illustrates the effectiveness of our proposed methods.

paragraphs: Jaccard similarity is useful in machine learning and search, but large-scale applications often require compact hashing estimates rather than direct comparisons. For binary data, one permutation hashing with densification accelerates traditional minwise hashing while retaining unbiased, accurate estimates. This paper studies how the densification stage can further improve estimation quality.

The proposed strategy introduces re-randomization during densification. The authors describe it as capable of attaining the smallest variance among densification schemes. Variance matters because it captures how much the estimate fluctuates: reducing it makes the hashing estimate more reliable while preserving the computational motivation for using one permutation.

The same idea motivates an extension from binary inputs to weighted, non-binary data, called bin-wise consistent weighted sampling. The paper analyzes this algorithm and compares it with a recent alternative. Experiments across multiple datasets support the effectiveness of the proposed methods. Together, the contributions improve a component of binary similarity hashing and extend the approach to a broader kind of data.
summary.tldr: Re-randomized densification targets lower-variance similarity estimates and motivates bin-wise consistent weighted sampling for non-binary data.

title: Re-randomized Densification for One Permutation Hashing and Bin-wise Consistent Weighted Sampling

abstract: Proximal policy optimization (PPO) is one of the most popular deep reinforcement learning (RL) methods, achieving state-of-the-art performance across a wide range of challenging tasks. However, as a model-free RL method, the success of PPO relies heavily on the effectiveness of its exploratory policy search. In this paper, we give an in-depth analysis on the exploration behavior of PPO, and show that PPO is prone to suffer from the risk of lack of exploration especially under the case of bad initialization, which may lead to the failure of training or being trapped in bad local optima. To address these issues, we proposed a novel policy optimization method, named Trust Region-Guided PPO (TRGPPO), which adaptively adjusts the clipping range within the trust region. We formally show that this method not only improves the exploration ability within the trust region but enjoys a better performance bound compared to the original PPO as well. Extensive experiments verify the advantage of the proposed method.

In this paper, we give an in-depth analysis on the exploration behavior of PPO, and show that PPO is prone to suffer from the risk of lack of exploration especially under the case of bad initialization, which may lead to the failure of training or being trapped in bad local optima. To address these issues, we proposed a novel policy optimization method, named Trust Region-Guided PPO (TRGPPO), which adaptively adjusts the clipping range within the trust region. paragraphs: Proximal policy optimization learns by searching for better action-selection policies. The effectiveness of that search depends on exploration. This paper analyzes PPO's exploration behavior and finds that it can explore inadequately, especially with a poor initialization. That behavior can cause training to fail or leave it trapped in a poor local optimum.

The proposed Trust Region-Guided PPO adapts the clipping range within a trust region. Clipping controls how policy changes enter the optimization objective, so changing its range affects which updates the search can pursue. The method uses the trust-region structure to guide that adjustment, directly addressing the exploration issue identified in the analysis.

The authors formally show improved exploration within the trust region and a better performance bound than original PPO. Extensive experiments also support the method's advantage. The findings connect a specific optimization mechanism to exploration quality: adjusting clipping with trust-region guidance can improve the search, with both theoretical and empirical support for the proposed modification.
summary.tldr: Trust Region-Guided PPO adaptively adjusts clipping to improve exploration and obtains a better performance bound than original PPO.

title: Trust Region-Guided Proximal Policy Optimization

abstract: Causal identification is the problem of deciding whether a post-interventional distribution is computable from a combination of qualitative knowledge about the data-generating process, which is encoded in a causal diagram, and an observational distribution. A generalization of this problem restricts the qualitative knowledge to a class of Markov equivalent causal diagrams, which, unlike a single, fully-specified causal diagram, can be inferred from the observational distribution. Recent work by (Jaber et al., 2019a) devised a complete algorithm for the identification of unconditional causal effects given a Markov equivalence class of causal diagrams. However, there are identifiable conditional causal effects that cannot be handled by that algorithm. In this work, we derive an algorithm to identify conditional effects, which are particularly useful for evaluating conditional plans or policies.

A generalization of this problem restricts the qualitative knowledge to a class of Markov equivalent causal diagrams, which, unlike a single, fully-specified causal diagram, can be inferred from the observational distribution. Recent work by (Jaber et al., 2019a) devised a complete algorithm for the identification of unconditional causal effects given a Markov equivalence class of causal diagrams. However, there are identifiable conditional causal effects that cannot be handled by that algorithm. In this work, we derive an algorithm to identify conditional effects, which are particularly useful for evaluating conditional plans or policies.

paragraphs: Causal identification asks whether the distribution produced by an intervention can be computed from observational data and qualitative knowledge of causal relationships. That knowledge is often represented by a causal diagram. This paper considers the harder situation where the available information determines only a class of Markov equivalent diagrams, rather than one fully specified diagram.

Working with an equivalence class preserves uncertainty about the causal structure instead of choosing a single diagram. The paper focuses on conditional causal effects, which describe intervention outcomes conditional on additional information. These effects are particularly relevant when evaluating plans or policies whose decisions depend on observed conditions.

An earlier algorithm addressed unconditional effects given a Markov equivalence class, but some identifiable conditional effects fall outside what that algorithm can handle. The authors derive an algorithm for identifying conditional effects to address this gap. The contribution concerns what intervention quantities can be recovered despite structural ambiguity. It extends the available identification tools toward conditional policy evaluation without requiring the starting knowledge to specify one complete causal diagram.
summary.tldr: An identification algorithm addresses conditional causal effects when causal knowledge specifies only a Markov equivalence class.

title: Identification of Conditional Causal Effects under Markov Equivalence

abstract: The use of neural networks in safety-critical computer vision systems calls for their robustness certification against natural geometric transformations (e.g., rotation, scaling). However, current certification methods target mostly norm-based pixel perturbations and cannot certify robustness against geometric transformations. In this work, we propose a new method to compute sound and asymptotically optimal linear relaxations for any composition of transformations. Our method is based on a novel combination of sampling and optimization. We implemented the method in a system called DeepG and demonstrated that it certifies significantly more complex geometric transformations than existing methods on both defended and undefended networks while scaling to large architectures.
originalAbstract: The use of neural networks in safety-critical computer vision systems calls for their robustness certification against natural geometric transformations (e.g., rotation, scaling). However, current certification methods target mostly norm-based pixel perturbations and cannot certify robustness against geometric transformations. In this work, we propose a new method to compute sound and asymptotically optimal linear relaxations for any composition of transformations. Our method is based on a novel combination of sampling and optimization. We implemented the method in a system called DeepG and demonstrated that it certifies significantly more complex geometric transformations than existing methods on both defended and undefended networks while scaling to large architectures.

paragraphs: A vision model can encounter an image that has been rotated or scaled without its underlying content changing. Certifying robustness means establishing that specified changes cannot undermine the model’s prediction. The paper addresses geometric transformations, which are poorly served by certification methods focused on bounded changes to individual pixel values.

The proposed method combines sampling with optimization to construct linear relaxations of compositions of transformations. These relaxations provide a simpler mathematical description that safely covers the transformations being analyzed. The authors establish soundness and asymptotic optimality: the bounds remain valid, and their approximation quality has an optimal limiting behavior. Asymptotic optimality is a limiting guarantee, rather than a claim that every finite computation is exact.

The implementation, DeepG, certifies substantially more complex geometric transformations than existing methods in the reported evaluation. It works with both defended and undefended networks and scales to large architectures. The contribution is therefore a way to obtain formal guarantees for richer geometric changes, extending the range of transformations that robustness certification can address.
summary.tldr: DeepG combines sampling and optimization to certify neural-network robustness against complex compositions of geometric transformations.

title: Certifying Geometric Robustness of Neural Networks

abstract: Linear regression is an important tool across many fields that work with sensitive human-sourced data. Significant prior work has focused on producing differentially private point estimates, which provide a privacy guarantee to individuals while still allowing modelers to draw insights from data by estimating regression coefficients. We investigate the problem of Bayesian linear regression, with the goal of computing posterior distributions that correctly quantify uncertainty given privately released statistics. We show that a naive approach that ignores the noise injected by the privacy mechanism does a poor job in realistic data settings. We then develop noise-aware methods that perform inference over the privacy mechanism and produce correct posteriors across a wide range of scenarios.
originalAbstract: Linear regression is an important tool across many fields that work with sensitive human-sourced data. Significant prior work has focused on producing differentially private point estimates, which provide a privacy guarantee to individuals while still allowing modelers to draw insights from data by estimating regression coefficients. We investigate the problem of Bayesian linear regression, with the goal of computing posterior distributions that correctly quantify uncertainty given privately released statistics. We show that a naive approach that ignores the noise injected by the privacy mechanism does a poor job in realistic data settings. We then develop noise-aware methods that perform inference over the privacy mechanism and produce correct posteriors across a wide range of scenarios.

paragraphs: Linear regression is often applied to sensitive information about people. Differential privacy allows statistics to be released with individual privacy guarantees, but the privacy mechanism introduces noise. This paper asks how Bayesian regression should quantify uncertainty when those noisy statistics are the information available for inference.

The distinction matters because a point estimate and a posterior distribution answer different questions. A coefficient estimate summarizes a relationship, while a posterior also expresses uncertainty about that relationship. The authors show that a naive procedure which ignores the added privacy noise performs poorly in realistic data settings. Treating the released statistics as if they were unperturbed fails to account properly for the information available.

The proposed methods explicitly incorporate the privacy mechanism into inference. They account for its noise when constructing posterior distributions and produce correct posteriors across a wide range of scenarios. The contribution is a way to make Bayesian uncertainty assessment reflect the process that generated the private release, extending the focus beyond privately estimating regression coefficients alone.
summary.tldr: Noise-aware Bayesian regression accounts for the privacy mechanism to quantify uncertainty correctly from privately released statistics.

title: Differentially Private Bayesian Linear Regression

abstract: Recent neural models for image captioning usually employ an encoder-decoder framework with an attention mechanism. However, the attention mechanism in such a framework aligns one single (attended) image feature vector to one caption word, assuming one-to-one mapping from source image regions and target caption words, which is never possible. In this paper, we propose a novel attention model, namely Adaptive Attention Time (AAT), to align the source and the target adaptively for image captioning. AAT allows the framework to learn how many attention steps to take to output a caption word at each decoding step. With AAT, an image region can be mapped to an arbitrary number of caption words while a caption word can also attend to an arbitrary number of image regions. AAT is deterministic and differentiable, and doesn't introduce any noise to the parameter gradients. In this paper, we empirically show that AAT improves over state-of-the-art methods on the task of image captioning. Code is available at https://github.com/husthuaan/AAT.

paragraphs: Image captioning systems commonly use attention to connect image information with the words they generate. The paper challenges a fixed arrangement in which each output word receives one attended image feature vector. Describing an image can require more flexible relationships between visual regions and words, motivating a change to how attention proceeds during caption generation.

The proposed Adaptive Attention Time model learns how many attention steps to take before producing each word. This allows a word to attend to multiple image regions and allows an image region to contribute to multiple words. The central change is therefore the amount of attention computation associated with each decoding step, giving the system flexibility in how it aligns visual content with language.

The attention procedure is deterministic and differentiable, and the authors state that it introduces no noise into parameter gradients. Their experiments report improvements over state-of-the-art image captioning methods. These findings support adapting attention timing as a useful part of caption generation, alongside deciding which visual information should influence the next word.
summary.tldr: Adaptive Attention Time improves image captioning by learning how many attention steps to use when generating each word.

title: Adaptively Aligned Image Captioning via Adaptive Attention Time

abstract: To learn intrinsic low-dimensional structures from high-dimensional data that most discriminate between classes, we propose the principle of {\em Maximal Coding Rate Reduction} ($\text{MCR}^2$), an information-theoretic measure that maximizes the coding rate difference between the whole dataset and the sum of each individual class. We clarify its relationships with most existing frameworks such as cross-entropy, information bottleneck, information gain, contractive and contrastive learning, and provide theoretical guarantees for learning diverse and discriminative features. The coding rate can be accurately computed from finite samples of degenerate subspace-like distributions and can learn intrinsic representations in supervised, self-supervised, and unsupervised settings in a unified manner. Empirically, the representations learned using this principle alone are significantly more robust to label corruptions in classification than those using cross-entropy, and can lead to state-of-the-art results in clustering mixed data from self-learned invariant features.

We clarify its relationships with most existing frameworks such as cross-entropy, information bottleneck, information gain, contractive and contrastive learning, and provide theoretical guarantees for learning diverse and discriminative features. The coding rate can be accurately computed from finite samples of degenerate subspace-like distributions and can learn intrinsic representations in supervised, self-supervised, and unsupervised settings in a unified manner. paragraphs: Useful representations should expose low-dimensional structure while preserving distinctions between classes. This paper proposes maximal coding rate reduction, or MCR², as an information-theoretic objective for that purpose. It maximizes the difference between the coding rate of the full dataset and the combined coding rates of the individual classes.

The comparison encourages representations that retain diversity across the dataset while making class-specific structure compact. The authors provide theoretical guarantees for diverse, discriminative features and relate the objective to cross-entropy, information bottleneck, information gain, and contractive and contrastive learning. They also show that coding rates can be accurately computed from finite samples for degenerate distributions with subspace-like structure.

The principle supports supervised, self-supervised, and unsupervised representation learning within one framework. In the reported classification experiments, using this objective alone produces substantially greater robustness to corrupted labels than cross-entropy. The authors also report that self-learned invariant features can yield state-of-the-art clustering of mixed data. These findings support coding-rate reduction as a representation objective with benefits extending beyond standard classification accuracy.
summary.tldr: MCR² learns diverse, class-discriminative representations through coding-rate differences, with reported benefits for label-corruption robustness and clustering.

title: Learning Diverse and Discriminative Representations via the Principle of Maximal Coding Rate Reduction

abstract: For mental disorders, patients' underlying mental states are non-observed latent constructs which have to be inferred from observed multi-domain measurements such as diagnostic symptoms and patient functioning scores. Additionally, substantial heterogeneity in the disease diagnosis between patients needs to be addressed for optimizing individualized treatment policy in order to achieve precision medicine. To address these challenges, we propose an integrated learning framework that can simultaneously learn patients' underlying mental states and recommend optimal treatments for each individual. This learning framework is based on the measurement theory in psychiatry for modeling multiple disease diagnostic measures as arising from the underlying causes (true mental states). It allows incorporation of the multivariate pre- and post-treatment outcomes as well as biological measures while preserving the invariant structure for representing patients' latent mental states. A multi-layer neural network is used to allow complex treatment effect heterogeneity. Optimal treatment policy can be inferred for future patients by comparing their potential mental states under different treatments given the observed multi-domain pre-treatment measurements. Experiments on simulated data and a real-world clinical trial data show that the learned treatment polices compare favorably to alternative methods on heterogeneous treatment effects, and have broad utilities which lead to better patient outcomes on multiple domains.

paragraphs: Patients’ underlying mental states are not directly observed; they must be inferred from measurements such as symptoms and functioning scores. Treatment choice also needs to account for substantial differences between patients. This paper develops an integrated framework that learns latent mental states and individualized treatment recommendations together, drawing information from multiple outcome domains.

The framework follows a psychiatric measurement model in which observed diagnostic measures arise from underlying mental states. It incorporates measurements before and after treatment, along with biological measures, while preserving an invariant structure for representing those states. A multilayer neural network models complex differences in treatment effects between patients.

For a future patient, the policy compares potential mental states under different treatments using that patient’s observed pretreatment measurements. Experiments on simulated data and data from a clinical trial find that the learned policies compare favorably with alternatives for heterogeneous treatment effects and support better outcomes across multiple domains. These results concern the evaluated policies and data, connecting integrated outcome representation to individualized treatment selection.
summary.tldr: An integrated latent-state model combines multiple measurements to learn individualized treatment policies that compare favorably with alternatives in simulation and clinical-trial data.

title: Representation Learning for Integrating Multi-domain Outcomes to Optimize Individualized Treatment

abstract: We propose a framework that lifts the capabilities of graph convolutional networks (GCNs) to scenarios where no input graph is given and increases their robustness to adversarial attacks. We formulate a joint probabilistic model that considers a prior distribution over graphs along with a GCN-based likelihood and develop a stochastic variational inference algorithm to estimate the graph posterior and the GCN parameters jointly. To address the problem of propagating gradients through latent variables drawn from discrete distributions, we use their continuous relaxations known as Concrete distributions. We show that, on real datasets, our approach can outperform state-of-the-art Bayesian and non-Bayesian graph neural network algorithms on the task of semi-supervised classification in the absence of graph data and when the network structure is subjected to adversarial perturbations.
originalAbstract: We propose a framework that lifts the capabilities of graph convolutional networks (GCNs) to scenarios where no input graph is given and increases their robustness to adversarial attacks. We formulate a joint probabilistic model that considers a prior distribution over graphs along with a GCN-based likelihood and develop a stochastic variational inference algorithm to estimate the graph posterior and the GCN parameters jointly. To address the problem of propagating gradients through latent variables drawn from discrete distributions, we use their continuous relaxations known as Concrete distributions. We show that, on real datasets, our approach can outperform state-of-the-art Bayesian and non-Bayesian graph neural network algorithms on the task of semi-supervised classification in the absence of graph data and when the network structure is subjected to adversarial perturbations.

paragraphs: Graph convolutional networks use relationships between examples, but a suitable input graph may be unavailable or corrupted by adversarial changes. This paper develops a probabilistic framework for learning under both circumstances. It treats graph structure as something to infer jointly with the network rather than requiring it to be fully supplied.

The model combines a prior distribution over graphs with a likelihood defined through a graph convolutional network. A stochastic variational inference algorithm estimates the graph posterior and network parameters together. Because graph-related latent variables are discrete, the method uses continuous Concrete relaxations to propagate gradients through their sampled values during optimization.

Experiments on real datasets examine semi-supervised classification with missing graph data and with adversarially perturbed network structure. The authors show that their method can outperform state-of-the-art Bayesian and non-Bayesian graph-network approaches in these settings. The contribution is a unified way to learn uncertain graph structure and a predictor together, extending where graph convolution can be applied and improving robustness in the evaluated attack settings.
summary.tldr: A variational framework jointly infers graph structure and GCN parameters for classification without supplied graphs or under adversarial graph perturbations.

title: Variational Inference for Graph Convolutional Networks in the Absence of Graph Data and Adversarial Settings

abstract: We analyze continuous-time mirror descent applied to sparse phase retrieval, which is the problem of recovering sparse signals from a set of magnitude-only measurements. We apply mirror descent to the unconstrained empirical risk minimization problem (batch setting), using the square loss and square measurements. We provide a full convergence analysis of the algorithm in this non-convex setting and prove that, with the hypentropy mirror map, mirror descent recovers any $k$-sparse vector $\mathbf{x}^\star\in\mathbb{R}^n$ with minimum (in modulus) non-zero entry on the order of $\| \mathbf{x}^\star \|_2/\sqrt{k}$ from $k^2$ Gaussian measurements, modulo logarithmic terms. This yields a simple algorithm which, unlike most existing approaches to sparse phase retrieval, adapts to the sparsity level, without including thresholding steps or adding regularization terms. Our results also provide a principled theoretical understanding for Hadamard Wirtinger flow [54], as Euclidean gradient descent applied to the empirical risk problem with Hadamard parametrization can be recovered as a first-order approximation to mirror descent in discrete time.

This paper studies a continuous-time version of mirror descent applied to an unconstrained batch objective using squared measurements and a squared-error loss.

The central result is a convergence guarantee for a particular geometry, specified by the hypentropy mirror map. Recovery is proved for a k-sparse signal when its smallest nonzero entry has magnitude on the order of the signal’s Euclidean norm divided by the square root of k. Under that condition, the required number of Gaussian measurements scales as k squared, apart from logarithmic factors.

The approach matters because it adapts to sparsity without adding a regularization penalty or explicitly thresholding entries. The paper also connects the analysis to Hadamard Wirtinger flow: gradient descent using a Hadamard parametrization arises as a first-order discrete-time approximation to mirror descent. This supplies a theoretical explanation for that related method while keeping the recovery claim tied to its stated assumptions.
summary.tldr: Continuous-time mirror descent recovers sparse signals from magnitude-only Gaussian measurements under stated signal conditions, without thresholding or regularization.

title: A Continuous-Time Mirror Descent Approach to Sparse Phase Retrieval

abstract: Boosting is an algorithmic approach which is based on the idea of combining weak and moderately inaccurate hypotheses to a strong and accurate one. In this work we study multiclass boosting with a possibly large number of classes or categories. Multiclass boosting can be formulated in various ways. Here, we focus on an especially natural formulation in which the weak hypotheses are assumed to belong to an ''easy-to-learn'' base class, and the weak learner is an agnostic PAC learner for that class with respect to the standard classification loss. This is in contrast with other, more complicated losses as have often been considered in the past. The goal of the overall boosting algorithm is then to learn a combination of weak hypotheses by repeatedly calling the weak learner.We study the resources required for boosting, especially how theydepend on the number of classes $k$, for both the booster and weak learner.We find that the boosting algorithm itself only requires $O(\log k)$samples, as we show by analyzing a variant of AdaBoost for oursetting. In stark contrast, assuming typical limits on the number of weak-learner calls,we prove that the number of samples required by a weak learner is at least polynomial in $k$, exponentially more than thenumber of samples needed by the booster.Alternatively, we prove that the weak learner's accuracy parametermust be smaller than an inverse polynomial in $k$, showing that the returned weakhypotheses must be nearly the best in their class when $k$ is large.We also prove a trade-off between number of oracle calls and theresources required of the weak learner, meaning that the fewer calls to theweak learner the more that is demanded on each call.

paragraphs: Boosting combines relatively inaccurate predictors into a stronger predictor. This paper asks how its resource demands change when there are many possible classes. It studies a formulation where the weak learner learns an easy base class under ordinary classification loss, using an agnostic PAC guarantee rather than a more complicated loss.

The analysis separates the resources used by the booster from those required by its weak-learning subroutine. A variant of AdaBoost needs only logarithmically many samples in the number of classes, k. In contrast, under typical restrictions on the number of weak-learner calls, the authors prove a polynomial-in-k sample requirement for the weak learner.

An alternative result requires the weak learner's accuracy parameter to be smaller than an inverse polynomial in k, demanding hypotheses close to the best available in their class. A further tradeoff links fewer calls to greater demands per call. The findings reveal that an apparently inexpensive boosting procedure can depend on a substantially more demanding weak learner as the class count grows.
summary.tldr: Multiclass boosting can have low sample demands while imposing much larger sample or accuracy requirements on its weak learner.

title: Multiclass Boosting and the Cost of Weak Learning

abstract: We address the problem of sequential prediction with expert advice in a non-stationary environment with long-term memory guarantees in the sense of Bousquet and Warmuth [4]. We give a linear-time algorithm that improves on the best known regret bound [27]. This algorithm incorporates a relative entropy projection step. This projection is advantageous over previous weight-sharing approaches in that weight updates may come with implicit costs as in for example portfolio optimization. We give an algorithm to compute this projection step in linear time, which may be of independent interest.

paragraphs: Sequential prediction with expert advice asks a learner to combine recommendations while outcomes arrive over time. When conditions change, the most useful expert can change too. This paper studies that non-stationary setting while seeking long-term memory guarantees, so its target goes beyond identifying a single expert that performs well throughout the sequence.

The authors give a linear-time algorithm with an improved regret bound over the previously best-known result. Regret measures the performance gap relative to the comparison strategy used in the analysis. The algorithm incorporates a relative entropy projection, making this projection an essential part of how the learner updates its expert weights.

This update mechanism has an advantage over earlier weight-sharing approaches when changing weights carries implicit costs, as can happen in portfolio optimization. The authors also supply a linear-time algorithm for computing the projection itself. That matters because an efficient outer learning procedure would lose its practical appeal if this internal step were expensive. The paper thus contributes both a stronger prediction guarantee and an efficient computational primitive that may be useful separately.
summary.tldr: A linear-time expert-tracking algorithm improves regret guarantees using a relative entropy projection that can also be computed in linear time.

title: Improved Regret Bounds for Tracking Experts with Memory

abstract: Gathering training data is a key step of any supervised learning task, and it is both critical and expensive. Critical, because the quantity and quality of the training data has a high impact on the performance of the learned function. Expensive, because most practical cases rely on humans-in-the-loop to label the data. The process of determining the correct labels is much more expensive than comparing two items to see whether they belong to the same class. Thus motivated, we propose a setting for training data gathering where the human experts perform the comparatively cheap task of answering pairwise queries, and the computer groups the items into classes (which can be labeled cheaply at the very end of the process). Given the items, we consider two random models for the classes: one where the set partition they form is drawn uniformly, the other one where each item chooses its class independently following a fixed distribution. In the first model, we characterize the algorithms that minimize the average number of queries required to cluster the items and analyze their complexity. In the second model, we analyze a specific algorithm family, propose as a conjecture that they reach the minimum average number of queries and compare their performance to a random approach. We also propose solutions to handle errors or inconsistencies in the experts' answers.

paragraphs: Creating labeled training data often requires expensive expert judgment. This paper studies a cheaper interaction: asking whether two items belong to the same class. A computer uses these pairwise answers to assemble groups, after which experts can assign labels to the groups. The central question is how to minimize the number of comparisons.

The authors analyze two probabilistic models of how classes are formed. In the first, the partition of items into classes is chosen uniformly at random. They characterize algorithms that minimize the average query count and analyze their complexity. In the second, each item independently chooses a class according to a fixed distribution.

For that second model, the authors study a particular algorithm family and compare it with a random strategy. Its average-query optimality remains a conjecture, rather than a proved result. They also propose ways to accommodate incorrect or inconsistent expert answers. The contribution connects annotation cost to explicit mathematical models while distinguishing established optimality from a promising unresolved claim.
summary.tldr: Pairwise expert comparisons can support cheaper training-data labeling, with query-optimal clustering algorithms established under one random class model.

title: Active clustering for labeling training data

abstract: Existing approaches to unsupervised object discovery (UOD) do not scale up to large datasets without approximations that compromise their performance. We propose a novel formulation of UOD as a ranking problem, amenable to the arsenal of distributed methods available for eigenvalue problems and link analysis. Through the use of self-supervised features, we also demonstrate the first effective fully unsupervised pipeline for UOD. Extensive experiments on COCO~\cite{Lin2014cocodataset} and OpenImages~\cite{openimages} show that, in the single-object discovery setting where a single prominent object is sought in each image, the proposed LOD (Large-scale Object Discovery) approach is on par with, or better than the state of the art for medium-scale datasets (up to 120K images), and over 37\% better than the only other algorithms capable of scaling up to 1.7M images. In the multi-object discovery setting where multiple objects are sought in each image, the proposed LOD is over 14\% better in average precision (AP) than all other methods for datasets ranging from 20K to 1.7M images. Using self-supervised features, we also show that the proposed method obtains state-of-the-art UOD performance on OpenImages.

paragraphs: Unsupervised object discovery seeks objects in images without object annotations. Existing approaches face a scaling problem: handling large collections can require approximations that hurt performance. This paper reformulates discovery as a ranking task, allowing it to draw on distributed techniques for eigenvalue problems and link analysis rather than relying on those compromises.

The resulting Large-scale Object Discovery approach, or LOD, also uses self-supervised features to form a fully unsupervised pipeline. This addresses the source of the image representation as well as the discovery procedure itself. The authors evaluate both finding one prominent object per image and finding multiple objects within each image.

On COCO and OpenImages, single-object results match or exceed prior state of the art at medium scale, up to 120,000 images. At 1.7 million images, the reported improvement exceeds 37% over the other scalable algorithms. Self-supervised features also yield state-of-the-art discovery performance on OpenImages.
summary.tldr: LOD turns unsupervised object discovery into a ranking problem that scales to millions of images while improving reported discovery performance.

title: Large-Scale Unsupervised Object Discovery

abstract: The multiplicative structure of parameters and input data in the first layer of neural networks is explored to build connection between the landscape of the loss function with respect to parameters and the landscape of the model function with respect to input data. By this connection, it is shown that flat minima regularize the gradient of the model function, which explains the good generalization performance of flat minima. Then, we go beyond the flatness and consider high-order moments of the gradient noise, and show that Stochastic Gradient Dascent (SGD) tends to impose constraints on these moments by a linear stability analysis of SGD around global minima. Together with the multiplicative structure, we identify the Sobolev regularization effect of SGD, i.e. SGD regularizes the Sobolev seminorms of the model function with respect to the input data. Finally, bounds for generalization error and adversarial robustness are provided for solutions found by SGD under assumptions of the data distribution.

paragraphs: This paper connects two views of a neural network: how its loss changes when parameters move and how its output changes when inputs move. The link comes from the multiplicative interaction between input data and first-layer parameters. Using this relationship, the authors show how flat minima constrain the model’s input gradient, offering an explanation for their generalization behavior.

The analysis then extends beyond flatness to higher-order moments of gradient noise. By examining the linear stability of stochastic gradient descent around global minima, the authors show that SGD tends to constrain these moments. Combining this with the first-layer relationship translates properties of the optimization process into restrictions on the learned function.

The resulting effect is described as Sobolev regularization: SGD controls derivative-based measures of the model function with respect to its inputs. The paper also derives bounds on generalization error and adversarial robustness under assumptions about the data distribution. These conditional guarantees connect training stability with input smoothness, while keeping the conclusions tied to the setting of the analysis.
summary.tldr: The paper links SGD stability to input smoothness and derives conditional generalization and adversarial-robustness bounds.

title: On Linear Stability of SGD and Input-Smoothness of Neural Networks

abstract: We develop machinery to design efficiently computable and \emph{consistent} estimators, achieving estimation error approaching zero as the number of observations grows, when facing an oblivious adversary that may corrupt responses in all but an $\alpha$ fraction of the samples.As concrete examples, we investigate two problems: sparse regression and principal component analysis (PCA).For sparse regression, we achieve consistency for optimal sample size $n\gtrsim (k\log d)/\alpha^2$ and optimal error rate $O(\sqrt{(k\log d)/(n\cdot \alpha^2)})$where $n$ is the number of observations, $d$ is the number of dimensions and $k$ is the sparsity of the parameter vector, allowing the fraction of inliers to be inverse-polynomial in the number of samples.Prior to this work, no estimator was known to be consistent when the fraction of inliers $\alpha$ is $o(1/\log \log n)$, even for (non-spherical) Gaussian design matrices.Results holding under weak design assumptions and in the presence of such general noise have only been shown in dense setting (i.e., general linear regression) very recently by d'Orsi et al.~\cite{ICML-linear-regression}.In the context of PCA, we attain optimal error guarantees under broad spikiness assumptions on the parameter matrix (usually used in matrix completion). Previous works could obtain non-trivial guarantees only under the assumptions that the measurement noise corresponding to the inliers is polynomially small in $n$ (e.g., Gaussian with variance $1/n^2$).To devise our estimators, we equip the Huber loss with non-smooth regularizers such as the $\ell_1$ norm or the nuclear norm, and extend d'Orsi et al.'s approach~\cite{ICML-linear-regression} in a novel way to analyze the loss function.Our machinery appears to be easily applicable to a wide range of estimation problems.We complement these algorithmic results with statistical lower bounds showing that the fraction of inliers that our PCA estimator can deal with is optimal up to a constant factor.

paragraphs: This paper studies estimation when an oblivious adversary can corrupt responses in all but an α fraction of observations. The goal is consistency: estimation error should approach zero as more observations become available. The authors develop efficiently computable estimators for sparse regression and principal component analysis, addressing settings in which reliable observations may be a small minority.

Their construction combines the Huber loss with nonsmooth regularizers, including the ℓ1 norm and nuclear norm. For sparse regression, they obtain optimal sample-size scaling of roughly k log(d)/α² and an optimal error rate proportional to the square root of k log(d)/(nα²). Here k measures sparsity, d is dimension, and n is the observation count. The analysis allows the inlier fraction to be inverse-polynomial in sample size.

For PCA, the authors establish optimal error guarantees under broad assumptions controlling matrix spikiness. They also prove statistical lower bounds showing that the inlier fraction their PCA estimator tolerates is optimal up to a constant factor. Together, the results explain when strong corruption can coexist with accurate estimation under the stated adversarial and structural assumptions.
summary.tldr: Regularized Huber-loss estimators achieve consistent sparse regression and PCA under severe oblivious corruption, with optimal guarantees in the stated settings.

title: Consistent Estimation for PCA and Sparse Regression with Oblivious Outliers

abstract: Universal Semi-Supervised Learning (UniSSL) aims to solve the open-set problem where both the class distribution (i.e., class set) and feature distribution (i.e., feature domain) are different between labeled dataset and unlabeled dataset. Such a problem seriously hinders the realistic landing of classical SSL. Different from the existing SSL methods targeting at the open-set problem that only study one certain scenario of class distribution mismatch and ignore the feature distribution mismatch, we consider a more general case where a mismatch exists in both class and feature distribution. In this case, we propose a ''Class-shAring data detection and Feature Adaptation'' (CAFA) framework which requires no prior knowledge of the class relationship between the labeled dataset and unlabeled dataset. Particularly, CAFA utilizes a novel scoring strategy to detect the data in the shared class set. Then, it conducts domain adaptation to fully exploit the value of the detected class-sharing data for better semi-supervised consistency training. Exhaustive experiments on several benchmark datasets show the effectiveness of our method in tackling open-set problems.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised learning uses unlabeled data alongside labeled examples, but the two collections may differ in both the classes they contain and their feature distributions. This paper studies that combined mismatch under the name Universal Semi-Supervised Learning. Its setting broadens approaches that consider only a particular class mismatch while leaving feature-domain differences unaddressed.

The proposed CAFA framework first scores unlabeled examples to identify data belonging to classes shared with the labeled collection. It then applies domain adaptation to the detected examples so they can contribute more effectively to semi-supervised consistency training. The framework requires no prior knowledge of the relationship between the two datasets' class sets.

Experiments across several benchmark datasets demonstrate effectiveness on open-set problems. The approach matters because deciding which unlabeled examples are relevant and accounting for how they differ from labeled data are connected challenges. Detecting shared classes addresses relevance, while adapting their feature distributions helps the training procedure use those examples. CAFA combines both operations within one framework for the more general mismatch setting.
summary.tldr: CAFA identifies shared-class unlabeled data and adapts its features to support semi-supervised learning when both classes and domains differ.

title: Universal Semi-Supervised Learning

abstract: Self-supervised pre-training has drawn increasing attention in recent years due to its superior performance on numerous downstream tasks after fine-tuning. However, it is well-known that deep learning models lack the robustness to adversarial examples, which can also invoke security issues to pre-trained models, despite being less explored. In this paper, we delve into the robustness of pre-trained models by introducing Pre-trained Adversarial Perturbations (PAPs), which are universal perturbations crafted for the pre-trained models to maintain the effectiveness when attacking fine-tuned ones without any knowledge of the downstream tasks. To this end, we propose a Low-Level Layer Lifting Attack (L4A) method to generate effective PAPs by lifting the neuron activations of low-level layers of the pre-trained models. Equipped with an enhanced noise augmentation strategy, L4A is effective at generating more transferable PAPs against the fine-tuned models. Extensive experiments on typical pre-trained vision models and ten downstream tasks demonstrate that our method improves the attack success rate by a large margin compared to the state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: Pretrained vision models are adapted to many downstream tasks, raising the question of whether an attack prepared before adaptation can remain effective afterward. This paper introduces pretrained adversarial perturbations, or PAPs: universal perturbations crafted using a pretrained model without knowledge of the downstream tasks they will later target.

The proposed Low-Level Layer Lifting Attack generates these perturbations by increasing neuron activations in the pretrained model's lower layers. It also uses an enhanced noise augmentation strategy to improve transfer to fine-tuned models. The intended transfer is therefore across adaptation: the attack is constructed against the shared pretrained starting point and evaluated against models derived from it.

Experiments cover typical pretrained vision models and ten downstream tasks. The authors report a large improvement in attack success rate over existing methods. This provides empirical evidence that perturbations can retain effectiveness through fine-tuning even when downstream-task information is unavailable during attack construction. The contribution highlights robustness of pretrained representations as relevant to the security of their later adaptations.
summary.tldr: PAPs exploit pretrained models to create perturbations that transfer effectively to tested fine-tuned models without downstream-task knowledge.

title: Pre-trained Adversarial Perturbations

abstract: Gradient descent during the learning process of a neural network can be subject to many instabilities. The spectral density of the Jacobian is a key component for analyzing stability. Following the works of Pennington et al., such Jacobians are modeled using free multiplicative convolutions from Free Probability Theory (FPT).We present a reliable and very fast method for computing the associated spectral densities, for given architecture and initialization. This method has a controlled and proven convergence. Our technique is based on an homotopy method: it is an adaptative Newton-Raphson scheme which chains basins of attraction. We find contiguous lilypad-like basins and step from one to the next, heading towards the objective.In order to demonstrate the relevance of our method we show that the relevant FPT metrics computed before training are highly correlated to final test losses – up to 85%. We also give evidence that a very desirable feature for neural networks is the hyperbolicity of their Jacobian at initialization, while remaining at the edge of chaos.

paragraphs: Neural network training can become unstable, and the spectral density of the network's Jacobian offers a way to analyze that behavior. This paper works with a free-probability model of those Jacobians to calculate spectral densities for a chosen architecture and initialization. The aim is to make these calculations reliable and fast enough to inform analysis before training.

The computational method uses homotopy: it progresses toward the desired solution through a sequence of related problems. An adaptive Newton–Raphson procedure moves between neighbouring regions in which its iterations converge. The authors provide a controlled, proven convergence result for this calculation, making the numerical procedure a central contribution alongside its application to neural networks.

In experiments, free-probability metrics calculated before training correlate strongly with final test losses, with reported correlations reaching 85%. This supports their relevance as indicators of eventual performance, without establishing that they determine it. The authors also present evidence favouring Jacobian hyperbolicity at initialization while the network remains at the edge of chaos.
summary.tldr: A fast, convergent spectral calculation yields pre-training metrics that correlate strongly with final losses in the reported experiments.

title: Free Probability for predicting the performance of feed-forward fully connected neural networks

abstract: The lack of publicly available high-quality and accurately labeled datasets has long been a major bottleneck for singing voice synthesis (SVS). To tackle this problem, we present M4Singer, a free-to-use Multi-style, Multi-singer Mandarin singing collection with elaborately annotated Musical scores as well as its benchmarks. Specifically, 1) we construct and release a large high-quality Chinese singing voice corpus, which is recorded by 20 professional singers, covering 700 Chinese pop songs as well as all the four SATB types (i.e., soprano, alto, tenor, and bass); 2) we take extensive efforts to manually compose the musical scores for each recorded song, which are necessary to the study of the prosody modeling for SVS. 3) To facilitate the use and demonstrate the quality of M4Singer, we conduct four different benchmark experiments: score-based SVS, controllable singing voice (CSV), singing voice conversion (SVC) and automatic music transcription (AMT).

paragraphs: Singing voice synthesis depends on recordings paired with accurate musical information. A shortage of public, high-quality, carefully labeled data has limited work in this area. M4Singer addresses that resource problem with a free-to-use Mandarin singing collection that includes multiple singers, styles, and manually prepared musical scores.

The authors manually compose scores for each recorded song, supplying information needed to study prosody modeling in singing synthesis. The scores are thus a central part of the resource, alongside the audio recordings.

Four benchmark experiments demonstrate uses of the collection: score-based singing synthesis, controllable singing voice, singing voice conversion, and automatic music transcription. These tasks cover generating singing, controlling it, converting voices, and recovering musical information from audio. The paper's contribution is a shared dataset with accompanying benchmarks, intended to make several strands of singing research easier to develop and evaluate.
summary.tldr: M4Singer provides Mandarin singing recordings from 20 professional singers across 700 songs, with manually prepared scores and four benchmark tasks.

title: M4Singer: A Multi-Style, Multi-Singer and Musical Score Provided Mandarin Singing Corpus

abstract: Modeling the energy and forces of atomic systems is a fundamental problem in computational chemistry with the potential to help address many of the world’s most pressing problems, including those related to energy scarcity and climate change. These calculations are traditionally performed using Density Functional Theory, which is computationally very expensive. Machine learning has the potential to dramatically improve the efficiency of these calculations from days or hours to seconds.We propose the Spherical Channel Network (SCN) to model atomic energies and forces. The SCN is a graph neural network where nodes represent atoms and edges their neighboring atoms. The atom embeddings are a set of spherical functions, called spherical channels, represented using spherical harmonics. We demonstrate, that by rotating the embeddings based on the 3D edge orientation, more information may be utilized while maintaining the rotational equivariance of the messages. While equivariance is a desirable property, we find that by relaxing this constraint in both message passing and aggregation, improved accuracy may be achieved. We demonstrate state-of-the-art results on the large-scale Open Catalyst 2020 dataset in both energy and force prediction for numerous tasks and metrics.

paragraphs: Predicting atomic energies and forces is central to computational chemistry, but traditional density-functional calculations are expensive. This paper introduces the Spherical Channel Network as a learned model for those quantities. It represents an atomic system as a graph, with atoms as nodes and connections linking neighboring atoms.

Each atom’s representation contains spherical functions, called spherical channels, expressed using spherical harmonics. The network rotates these representations according to the three-dimensional orientation of each edge. The authors show that this can allow messages to use more information while retaining rotational equivariance, meaning their transformation remains consistent with rotation.

The paper also investigates relaxing equivariance in message passing and aggregation. Although equivariance is desirable, the authors find that loosening it can improve accuracy. On the large Open Catalyst 2020 dataset, the network achieves state-of-the-art energy and force prediction across numerous tasks and metrics. The findings connect a direction-sensitive representation with strong empirical performance, while showing that strict enforcement of the symmetry is not always the most accurate choice in the evaluated setting.
summary.tldr: Spherical Channel Networks use orientation-aware atomic representations to achieve strong energy and force predictions, with accuracy gains possible from relaxed equivariance.

title: Spherical Channels for Modeling Atomic Interactions

abstract: LiDAR point clouds, which are usually scanned by rotating LiDAR sensors continuously, capture precise geometry of the surrounding environment and are crucial to many autonomous detection and navigation tasks. Though many 3D deep architectures have been developed, efficient collection and annotation of large amounts of point clouds remain one major challenge in the analytics and understanding of point cloud data. This paper presents PolarMix, a point cloud augmentation technique that is simple and generic but can mitigate the data constraint effectively across various perception tasks and scenarios. PolarMix enriches point cloud distributions and preserves point cloud fidelity via two cross-scan augmentation strategies that cut, edit, and mix point clouds along the scanning direction. The first is scene-level swapping which exchanges point cloud sectors of two LiDAR scans that are cut along the LiDAR scanning direction. The second is instance-level rotation and paste which crops point instances from one LiDAR scan, rotates them by multiple angles (to create multiple copies), and paste the rotated point instances into other scans. Extensive experiments show that PolarMix achieves superior performance consistently across different perception tasks and scenarios. In addition, it can work as a plug-and-play for various 3D deep architectures and also performs well for unsupervised domain adaptation.

paragraphs: LiDAR point clouds capture detailed geometry, but collecting and labeling enough of them remains difficult. Its augmentations follow the scanning direction of rotating LiDAR sensors, aiming to enrich the data distribution while preserving the fidelity of the point clouds.

These operations introduce variation at both scene and object scales.

Experiments report consistently superior performance across multiple perception tasks and scenarios. The method can be added to different 3D network architectures and also performs well in unsupervised domain adaptation. Its contribution is a broadly applicable augmentation procedure that uses the organization of LiDAR scans to make existing data more useful.
summary.tldr: PolarMix augments LiDAR data by swapping scan sectors and rotating and pasting object instances, improving multiple perception tasks.

title: PolarMix: A General Data Augmentation Technique for LiDAR Point Clouds

abstract: Given data from diverse sets of distinct distributions, domain generalization aims to learn models that generalize to unseen distributions. A common approach is designing a data-driven surrogate penalty to capture generalization and minimize the empirical risk jointly with the penalty. We argue that a significant failure mode of this recipe is an excess risk due to an erroneous penalty or hardness in joint optimization. We present an approach that eliminates this problem. Instead of jointly minimizing empirical risk with the penalty, we minimize the penalty under the constraint of optimality of the empirical risk. This change guarantees that the domain generalization penalty cannot impair optimization of the empirical risk, \ie, in-distribution performance. To solve the proposed optimization problem, we demonstrate an exciting connection to rate-distortion theory and utilize its tools to design an efficient method. Our approach can be applied to any penalty-based domain generalization method, and we demonstrate its effectiveness by applying it to three examplar methods from the literature, showing significant improvements.
