paragraphs: Domain generalization aims to learn from several observed distributions and perform well on unseen ones. A common strategy combines training error with a penalty intended to encourage generalization. The paper argues that an inaccurate penalty, or difficulty optimizing both terms together, can needlessly worsen performance on the training distributions.

The authors reverse the relationship between these objectives. They minimize the generalization penalty subject to the requirement that empirical risk remain optimal. Under this formulation, the penalty cannot impair optimization of empirical risk. This protects the training-distribution objective without requiring the penalty itself to perfectly capture what will generalize.

To solve the constrained problem efficiently, the authors connect it to rate-distortion theory and use tools from that area. They describe the approach as applicable to any penalty-based domain generalization method and demonstrate significant improvements on three examples from prior work. The guarantee concerns preserving empirical-risk optimality; the improvements in domain generalization are demonstrated experimentally. This distinction explains both the method's firm protection and its practical motivation.
summary.tldr: The method optimizes a domain-generalization penalty while constraining empirical risk to remain optimal.

title: Domain Generalization without Excess Empirical Risk

abstract: This paper explores the possibility of near-optimally solving multi-agent, multi-task NP-hard planning problems with time-dependent rewards using a learning-based algorithm. In particular, we consider a class of robot/machine scheduling problems called the multi-robot reward collection problem (MRRC). Such MRRC problems well model ride-sharing, pickup-and-delivery, and a variety of related problems. In representing the MRRC problem as a sequential decision-making problem, we observe that each state can be represented as an extension of probabilistic graphical models (PGMs), which we refer to as random PGMs. We then develop a mean-field inference method for random PGMs. We then propose (1) an order-transferable Q-function estimator and (2) an order-transferability-enabled auction to select a joint assignment in polynomial-time. These result in a reinforcement learning framework with at least $1-1/e$ optimality. Experimental results on solving MRRC problems highlight the near-optimality and transferability of the proposed methods. We also consider identical parallel machine scheduling problems (IPMS) and minimax multiple traveling salesman problems (minimax-mTSP).

paragraphs: Assigning multiple robots or machines to tasks becomes difficult when rewards depend on timing and assignments interact. The paper studies this through the multi-robot reward collection problem, which models settings such as ride-sharing and pickup-and-delivery. Its aim is to learn near-optimal planning behavior for this NP-hard problem class.

The authors formulate planning as sequential decision making and represent each state using an extension of probabilistic graphical models called random PGMs. They develop a mean-field inference method for these representations. Building on this, they introduce an order-transferable estimator of action values and an auction that uses this property to select a joint assignment in polynomial time.

These components form a reinforcement-learning framework with a stated optimality guarantee of at least 1−1/e. Experiments on reward-collection problems support the methods' near-optimality and transferability. The paper also considers identical parallel machine scheduling and minimax multiple traveling-salesman problems. The contribution combines structured inference, learned action evaluation, and efficient assignment selection for the planning settings studied.
summary.tldr: Structured graph inference and an auction-based assignment mechanism support learned multi-agent planning with a stated approximation guarantee.

title: Learning NP-Hard Multi-Agent Assignment Planning using GNN: Inference on a Random Graph and Provable Auction-Fitted Q-learning

abstract: Peer prediction refers to a collection of mechanisms for eliciting information from human agents when direct verification of the obtained information is unavailable. They are designed to have a game-theoretic equilibrium where everyone reveals their private information truthfully. This result holds under the assumption that agents are Bayesian and they each adopt a fixed strategy across all tasks. Human agents however are observed in many domains to exhibit learning behavior in sequential settings. In this paper, we explore the dynamics of sequential peer prediction mechanisms when participants are learning agents. We first show that the notion of no regret alone for the agents’ learning algorithms cannot guarantee convergence to the truthful strategy. We then focus on a family of learning algorithms where strategy updates only depend on agents’ cumulative rewards and prove that agents' strategies in the popular Correlated Agreement (CA) mechanism converge to truthful reporting when they use algorithms from this family. This family of algorithms is not necessarily no-regret, but includes several familiar no-regret learning algorithms (e.g multiplicative weight update and Follow the Perturbed Leader) as special cases. Simulation of several algorithms in this family as well as the $\epsilon$-greedy algorithm, which is outside of this family, shows convergence to the truthful strategy in the CA mechanism.

paragraphs: Peer-prediction mechanisms reward reports when their truth cannot be checked directly. Traditional guarantees identify an equilibrium where everyone reports honestly, assuming Bayesian agents use fixed strategies across tasks. This paper asks what happens when participants instead learn and change their reporting behavior over a sequence of interactions.

The authors first show that no-regret learning alone does not guarantee convergence to truthful reporting. They then analyze a family of learning algorithms whose strategy updates depend only on cumulative rewards. For agents using algorithms in this family, they prove convergence to truthful reporting under the Correlated Agreement mechanism. The family includes multiplicative weight update and Follow the Perturbed Leader, but is not defined by the no-regret property.

The latter is empirical evidence rather than an extension of the theorem. The paper’s central contribution is to distinguish the existence of a truthful equilibrium from whether learning agents actually approach it, and to identify an algorithm family for which that dynamic behavior can be established.
summary.tldr: No-regret learning alone cannot ensure honesty, but a specified reward-based learning family converges to truthful reporting under Correlated Agreement.

title: Peer Prediction for Learning Agents

abstract: In this paper we show that our Machine Learning (ML) approach, CoMLSim (Composable Machine Learning Simulator), can simulate PDEs on highly-resolved grids with higher accuracy and generalization to out-of-distribution source terms and geometries than traditional ML baselines. Our unique approach combines key principles of traditional PDE solvers with local-learning and low-dimensional manifold techniques to iteratively simulate PDEs on large computational domains. The proposed approach is validated on more than 5 steady-state PDEs across different PDE conditions on highly-resolved grids and comparisons are made with the commercial solver, Ansys Fluent as well as 4 other state-of-the-art ML methods. The numerical experiments show that our approach outperforms ML baselines in terms of 1) accuracy across quantitative metrics and 2) generalization to out-of-distribution conditions as well as domain sizes. Additionally, we provide results for a large number of ablations experiments conducted to highlight components of our approach that strongly influence the results. We conclude that our local-learning and iterative-inferencing approach reduces the challenge of generalization that most ML models face.

Our unique approach combines key principles of traditional PDE solvers with local-learning and low-dimensional manifold techniques to iteratively simulate PDEs on large computational domains. The proposed approach is validated on more than 5 steady-state PDEs across different PDE conditions on highly-resolved grids and comparisons are made with the commercial solver, Ansys Fluent as well as 4 other state-of-the-art ML methods. The numerical experiments show that our approach outperforms ML baselines in terms of 1) accuracy across quantitative metrics and 2) generalization to out-of-distribution conditions as well as domain sizes. Additionally, we provide results for a large number of ablations experiments conducted to highlight components of our approach that strongly influence the results. We conclude that our local-learning and iterative-inferencing approach reduces the challenge of generalization that most ML models face.

paragraphs: CoMLSim addresses the problem of using machine learning to simulate steady-state partial differential equations on finely resolved grids. Its central idea is to combine principles from traditional numerical solvers with learning that operates locally. The method also uses low-dimensional representations and repeated inference steps to build simulations across large computational domains.

This combination matters because the paper targets generalization across more than the conditions represented during training. The evaluated changes include unfamiliar source terms, geometries, and domain sizes. Local learning and iterative simulation provide the organizing approach for handling these changes, rather than treating each large simulation as an entirely separate prediction problem.

The authors validate CoMLSim on more than five steady-state PDEs under different conditions, comparing it with Ansys Fluent and four machine-learning methods. Their numerical experiments show better accuracy and generalization than the machine-learning baselines. Component-removal experiments also identify parts of the approach that strongly affect results. These findings support the authors’ conclusion that local learning and iterative inference reduce generalization difficulties in the settings tested; they do not establish superiority over the commercial solver.
summary.tldr: CoMLSim combines local learning with iterative PDE simulation to improve accuracy and generalization over tested machine-learning baselines.

title: A composable machine-learning approach for steady-state simulations on high-resolution grids

abstract: In the stochastic contextual low-rank matrix bandit problem, the expected reward of an action is given by the inner product between the action's feature matrix and some fixed, but initially unknown $d_1$ by $d_2$ matrix $\Theta^*$ with rank $r \ll \{d_1, d_2\}$, and an agent sequentially takes actions based on past experience to maximize the cumulative reward. In this paper, we study the generalized low-rank matrix bandit problem, which has been recently proposed in \cite{lu2021low} under the Generalized Linear Model (GLM) framework. To overcome the computational infeasibility and theoretical restrain of existing algorithms on this problem, we first propose the G-ESTT framework that modifies the idea from \cite{jun2019bilinear} by using Stein's method on the subspace estimation and then leverage the estimated subspaces via a regularization idea. Furthermore, we remarkably improve the efficiency of G-ESTT by using a novel exclusion idea on the estimated subspace instead, and propose the G-ESTS framework. We also show that both of our methods are the first algorithm to achieve the optimal $\tilde{O}((d_1+d_2)r\sqrt{T})$ bound of regret presented in \cite{lu2021low} up to logarithm terms under some mild conditions, which improves upon the current regret of $\tilde{O}((d_1+d_2)^{3/2} \sqrt{rT})$~\citep{lu2021low}. For completeness, we conduct experiments to illustrate that our proposed algorithms, especially G-ESTS, are also computationally tractable and consistently outperform other state-of-the-art (generalized) linear matrix bandit methods based on a suite of simulations.

paragraphs: Matrix bandits describe sequential decisions whose rewards depend on an unknown matrix and an action's feature matrix. When the unknown matrix has low rank, it contains structure that could make learning easier than estimating all its entries independently. This paper studies a generalized version using a generalized linear model and seeks algorithms that are both computationally practical and theoretically strong.

The first framework, G-ESTT, uses Stein's method to estimate relevant subspaces and then incorporates those estimates through regularization. The second, G-ESTS, replaces that regularization approach with an exclusion mechanism on the estimated subspace. The authors report that this change substantially improves computational efficiency while retaining the desired learning guarantee.

Under mild conditions, both frameworks achieve the stated optimal regret rate, up to logarithmic factors: (d1 + d2)r√T, where r is the unknown matrix's rank. This improves the previously stated dependence on matrix dimensions and rank. Simulations also show computational tractability and consistent gains over the compared matrix-bandit methods, particularly for G-ESTS. Together, the results show how estimated low-rank structure can support both efficient computation and stronger sequential-learning guarantees.
summary.tldr: G-ESTT and G-ESTS exploit estimated low-rank subspaces to achieve improved regret guarantees and practical computation for generalized matrix bandits.

title: Efficient Frameworks for Generalized Low-Rank Matrix Bandit Problems

abstract: The goal of robust reinforcement learning (RL) is to learn a policy that is robust against the uncertainty in model parameters. Parameter uncertainty commonly occurs in many real-world RL applications due to simulator modeling errors, changes in the real-world system dynamics over time, and adversarial disturbances. Robust RL is typically formulated as a max-min problem, where the objective is to learn the policy that maximizes the value against the worst possible models that lie in an uncertainty set. In this work, we propose a robust RL algorithm called Robust Fitted Q-Iteration (RFQI), which uses only an offline dataset to learn the optimal robust policy. Robust RL with offline data is significantly more challenging than its non-robust counterpart because of the minimization over all models present in the robust Bellman operator. This poses challenges in offline data collection, optimization over the models, and unbiased estimation. In this work, we propose a systematic approach to overcome these challenges, resulting in our RFQI algorithm. We prove that RFQI learns a near-optimal robust policy under standard assumptions and demonstrate its superior performance on standard benchmark problems.

paragraphs: Robust reinforcement learning seeks a policy that performs well despite uncertainty about the environment. Its objective considers the worst-performing model within a specified uncertainty set. This is relevant when a simulator is imperfect, system dynamics change, or disturbances affect behavior. The paper asks how to learn such a policy using only previously collected data.

The proposed Robust Fitted Q-Iteration algorithm, RFQI, addresses this offline setting. Robustness introduces an inner minimization over possible models into the Bellman operator used for learning. With a fixed dataset, that extra optimization creates difficulties involving data collection, optimization over models, and unbiased estimation. The authors develop a systematic approach to handle these challenges together.

Under standard assumptions, the paper proves that RFQI learns a near-optimal robust policy. Benchmark experiments also show superior performance. The guarantee concerns robustness within the modeled uncertainty set and is conditional on the assumptions, so the stated theoretical result is more specific than unconditional protection against any environmental change. Its significance is obtaining a principled robust-learning procedure from offline data alone.
summary.tldr: RFQI learns robust policies from offline data and has a near-optimality guarantee under standard assumptions.

title: Robust Reinforcement Learning using Offline Data

abstract: Given a monocular video, segmenting and decoupling dynamic objects while recovering the static environment is a widely studied problem in machine intelligence. Existing solutions usually approach this problem in the image domain, limiting their performance and understanding of the environment. We introduce Decoupled Dynamic Neural Radiance Field (D^2NeRF), a self-supervised approach that takes a monocular video and learns a 3D scene representation which decouples moving objects, including their shadows, from the static background. Our method represents the moving objects and the static background by two separate neural radiance fields with only one allowing for temporal changes. A naive implementation of this approach leads to the dynamic component taking over the static one as the representation of the former is inherently more general and prone to overfitting. To this end, we propose a novel loss to promote correct separation of phenomena. We further propose a shadow field network to detect and decouple dynamically moving shadows. We introduce a new dataset containing various dynamic objects and shadows and demonstrate that our method can achieve better performance than state-of-the-art approaches in decoupling dynamic and static 3D objects, occlusion and shadow removal, and image segmentation for moving objects. Project page: https://d2nerf.github.io/

paragraphs: D^2NeRF learns to separate moving objects from a stationary environment using a video from a single camera. It builds a three-dimensional scene representation through self-supervision, extending the separation problem beyond individual images. The intended decomposition includes moving shadows, which also change the observed scene even though they are not separate solid objects.

The method uses two neural radiance fields, one for the static background and one that can change over time. Simply combining those fields creates a problem: the more flexible dynamic field can absorb content that belongs in the static field. A new loss encourages the intended separation, while an additional shadow field network identifies and separates moving shadows.

The authors introduce a dataset containing varied moving objects and shadows. They demonstrate that the method can outperform leading approaches in separating dynamic and static 3D content, removing occlusions and shadows, and segmenting moving objects in images. The contribution connects these tasks through one scene decomposition, with explicit mechanisms for controlling the dynamic representation's flexibility.
summary.tldr: D^2NeRF separates moving objects and shadows from a static 3D environment learned from a single-camera video.

title: D^2NeRF: Self-Supervised Decoupling of Dynamic and Static Objects from a Monocular Video

abstract: Text-to-image generation and image captioning are recently emerged as a new experimental paradigm to assess machine intelligence. They predict continuous quantity accompanied by their sampling techniques in the generation, making evaluation complicated and intractable to get marginal distributions. Based on a recent trend that multimodal generative evaluations exploit a vison-and-language pre-trained model, we propose the negative Gaussian cross-mutual information using the CLIP features as a unified metric, coined by Mutual Information Divergence (MID). To validate, we extensively compare it with competing metrics using carefully-generated or human-annotated judgments in text-to-image generation and image captioning tasks. The proposed MID significantly outperforms the competitive methods by having consistency across benchmarks, sample parsimony, and robustness toward the exploited CLIP model. We look forward to seeing the underrepresented implications of the Gaussian cross-mutual information in multimodal representation learning and future works based on this novel proposition.

paragraphs: Evaluating text-to-image generation and image captioning is difficult because the systems generate outputs through sampling, and the relevant marginal distributions are intractable to obtain. This paper proposes one metric for both tasks, using representations from a pretrained vision-language model to assess the relationship between visual and textual information.

The metric is called Mutual Information Divergence, or MID. It uses negative Gaussian cross-mutual information computed from CLIP features. This gives evaluation a shared representation space across the two generation directions: producing an image from text and producing text from an image. The authors compare MID with competing metrics using carefully generated judgments or human annotations.

The reported comparisons favor MID in consistency across benchmarks, economy in the number of samples needed, and robustness to the CLIP model used for feature extraction. These findings support its usefulness as a common multimodal evaluation measure in the studied tasks. The authors also propose Gaussian cross-mutual information as a promising subject for further work on multimodal representation learning, extending the research direction beyond this metric.
summary.tldr: MID uses Gaussian cross-mutual information in CLIP feature space to evaluate image-text generation, with reported advantages in consistency, sample efficiency, and robustness.

title: Mutual Information Divergence: A Unified Metric for Multimodal Generative Models

abstract: The implicit bias of neural networks has been extensively studied in recent years. Lyu and Li (2019) showed that in homogeneous networks trained with the exponential or the logistic loss, gradient flow converges to a KKT point of the max margin problem in parameter space. However, that leaves open the question of whether this point will generally be an actual optimum of the max margin problem. In this paper, we study this question in detail, for several neural network architectures involving linear and ReLU activations. Perhaps surprisingly, we show that in many cases, the KKT point is not even a local optimum of the max margin problem. On the flip side, we identify multiple settings where a local or global optimum can be guaranteed.

paragraphs: This paper examines what gradient-based training implicitly favors in neural networks. Prior theory for homogeneous networks trained with exponential or logistic loss connects gradient flow to a Karush–Kuhn–Tucker point of a parameter-space maximum-margin problem. The unresolved issue is whether reaching such a point also means reaching an actual optimum.

The authors investigate this distinction across several architectures using linear and ReLU activations. They show that, in many cases, the point reached is not even a local optimum of the margin objective. Thus, the previously established optimization conditions alone do not justify concluding that training maximizes the margin.

The paper also identifies multiple settings in which local or global optimality can be guaranteed. Its contribution is therefore a more precise account of when margin-maximization interpretations are valid. The negative results separate convergence to a qualifying stationary point from true optimization, while the positive results establish circumstances where the stronger conclusion is supported.
summary.tldr: Gradient-flow convergence to a maximum-margin KKT point need not yield even a local optimum, though some settings admit stronger guarantees.

title: On Margin Maximization in Linear and ReLU Networks

abstract: Analyzing the spatiotemporal behavior of multiple agents is of great interest to many communities. Existing probabilistic models in this realm are formalized either in an unsupervised framework, where the latent space is described by discrete or continuous variables, or in a supervised framework, where weakly preserved labels add explicit information to continuous latent representations. To overcome inherent limitations, we propose a novel objective function for processing multi-agent trajectories based on semi-supervised variational autoencoders, where equivariance and interaction of agents are captured via customized graph networks. The resulting architecture disentangles discrete and continuous latent effects and provides a natural solution for injecting expensive domain knowledge into interactive sequential systems. Empirically, our model not only outperforms various state-of-the-art baselines in trajectory forecasting, but also learns to effectively leverage unsupervised multi-agent sequences for classification tasks on interactive real-world sports datasets.

paragraphs: Understanding multiple agents moving together requires representing both individual trajectories and interactions between agents. This paper develops a semi-supervised generative approach for that setting. It aims to combine unlabeled sequences with valuable domain knowledge, rather than placing the entire learning problem in either a supervised or an unsupervised framework.

The method introduces an objective based on semi-supervised variational autoencoders. Customized graph networks capture interactions and equivariance, while the architecture separates discrete and continuous effects in its latent representation. This separation gives different forms of variation distinct roles within the model and provides a way to incorporate expensive domain knowledge into interactive sequence modeling.

Experiments show that the model outperforms several state-of-the-art comparison methods in trajectory forecasting. On real-world sports datasets involving interacting agents, it also uses unlabeled multiagent sequences effectively for classification. The findings demonstrate benefits for both predicting movement and learning classifications from sequences. The contribution joins relational modeling with semi-supervision, allowing available labels and unlabeled interaction data to contribute within the same generative framework.
summary.tldr: A semi-supervised generative model combines graph-based interaction modeling with discrete and continuous latent effects to improve multiagent trajectory learning.

title: Semi-Supervised Generative Models for Multiagent Trajectories

abstract: Weight decay is a simple yet powerful regularization technique that has been very widely used in training of deep neural networks (DNNs). While weight decay has attracted much attention, previous studies fail to discover some overlooked pitfalls on large gradient norms resulted by weight decay. In this paper, we discover that, weight decay can unfortunately lead to large gradient norms at the final phase (or the terminated solution) of training, which often indicates bad convergence and poor generalization. To mitigate the gradient-norm-centered pitfalls, we present the first practical scheduler for weight decay, called the Scheduled Weight Decay (SWD) method that can dynamically adjust the weight decay strength according to the gradient norm and significantly penalize large gradient norms during training. Our experiments also support that SWD indeed mitigates large gradient norms and often significantly outperforms the conventional constant weight decay strategy for Adaptive Moment Estimation (Adam).

paragraphs: Weight decay is widely used to regularize neural-network training, but this paper identifies a potential problem with its effect on gradients. The authors find that it can produce large gradient norms late in training or at the final solution. They describe those large norms as often indicating poor convergence and generalization, so a useful regularizer can also introduce an undesirable training behavior.

To address this issue, the paper proposes Scheduled Weight Decay, or SWD. It dynamically changes the strength of weight decay according to the gradient norm and strongly penalizes large gradient norms during training. This makes the regularization schedule responsive to a measured feature of the optimization process, rather than holding its strength constant throughout training.

The experiments support SWD's ability to mitigate large gradient norms. They also show that it often significantly outperforms conventional constant weight decay when used with Adam. The finding is therefore an empirical case for gradient-aware scheduling in that setting, with improvements described as frequent rather than universal across every training problem.
summary.tldr: Scheduled Weight Decay adjusts regularization using gradient norms to mitigate a potential convergence problem and often improves on constant weight decay with Adam.

title: On the Overlooked Pitfalls of Weight Decay and How to Mitigate Them: A Gradient-Norm Perspective

abstract: The early theory of actor-critic methods considered convergence using linear function approximators for the policy and value functions. Recent work has established convergence using neural network approximators with a single hidden layer. In this work we are taking the natural next step and establish convergence using deep neural networks with an arbitrary number of hidden layers, thus closing a gap between theory and practice. We show that actor-critic updates projected on a ball around the initial condition will converge to a neighborhood where the average of the squared gradients is $\tilde{O} \left( 1/\sqrt{m} \right) + O \left( \epsilon \right)$, with $m$ being the width of the neural network and $\epsilon$ the approximation quality of the best critic neural network over the projected set.
originalAbstract: The early theory of actor-critic methods considered convergence using linear function approximators for the policy and value functions. Recent work has established convergence using neural network approximators with a single hidden layer. In this work we are taking the natural next step and establish convergence using deep neural networks with an arbitrary number of hidden layers, thus closing a gap between theory and practice. We show that actor-critic updates projected on a ball around the initial condition will converge to a neighborhood where the average of the squared gradients is $\tilde{O} \left( 1/\sqrt{m} \right) + O \left( \epsilon \right)$, with $m$ being the width of the neural network and $\epsilon$ the approximation quality of the best critic neural network over the projected set.

paragraphs: Actor-critic methods learn a policy together with a value estimator, called the critic. Earlier convergence theory covered linear approximators and, more recently, neural networks with one hidden layer. This paper extends the analysis to deep networks with an arbitrary number of hidden layers, bringing the theoretical setting closer to the architectures used in practice.

The guarantee applies to updates that are projected onto a ball around the initial parameters. This keeps the optimization within a specified region. Under this restriction, the authors establish convergence to a neighborhood measured through the average squared gradients. The bound contains a term of order one over the square root of network width, up to logarithmic factors, and a term proportional to critic approximation error.

The result therefore connects the remaining gradient size to both network width and the best critic available within the permitted region. Greater width reduces one contribution, while critic approximation quality controls another. The stated guarantee concerns approximate stationarity under projected updates; it does not establish convergence to a globally optimal policy.
summary.tldr: The paper proves approximate convergence for projected actor-critic updates with arbitrarily deep networks, with error depending on network width and critic approximation quality.

title: Convergence of Actor-Critic with Multi-Layer Neural Networks

abstract: The computation necessary for training Transformer-based language models has skyrocketed in recent years.This trend has motivated research on efficient training algorithms designed to improve training, validation, and downstream performance faster than standard training. In this work, we revisit three categories of such algorithms: dynamic architectures (layer stacking, layer dropping), batch selection (selective backprop., RHO-loss), and efficient optimizers (Lion, Sophia). When pre-training BERT and T5 with a fixed computation budget using such methods, we find that their training, validation, and downstream gains vanish compared to a baseline with a fully-decayed learning rate. We define an evaluation protocol that enables computation to be done on arbitrary machines by mapping all computation time to a reference machine which we call reference system time. We discuss the limitations of our proposed protocol and release our code to encourage rigorous research in efficient training procedures: https://github.com/JeanKaddour/NoTrainNoGain.

paragraphs: Algorithms for efficient language-model training promise better results within a given amount of computation. This paper reexamines three families of such methods: changing the architecture during training, selecting which batches receive computation, and using alternative optimizers. The investigation asks whether their reported advantages remain when the comparison uses a fixed computational budget and a baseline whose learning rate has fully decayed.

The authors study BERT and T5 pretraining, including layer stacking and dropping, selective backpropagation and RHO-loss, and the Lion and Sophia optimizers. In these evaluations, the methods’ advantages in training, validation, and downstream performance disappear relative to that baseline. The finding emphasizes that the baseline’s learning-rate schedule is consequential when judging training efficiency.

The paper also proposes reference system time, an evaluation protocol that maps computation performed on different machines to a common reference machine. This is intended to enable comparisons across hardware, and the authors discuss the protocol’s limitations. The results challenge the tested efficiency gains under the stated setup, without establishing that these methods cannot help in other training settings.
summary.tldr: In fixed-budget BERT and T5 experiments, several efficient-training methods lose their advantage against a baseline with a fully decayed learning rate.

title: No Train No Gain: Revisiting Efficient Training Algorithms For Transformer-based Language Models

abstract: To the best of our knowledge, there are no methods today for training differentially private regression models on sparse input data. To remedy this, we adapt the Frank-Wolfe algorithm for $L_1$ penalized linear regression to be aware of sparse inputs and to use them effectively. In doing so, we reduce the training time of the algorithm from $\mathcal{O}( T D S + T N S)$ to $\mathcal{O}(N S + T \sqrt{D} \log{D} + T S^2)$, where $T$ is the number of iterations and a sparsity rate $S$ of a dataset with $N$ rows and $D$ features. Our results demonstrate that this procedure can reduce runtime by a factor of up to $2,200\times$, depending on the value of the privacy parameter $\epsilon$ and the sparsity of the dataset.

In doing so, we reduce the training time of the algorithm from $\mathcal{O}( T D S + T N S)$ to $\mathcal{O}(N S + T \sqrt{D} \log{D} + T S^2)$, where $T$ is the number of iterations and a sparsity rate $S$ of a dataset with $N$ rows and $D$ features. paragraphs: The paper addresses the computational cost of training differentially private regression models on sparse inputs. Its starting point is that sparsity should help reduce training work, yet the authors identify a lack of methods designed to exploit it in this setting. Their contribution adapts Frank-Wolfe optimization to make effective use of sparse data.

Specifically, the abstract describes a sparse-aware adaptation of Frank-Wolfe for ℓ1-penalized linear regression. The stated training cost changes from O(TDS + TNS) to O(NS + T√D log D + TS²), where T is the iteration count, N is the number of rows, D is the feature count, and S describes sparsity. The new expression separates an NS term from the terms repeated over iterations.

This matters because the former bound repeatedly includes work proportional to both feature count and dataset size. The reported runtime reduction reaches up to 2,200 times, depending on sparsity and the privacy parameter ε. That figure is a best reported speedup under particular conditions, while the complexity expressions explain how the benefit depends on the problem’s dimensions.
summary.tldr: Sparse-aware Frank-Wolfe iterations reduce the training cost of differentially private regression, with reported speedups reaching 2,200 times.

title: Scaling Up Differentially Private LASSO Regularized Logistic Regression via Faster Frank-Wolfe Iterations

abstract: We propose Pgx, a suite of board game reinforcement learning (RL) environments written in JAX and optimized for GPU/TPU accelerators. By leveraging JAX's auto-vectorization and parallelization over accelerators, Pgx can efficiently scale to thousands of simultaneous simulations over accelerators. In our experiments on a DGX-A100 workstation, we discovered that Pgx can simulate RL environments 10-100x faster than existing implementations available in Python. Pgx includes RL environments commonly used as benchmarks in RL research, such as backgammon, chess, shogi, and Go. Additionally, Pgx offers miniature game sets and baseline models to facilitate rapid research cycles. We demonstrate the efficient training of the Gumbel AlphaZero algorithm with Pgx environments. Overall, Pgx provides high-performance environment simulators for researchers to accelerate their RL experiments. Pgx is available at https://github.com/sotetsuk/pgx.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning experiments need environments that repeatedly simulate the consequences of an agent’s actions. Pgx provides board-game environments designed to run efficiently on GPUs and TPUs. The suite includes established research games such as backgammon, chess, shogi, and Go. It also provides smaller games and baseline models to support rapid experimentation. These components give researchers both substantial benchmark environments and more compact settings for shorter development cycles within the same suite.

On a DGX-A100 workstation, the authors report simulation speeds ten to one hundred times faster than existing Python implementations. They also demonstrate efficient training of Gumbel AlphaZero using Pgx environments. The speed comparison concerns environment simulation on the reported hardware; the training demonstration shows how those accelerated environments can contribute to a complete reinforcement learning experiment.
summary.tldr: Pgx runs thousands of board-game simulations on accelerators, with reported simulation speedups of 10–100× on a DGX-A100.

title: Pgx: Hardware-Accelerated Parallel Game Simulators for Reinforcement Learning

abstract: In deep learning theory, the covariance matrix of the representations serves as aproxy to examine the network’s trainability. Motivated by the success of Transform-ers, we study the covariance matrix of a modified Softmax-based attention modelwith skip connections in the proportional limit of infinite-depth-and-width. Weshow that at initialization the limiting distribution can be described by a stochasticdifferential equation (SDE) indexed by the depth-to-width ratio. To achieve awell-defined stochastic limit, the Transformer’s attention mechanism is modifiedby centering the Softmax output at identity, and scaling the Softmax logits by awidth-dependent temperature parameter. We examine the stability of the networkthrough the corresponding SDE, showing how the scale of both the drift and diffu-sion can be elegantly controlled with the aid of residual connections. The existenceof a stable SDE implies that the covariance structure is well-behaved, even for verylarge depth and width, thus preventing the notorious issues of rank degeneracyin deep attention models. Finally, we show, through simulations, that the SDEprovides a surprisingly good description of the corresponding finite-size model.We coin the name shaped Transformer for these architectural modifications.

paragraphs: This paper uses the covariance of internal representations to study the behavior of very deep and wide attention networks. Covariance acts as a proxy for trainability, describing how representations relate to one another. The analysis considers initialization as depth and width grow together proportionally, rather than increasing one while keeping the other fixed.

To obtain a well-defined limit, the authors modify attention by centering the Softmax output at the identity and introducing a width-dependent temperature for its logits. The limiting covariance distribution follows a stochastic differential equation indexed by the depth-to-width ratio. Residual connections provide control over both its drift and diffusion, the components governing systematic change and random fluctuation.

A stable limiting equation implies well-behaved covariance even at very large scale, preventing the rank degeneracy addressed by the analysis. Simulations also show that the equation describes corresponding finite models surprisingly well. These architectural changes define the shaped Transformer, connecting attention design to a tractable account of representation stability at initialization.
summary.tldr: Modified attention and residual connections yield a tractable, stable covariance limit as Transformer depth and width grow together.

title: The Shaped Transformer: Attention Models in the Infinite Depth-and-Width Limit

abstract: In practice, encoding invariances into models improves sample complexity. In this work, we study this phenomenon from a theoretical perspective. In particular, we provide minimax optimal rates for kernel ridge regression on compact manifolds, with a target function that is invariant to a group action on the manifold. Our results hold for any smooth compact Lie group action, even groups of positive dimension. For a finite group, the gain effectively multiplies the number of samples by the group size. For groups of positive dimension, the gain is observed by a reduction in the manifold's dimension, in addition to a factor proportional to the volume of the quotient space. Our proof takes the viewpoint of differential geometry, in contrast to the more common strategy of using invariant polynomials. This new geometric viewpoint on learning with invariances may be of independent interest.

Our results hold for any smooth compact Lie group action, even groups of positive dimension. For a finite group, the gain effectively multiplies the number of samples by the group size. paragraphs: Encoding invariance means building in transformations under which the target function stays unchanged. Such structure can reduce how much training data a model needs. This paper quantifies that benefit for kernel ridge regression on compact manifolds, assuming the target function is invariant under a smooth action of a compact Lie group.

The authors establish minimax-optimal rates and distinguish two forms of improvement. For finite groups, using invariance has an effect equivalent to multiplying the sample count by the group's size. For groups with positive dimension, the benefit includes reducing the manifold's effective dimension, together with a factor proportional to the volume of the quotient space.

These results make the role of symmetry precise within the stated regression setting: different kinds of transformation groups change sample requirements in different ways. The proof uses differential geometry rather than the more common approach based on invariant polynomials. Besides establishing the rates, the paper presents this geometric viewpoint as a potentially useful foundation for further analysis of learning with invariances.
summary.tldr: The paper derives minimax-optimal gains from group invariance in kernel ridge regression, separating finite-group sample gains from continuous-symmetry dimension reductions.

title: The Exact Sample Complexity Gain from Invariances for Kernel Regression

abstract: This paper explores the impact of occlusions in video action detection. We facilitatethis study by introducing five new benchmark datasets namely O-UCF and O-JHMDB consisting of synthetically controlled static/dynamic occlusions, OVIS-UCF and OVIS-JHMDB consisting of occlusions with realistic motions and Real-OUCF for occlusions in realistic-world scenarios. We formally confirm an intuitiveexpectation: existing models suffer a lot as occlusion severity is increased andexhibit different behaviours when occluders are static vs when they are moving.We discover several intriguing phenomenon emerging in neural nets: 1) transformerscan naturally outperform CNN models which might have even used occlusion as aform of data augmentation during training 2) incorporating symbolic-componentslike capsules to such backbones allows them to bind to occluders never even seenduring training and 3) Islands of agreement (similar to the ones hypothesized inHinton et Al’s GLOM) can emerge in realistic images/videos without instance-levelsupervision, distillation or contrastive-based objectives(eg. video-textual training).Such emergent properties allow us to derive simple yet effective training recipeswhich lead to robust occlusion models inductively satisfying the first two stages ofthe binding mechanism (grouping/segregation). Models leveraging these recipesoutperform existing video action-detectors under occlusion by 32.3% on O-UCF,32.7% on O-JHMDB & 2.6% on Real-OUCF in terms of the vMAP metric. The code for this work has been released at https: //github.com/rajatmodi62/OccludedActionBenchmark.

paragraphs: Recognizing actions becomes harder when objects obscure the action in a video. This paper introduces five benchmarks covering controlled static and moving occlusions, occluders with realistic motion, and real-world occlusion scenarios. The evaluations confirm that increasing obstruction hurts existing models and that static and moving occluders produce different behaviors.

The authors observe that transformers can outperform convolutional models even when those models received occlusion augmentation during training. Adding capsule-like symbolic components enables binding to previously unseen occluders. They also observe groups of agreeing representations, described as islands of agreement, without instance-level supervision, distillation, or contrastive objectives. These observations motivate training recipes for grouping and separating visual information.

Models using those recipes outperform existing action detectors under occlusion, with reported vMAP improvements of 32.3% on O-UCF, 32.7% on O-JHMDB, and 2.6% on Real-OUCF. The work contributes both evaluation resources and training methods. Its findings connect observed representation behavior to improved detection when relevant action content is partially hidden.
summary.tldr: Five occlusion benchmarks reveal model behaviors that motivate training recipes improving video action detection under partial obstruction.

title: On Occlusions in Video Action Detection: Benchmark Datasets And Training Recipes

abstract: Pre-training datasets are critical for building state-of-the-art machine learning models, motivating rigorous study on their impact on downstream tasks. In this work, we study the impact of the trade-off between the intra-class diversity (the number of samples per class) and the inter-class diversity (the number of classes) of a supervised pre-training dataset. Empirically, we found that with the size of the pre-training dataset fixed, the best downstream performance comes with a balance on the intra-/inter-class diversity. To understand the underlying mechanism, we show theoretically that the downstream performance depends monotonically on both types of diversity. Notably, our theory reveals that the optimal class-to-sample ratio (#classes / #samples per class) is invariant to the size of the pre-training dataset, which motivates an application of predicting the optimal number of pre-training classes. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this application by an improvement of around 2 points on the downstream tasks when using ImageNet as the pre-training dataset.
originalAbstract: Pre-training datasets are critical for building state-of-the-art machine learning models, motivating rigorous study on their impact on downstream tasks. In this work, we study the impact of the trade-off between the intra-class diversity (the number of samples per class) and the inter-class diversity (the number of classes) of a supervised pre-training dataset. Empirically, we found that with the size of the pre-training dataset fixed, the best downstream performance comes with a balance on the intra-/inter-class diversity. To understand the underlying mechanism, we show theoretically that the downstream performance depends monotonically on both types of diversity. Notably, our theory reveals that the optimal class-to-sample ratio (#classes / #samples per class) is invariant to the size of the pre-training dataset, which motivates an application of predicting the optimal number of pre-training classes. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this application by an improvement of around 2 points on the downstream tasks when using ImageNet as the pre-training dataset.

paragraphs: A supervised pre-training dataset can contain many classes, many examples within each class, or some balance between the two. With a fixed total number of examples, increasing one kind of diversity reduces room for the other. This paper studies how that allocation affects performance on tasks learned after pre-training.

The experiments find that downstream performance is best when the two forms of diversity are balanced. The theory shows that performance depends monotonically on both forms, explaining why the fixed-size constraint creates a meaningful trade-off. It also reveals that the optimal ratio of class count to examples per class is invariant to total dataset size within the theoretical analysis.

That result motivates a method for predicting how many pre-training classes to use. Applied with ImageNet as the pre-training dataset, the method improves downstream performance by around two points. The paper therefore connects dataset composition to transfer quality and uses its theoretical account to guide a concrete choice about how a pre-training dataset should be organized.
summary.tldr: Balancing class count and examples per class improves supervised pre-training, and a theoretical ratio helps predict a useful class count.

title: On the Trade-off of Intra-/Inter-class Diversity for Supervised Pre-training

abstract: We introduce general tools for designing efficient private estimation algorithms, in the high-dimensional settings, whose statistical guarantees almost match those of the best known non-private algorithms.To illustrate our techniques, we consider two problems: recovery of stochastic block models and learning mixtures of spherical Gaussians.For the former, we present the first efficient $(\epsilon, \delta)$-differentially private algorithm for both weak recovery and exact recovery. Previously known algorithms achieving comparable guarantees required quasi-polynomial time. For the latter, we design an $(\epsilon, \delta)$-differentially private algorithm that recovers the centers of the $k$-mixture when the minimum separation is at least $O(k^{1/t}\sqrt{t})$. For all choices of $t$, this algorithm requires sample complexity $n\geq k^{O(1)}d^{O(t)}$ and time complexity $(nd)^{O(t)}$. Prior work required either an additional additive $\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})$ term in the minimum separation or an explicit upper bound on the Euclidean norm of the centers.

The contribution combines stronger computational guarantees with fewer restrictions of those particular kinds.
summary.tldr: New private estimation tools improve recovery algorithms for stochastic block models and separated spherical Gaussian mixtures.

title: Private estimation algorithms for stochastic block models and mixture models

abstract: Recent works have shown the promise of learning pre-trained models for 3D molecular representation.However, existing pre-training models focus predominantly on equilibrium data and largely overlook off-equilibrium conformations.It is challenging to extend these methods to off-equilibrium data because their training objective relies on assumptions ofconformations being the local energy minima. We address this gap by proposing a force-centric pretraining model for 3D molecular conformations covering both equilibrium and off-equilibrium data.For off-equilibrium data, our model learns directly from their atomic forces. For equilibrium data, we introduce zero-force regularization and forced-based denoising techniques to approximate near-equilibrium forces.We obtain a unified pre-trained model for 3D molecular representation with over 15 million diverse conformations. Experiments show that, with our pre-training objective, we increase forces accuracy by around 3 times compared to the un-pre-trained Equivariant Transformer model. By incorporating regularizations on equilibrium data, we solved the problem of unstable MD simulations in vanilla Equivariant Transformers, achieving state-of-the-art simulation performance with 2.45 times faster inference time than NequIP. As a powerful molecular encoder, our pre-trained model achieves on-par performance with state-of-the-art property prediction tasks.

For off-equilibrium structures, the model learns directly from atomic forces. For equilibrium data, zero-force regularization and force-based denoising approximate nearby forces. The unified model is pretrained on more than 15 million diverse conformations.

Property prediction is comparable to state-of-the-art methods. These comparisons concern the evaluated configurations; the abstract does not specify the underlying force-error metric or guarantee stable simulation for every molecular system.
summary.tldr: Force-centered pretraining unifies equilibrium and off-equilibrium molecular conformations.

title: May the Force be with You: Unified Force-Centric Pre-Training for 3D Molecular Conformations

abstract: State-space models have gained popularity in sequence modelling due to their simple and efficient network structures. However, the absence of nonlinear activation along the temporal direction limits the model's capacity. In this paper, we prove that stacking state-space models with layer-wise nonlinear activation is sufficient to approximate any continuous sequence-to-sequence relationship. Our findings demonstrate that the addition of layer-wise nonlinear activation enhances the model's capacity to learn complex sequence patterns. Meanwhile, it can be seen both theoretically and empirically that the state-space models do not fundamentally resolve the issue of exponential decaying memory. Theoretical results are justified by numerical verifications.

Our findings demonstrate that the addition of layer-wise nonlinear activation enhances the model's capacity to learn complex sequence patterns. Meanwhile, it can be seen both theoretically and empirically that the state-space models do not fundamentally resolve the issue of exponential decaying memory. Theoretical results are justified by numerical verifications.

paragraphs: State-space models offer simple and efficient structures for processing sequences. However, a lack of nonlinear activation along the time direction restricts their capacity. This paper investigates whether introducing nonlinearities between stacked layers can supply the expressive power needed to model complicated relationships between input and output sequences.

The authors prove that stacking state-space models with layer-wise nonlinear activation is sufficient to approximate any continuous sequence-to-sequence relationship. The result identifies an architectural route to universal approximation: complex sequence mappings can be represented through the combination of stacked state-space layers and nonlinear transformations between them. It is a statement about representational capacity.

The paper also finds, both theoretically and empirically, that these models do not fundamentally eliminate exponentially decaying memory. Thus, stronger approximation capacity coexists with a continuing tendency for information from the past to fade exponentially. Numerical verifications support the theoretical findings. Taken together, the results distinguish two properties that can otherwise be conflated: the ability to express complex sequence relationships and the behavior of memory over time.
summary.tldr: Layer-wise nonlinearities make stacked state-space models universal approximators, while exponentially decaying memory remains.

title: State-space models with layer-wise nonlinearity are universal approximators with exponential decaying memory

abstract: While large language models (LMs) have shown remarkable capabilities across numerous tasks, they often struggle with simple reasoning and planning in physical environments, such as understanding object permanence or planning household activities. The limitation arises from the fact that LMs are trained only on written text and miss essential embodied knowledge and skills. In this paper, we propose a new paradigm of enhancing LMs by finetuning them with world models, to gain diverse embodied knowledge while retaining their general language capabilities. Our approach deploys an embodied agent in a world model, particularly a simulator of the physical world (VirtualHome), and acquires a diverse set of embodied experiences through both goal-oriented planning and random exploration. These experiences are then used to finetune LMs to teach diverse abilities of reasoning and acting in the physical world, e.g., planning and completing goals, object permanence and tracking, etc. Moreover, it is desirable to preserve the generality of LMs during finetuning, which facilitates generalizing the embodied knowledge across tasks rather than being tied to specific simulations. We thus further introduce the classical elastic weight consolidation (EWC) for selective weight updates, combined with low-rank adapters (LoRA) for training efficiency. Extensive experiments show our approach substantially improves base LMs on 18 downstream tasks by 64.28% on average. In particular, the small LMs (1.3B, 6B, and 13B) enhanced by our approach match or even outperform much larger LMs (e.g., ChatGPT).

Experiments report an average improvement of 64.28% over base models across 18 downstream tasks. Enhanced models with 1.3 billion, 6 billion, and 13 billion parameters match or outperform much larger models, including ChatGPT, in the reported comparisons. These results support the value of simulator-generated experience for the evaluated tasks, rather than establishing that model size ceases to matter across language modeling generally.
summary.tldr: Fine-tuning on simulated embodied experiences improves language models' tested physical reasoning and planning abilities.

title: Language Models Meet World Models: Embodied Experiences Enhance Language Models

abstract: In many scientific applications, we observe a system in different conditions in which its components may change, rather than in isolation. In our work, we are interested in explaining the generating process of such a multi-context system using a finite mixture of causal mechanisms. Recent work shows that this causal model is identifiable from data, but is limited to settings where the sparse mechanism shift hypothesis holds and only a subset of the causal conditionals change. As this assumption is not easily verifiable in practice, we study the more general principle that mechanism shifts are independent, which we formalize using the algorithmic notion of independence. We introduce an approach for causal discovery beyond partially directed graphs using Gaussian Process models, and give conditions under which we provably identify the correct causal model. In our experiments, we show that our method performs well in a range of synthetic settings, on realistic gene expression simulations, as well as on real-world cell signaling data.

paragraphs: Scientific systems are often observed under several conditions, with their components changing between contexts. This paper seeks to explain such observations using a finite mixture of causal mechanisms. Previous identifiability results relied on sparse mechanism shifts, meaning that only a subset of the causal conditionals changed, an assumption that can be difficult to verify.

The authors instead study the more general principle that mechanism changes are independent, formalized through algorithmic independence. This changes the organizing assumption from how many mechanisms shift to the independence of those shifts. They develop a Gaussian Process approach to causal discovery that goes beyond partially directed graphs and state conditions under which it provably identifies the correct causal model.

Experiments examine synthetic settings, realistic gene expression simulations, and real cell signaling data, with good performance reported across these settings. The work connects changes across contexts to causal identification under a different set of assumptions. Its identification claim remains conditional: the theorem provides conditions for recovering the model rather than promising recovery from every collection of changing observations.
summary.tldr: A Gaussian Process method learns causal models from multiple contexts by exploiting independent mechanism changes under stated identification conditions.

title: Learning Causal Models under Independent Changes

abstract: Learning complex physical dynamics purely from data is challenging due to the intrinsic properties of systems to be satisfied. Incorporating physics-informed priors, such as in Hamiltonian Neural Networks (HNNs), achieves high-precision modeling for energy-conservative systems. However, real-world systems often deviate from strict energy conservation and follow different physical priors. To address this, we present a framework that achieves high-precision modeling for a wide range of dynamical systems from the numerical aspect, by enforcing Time-Reversal Symmetry (TRS) via a novel regularization term. It helps preserve energies for conservative systems while serving as a strong inductive bias for non-conservative, reversible systems. While TRS is a domain-specific physical prior, we present the first theoretical proof that TRS loss can universally improve modeling accuracy by minimizing higher-order Taylor terms in ODE integration, which is numerically beneficial to various systems regardless of their properties, even for irreversible systems. By integrating the TRS loss within neural ordinary differential equation models, the proposed model TREAT demonstrates superior performance on diverse physical systems. It achieves a significant 11.5% MSE improvement in a challenging chaotic triple-pendulum scenario, underscoring TREAT’s broad applicability and effectiveness.

paragraphs: Learning physical motion from data is difficult because predictions must reflect the structure of the underlying system. Energy-conservation priors can help, but many real systems do not conserve energy. This paper proposes a regularization term based on time-reversal symmetry and investigates why it can help beyond systems that physically possess that symmetry.

The term supports energy preservation in conservative systems and provides an inductive bias for reversible, non-conservative systems. The authors also give a numerical argument for broader usefulness: they prove that the time-reversal loss can improve modeling accuracy by minimizing higher-order Taylor terms in ordinary differential equation integration. This connects the loss to numerical accuracy even for irreversible systems.

The proposed model, TREAT, incorporates the loss into neural ordinary differential equations. Experiments across diverse physical systems report superior performance, including an 11.5% mean-squared-error improvement for a chaotic triple pendulum. The contribution is both a practical regularizer and an explanation of how a physically motivated constraint can provide numerical benefits outside its original physical setting.
summary.tldr: TREAT uses time-reversal regularization to improve neural dynamical models, supported by a numerical analysis and experiments across varied physical systems.

title: Physics-Informed Regularization for Domain-Agnostic Dynamical System Modeling

abstract: While in-context learning is commonly associated with causal language models, such as GPT, we demonstrate that this capability also 'emerges' in masked language models. Through an embarrassingly simple inference technique, we enable an existing masked model, DeBERTa, to perform generative tasks without additional training or architectural changes. Our evaluation reveals that the masked and causal language models behave very differently, as they clearly outperform each other on different categories of tasks. These complementary strengths suggest that the field's focus on causal models for in-context learning may be limiting – both architectures can develop these capabilities, but with distinct advantages; pointing toward promising hybrid approaches that combine the strengths of both objectives.

paragraphs: In-context learning is usually associated with causal language models, which generate text by predicting what comes next. This paper asks whether masked language models can also exhibit that ability. The distinction matters because an architecture's usual training objective may obscure capabilities that become accessible through a different way of using it at inference time.

The authors demonstrate generative in-context learning with an existing DeBERTa model using a simple inference technique. The approach requires neither additional training nor architectural changes. The contribution therefore concerns how an already trained masked model is used: it shows that generative task performance can be elicited without first rebuilding the model as a causal language model.

The evaluation finds different strengths across task categories, with masked and causal models each clearly outperforming the other in different areas. This supports a broader view of in-context learning across architectures, rather than establishing one architecture as uniformly superior. The authors suggest that hybrid approaches could combine these complementary strengths; the abstract presents that as a promising direction, rather than an evaluated hybrid system.
summary.tldr: A simple inference technique enables DeBERTa to perform generative in-context learning without retraining, revealing strengths complementary to causal models.

title: BERTs are Generative In-Context Learners

abstract: Advances in latent diffusion models (LDMs) have revolutionized high-resolution image generation, but the design space of the autoencoder that is central to these systems remains underexplored. In this paper, we introduce LiteVAE, a new autoencoder design for LDMs, which leverages the 2D discrete wavelet transform to enhance scalability and computational efficiency over standard variational autoencoders (VAEs) with no sacrifice in output quality. We investigate the training methodologies and the decoder architecture of LiteVAE and propose several enhancements that improve the training dynamics and reconstruction quality. Our base LiteVAE model matches the quality of the established VAEs in current LDMs with a six-fold reduction in encoder parameters, leading to faster training and lower GPU memory requirements, while our larger model outperforms VAEs of comparable complexity across all evaluated metrics (rFID, LPIPS, PSNR, and SSIM).

paragraphs: Latent diffusion systems depend on an autoencoder that maps images into a compressed representation and reconstructs them. Although image generation has advanced rapidly, this component’s design remains comparatively underexplored. LiteVAE investigates how to make the autoencoder more efficient while preserving the quality needed by latent diffusion models.

Its design incorporates the two-dimensional discrete wavelet transform to improve scalability and computational efficiency. The authors also study training methods and the decoder architecture, introducing changes that improve training dynamics and reconstruction quality. This treats both the representation design and the way it is trained as opportunities to reduce the cost of the autoencoder.

The base LiteVAE matches the quality of established autoencoders used in current latent diffusion systems while using one-sixth as many encoder parameters. The authors connect this reduction to faster training and lower GPU memory requirements. Their larger model also exceeds similarly complex VAEs on every evaluated metric: rFID, LPIPS, PSNR, and SSIM. The results support efficiency gains at the base size and quality gains at comparable larger complexity.
summary.tldr: LiteVAE uses wavelet-based autoencoder design to match established reconstruction quality with six times fewer encoder parameters.

title: LiteVAE: Lightweight and Efficient Variational Autoencoders for Latent Diffusion Models

abstract: Existing super-resolution (SR) methods optimize all model weights equally using $\mathcal{L}_1$ or $\mathcal{L}_2$ losses by uniformly sampling image patches without considering dataset imbalances or parameter redundancy, which limits their performance. To address this, we formulate the image SR task as an imbalanced distribution transfer learning problem from a statistical probability perspective, proposing a plug-and-play Weight-Balancing framework (WBSR) to achieve balanced model learning without changing the original model structure and training data. Specifically, we develop a Hierarchical Equalization Sampling (HES) strategy to address data distribution imbalances, enabling better feature representation from texture-rich samples. To tackle model optimization imbalances, we propose a Balanced Diversity Loss (BDLoss) function, focusing on learning texture regions while disregarding redundant computations in smooth regions. After joint training of HES and BDLoss to rectify these imbalances, we present a gradient projection dynamic inference strategy to facilitate accurate and efficient inference. Extensive experiments across various models, datasets, and scale factors demonstrate that our method achieves comparable or superior performance to existing approaches with about 34\% reduction in computational cost.

After joint training of HES and BDLoss to rectify these imbalances, we present a gradient projection dynamic inference strategy to facilitate accurate and efficient inference. paragraphs: Image super-resolution models commonly train on uniformly sampled patches and optimize weights using standard reconstruction losses. This paper argues that such training overlooks imbalances in image content and redundancy in model computation. WBSR reframes super-resolution as an imbalanced distribution transfer problem and provides a framework that can be added without changing the original model structure or training data.

Hierarchical Equalization Sampling addresses the distribution of training examples, helping the model learn from texture-rich content. Balanced Diversity Loss addresses optimization, concentrating learning on textured regions while reducing attention to redundant computation in smooth regions. These components are trained jointly to balance how different image content influences the model.

The framework then uses a gradient projection strategy for dynamic inference. Experiments across different models, datasets, and enlargement factors report comparable or better performance with approximately 34% lower computational cost. The findings support treating training imbalance and inference efficiency together, using the differing demands of textured and smooth image regions to improve the allocation of model effort.
summary.tldr: WBSR balances super-resolution training and adds dynamic inference, achieving comparable or better quality with about 34% less computation.

title: Rethinking Imbalance in Image Super-Resolution for Efficient Inference

abstract: The cost of ranking becomes significant in the new stage of deep learning. We propose ST$_k$, a fully differentiable module with a single trainable parameter, designed to solve the Top-k problem without requiring additional time or GPU memory. Due to its fully differentiable nature, ST$_k$ can be embedded end-to-end into neural networks and optimize the Top-k problems within a unified computational graph. We apply ST$_k$ to the Average Top-k Loss (AT$_k$), which inherently faces a Top-k problem. The proposed ST$_k$ Loss outperforms AT$_k$ Loss and achieves the best average performance on multiple benchmarks, with the lowest standard deviation. With the assistance of ST$_k$ Loss, we surpass the state-of-the-art (SOTA) on both CIFAR-100-LT and Places-LT leaderboards.
