paragraphs: Selecting the top k items is a recurring operation in deep learning, and the cost of ranking can become significant. This paper proposes ST_k, a fully differentiable module with a single trainable parameter. The authors design it to solve top-k problems without requiring additional time or GPU memory.

Full differentiability allows the selection module to participate in end-to-end optimization within a neural network's computational graph. The authors apply it to Average Top-k Loss, an objective that itself requires top-k selection. This produces ST_k Loss, connecting the proposed selection mechanism directly to the loss used for model training.

Across multiple benchmarks, ST_k Loss outperforms Average Top-k Loss and achieves the best reported average performance with the lowest standard deviation. The authors also report surpassing the state of the art on the CIFAR-100-LT and Places-LT leaderboards using this loss. These findings support the module's value through its demonstrated loss-function application, while its differentiable design makes integration into a unified training computation possible.
summary.tldr: ST_k makes top-k selection differentiable with one trainable parameter and improves benchmark performance when incorporated into a training loss.

title: ST$_k$: A Scalable Module for Solving Top-k Problems

abstract: Mixed time series (MiTS) comprising both continuous variables (CVs) and discrete variables (DVs) are frequently encountered yet under-explored in time series analysis. Essentially, CVs and DVs exhibit different temporal patterns and distribution types. Overlooking these heterogeneities would lead to insufficient and imbalanced representation learning, bringing biased results. This paper addresses the problem with two insights: 1) DVs may originate from intrinsic latent continuous variables (LCVs), which lose fine-grained information due to extrinsic discretization; 2) LCVs and CVs share similar temporal patterns and interact spatially. Considering these similarities and interactions, we propose a general MiTS analysis framework MiTSformer, which recovers LCVs behind DVs for sufficient and balanced spatial-temporal modeling by designing two essential inductive biases: 1) hierarchically aggregating multi-scale temporal context information to enrich the information granularity of DVs; 2) adaptively learning the aggregation processes via the adversarial guidance from CVs. Subsequently, MiTSformer captures complete spatial-temporal dependencies within and across LCVs and CVs via cascaded self- and cross-attention blocks. Empirically, MiTSformer achieves consistent SOTA on five mixed time series analysis tasks, including classification, extrinsic regression, anomaly detection, imputation, and long-term forecasting. The code is available at https://github.com/chunhuiz/MiTSformer.
originalAbstract: Mixed time series (MiTS) comprising both continuous variables (CVs) and discrete variables (DVs) are frequently encountered yet under-explored in time series analysis. Essentially, CVs and DVs exhibit different temporal patterns and distribution types. Overlooking these heterogeneities would lead to insufficient and imbalanced representation learning, bringing biased results. This paper addresses the problem with two insights: 1) DVs may originate from intrinsic latent continuous variables (LCVs), which lose fine-grained information due to extrinsic discretization; 2) LCVs and CVs share similar temporal patterns and interact spatially. Considering these similarities and interactions, we propose a general MiTS analysis framework MiTSformer, which recovers LCVs behind DVs for sufficient and balanced spatial-temporal modeling by designing two essential inductive biases: 1) hierarchically aggregating multi-scale temporal context information to enrich the information granularity of DVs; 2) adaptively learning the aggregation processes via the adversarial guidance from CVs. Subsequently, MiTSformer captures complete spatial-temporal dependencies within and across LCVs and CVs via cascaded self- and cross-attention blocks. Empirically, MiTSformer achieves consistent SOTA on five mixed time series analysis tasks, including classification, extrinsic regression, anomaly detection, imputation, and long-term forecasting. The code is available at https://github.com/chunhuiz/MiTSformer.

paragraphs: Mixed time series contain both continuous measurements and discrete values. These two kinds of variables can have different distributions and patterns over time, making it difficult to learn useful representations of both together. MiTSformer addresses the resulting risk that a model represents one kind of variable more effectively than the other.

The approach starts from the possibility that discrete observations arise from underlying continuous quantities whose detail was lost through discretization. It attempts to recover representations of those quantities by combining temporal context at several scales. Guidance from the continuous variables, delivered through adversarial learning, helps adapt this aggregation process. Attention blocks then model relationships over time and across the recovered and originally continuous variables.

The authors report consistently leading results across five tasks: classification, regression, anomaly detection, filling missing values, and long-term forecasting. These findings support using a shared framework across different mixed-data problems. The interpretation of discrete variables as potentially hiding continuous information is a motivating premise of the method, rather than a claim that every discrete observation has such an origin.
summary.tldr: MiTSformer models mixed time series by recovering continuous representations behind discrete variables and aligning them with continuous measurements.

title: Addressing Spatial-Temporal Heterogeneity: General Mixed Time Series Analysis via Latent Continuity Recovery and Alignment

abstract: Unsupervised out-of-distribution (OOD) detection aims to identify out-of-domain data by learning only from unlabeled In-Distribution (ID) training samples, which is crucial for developing a safe real-world machine learning system. Current reconstruction-based method provides a good alternative approach, by measuring the reconstruction error between the input and its corresponding generative counterpart in the pixel/feature space. However, such generative methods face the key dilemma, $i.e.$, improving the reconstruction power of the generative model, while keeping compact representation of the ID data. To address this issue, we propose the diffusion-based layer-wise semantic reconstruction approach for unsupervised OOD detection. The innovation of our approach is that we leverage the diffusion model's intrinsic data reconstruction ability to distinguish ID samples from OOD samples in the latent feature space. Moreover, to set up a comprehensive and discriminative feature representation, we devise a multi-layer semantic feature extraction strategy. Through distorting the extracted features with Gaussian noises and applying the diffusion model for feature reconstruction, the separation of ID and OOD samples is implemented according to the reconstruction errors. Extensive experimental results on multiple benchmarks built upon various datasets demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance in terms of detection accuracy and speed.

paragraphs: Unsupervised out-of-distribution detection learns from unlabeled examples of familiar data and tries to recognize unfamiliar inputs later. Reconstruction methods approach this by comparing an input with a generated reconstruction. The paper identifies a tension between making reconstruction powerful and keeping the learned representation focused on the in-distribution data.

The proposed method uses diffusion to reconstruct semantic features rather than relying solely on reconstruction in pixel space. It extracts features from multiple layers to build a more comprehensive representation, adds Gaussian noise to those features, and reconstructs them with a diffusion model. Reconstruction errors then provide the basis for separating familiar and unfamiliar samples.

This design brings the diffusion model's reconstruction ability into a feature space containing information from several layers. The authors report state-of-the-art detection accuracy and speed on multiple benchmarks built from different datasets. The findings support the combination of multilayer semantic representation and diffusion reconstruction as an effective detector in those evaluations, using only unlabeled in-distribution samples for training.
summary.tldr: The method detects unfamiliar inputs through diffusion reconstruction errors on noisy semantic features extracted from multiple layers.

title: Diffusion-based Layer-wise Semantic Reconstruction for Unsupervised Out-of-Distribution Detection

abstract: In many Deep Reinforcement Learning (RL) problems, decisions in a trained policy vary in significance for the expected safety and performance of the policy. Since RL policies are very complex, testing efforts should concentrate on states in which the agent's decisions have the highest impact on the expected outcome. In this paper, we propose a novel model-based method to rigorously compute a ranking of state importance across the entire state space. We then focus our testing efforts on the highest-ranked states. In this paper, we focus on testing for safety. However, the proposed methods can be easily adapted to test for performance. In each iteration, our testing framework computes optimistic and pessimistic safety estimates. These estimates provide lower and upper bounds on the expected outcomes of the policy execution across all modeled states in the state space. Our approach divides the state space into safe and unsafe regions upon convergence, providing clear insights into the policy's weaknesses. Two important properties characterize our approach. (1) Optimal Test-Case Selection: At any time in the testing process, our approach evaluates the policy in the states that are most critical for safety. (2) Guaranteed Safety: Our approach can provide formal verification guarantees over the entire state space by sampling only a fraction of the policy. Any safety properties assured by the pessimistic estimate are formally proven to hold for the policy. We provide a detailed evaluation of our framework on several examples, showing that our method discovers unsafe policy behavior with low testing effort.

summary.tldr: A model-based testing framework prioritizes safety-critical decisions and can establish formal policy guarantees from evaluating only a fraction of its behavior.

title: Test Where Decisions Matter: Importance-driven Testing for Deep Reinforcement Learning

abstract: This paper aims to discuss the impact of random initialization of neural networks in the neural tangent kernel (NTK) theory, which is ignored by most recent works in the NTK theory. It is well known that as the network's width tends to infinity, the neural network with random initialization converges to a Gaussian process \(f^{\mathrm{GP}}\), which takes values in \(L^{2}(\mathcal{X})\), where \(\mathcal{X}\) is the domain of the data. In contrast, to adopt the traditional theory of kernel regression, most recent works introduced a special mirrored architecture and a mirrored (random) initialization to ensure the network's output is identically zero at initialization. Therefore, it remains a question whether the conventional setting and mirrored initialization would make wide neural networks exhibit different generalization capabilities. In this paper, we first show that the training dynamics of the gradient flow of neural networks with random initialization converge uniformly to that of the corresponding NTK regression with random initialization \(f^{\mathrm{GP}}\). We then show that \(\mathbf{P}(f^{\mathrm{GP}} \in [\mathcal{H}^{\mathrm{NT}}]^{s}) = 1\) for any \(s < \frac{3}{d+1}\) and \(\mathbf{P}(f^{\mathrm{GP}} \in [\mathcal{H}^{\mathrm{NT}}]^{s}) = 0\) for any \(s \geq \frac{3}{d+1}\), where \([\mathcal{H}^{\mathrm{NT}}]^{s}\) is the real interpolation space of the RKHS \(\mathcal{H}^{\mathrm{NT}}\) associated with the NTK. Consequently, the generalization error of the wide neural network trained by gradient descent is \(\Omega(n^{-\frac{3}{d+3}})\), and it still suffers from the curse of dimensionality. Thus, the NTK theory may not explain the superior performance of neural networks.

paragraphs: Neural tangent kernel theory connects very wide neural networks to kernel regression. Many analyses simplify this connection by using mirrored architectures and initialization so that the initial network output is exactly zero. This paper asks what changes when ordinary random initialization instead produces a nonzero random function.

The authors first prove that gradient-flow training dynamics converge uniformly to those of the corresponding kernel regression problem with a Gaussian-process initial function. They then characterize that function's regularity in interpolation spaces associated with the neural tangent kernel. Almost surely, membership holds below the threshold 3/(d+1) and fails at or above it.

The resulting generalization-error lower bound is of order n raised to −3/(d+3), where n is sample size and d is data dimension. As dimension grows, this bound reflects the curse of dimensionality. The result shows why initialization matters to the theory's account of generalization and supports the authors' qualified conclusion that NTK theory may not explain neural networks' superior empirical performance.
summary.tldr: Accounting for ordinary random initialization yields an NTK generalization lower bound that retains the curse of dimensionality.

title: On the Impacts of the Random Initialization in the Neural Tangent Kernel Theory

abstract: Aligning large language models (LLMs) with human objectives is crucial for real-world applications. However, fine-tuning LLMs for alignment often suffers from unstable training and requires substantial computing resources. Test-time alignment techniques, such as prompting and guided decoding, do not modify the underlying model, and their performance remains dependent on the original model's capabilities. To address these challenges, we propose aligning LLMs through representation editing. The core of our method is to view a pre-trained autoregressive LLM as a discrete-time stochastic dynamical system. To achieve alignment for specific objectives, we introduce external control signals into the state space of this language dynamical system. We train a value function directly on the hidden states according to the Bellman equation, enabling gradient-based optimization to obtain the optimal control signals at test time. Our experiments demonstrate that our method outperforms existing test-time alignment techniques while requiring significantly fewer resources compared to fine-tuning methods. Our code is available at [https://github.com/Lingkai-Kong/RE-Control](https://github.com/Lingkai-Kong/RE-Control).

paragraphs: This paper approaches language-model alignment as a problem of controlling the model’s internal state during generation. Fine-tuning can demand substantial computing resources and suffer from unstable training. Existing techniques that operate at test time, such as prompting and guided decoding, also remain dependent on the original model’s capabilities. The authors investigate representation editing as another way to pursue specific objectives.

They describe an autoregressive language model as a stochastic dynamical system that evolves in discrete steps. External control signals intervene in its hidden representations. To choose those signals, the method trains a value function directly on hidden states using the Bellman equation, connecting internal states to the objective the controller seeks to achieve.

At test time, gradient-based optimization uses this value function to find control signals. Experiments report better performance than existing test-time alignment techniques and substantially lower resource requirements than fine-tuning approaches. These findings support using learned evaluations of internal states to guide generation, with the alignment intervention expressed directly through the model’s representations.
summary.tldr: The method aligns language models by learning a value function that guides edits to hidden states during generation.

title: Aligning Large Language Models with Representation Editing: A Control Perspective

abstract: Accurately quantifying tree cover is an important metric for ecosystem monitoring and for assessing progress in restored sites. Recent works have shown that deep learning-based segmentation algorithms are capable of accurately mapping trees at country and continental scales using high-resolution aerial and satellite imagery. Mapping at high (ideally sub-meter) resolution is necessary to identify individual trees, however there are few open-access datasets containing instance level annotations and those that exist are small or not geographically diverse. We present a novel open-access dataset for individual tree crown delineation (TCD) in high-resolution aerial imagery sourced from OpenAerialMap (OAM). Our dataset, OAM-TCD, comprises 5072 2048x2048 px images at 10 cm/px resolution with associated human-labeled instance masks for over 280k individual and 56k groups of trees. By sampling imagery from around the world, we are able to better capture the diversity and morphology of trees in different terrestrial biomes and in both urban and natural environments. Using our dataset, we train reference instance and semantic segmentation models that compare favorably to existing state-of-the-art models. We assess performance through k-fold cross-validation and comparison with existing datasets; additionally we demonstrate compelling results on independent aerial imagery captured over Switzerland and compare to municipal tree inventories and LIDAR-derived canopy maps in the city of Zurich. Our dataset, models and training/benchmark code are publicly released under permissive open-source licenses: Creative Commons (majority CC BY 4.0), and Apache 2.0 respectively.

Identifying individual trees requires detailed imagery and annotations, but available open datasets have often been small or geographically limited. OAM-TCD addresses this gap with globally sampled aerial imagery and human-labeled masks for individual tree crowns and groups of trees.

summary.tldr: OAM-TCD provides globally diverse, high-resolution aerial images and extensive tree annotations, alongside reference models and open benchmarking resources.

title: OAM-TCD: A globally diverse dataset of high-resolution tree cover maps

abstract: The notion of algorithmic fairness has been actively explored from various aspects of fairness, such as counterfactual fairness (CF) and group fairness (GF). However, the exact relationship between CF and GF remains to be unclear, especially in image classification tasks; the reason is because we often cannot collect counterfactual samples regarding a sensitive attribute, essential for evaluating CF, from the existing images (e.g., a photo of the same person but with different secondary sex characteristics). In this paper, we construct new image datasets for evaluating CF by using a high-quality image editing method and carefully labeling with human annotators. Our datasets, CelebA-CF and LFW-CF, build upon the popular image GF benchmarks; hence, we can evaluate CF and GF simultaneously. We empirically observe that CF does not imply GF in image classification, whereas previous studies on tabular datasets observed the opposite. We theoretically show that it could be due to the existence of a latent attribute $G$ that is correlated with, but not caused by, the sensitive attribute (e.g., secondary sex characteristics are highly correlated with hair length). From this observation, we propose a simple baseline, Counterfactual Knowledge Distillation (CKD), to mitigate such correlation with the sensitive attributes. Extensive experimental results on CelebA-CF and LFW-CF demonstrate that CF-achieving models satisfy GF if we successfully reduce the reliance on $G$ (e.g., using CKD).

paragraphs: Evaluating counterfactual fairness in images requires examples that differ in a sensitive attribute while representing the relevant counterfactual comparison. Such examples are difficult to obtain from existing photographs. The authors use high-quality image editing and careful human annotation to create CelebA-CF and LFW-CF, extending benchmarks that already support group-fairness evaluation.

These datasets allow both fairness notions to be assessed together. The experiments show that counterfactual fairness does not imply group fairness in the studied image-classification settings. The theoretical analysis identifies a possible explanation: a latent attribute can be correlated with a sensitive attribute without being caused by it. Reliance on that attribute can help explain why the two fairness criteria diverge.

The authors propose Counterfactual Knowledge Distillation to mitigate the relevant correlations. Experiments on both datasets show that models achieving counterfactual fairness also satisfy group fairness when their reliance on the latent attribute is successfully reduced. The condition matters: the result connects the fairness notions through a successful reduction in that reliance, rather than establishing that counterfactual fairness alone guarantees group fairness.
summary.tldr: New image datasets show that counterfactual fairness need not imply group fairness, with correlated latent attributes offering a possible explanation.

title: Do Counterfactually Fair Image Classifiers Satisfy Group Fairness? -- A Theoretical and Empirical Study

abstract: The recently-proposed framework of Predict+Optimize tackles optimization problems with parameters that are unknown at solving time, in a supervised learning setting. Prior frameworks consider only the scenario where all unknown parameters are (eventually) revealed simultaneously. In this work, we propose Multi-Stage Predict+Optimize, a novel extension catering to applications where unknown parameters are revealed in sequential stages, with optimization decisions made in between. We further develop three training algorithms for neural networks (NNs) for our framework as proof of concept, both of which handle all mixed integer linear programs. The first baseline algorithm is a natural extension of prior work, training a single NN which makes a single prediction of unknown parameters. The second and third algorithms instead leverage the possibility of updating parameter predictions between stages, and trains one NN per stage. To handle the interdependency between the neural networks, we adopt sequential and parallelized versions of coordinate descent for training. Experimentation on three benchmarks demonstrates the superior learning performance of our methods over classical approaches.

paragraphs: Predict+Optimize learns predictions for parameters that an optimization problem needs but that are not known when decisions must be made. This paper extends that framework to situations where information arrives in stages, with decisions occurring between revelations. Such a setting gives later predictions access to information unavailable at the beginning.

The authors develop three neural-network training algorithms for mixed integer linear programs. The first extends earlier work by using one network to make a single prediction of the unknown parameters. The other two use a separate network at each stage, allowing predictions to change as additional information becomes available.

Training the stage-specific networks requires handling their interdependence: decisions and predictions at different stages belong to the same overall problem. The authors use sequential and parallelized forms of coordinate descent to manage these dependencies. Experiments on three benchmarks report superior learning performance over classical approaches. The contribution is a framework and proof-of-concept algorithms that explicitly incorporate the timing of information, allowing prediction and optimization to adapt across a sequence of decisions.
summary.tldr: Multi-Stage Predict+Optimize updates predictions as information arrives between optimization decisions.

title: Multi-Stage Predict+Optimize for (Mixed Integer) Linear Programs

abstract: The ability to invent novel and interesting problems is a remarkable feature of human intelligence that drives innovation, art, and science. We propose a method that aims to automate this process by harnessing the power of state-of-the-art generative models to produce a diversity of challenging yet solvable problems, here in the context of Python programming puzzles. Inspired by the intrinsically motivated literature, Autotelic CodE Search (ACES) jointly optimizes for the diversity and difficulty of generated problems. We represent problems in a space of LLM-generated semantic descriptors describing the programming skills required to solve them (e.g. string manipulation, dynamic programming, etc.) and measure their difficulty empirically as a linearly decreasing function of the success rate of \textit{Llama-3-70B}, a state-of-the-art LLM problem solver. ACES iteratively prompts a large language model to generate difficult problems achieving a diversity of target semantic descriptors (goal-directed exploration) using previously generated problems as in-context examples. ACES generates problems that are more diverse and more challenging than problems produced by baseline methods and three times more challenging than problems found in existing Python programming benchmarks on average across 11 state-of-the-art code LLMs.

paragraphs: ACES investigates whether a generative model can invent programming problems that are both varied and challenging. Its setting is Python puzzles, where the aim is to produce difficult but solvable tasks. The approach jointly pursues difficulty and diversity, so generating more problems is tied to exploring different combinations of programming skills.

The method describes each puzzle using semantic descriptors generated by a language model, such as string manipulation or dynamic programming. These descriptors organize the space of possible problems. Difficulty is measured empirically from Llama-3-70B's success rate: lower success means higher difficulty. ACES repeatedly asks a language model to target different descriptors, using previously generated puzzles as examples to guide further exploration.

The resulting problems were more diverse and challenging than those from the tested baseline methods. Across 11 code language models, the authors report that they were three times more challenging than existing Python benchmark problems on average. This finding concerns difficulty measured through model performance, connecting problem generation to the observed capabilities of the solvers.
summary.tldr: ACES generates varied Python puzzles by targeting programming skills and using solver success rates to guide difficulty.

title: ACES: Generating a Diversity of Challenging Programming Puzzles with Autotelic Generative Models

abstract: In this work we design graph neural network architectures that capture optimalapproximation algorithms for a large class of combinatorial optimization problems,using powerful algorithmic tools from semidefinite programming (SDP). Concretely, we prove that polynomial-sized message-passing algorithms can representthe most powerful polynomial time algorithms for Max Constraint SatisfactionProblems assuming the Unique Games Conjecture. We leverage this result toconstruct efficient graph neural network architectures, OptGNN, that obtain high quality approximate solutions on landmark combinatorial optimization problemssuch as Max-Cut, Min-Vertex-Cover, and Max-3-SAT. Our approach achievesstrong empirical results across a wide range of real-world and synthetic datasetsagainst solvers and neural baselines. Finally, we take advantage of OptGNN’sability to capture convex relaxations to design an algorithm for producing boundson the optimal solution from the learned embeddings of OptGNN.

These problems ask for the best discrete arrangement or selection, but finding an exact solution can be computationally demanding. The authors build on semidefinite programming, which supplies mathematical relaxations for obtaining approximate solutions.

Their central theoretical result concerns Max Constraint Satisfaction Problems. Assuming the Unique Games Conjecture, they prove that polynomial-sized message-passing algorithms can represent the strongest polynomial-time approximation algorithms for this class. This is a conditional statement about what these architectures can express; it does not establish that ordinary neural-network training will automatically discover an optimal approximation algorithm.

The authors use this connection to construct OptGNN architectures and evaluate them on problems including Max-Cut, Min-Vertex-Cover, and Max-3-SAT. They report strong empirical results against solvers and neural baselines on real and synthetic datasets. They also develop a way to derive bounds on the optimal solution from learned embeddings, connecting the network's output to mathematical information about solution quality.
summary.tldr: OptGNN connects graph neural networks to powerful approximation algorithms, with a conditional expressiveness guarantee and strong empirical optimization results.

title: Are Graph Neural Networks Optimal Approximation Algorithms?

abstract: Recently, there has been growing evidence that if the width and depth of a neural network are scaled toward the so-called rich feature learning limit ($\mu$P and its depth extension), then some hyperparameters --- such as the learning rate --- exhibit transfer from small to very large models. From an optimization perspective, this phenomenon is puzzling, as it implies that the loss landscape is consistently similar across very different model sizes. In this work, we study the landscape through the lens of the Hessian, with a focus on its largest eigenvalue (i.e. the sharpness), and find that certain spectral properties under $\mu$P are largely independent of the width and depth of the network along the training trajectory. We name this property *super consistency* of the landscape. On the other hand, we show that in the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) and other scaling regimes, the sharpness exhibits very different dynamics at different scales. But what causes these differences in the sharpness dynamics? Through a connection between the Hessian's and the NTK's spectrum, we argue that the cause lies in the presence (for $\mu$P) or progressive absence (for the NTK scaling) of feature learning.We corroborate our claims with a substantial suite of experiments, covering a wide range of datasets and architectures: from ResNets and Vision Transformers trained on benchmark vision datasets to Transformers-based language models trained on WikiText.

paragraphs: A learning rate chosen for a small network can sometimes remain useful for a much larger one when the models follow particular scaling rules. This is surprising because changing network size could change the optimization problem substantially. The paper investigates this transfer through the curvature of the loss landscape, focusing on the Hessian and its largest eigenvalue, called sharpness.

Under the rich feature-learning scaling known as μP and its depth extension, the authors find that certain spectral properties remain largely independent of network width and depth throughout training. Experiments cover ResNets, Vision Transformers, and language Transformers, including training on WikiText. The findings offer an optimization-based explanation for learning-rate transfer through consistency in selected landscape properties.
summary.tldr: Under μP scaling, largely size-independent loss-curvature dynamics help explain why learning rates can transfer between small and large networks.

title: Super Consistency of Neural Network Landscapes and Learning Rate Transfer

abstract: How to decode human vision through neural signals has attracted a long-standing interest in neuroscience and machine learning. Modern contrastive learning and generative models improved the performance of visual decoding and reconstruction based on functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI). However, the high cost and low temporal resolution of fMRI limit their applications in brain-computer interfaces (BCIs), prompting a high need for visual decoding based on electroencephalography (EEG). In this study, we present an end-to-end EEG-based visual reconstruction zero-shot framework, consisting of a tailored brain encoder, called the Adaptive Thinking Mapper (ATM), which projects neural signals from different sources into the shared subspace as the clip embedding, and a two-stage multi-pipe EEG-to-image generation strategy. In stage one, EEG is embedded to align the high-level clip embedding, and then the prior diffusion model refines EEG embedding into image priors. A blurry image also decoded from EEG for maintaining the low-level feature. In stage two, we input both the high-level clip embedding, the blurry image and caption from EEG latent to a pre-trained diffusion model. Furthermore, we analyzed the impacts of different time windows and brain regions on decoding and reconstruction. The versatility of our framework is demonstrated in the magnetoencephalogram (MEG) data modality. The experimental results indicate that our EEG-based visual zero-shot framework achieves SOTA performance in classification, retrieval and reconstruction, highlighting the portability, low cost, and high temporal resolution of EEG, enabling a wide range of BCI applications. Our code is available at https://github.com/ncclab-sustech/EEG_Image_decode.

EEG is attractive for this task because it offers portability, low cost, and high temporal resolution compared with fMRI. This paper presents a zero-shot visual decoding and reconstruction framework that translates EEG measurements into information a pretrained image generator can use.

Its Adaptive Thinking Mapper encodes neural signals into a space aligned with CLIP embeddings. In the first generation stage, a prior diffusion model refines the EEG embedding into image priors, while a separately decoded blurry image preserves lower-level visual information. The second stage supplies the high-level embedding, blurry image, and a caption derived from the EEG latent representation to a pretrained diffusion model.

The authors also analyze how recording time windows and brain regions affect decoding and reconstruction, and demonstrate the framework on MEG signals. Experiments report state-of-the-art performance for EEG-based zero-shot classification, retrieval, and reconstruction. The approach combines semantic and lower-level cues from neural signals, supporting several visual decoding tasks within one framework and demonstrating applicability across more than one neural recording modality.
summary.tldr: An EEG encoder and two-stage diffusion pipeline combine semantic and low-level neural cues for zero-shot visual decoding and reconstruction.

title: Visual Decoding and Reconstruction via EEG Embeddings with Guided Diffusion

abstract: A wide array of sequence models are built on a framework modeled after Transformers, comprising alternating sequence mixer and channel mixer layers. This paper studies a unifying *matrix mixer* view of sequence mixers that can be conceptualized as a linear map on the input sequence. This framework encompasses a broad range of well-known sequence models, including the self-attention of Transformers as well as recent strong alternatives such as structured state space models (SSMs), and allows understanding downstream characteristics such as efficiency and expressivity through properties of their structured matrix class. We identify a key axis of matrix parameterizations termed *sequence alignment*, which increases the flexibility and performance of matrix mixers, providing insights into the strong performance of Transformers and recent SSMs such as Mamba. Furthermore, the matrix mixer framework offers a systematic approach to developing sequence mixers with desired properties, allowing us to develop several new sub-quadratic sequence models. In particular, we propose a natural bidirectional extension of the Mamba model (**Hydra**), parameterized as a *quasiseparable matrix mixer*, which demonstrates superior performance over other sequence models including Transformers on non-causal tasks. As a drop-in replacement for attention layers, \name outperforms BERT by 0.8 points on the GLUE benchmark and ViT by 2% Top-1 accuracy on ImageNet.

This paper studies that operation through a matrix mixer view, treating sequence mixing as a linear map on the input sequence. The framework encompasses Transformer attention and structured state space models, allowing their efficiency and expressive capacity to be examined through the structure of their mixing matrices.

The authors identify sequence alignment as an important dimension of matrix parameterization that improves flexibility and performance. They then use the framework to design several models with sub-quadratic sequence mixing. Hydra is a bidirectional extension of Mamba built as a quasiseparable matrix mixer, intended for non-causal tasks where information can flow in both sequence directions.

In the reported evaluations, Hydra outperforms other sequence models, including Transformers. Used in place of attention layers, it exceeds BERT by 0.8 points on GLUE and ViT by 2% Top-1 accuracy on ImageNet. The results connect a general mathematical view of sequence mixing to a concrete architecture with strong language and image task performance.
summary.tldr: Hydra uses a unified matrix-mixer framework to extend Mamba bidirectionally, outperforming the reported Transformer comparisons on non-causal tasks.

title: Hydra: Bidirectional State Space Models Through Generalized Matrix Mixers

abstract: Large vision-language models (VLMs) fine-tuned on specialized visual instruction-following data have exhibited impressive language reasoning capabilities across various scenarios. However, this fine-tuning paradigm may not be able to efficiently learn optimal decision-making agents in multi-step goal-directed tasks from interactive environments. To address this challenge, we propose an algorithmic framework that fine-tunes VLMs with reinforcement learning (RL). Specifically, our framework provides a task description and then prompts the VLM to generate chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning, enabling the VLM to efficiently explore intermediate reasoning steps that lead to the final text-based action. Next, the open-ended text output is parsed into an executable action to interact with the environment to obtain goal-directed task rewards. Finally, our framework uses these task rewards to fine-tune the entire VLM with RL. Empirically, we demonstrate that our proposed framework enhances the decision-making capabilities of VLM agents across various tasks, enabling 7b models to outperform commercial models such as GPT4-V or Gemini. Furthermore, we find that CoT reasoning is a crucial component for performance improvement, as removing the CoT reasoning results in a significant decrease in the overall performance of our method.

paragraphs: Following visual instructions and making good decisions over several interactions are related but different capabilities. A vision-language model may produce convincing responses yet struggle to choose actions that accomplish a goal over time. This paper investigates reinforcement learning as a way to train such models directly through interaction and task rewards.

The framework gives the model a task description and prompts it to produce intermediate reasoning followed by a text-based action. That text is parsed into an executable action, allowing the model to interact with its environment. Rewards from the resulting task behavior are then used to fine-tune the entire vision-language model, connecting its outputs to goal achievement.

Across the evaluated tasks, the authors report improved decision-making, with seven-billion-parameter models outperforming commercial models including GPT4-V or Gemini. Removing the intermediate reasoning substantially reduces performance in their method. These findings support both reward-driven adaptation and the reasoning component within the tested framework; they do not establish superiority across every use of vision-language models.
summary.tldr: The framework fine-tunes vision-language models through interactive task rewards, improving multistep decision-making in the evaluated environments.

title: Fine-Tuning Large Vision-Language Models as Decision-Making Agents via Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are widely used in today's tasks of natural language processing. To support applications like multi-turn chats, document understanding, and content generation, models with long context lengths are growing in importance.However, managing long contexts brings substantial challenges due to the expansion of key-value cache (KV cache). Longer KV cache requires larger memory, limiting the batch-size thus decreasing throughput. Also, computing attention over long KV cache incurs more memory access, hurting the end-to-end latency.Prior works find that it is sufficient to use only the recent and high-impact tokens for attention computation, allowing the eviction of less vital tokens to shrink cache size.Nonetheless, we observe a dynamic shift in token importance across different decoding steps. Tokens initially evicted might regain importance after certain decoding steps.To address this, we propose ArkVale, a page-based KV cache manager that can recognize and recall currently important tokens evicted before. We asynchronously copy the filled page into external memory (e.g., CPU memory) as backup and summarize it into a much smaller digest by constructing the bounding-volume of its keys. Before attention computation, we measure all pages' importance based on their digests, recall the important ones, evict the unimportant ones, and select the top-ranked pages for attention computation. Experiment results show that ArkVale performs well on various long context tasks with negligible accuracy loss under 2k$\sim$4k cache budget and can improve decoding latency to $2.2\times$ and batching throughput to $4.6\times$ because it applies attention on only a small subset of pages and reduce per-sample memory usage of KV cache.

paragraphs: Long-context language models store keys and values from earlier tokens so that later generation can attend to them. This cache consumes memory and makes attention more expensive as context grows. Removing less useful tokens helps, but ArkVale starts from an important observation: a token that appears unimportant now may become useful again during later decoding steps.

ArkVale manages the cache in pages and makes eviction reversible. It asynchronously backs up completed pages in external memory, such as CPU memory, and creates a compact summary of each page using a bounding volume of its keys. Before attention, these summaries help rank pages, bring important ones back, and remove less important ones.

Attention then uses only selected pages. Experiments report negligible accuracy loss on various long-context tasks with cache budgets of 2k–4k, alongside decoding speedups of 2.2 times and batching throughput improvements of 4.6 times. The central contribution is a cache policy that responds to changing relevance while reducing active memory use and attention work.
summary.tldr: ArkVale reduces long-context inference costs by evicting cache pages while retaining the ability to recall them when their tokens become relevant again.

title: ArkVale: Efficient Generative LLM Inference with Recallable Key-Value Eviction

abstract: The Multi-modal Large Language Model (MLLM) based Referring Expression Generation (REG) task has gained increasing popularity, which aims to generate an unambiguous text description that applies to exactly one object or region in the image by leveraging foundation models. We empirically found that there exists a potential trade-off between the detailedness and the correctness of the descriptions for the referring objects. On the one hand, generating sentences with more details is usually required in order to provide more precise object descriptions. On the other hand, complicated sentences could easily increase the probability of hallucinations. To address this issue, we propose a training-free framework, named ``unleash-then-eliminate'', which first elicits the latent information in the intermediate layers, and then adopts a cycle-consistency-based decoding method to alleviate the production of hallucinations. Furthermore, to reduce the computational load of cycle-consistency-based decoding, we devise a Probing-based Importance Estimation method to statistically estimate the importance weights of intermediate layers within a subset. These importance weights are then incorporated into the decoding process over the entire dataset, intervening in the next token prediction from intermediate layers.Extensive experiments conducted on the RefCOCOg and PHD benchmarks show that our proposed framework could outperform existing methods on both semantic and hallucination-related metrics. Code will be made available in https://github.com/Glupayy/unleash-eliminate.

paragraphs: Referring expression generation produces a description that uniquely identifies one object or region in an image. More detail can help distinguish the target, but the authors observe a potential trade-off: complicated descriptions can also increase hallucinations. The challenge is to use a multimodal model's region knowledge while keeping its descriptions correct.

The proposed training-free framework, called unleash-then-eliminate, first draws out information held in intermediate model layers. It then uses cycle-consistency-based decoding to reduce hallucinations. This combines access to latent region information with a decoding procedure intended to control unsupported content as the description is generated.

Because that decoding process can be computationally demanding, the authors introduce Probing-based Importance Estimation. It estimates intermediate-layer importance weights on a subset and then uses those weights during next-token prediction across the full dataset. Experiments on RefCOCOg and PHD show that the framework can outperform existing methods on both semantic and hallucination-related measures. The findings support using intermediate representations to improve descriptive content while also addressing its reliability.
summary.tldr: A training-free decoding framework uses intermediate-layer region information to improve referring descriptions and reduce hallucinations.

title: Unleashing Region Understanding in Intermediate Layers for MLLM-based Referring Expression Generation

abstract: Spatiotemporal learning has become a pivotal technique to enable urban intelligence. Traditional spatiotemporal models mostly focus on a specific task by assuming a same distribution between training and testing sets. However, given that urban systems are usually dynamic, multi-sourced with imbalanced data distributions, current specific task-specific models fail to generalize to new urban conditions and adapt to new domains without explicitly modeling interdependencies across various dimensions and types of urban data. To this end, we argue that there is an essential to propose a Continuous Multi-task Spatio-Temporal learning framework (CMuST) to empower collective urban intelligence, which reforms the urban spatiotemporal learning from single-domain to cooperatively multi-dimensional and multi-task learning. Specifically, CMuST proposes a new multi-dimensional spatiotemporal interaction network (MSTI) to allow cross-interactions between context and main observations as well as self-interactions within spatial and temporal aspects to be exposed, which is also the core for capturing task-level commonality and personalization. To ensure continuous task learning, a novel Rolling Adaptation training scheme (RoAda) is devised, which not only preserves task uniqueness by constructing data summarization-driven task prompts, but also harnesses correlated patterns among tasks by iterative model behavior modeling. We further establish a benchmark of three cities for multi-task spatiotemporal learning, and empirically demonstrate the superiority of CMuST via extensive evaluations on these datasets. The impressive improvements on both few-shot streaming data and new domain tasks against existing SOAT methods are achieved. Code is available at https://github.com/DILab-USTCSZ/CMuST.

paragraphs: Urban data changes over time, comes from multiple sources, and can be unevenly distributed. Models trained for one task under an assumption that training and testing distributions match can struggle with new conditions. CMuST addresses this by learning across multiple spatiotemporal tasks while explicitly representing connections among different dimensions of urban data.

Its interaction network models relationships between contextual information and main observations, alongside interactions within spatial and temporal dimensions. This supports learning patterns shared across tasks while retaining task-specific characteristics. A Rolling Adaptation training scheme then enables continued learning: prompts derived from data summaries represent individual tasks, while iterative modeling of model behavior captures relationships among tasks.

The authors introduce a three-city benchmark and report improvements over existing state-of-the-art methods in extensive evaluations. These include settings with few-shot streaming data and tasks from new domains. The results support the idea that urban prediction benefits from jointly learning shared structure and task individuality, with continued adaptation providing a way to use that structure as new data and tasks arrive.
summary.tldr: CMuST combines cross-task spatiotemporal interactions with rolling adaptation to improve learning from streaming urban data and new domains.

title: Get Rid of Isolation: A Continuous Multi-task Spatio-Temporal Learning Framework

abstract: Last-layer retraining methods have emerged as an efficient framework for correcting existing base models. Within this framework, several methods have been proposed to deal with correcting models for subgroup fairness with and without group membership information. Importantly, prior work has demonstrated that many methods are susceptible to noisy labels. To this end, we propose a drop-in correction for label noise in last-layer retraining, and demonstrate that it achieves state-of-the-art worst-group accuracy for a broad range of symmetric label noise and across a wide variety of datasets exhibiting spurious correlations. Our proposed approach uses label spreading on a latent nearest neighbors graph and has minimal computational overhead compared to existing methods.

Importantly, prior work has demonstrated that many methods are susceptible to noisy labels. paragraphs: Retraining a model’s final layer offers an efficient way to correct an existing predictor for subgroup fairness. However, these corrections can be vulnerable to incorrect training labels. This paper targets that weakness by introducing a label-noise correction that can be added to last-layer retraining methods, preserving the appeal of making a relatively small model adjustment.

The approach uses label spreading on a nearest-neighbor graph built in the model’s latent representation. In plain terms, examples are connected according to their similarity in the learned feature space, and label information is spread through those connections. This makes relationships among represented examples part of the correction procedure, addressing noise in the labels used for retraining.

The authors report state-of-the-art worst-group accuracy across a broad range of symmetric label noise and multiple datasets containing spurious correlations. Worst-group accuracy focuses attention on the subgroup with the weakest performance. The method adds minimal computational overhead relative to existing approaches, suggesting that improved robustness can be incorporated without losing the efficiency motivating last-layer correction.
summary.tldr: Spreading labels through a latent nearest-neighbor graph improves the robustness of last-layer fairness corrections under symmetric label noise with little added computation.

title: Enhancing Robustness of Last Layer Two-Stage Fair Model Corrections

abstract: Although 3D Gaussian Splatting has been widely studied because of its realistic and efficient novel-view synthesis, it is still challenging to extract a high-quality surface from the point-based representation. Previous works improve the surface by incorporating geometric priors from the off-the-shelf normal estimator. However, there are two main limitations: 1) Supervising normal rendered from 3D Gaussians updates only the rotation parameter while neglecting other geometric parameters; 2) The inconsistency of predicted normal maps across multiple views may lead to severe reconstruction artifacts. In this paper, we propose a Depth-Normal regularizer that directly couples normal with other geometric parameters, leading to full updates of the geometric parameters from normal regularization. We further propose a confidence term to mitigate inconsistencies of normal predictions across multiple views. Moreover, we also introduce a densification and splitting strategy to regularize the size and distribution of 3D Gaussians for more accurate surface modeling. Compared with Gaussian-based baselines, experiments show that our approach obtains better reconstruction quality and maintains competitive appearance quality at faster training speed and 100+ FPS rendering. Our code will be made open-source upon paper acceptance.

paragraphs: 3D Gaussian Splatting can render realistic views efficiently, but extracting a clean surface from its point-based representation remains difficult. Existing approaches use predicted surface normals as geometric guidance. The paper identifies two problems: supervising rendered normals can update only Gaussian rotation, and normal predictions that disagree across views can introduce serious reconstruction artifacts.

VCR-GauS introduces a depth-normal regularizer that connects normals to other geometric parameters, allowing normal-based supervision to update the full geometry. A confidence term reduces the effect of inconsistencies between normal predictions from different viewpoints. The method also controls the size and distribution of Gaussians through a densification and splitting strategy, supporting more accurate surface modeling.

Compared with Gaussian-based baselines, experiments show better surface reconstruction while retaining competitive appearance quality. The authors also report faster training and rendering above 100 frames per second. These results connect improvements in geometric supervision to the practical goal of extracting better surfaces while preserving efficient rendering. The approach addresses both incomplete parameter updates and disagreement in the geometric guidance.
summary.tldr: VCR-GauS couples depth and normal supervision, handles cross-view inconsistency, and refines Gaussian placement to improve surface reconstruction while retaining fast rendering.

title: VCR-GauS: View Consistent Depth-Normal Regularizer for Gaussian Surface Reconstruction

abstract: A common problem in LLM evaluation is how to choose a subset of metrics from a full suite of possible metrics. Subset selection is usually done for efficiency or interpretability reasons, and the goal is often to select a "representative" subset of metrics. However, "representative" is rarely clearly defined. In this work, we use ideas from social choice theory to formalize two notions of representation for the selection of a subset of evaluation metrics. We first introduce *positional representation*, which guarantees every alternative is sufficiently represented at every position cutoff. We then introduce *positional proportionality*, which guarantees no alternative is proportionally over- or under-represented by more than a small error at any position. We prove upper and lower bounds on the smallest number of metrics needed to guarantee either of these properties in the worst case. We also study a generalized form of each property that allows for additional input on groups of metrics that must be represented. Finally, we tie theory to practice through real-world case studies on both LLM evaluation and hospital quality evaluation.

paragraphs: Smaller evaluation suites can save computation and make results easier to interpret, but choosing a representative subset of metrics requires defining what representation means. Metritocracy uses social choice theory to formalize this question. It examines how metric selection preserves the positions of the alternatives being evaluated, such as language models or hospitals.

The first proposed property, positional representation, requires every alternative to receive sufficient representation at every ranking-position cutoff. The second, positional proportionality, controls how far an alternative can be proportionally overrepresented or underrepresented at any position. These definitions turn an informal preference for a balanced subset into explicit properties that can be analyzed.

The authors prove upper and lower bounds on the smallest metric subset needed to guarantee each property in the worst case. They also generalize the properties to incorporate specified groups of metrics that must be represented. Case studies in language-model and hospital-quality evaluation connect the theory to practical selection problems, clarifying what a reduced benchmark can be required to preserve.
summary.tldr: Metritocracy defines formal representation guarantees for reduced metric suites and bounds how many metrics are needed to achieve them.

title: Metritocracy: Representative Metrics for Lite Benchmarks

abstract: Modern deep generative models can now produce high-quality synthetic samples that are often indistinguishable from real training data. A growing body of research aims to understand why recent methods, such as diffusion and flow matching techniques, generalize so effectively. Among the proposed explanations are the inductive biases of deep learning architectures and the stochastic nature of the conditional flow matching loss. In this work, we rule out the noisy nature of the loss as a key factor driving generalization in flow matching. First, we empirically show that in high-dimensional settings, the stochastic and closed-form versions of the flow matching loss yield nearly equivalent losses. Then, using state-of-the-art flow matching models on standard image datasets, we demonstrate that both variants achieve comparable statistical performance, with the surprising observation that using the closed-form can even improve performance.

paragraphs: This paper examines why flow-matching generative models generalize effectively. One proposed explanation is the randomness in their conditional training targets; another concerns the inductive biases of neural architectures. The researchers isolate the target-randomness explanation by comparing stochastic and closed-form versions of the flow-matching training loss.

Their first empirical finding is that these two losses become nearly equivalent in high-dimensional settings. They then train state-of-the-art flow-matching models on standard image datasets using both variants. This comparison tests whether the stochastic target formulation provides a meaningful performance advantage when the alternative removes that source of target randomness.

Both formulations achieve comparable statistical performance, and the closed-form version can even perform better. The paper therefore argues against noisy targets being a key driver of flow-matching generalization. The result narrows the explanations supported by these experiments: effective generation persists without relying on that particular source of randomness. It does not establish which alternative explanation accounts for the remaining generalization behavior.
summary.tldr: Comparisons with a closed-form loss argue against target stochasticity being a key cause of flow-matching generalization.

title: On the Closed-Form of Flow Matching: Generalization Does Not Arise from Target Stochasticity

abstract: We introduce native-resolution image synthesis, a novel paradigm in generative modeling capable of synthesizing images at arbitrary resolutions and aspect ratios. This approach overcomes the limitations of standard fixed-resolution, square-image methods by inherently handling variable-length visual tokens—a core challenge for conventional techniques. To this end, we propose the Native-resolution diffusion Transformer (NiT), an architecture that explicitly models varying resolutions and aspect ratios within its denoising process. Unconstrained by fixed formats, NiT learns intrinsic visual distributions from images encompassing a wide range of resolutions and aspect ratios. Notably, a single NiT model simultaneously achieves the state-of-the-art performance on both ImageNet-256x256 and 512x512 benchmarks. Surprisingly, akin to the robust zero-shot capabilities seen in advanced Large Language Models, NiT, pretrained solely on ImageNet, demonstrates excellent zero-shot generalization performance. It successfully generates high-fidelity images at previously unseen high resolutions (e.g., 1024x1024, 1536x1536) and diverse aspect ratios (e.g., 16:9,3:1, 4:3), as shown in Figure 1. These findings indicate the significant potential of native-resolution modeling as a bridge between visual generative modeling and advanced LLM methodologies.

A single NiT model achieves state-of-the-art performance on both the 256-by-256 and 512-by-512 ImageNet benchmarks, supporting the value of learning across resolutions in a shared model.

Examples include 1024-by-1024 and 1536-by-1536 images, as well as 16:9, 3:1, and 4:3 formats. These results demonstrate strong generalization in the evaluated settings and suggest that variable-length visual modeling could connect image generation more closely with methods used in advanced language models.
summary.tldr: NiT models varying image resolutions and aspect ratios directly, achieving strong ImageNet results and zero-shot generation at previously unseen formats.

title: Native-Resolution Image Synthesis

abstract: Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown promise in function-level code generation, yet repository-level software engineering tasks remain challenging. Current solutions predominantly rely on proprietary LLM agents, which introduce unpredictability and limit accessibility, raising concerns about data privacy and model customization. This paper investigates whether open-source LLMs can effectively address repository-level tasks without requiring agent-based approaches. We demonstrate this is possible by enabling LLMs to comprehend functions and files within codebases through their semantic information and structural dependencies. To this end, we introduce Code Graph Models (CGMs), which integrate repository code graph structures into the LLM's attention mechanism and map node attributes to the LLM's input space using a specialized adapter. When combined with an agentless graph RAG framework, our approach achieves a 43.00% resolution rate on the SWE-bench Lite benchmark using the open-source Qwen2.5-72B model. This performance ranks first among open weight models, second among methods with open-source systems, and eighth overall, surpassing the previous best open-source model-based method by 12.33%.

paragraphs: Repository-level software tasks require understanding how functions and files fit together, beyond generating a single function in isolation. This paper investigates whether open-source language models can handle such tasks without an agent-based approach. Its central idea is to expose both the meaning of code and the structural dependencies connecting a repository.

Code Graph Models incorporate a repository’s graph structure directly into the language model’s attention mechanism. A specialized adapter translates attributes of graph nodes into the model’s input space. The resulting model is paired with an agentless graph retrieval-augmented generation framework, connecting graph-informed representation with retrieval of repository information for the task.

Using Qwen2.5-72B, the combined system achieves a 43.00% resolution rate on SWE-bench Lite. The abstract reports first place among open-weight models, second among methods with open-source systems, and eighth overall in its comparison. These results support the feasibility of repository-level problem solving with an open model and explicit code structure, while directly evaluating the combined model-and-retrieval approach.
summary.tldr: CGM integrates repository graphs into a language model and achieves 43.00% resolution on SWE-bench Lite with agentless graph retrieval.

title: Code Graph Model (CGM): A Graph-Integrated Large Language Model for Repository-Level Software Engineering Tasks

abstract: Biological brains demonstrate complex neural activity, where neural dynamics are critical to how brains process information. Most artificial neural networks ignore the complexity of individual neurons. We challenge that paradigm. By incorporating neuron-level processing and synchronization, we reintroduce neural timing as a foundational element. We present the Continuous Thought Machine (CTM), a model designed to leverage neural dynamics as its core representation. The CTM has two innovations: (1) neuron-level temporal processing}, where each neuron uses unique weight parameters to process incoming histories; and (2) neural synchronization as a latent representation. The CTM aims to strike a balance between neuron abstractions and biological realism. It operates at a level of abstraction that effectively captures essential temporal dynamics while remaining computationally tractable. We demonstrate the CTM's performance and versatility across a range of tasks, including solving 2D mazes, ImageNet-1K classification, parity computation, and more. Beyond displaying rich internal representations and offering a natural avenue for interpretation owing to its internal process, the CTM is able to perform tasks that require complex sequential reasoning. The CTM can also leverage adaptive compute, where it can stop earlier for simpler tasks, or keep computing when faced with more challenging instances. The goal of this work is to share the CTM and its associated innovations, rather than pushing for new state-of-the-art results. To that end, we believe the CTM represents a significant step toward developing more biologically plausible and powerful artificial intelligence systems. We provide an accompanying [interactive online demonstration](https://pub.sakana.ai/ctm/) and an [extended technical report](https://pub.sakana.ai/ctm/paper).

title: Continuous Thought Machines

abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) enhances large language models (LLMs) by integrating external knowledge, yet traditional RAG systems struggle with static workflows and limited adaptability for complex, multistep reasoning tasks. Agentic RAG systems, such as DeepResearch, address these issues through dynamic retrieval, iterative context refinement, and adaptive workflows. However, recent methods like Search-R1, which rely on outcome-based reinforcement learning, face challenges such as low exploration efficiency, gradient conflict, and sparse reward signals. To tackle these limitations, we introduce ReasonRAG, a novel method that leverages RAG-ProGUIDE—a high-quality dataset providing fine-grained, process-level rewards for query generation, evidence extraction, and answer generation. By employing process-supervised reinforcement learning, ReasonRAG enhances LLMs’ autonomous capabilities in search, query generation, evidence extraction, and answer synthesis. Experimental results show that ReasonRAG, utilizing RAG-ProGUIDE, outperforms existing approaches like Search-R1 and traditional RAG systems, achieving superior performance on five benchmark datasets with only 5k training instances—significantly fewer than the 90k required by Search-R1. Our code is available at https://github.com/Applied-Machine-Learning-Lab/ReasonRAG.

paragraphs: Agentic retrieval-augmented generation lets a model search, revise its context, and adapt its workflow while answering a question. Training such a system only on final outcomes can provide sparse feedback and make exploration inefficient. This paper studies a more detailed training signal that evaluates intermediate parts of the retrieval and reasoning process.

ReasonRAG uses RAG-ProGUIDE, a dataset containing fine-grained process rewards for query generation, evidence extraction, and answer generation. Process-supervised reinforcement learning uses these signals to improve the model’s autonomous search and synthesis abilities. This makes feedback available for distinct stages of the workflow, connecting the training objective to the decisions the agent makes along the way.

Across five benchmark datasets, ReasonRAG outperforms Search-R1 and traditional RAG systems using 5,000 training instances, compared with the 90,000 cited for Search-R1. The results support the value of process supervision in the evaluated agentic RAG setting. They demonstrate stronger performance with substantially fewer training examples for this method and dataset combination.
summary.tldr: ReasonRAG uses rewards for intermediate retrieval steps to outperform tested alternatives with 5,000 training instances.

title: Process vs. Outcome Reward: Which is Better for Agentic RAG Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Generative steganography has emerged as an active research area, yet its practical system is constrained by the inherent secret payload limitation caused by low entropy in generating stego texts. This payload limitation necessitates the use of lengthy stego texts or frequent transmissions, which increases the risk of suspicion by adversaries. Previous studies have mainly focused on payload enhancement through optimized entropy utilization while overlooking the crucial role of secret message processing. To address this gap, we propose StegoZip, a framework that leverages large language models to optimize secret message processing. StegoZip consists of two core components: semantic redundancy pruning and index-based compression coding. The former dynamically prunes the secret message to extract a low-semantic representation, whereas the latter further compresses it into compact binary codes. When integrated with state-of-the-art steganographic methods under lossless decoding, StegoZip achieves 2.5$\times$ the payload of the baselines while maintaining comparable processing time in practice. This enhanced payload significantly improves covertness by mitigating the risks associated with frequent transmissions while maintaining provable content security.

A low payload can require longer texts or more transmissions, increasing opportunities for suspicion. StegoZip approaches this capacity problem by processing the secret message before it is embedded.

The framework uses large language models in two complementary stages. Semantic redundancy pruning extracts a reduced representation of the message, and index-based compression coding turns that representation into compact binary codes. The aim is to reduce the space required for the secret itself, complementing previous work that focused on using the generated text’s available entropy more efficiently.

When combined with state-of-the-art steganographic methods under lossless decoding, StegoZip delivers 2.5 times the baseline payload with comparable practical processing time. The authors also report maintained provable content security and improved covertness through reduced transmission needs. These claims distinguish recovering the message and protecting its content from the operational benefit of carrying more information per transmission.
summary.tldr: StegoZip compresses secret messages before embedding, achieving 2.5 times the baseline payload under lossless decoding with comparable processing time.

title: StegoZip: Enhancing Linguistic Steganography Payload in Practice with Large Language Models

abstract: The matrix recovery (completion) problem, a central problem in data science, involves recovering a matrix $A$ from a relatively small random set of entries. While such a task is generally impossible, it has been shown that one can recover $A$ exactly in polynomial time, with high probability, under three basic and necessary assumptions: (1) the rank of $A$ is very small compared to its dimensions (low rank), (2) $A$ has delocalized singular vectors (incoherence), and (3) the sample size is sufficiently large. Various algorithms address this task, including convex optimization by Candes, Recht, and Tao (2009, 2010), alternating projection by Hardt and Wooters (2014), and low-rank approximation with gradient descent by Keshavan, Montanari, and Oh (2009, 2010). In applications, Candes and Plan (2009) noted that it is more realistic to assume noisy observations. In such cases, the above approaches provide approximate recovery with small root mean square error, which is difficult to convert into exact recovery. Recently, results by Abbe et al. (2017) and Bhardwaj et al. (2023) on approximation in the infinity norm showed that one can recover $A$ even in the noisy case, provided $A$ has bounded precision. However, beyond the three basic assumptions, they either required that the condition number of $A$ be small (2017) or that the gaps between consecutive singular values be large (2023). These additional assumptions conflict, with one requiring singular values to be close together and the other suggesting they should be far apart. It is thus natural to conjecture that neither is necessary. In this paper, we demonstrate that this is indeed the case. We propose a simple algorithm for exact recovery of noisy data, relying solely on the three basic assumptions. The core step of the algorithm is a straightforward truncated singular value decomposition, which is highly efficient. To analyze the algorithm, we prove a new infinity norm version of the classical Davis-Kahan perturbation theorem, improving an earlier result in (2023). Our proof employs a combinatorial contour integration argument and is entirely distinct from all previous approaches.

The underlying setting requires low rank, sufficiently spread-out singular vectors, and enough observations. For noisy data, bounded precision is also central to the exact-recovery discussion: the target entries have limited precision rather than arbitrary real-valued detail.

Those restrictions included either a small condition number or large gaps between successive singular values. Its main computational step is truncated singular value decomposition, giving the proposed algorithm a simple and efficient core.

Entrywise control matters because a small average error can still hide individual mistakes that obstruct exact recovery. The result strengthens the recovery analysis while retaining the basic structural and sampling setting described in the abstract.
summary.tldr: An efficient matrix-recovery method removes extra singular-value restrictions from exact recovery in the noisy, bounded-precision setting.

title: Fast exact recovery of noisy matrix from few entries: the infinity norm approach

abstract: Sign Language Translation (SLT) aims to map sign language videos to spoken language text. A common approach relies on gloss annotations as an intermediate representation, decomposing SLT into two sub-tasks: video-to-gloss recognition and gloss-to-text translation. While effective, this paradigm depends on expert-annotated gloss labels, which are costly and rarely available in existing datasets, limiting its scalability. To address this challenge, we propose a gloss-free pseudo gloss generation framework that eliminates the need for human-annotated glosses while preserving the structured intermediate representation. Specifically, we prompt a Large Language Model (LLM) with a few example text-gloss pairs using in-context learning to produce draft sign glosses from spoken language text. To enhance the correspondence between LLM-generated pseudo glosses and the sign sequences in video, we correct the ordering in the pseudo glosses for better alignment via a weakly supervised learning process. This reordering facilitates the incorporation of auxiliary alignment objectives, and allows for the use of efficient supervision via a Connectionist Temporal Classification (CTC) loss. We train our SLT model—consisting of a vision encoder and a translator—through a three-stage pipeline, which progressively narrows the modality gap between sign language and spoken language. Despite its simplicity, our approach outperforms previous state-of-the-art gloss-free frameworks on two SLT benchmarks and achieves competitive results compared to gloss-based methods.

This structure helps divide translation into manageable stages, but collecting expert gloss annotations is expensive. The paper develops a framework that generates pseudo glosses so a translation model can retain an intermediate structure without requiring human gloss annotations for its training videos.

Because the generated ordering may not match the signs in a video, a weakly supervised process then reorders the pseudo glosses.
