The findings suggest that automatically constructed, corrected intermediate labels can recover useful structure while reducing dependence on costly annotations.
summary.tldr: LLM-generated pseudo glosses, reordered to align with sign videos, improve translation without requiring expert gloss annotations for the training videos.

title: Bridging Sign and Spoken Languages: Pseudo Gloss Generation for Sign Language Translation

abstract: Foundation models demand advanced data processing for their vast, multimodal datasets.However, traditional frameworks struggle with the unique complexities of multimodal data.In response, we present Data-Juicer 2.0, a data processing system backed by 100+ data processing operators spanning text, image, video, and audio modalities, supporting more critical tasks including data analysis, synthesis, annotation, and foundation model post-training.With seamless compatibility and dedicated optimization for popular dataset hubs like Hugging Face and computing engines like Ray, it improves upon its predecessor in terms of usability, efficiency, and programmability.It features an easily accessible user interface layer that supports decoupled Python interactions, RESTful APIs, and conversational commands. Its new runtime layer offers adaptive execution across diverse scales and environments, abstracting away system complexities.Extensive empirical evaluations demonstrate Data-Juicer 2.0's remarkable performance and scalability, highlighting its capability to efficiently process TB-level data with 10k+ CPU cores. The system is publicly available and has been widely adopted in diverse research fields and real-world products such as Alibaba Cloud PAI. We actively maintain the system and share practical insights to foster research and applications of next-generation foundation models.

paragraphs: Foundation models require processing large collections of text, images, video, and audio. Supporting all of these formats introduces demands that traditional data frameworks struggle to meet. Data-Juicer 2.0 provides a system for this work, with more than 100 processing operators covering analysis, synthesis, annotation, and tasks associated with model post-training.

The system combines several ways to express processing work with a runtime that adapts execution to different environments and scales. Users can interact through Python, REST APIs, or conversational commands. Compatibility and targeted optimizations for resources such as Hugging Face datasets and the Ray computing engine help connect those interfaces to existing data and computing infrastructure.

Empirical evaluations demonstrate processing at terabyte scale using more than 10,000 CPU cores. The authors report improvements over the previous version in usability, efficiency, and programmability, alongside adoption in research and products including Alibaba Cloud PAI. The contribution links multimodal processing functionality with execution infrastructure, so that the same system supports both defining data operations and carrying them out at substantial scale.
summary.tldr: Data-Juicer 2.0 combines multimodal processing tools with adaptive execution for foundation-model data workflows at cloud scale.

title: Data-Juicer 2.0: Cloud-Scale Adaptive Data Processing for and with Foundation Models

abstract: Pause tokens, simple filler symbols such as "...", consistently improve Transformer performance on both language and mathematical tasks, yet their theoretical effect remains unexplained. We provide the first formal separation result, proving that adding pause tokens to constant-depth, logarithmic-width Transformers strictly increases their computational expressivity. With bounded-precision activations, Transformers without pause tokens compute only a strict subset of $\mathsf{AC}^0$ functions, while adding a polynomial number of pause tokens enables expressing the complete class. For logarithmic-precision Transformers, we show that adding pause tokens achieves expressivity equivalent to $\mathsf{TC}^0$, matching known upper bounds. Empirically, we demonstrate that two‑layer causally masked Transformers can learn parity when supplied with pause tokens, a function that they appear unable to learn without them. Our results provide a rigorous theoretical explanation for prior empirical findings, clarify how pause tokens interact with width, depth, and numeric precision, and position them as a distinct mechanism, complementary to chain-of-thought prompting, for enhancing Transformer reasoning.

paragraphs: Pause tokens are filler symbols that can improve Transformer performance without themselves supplying substantive task content. This paper gives a formal explanation for their computational effect. It studies Transformers whose depth is constant and whose width grows logarithmically, showing that adding pause tokens strictly increases expressivity.

For bounded-precision activations, models without pause tokens can compute only a strict subset of the function class AC⁰. Adding a polynomial number of pause tokens enables the complete class. Under logarithmic precision, pause tokens enable expressivity equivalent to TC⁰, matching known upper bounds. These statements depend on the specified depth, width, precision, and pause-token settings.

An empirical study also shows that two-layer causally masked Transformers can learn parity with pause tokens, while they appear unable to learn it without them. The experiment complements the formal separation without turning that observed learning difficulty into an unrestricted impossibility claim. Together, the results establish pause tokens as a computational mechanism that complements chain-of-thought prompting and clarify how their effects interact with architectural constraints.
summary.tldr: Under specified width and precision constraints, pause tokens provably expand what constant-depth Transformers can compute.

title: Pause Tokens Strictly Increase the Expressivity of Constant-Depth Transformers

abstract: In real-world decision-making problems, one needs to pick among multiple policies the one that performs best while respecting economic constraints. This motivates the problem of constrained best-arm identification for bandit problems where every arm is a joint distribution of reward and cost. We investigate the general case where reward and cost are dependent. The goal is to accurately identify the arm with the highest mean reward among all arms whose mean cost is below a given threshold. We prove information-theoretic lower bounds on the sample complexity for three models: Gaussian with fixed covariance, Gaussian with unknown covariance, and non-parametric distributions of rectangular support. We propose a combination of a sampling and a stopping rule that correctly identifies the constrained best arm and matches the optimal sample complexities for each of the three models. Simulations demonstrate the performance of our algorithms.

Simulations demonstrate the performance of our algorithms.

paragraphs: Choosing a policy often requires balancing performance against an economic constraint. This paper studies a bandit version of that problem: each available choice produces both a reward and a cost, and the objective is to identify the choice with the highest average reward among those whose average cost falls below a specified threshold.

The analysis allows reward and cost to be dependent, so their relationship is part of the statistical problem. The authors establish information-theoretic lower bounds on the number of observations needed under three distribution models: Gaussian outcomes with known covariance, Gaussian outcomes with unknown covariance, and non-parametric distributions supported within a rectangle. These bounds describe the sampling difficulty under each model.

The proposed method combines a rule for deciding what to sample with a rule for deciding when to stop. It correctly identifies the constrained best choice and matches the optimal sample complexities for the three models. Simulations demonstrate its performance. The contribution connects reliable selection under cost constraints with a precise account of how much evidence that selection requires.
summary.tldr: The paper gives sample-optimal methods for identifying the highest-reward option whose average cost satisfies a threshold, allowing dependent rewards and costs.

title: Constrained Best Arm Identification

abstract: Traditional reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms face significant limitations in handling long-term tasks with sparse rewards. Recent advancements have leveraged large language models (LLMs) to enhance RL by utilizing their world knowledge for task planning and reward generation. However, planning-based approaches often depend on pre-defined skill libraries and fail to optimize low-level control policies, while reward-based methods require extensive human feedback or exhaustive searching due to the complexity of tasks. In this paper, we propose the Progress Reward Model for RL (PRM4RL), a novel framework that integrates task planning and dense reward to enhance RL. For high-level planning, a complex task is decomposed into a series of simple manageable subtasks, with a subtask-oriented, fine-grained progress function designed to monitor task execution progress. For low-level reward generation, inspired by potential-based reward shaping, we use the progress function to construct a Progress Reward Model (PRM), providing theoretically grounded optimality and convergence guarantees, thereby enabling effective policy optimization. Experimental results on robotics control tasks demonstrate that our approach outperforms both LLM-based planning and reward methods, achieving state-of-the-art performance.

paragraphs: Long tasks with sparse rewards make reinforcement learning difficult because useful feedback may arrive only after substantial interaction. Language-model planning can help organize such tasks, but existing approaches may rely on predefined skills or leave low-level control unoptimized. PRM4RL connects high-level task decomposition with dense rewards for learning control policies.

The framework breaks a complex task into simpler subtasks and defines a fine-grained function that measures progress through them. It then uses this progress function to construct rewards, drawing on potential-based reward shaping. This links the plan to the feedback received during policy optimization, so progress toward subtasks becomes part of the learning signal.

The authors provide theoretical optimality and convergence guarantees for their progress-reward construction. In robotics-control experiments, the approach outperforms both language-model planning methods and language-model reward methods, with reported state-of-the-art performance. The contribution is the integration of planning and reward generation into a coordinated framework, supported by theoretical analysis and empirical results on the evaluated control tasks.
summary.tldr: PRM4RL turns language-model task plans into progress-based dense rewards, improving policy learning on evaluated robotics-control tasks.

title: Progress Reward Model for Reinforcement Learning via Large Language Models

abstract: Harnessing the event-driven characteristic, Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) present a promising avenue toward energy-efficient Transformer architectures. However, existing Spiking Transformers still suffer significant performance gaps compared to their Artificial Neural Network counterparts. Through comprehensive analysis, we attribute this gap to these two factors. First, the binary nature of spike trains limits Spiking Self-attention (SSA)’s capacity to capture negative–negative and positive–negative membrane potential interactions on Querys and Keys. Second, SSA typically omits Softmax functions to avoid energy-intensive multiply-accumulate operations, thereby failing to maintain row-stochasticity constraints on attention scores. To address these issues, we propose a Bipolar Self-attention (BSA) paradigm, effectively modeling multi-polar membrane potential interactions with a fully spike-driven characteristic. Specifically, we demonstrate that ternary matrix multiplication provides a closer approximation to real-valued computation on both distribution and local correlation, enabling clear differentiation between homopolar and heteropolar interactions. Moreover, we propose a shift-based Softmax approximation named Shiftmax, which efficiently achieves low-entropy activation and partly maintains row-stochasticity without non-linear operation, enabling precise attention allocation. Extensive experiments show that BSA achieves substantial performance improvements across various tasks, including image classification, semantic segmentation, and event-based tracking. These results establish its potential as a fundamental building block for energy-efficient Spiking Transformers.

paragraphs: Spiking Transformers aim to exploit event-driven computation for energy-efficient modeling, but their performance trails conventional neural Transformers. The authors identify two problems in spiking self-attention. Binary spikes cannot adequately represent interactions involving negative query and key membrane potentials. Omitting Softmax also removes the usual constraint that each attention row forms a normalized distribution.

Bipolar Self-attention addresses the first problem through ternary matrix multiplication while retaining fully spike-driven operation. The authors show that this better approximates real-valued computation in distribution and local correlation, distinguishing interactions between matching and opposing polarities. They also introduce Shiftmax, a shift-based approximation to Softmax that avoids nonlinear operations.

Shiftmax produces concentrated attention activations and partially preserves row normalization, supporting more precise allocation of attention. Experiments show substantial improvements in image classification, semantic segmentation, and event-based tracking. These results support Bipolar Self-attention as a possible building block for energy-efficient Spiking Transformers, with the normalization benefit explicitly described as partial.
summary.tldr: Bipolar Self-attention improves Spiking Transformers through signed interactions and an efficient, partially normalizing Softmax approximation.

title: Bipolar Self-attention for Spiking Transformers

abstract: We present Chain-of-Action (CoA), a novel visuomotor policy paradigm built upon Trajectory Autoregressive Modeling. Unlike conventional approaches that predict next step action(s) forward, CoA generates an entire trajectory by explicit backward reasoning with task-specific goals through an action-level Chain-of-Thought (CoT) process. This process is unified within a single autoregressive structure: (1) the first token corresponds to a stable keyframe action that encodes the task-specific goals; and (2) subsequent action tokens are generated autoregressively, conditioned on the initial keyframe and previously predicted actions. This backward action reasoning enforces a global-to-local structure, allowing each local action to be tightly constrained by the final goal. To further realize the action reasoning structure, CoA incorporates four complementary designs: continuous action token representation; dynamic stopping for variable-length trajectory generation; reverse temporal ensemble; and multi-token prediction to balance action chunk modeling with global structure. As a result, CoA gives strong spatial generalization capabilities while preserving the flexibility and simplicity of a visuomotor policy. Empirically, we observe that CoA outperforms representative imitation learning algorithms such as ACT and Diffusion Policy across 60 RLBench tasks and 8 real-world tasks.

paragraphs: Chain-of-Action changes how a robot constructs a movement trajectory from visual input. Instead of beginning with the next movement, it first generates a stable keyframe action representing the task goal. It then develops the trajectory through backward action reasoning, so the desired endpoint helps organize the intervening actions.

The entire process uses one autoregressive structure: each new action token depends on the initial goal keyframe and actions already predicted. This gives local movements a shared global reference. The design also represents actions continuously, allows generation to stop dynamically for different trajectory lengths, and incorporates reverse temporal ensembling. Multi-token prediction balances the modeling of action chunks with the overall trajectory structure.

The authors report better performance than representative imitation-learning methods, including ACT and Diffusion Policy, across 60 RLBench tasks and eight real-world tasks. They also report strong spatial generalization. The findings suggest that explicitly organizing action generation around a final goal can help a visually guided policy produce effective trajectories while retaining a relatively simple policy structure.
summary.tldr: Chain-of-Action generates robot trajectories through backward reasoning from a goal keyframe, improving manipulation performance in the reported evaluations.

title: Chain-of-Action: Trajectory Autoregressive Modeling for Robotic Manipulation

abstract: While model serving has unlocked unprecedented capabilities, the high cost of serving large-scale models continues to be a significant barrier to widespread accessibility and rapid innovation. Compiler optimizations have long driven substantial performance improvements, but existing compilers struggle with neural workloads due to the exponentially large and highly interdependent space of possible transformations. Although existing stochastic search techniques can be effective, they are often sample-inefficient and fail to leverage the structural context underlying compilation decisions. We set out to investigate the research question of whether reasoning with large language models (LLMs), without any retraining, can leverage the context-aware decision space of compiler optimizations to significantly improve sample efficiency. To that end, we introduce a novel compilation framework (dubbed Reasoning Compiler) that formulates optimization as a sequential, context-aware decision process guided by a large language model and structured Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS). The LLM acts as a proposal mechanism, suggesting hardware-informed transformations that reflect the current program state and accumulated performance feedback. MCTS incorporates the LLM-generated proposals to balance exploration and exploitation, facilitating structured, context-sensitive traversal of the expansive compiler optimization space. By achieving substantial speedups with markedly fewer samples than leading neural compilers, our approach demonstrates the potential of LLM-guided reasoning to transform the landscape of compiler optimization.

paragraphs: Compiler optimization can make neural-model serving faster, but the search space is enormous and its decisions are interdependent. A transformation that helps in one program state may interact differently with later choices. Reasoning Compiler investigates whether an existing language model can use this context to guide optimization more efficiently without retraining.

The framework treats compilation as a sequence of decisions and combines language-model proposals with Monte Carlo tree search. The language model suggests hardware-informed transformations using the current program state and accumulated performance feedback. Tree search then balances investigating new possibilities with pursuing promising choices, organizing the search around the proposals rather than exploring transformations without that guidance.

The authors report substantial speedups with markedly fewer evaluated samples than leading neural compilers. The finding supports the usefulness of language-model reasoning as a proposal mechanism within a structured search procedure. Its contribution is the combination: contextual suggestions guide the choices, while tree search manages how those choices are explored over multiple optimization steps.
summary.tldr: Reasoning Compiler combines an unretrained language model with tree search to find faster neural-program compilations using substantially fewer search samples.

title: REASONING COMPILER: LLM-Guided Optimizations for Efficient Model Serving

abstract: Diffusion models, though originally designed for generative tasks, have demonstrated impressive self-supervised representation learning capabilities. A particularly intriguing phenomenon in these models is the emergence of unimodal representation dynamics, where the quality of learned features peaks at an intermediate noise level. In this work, we conduct a comprehensive theoretical and empirical investigation of this phenomenon. Leveraging the inherent low-dimensionality structure of image data, we theoretically demonstrate that the unimodal dynamic emerges when the diffusion model successfully captures the underlying data distribution. The unimodality arises from an interplay between denoising strength and class confidence across noise scales. Empirically, we further show that, in classification tasks, the presence of unimodal dynamics reliably reflects the diffusion model’s generalization: it emerges when the model generate novel images and gradually transitions to a monotonically decreasing curve as the model begins to memorize the training data.

paragraphs: Diffusion models can learn features useful for recognition even though they are designed to generate data. A recurring observation is that feature quality peaks at an intermediate noise level, producing a curve with a single peak. This paper investigates why that pattern appears and what it reveals about the model’s learned distribution.

The theoretical analysis uses the low-dimensional structure underlying image data. It shows that the single-peaked behavior emerges when the diffusion model successfully captures the underlying distribution. The explanation involves the interaction between denoising strength and confidence about class identity across noise levels, connecting representation quality to the model’s behavior along the denoising process.

In classification experiments, the authors find that this curve also reflects generalization. The single peak appears when models generate novel images, while the curve gradually becomes monotonically decreasing as models begin memorizing training examples. The findings connect a feature-quality measurement to generative behavior, providing an empirically supported indication of generalization in the studied setting.
summary.tldr: The paper explains why diffusion features can peak at intermediate noise and finds that this pattern tracks generalization versus memorization in classification experiments.

title: Understanding Representation Dynamics of Diffusion Models via Low-Dimensional Modeling

abstract: We present TIDES, a text informed design approach for generating physically sound designs based on a textual description and a set of physical constraints. TIDES jointly optimizes structural (topology) and visual properties. A pre-trained text-image model is used to measure the design's visual alignment with a text prompt and a differentiable physics simulator is used to measure its physical performance. We evaluate TIDES on a series of structural optimization problems operating under different load and support conditions, at different resolutions, and experimentally in the lab by performing the 3-point bending test on 2D beam designs that are extruded and 3D printed. We find that it can jointly optimize the two objectives and return designs that satisfy engineering design requirements (compliance and density) while utilizing features specified by text.

paragraphs: A design described in words can have both a desired appearance and engineering requirements. TIDES addresses these objectives together, generating structures from a text description and a set of physical constraints. Its optimization changes structural topology and visual properties, so the resulting design can incorporate requested features while meeting specified mechanical requirements.

The method combines two sources of feedback. A pretrained text-image model measures visual agreement with the prompt, while a differentiable physics simulator measures physical performance. Using both within optimization connects the visual request to the structural consequences of design changes. This is the central mechanism for pursuing appearance and physical behavior together.

The authors evaluate structural optimization problems with different loads, support conditions, and resolutions. They also extrude two-dimensional beam designs, manufacture them through 3D printing, and perform laboratory three-point bending tests. Across the reported evaluation, TIDES produces designs that satisfy compliance and density requirements while using text-specified features. These results demonstrate joint optimization of the two objectives in the structural design settings studied.
summary.tldr: TIDES combines text-image guidance with differentiable physics to generate structures that incorporate requested visual features and meet engineering requirements.

title: Generating Physically Sound Designs from Text and a Set of Physical Constraints

abstract: This position paper argues that post-deployment monitoring in clinical AI is underdeveloped and proposes statistically valid and label-efficient testing frameworks as a principled foundation for ensuring reliability and safety in real-world deployment. A recent review found that only 9\% of FDA-registered AI-based healthcare tools include a post-deployment surveillance plan. Existing monitoring approaches are often manual, sporadic, and reactive, making them ill-suited for the dynamic environments in which clinical models operate. We contend that post-deployment monitoring should be grounded in label-efficient and statistically valid testing frameworks, offering a principled alternative to current practices. We use the term "statistically valid" to refer to methods that provide explicit guarantees on error rates (e.g., Type I/II error), enable formal inference under pre-defined assumptions, and support reproducibility—features that align with regulatory requirements. Specifically, we propose that the detection of changes in the data and model performance degradation should be framed as distinct statistical hypothesis testing problems. Grounding monitoring in statistical rigor ensures a reproducible and scientifically sound basis for maintaining the reliability of clinical AI systems. Importantly, it also opens new research directions for the technical community---spanning theory, methods, and tools for statistically principled detection, attribution, and mitigation of post-deployment model failures in real-world settings.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that clinical AI needs a stronger statistical foundation for monitoring after deployment. It cites a review in which only 9% of FDA-registered AI-based healthcare tools included a surveillance plan. Manual, occasional, reactive checks are presented as poorly suited to the changing environments where clinical models operate.

The proposed foundation is label-efficient statistical testing with explicit error-rate guarantees, inference under predefined assumptions, and reproducible procedures. The authors distinguish detecting changes in incoming data from detecting deterioration in model performance. Framing these as separate hypothesis-testing problems makes clear that they ask different questions and should have their own statistical treatment.

The paper's contribution is a methodological position and research agenda. It calls for monitoring methods that provide a reproducible basis for assessing reliability while limiting labeling demands. It also identifies opportunities to develop theory and tools for detecting failures, attributing their causes, and mitigating their effects. The proposed guarantees depend on stated assumptions, making those assumptions part of the monitoring framework.
summary.tldr: The paper argues for label-efficient, statistically valid monitoring that separately tests for data changes and clinical AI performance degradation.

title: Statistically Valid Post-Deployment Monitoring Should Be Standard for AI-Based Digital Health

abstract: Graphs are complex, non-Euclidean structures that require specialized models, such as Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), Graph Transformers, or kernel-based approaches, to effectively capture their relational patterns. This inherent complexity makes explaining GNNs decisions particularly challenging. Most existing explainable AI (XAI) methods for GNNs focus on identifying influential nodes or extracting subgraphs that highlight relevant motifs. However, these approaches often fall short of clarifying how such elements contribute to the final prediction. To overcome this limitation, logic-based explanations aim to derive explicit logical rules that reflect the model's decision-making process. Current logic-based methods are limited to post-hoc analyzes and are predominantly applied to graph classification, leaving a significant gap in intrinsically explainable GNN architectures. In this paper, we explore the potential of integrating logic reasoning directly into graph learning. We introduce LogiX-GIN, a novel, self-explainable GNN architecture that incorporates logic layers to produce interpretable logical rules as part of the learning process. Unlike post-hoc methods, LogiX-GIN provides faithful, transparent, and inherently interpretable explanations aligned with the model's internal computations. We evaluate LogiX-GIN across several graph-based tasks and show that it achieves competitive predictive performance while delivering clear, logic-based insights into its decision-making process.

Current logic-based methods are limited to post-hoc analyzes and are predominantly applied to graph classification, leaving a significant gap in intrinsically explainable GNN architectures. In this paper, we explore the potential of integrating logic reasoning directly into graph learning. We introduce LogiX-GIN, a novel, self-explainable GNN architecture that incorporates logic layers to produce interpretable logical rules as part of the learning process. Unlike post-hoc methods, LogiX-GIN provides faithful, transparent, and inherently interpretable explanations aligned with the model's internal computations. We evaluate LogiX-GIN across several graph-based tasks and show that it achieves competitive predictive performance while delivering clear, logic-based insights into its decision-making process.

paragraphs: Explaining a graph neural network often means highlighting influential nodes or subgraphs. Such highlights can show where relevant information lies without explaining how it supports the prediction. This paper investigates logical rules as a more explicit description of the decision process, focusing on explanations produced within the model's own learning architecture.

The proposed model, LogiX-GIN, incorporates logic layers into a graph neural network. These layers generate interpretable rules as part of learning, linking the explanation to the computations used for prediction. This addresses a gap in existing logic-based approaches, which the abstract describes as predominantly post-hoc analyses focused on graph classification.

Across several graph-based tasks, LogiX-GIN achieves competitive predictive performance while providing clear logical explanations. The authors characterize these explanations as faithful and aligned with the model's internal operations. The contribution is therefore an architecture that combines graph prediction and rule-based explanation within the same process, with experiments supporting the possibility of retaining useful predictive performance alongside this form of interpretability.
summary.tldr: LogiX-GIN embeds logic layers in a graph neural network so its predictions come with rules aligned with its internal computations.

title: On Logic-based Self-Explainable Graph Neural Networks

abstract: Recent progress in vision-language modeling for 3D medical imaging has been fueled by large-scale computed tomography (CT) corpora with paired free-text reports, stronger architectures, and powerful pretrained models. This has enabled applications such as automated report generation and text-conditioned 3D image synthesis. Yet, current approaches struggle with high-resolution, long-sequence volumes: contrastive pretraining often yields vision encoders that are misaligned with clinical language, and slice-wise tokenization blurs fine anatomy, reducing diagnostic performance on downstream tasks. We introduce BTB3D (Better Tokens for Better 3D), a causal convolutional encoder-decoder that unifies 2D and 3D training and inference while producing compact, frequency-aware volumetric tokens. A three-stage training curriculum enables (i) local reconstruction, (ii) overlapping-window tiling, and (iii) long-context decoder refinement, during which the model learns from short slice excerpts yet generalizes to scans exceeding $300$ slices without additional memory overhead. BTB3D sets a new state-of-the-art on two key tasks: it improves BLEU scores and increases clinical F1 by 40\% over CT2Rep, CT-CHAT, and Merlin for report generation; and it reduces FID by 75\% and halves FVD compared to GenerateCT and MedSyn for text-to-CT synthesis, producing anatomically consistent $512\times512\times241$ volumes. These results confirm that precise three-dimensional tokenization, rather than larger language backbones alone, is essential for scalable vision-language modeling in 3D medical imaging. The codebase is available at: https://github.com/ibrahimethemhamamci/BTB3D

title: Better Tokens for Better 3D: Advancing Vision-Language Modeling in 3D Medical Imaging

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel at zero-shot inference but continue to struggle with complex, multi-step reasoning. Recent methods that augment LLMs with intermediate reasoning steps such as Chain of Thought (CoT) and Program of Thought (PoT) improve performance but often produce undesirable solutions, especially in algorithmic domains. We introduce Per-Instance Program Synthesis (PIPS), a method that generates and refines programs at the instance level using structural feedback without relying on task-specific guidance or explicit test cases. To further improve performance, PIPS incorporates a confidence metric that dynamically chooses between direct inference and program synthesis on a per-instance basis. Experiments across three frontier LLMs and 30 benchmarks including all tasks of Big Bench Extra Hard (BBEH), visual question answering tasks, relational reasoning tasks, and mathematical reasoning tasks show that PIPS improves the absolute harmonic mean accuracy by up to 8.6\% and 9.4\% compared to PoT and CoT respectively, and reduces undesirable program generations by 65.1\% on the algorithmic tasks compared to PoT with Gemini-2.0-Flash.

paragraphs: Intermediate reasoning can improve language-model performance, but generated reasoning or programs can still produce undesirable solutions, particularly on algorithmic tasks. Per-Instance Program Synthesis addresses this by constructing and refining a program for the particular input being solved. The refinement uses structural feedback without requiring task-specific guidance or explicit test cases.

PIPS also includes a confidence measure that chooses between answering directly and using program synthesis for each instance. This makes the use of generated programs adaptive to the input. The method combines a refinement process with a decision about when that process should be used.

Experiments span three frontier language models and 30 benchmarks, covering difficult general reasoning, visual questions, relational reasoning, and mathematics. The reported absolute harmonic mean accuracy gains reach 8.6% over Program of Thought and 9.4% over Chain of Thought. On algorithmic tasks with Gemini-2.0-Flash, undesirable program generations fall by 65.1% relative to Program of Thought. These results support both improved accuracy and better program behavior in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: PIPS adaptively generates and refines programs for individual inputs, improving reasoning accuracy and reducing undesirable program outputs.

title: Once Upon an Input: Reasoning via Per-Instance Program Synthesis

abstract: Morphing is a long-standing problem in vision and computer graphics, requir- ing a time-dependent warping for feature alignment and a blending for smooth interpolation. Recently, multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) have been explored as implicit neural representations (INRs) for modeling such deformations, due to their meshlessness and differentiability; however, extracting coherent and accurate morphings from standard MLPs typically relies on costly regularizations, which often lead to unstable training and prevent effective feature alignment. To overcome these limitations, we propose FLOWING (FLOW morphING), a framework that recasts warping as the construction of a differential vector flow, naturally ensuring continuity, invertibility, and temporal coherence by encoding structural flow prop- erties directly into the network architectures. This flow-centric approach yields principled and stable transformations, enabling accurate and structure-preserving morphing of both 2D images and 3D shapes. Extensive experiments across a range of applications—including face and image morphing, as well as Gaussian Splatting morphing—show that FLOWING achieves state-of-the-art morphing quality with faster convergence. Code and pretrained models are available in https://schardong.github.io/flowing.
authors: João Paulo Silva do Monte Lima

paragraphs: FLOWING addresses morphing between images or shapes, where corresponding features must move into alignment while appearance changes smoothly over time. Neural representations based on multilayer perceptrons offer differentiable, mesh-free deformation models. However, the paper identifies costly regularization, unstable training, and poor feature alignment as obstacles when standard networks are used to produce coherent morphing sequences.

The proposed framework represents warping through a differential vector flow. It encodes structural properties of that flow directly into the network architecture, ensuring continuity, invertibility, and coherence over time. This design makes the transformation’s structure part of the representation itself, reducing dependence on costly regularization to obtain a well-behaved deformation.

These findings support the value of designing neural deformation architectures around flow properties: the same structural choices underpin both stable transformations and effective feature alignment.
summary.tldr: FLOWING builds structural flow properties into neural architectures to produce coherent image and shape morphing with faster convergence.

title: FLOWING: Implicit Neural Flows for Structure-Preserving Morphing

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in sensitive domains, where their ability to infer personal data from seemingly benign text introduces emerging privacy risks. While recent LLM-based anonymization methods help mitigate such risks, they often rely on proprietary models (e.g., GPT-4), raising concerns about cost and the potential exposure of sensitive data to untrusted external systems. To address this, we introduce $\textit{SElf-refining Anonymization with Language model}$ (SEAL), a novel distillation framework for training small language models (SLMs) to perform effective anonymization without relying on external models at inference time. SEAL leverages adversarial interactions between an LLM anonymizer and an inference model to collect trajectories of anonymized texts and inferred attributes, which are then used to distill anonymization and critique capabilities into SLMs through supervised fine-tuning and preference learning. The resulting models learn both to anonymize text and to evaluate their outputs, enabling iterative improvement of anonymization quality via self-refinement. Experiments on SynthPAI, a dataset of synthetic personal profiles and text comments, demonstrate that SLMs trained with SEAL achieve substantial improvements in anonymization capabilities. Notably, 8B models attain a privacy-utility trade-off comparable to that of the GPT-4 anonymizer and, with self-refinement, even surpass it in terms of privacy protection. These results highlight the effectiveness of our adversarial distillation framework for training SLMs as efficient anonymizers.

paragraphs: Language models can infer personal attributes from text that appears innocuous, creating a challenge for anonymization. Existing model-based anonymizers may rely on proprietary services, bringing cost and data-exposure concerns. SEAL trains smaller models to anonymize and critique text without needing external models during inference.

These interactions produce sequences of revised texts and inferred attributes. With self-refinement, they surpass it on privacy protection. The findings support distilling an interactive anonymization process into a smaller model, with the reported comparison grounded specifically in the synthetic-profile evaluation.
summary.tldr: SEAL distills anonymization and self-critique into smaller models that achieve strong privacy protection on synthetic-profile evaluations.

title: Self-Refining Language Model Anonymizers via Adversarial Distillation

abstract: Time-series anomaly detection is critical for ensuring safety in high-stakes applications, where robustness is a fundamental requirement rather than a mere performance metric. Addressing the vulnerability of these systems to adversarial manipulation is therefore essential. Existing defenses are largely heuristic or provide certified robustness only under $\ell_p$-norm constraints, which are incompatible with time-series data. In particular, $\ell_p$-norm fails to capture the intrinsic temporal structure in time series, causing small temporal distortions to significantly alter the $\ell_p$-norm measures. Instead, the similarity metric Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) is more suitable and widely adopted in the time-series domain, as DTW accounts for temporal alignment and remains robust to temporal variations. To date, however, there has been no certifiable robustness result in this metric that provides guarantees. In this work, we introduce the first DTW-certified robust defense in time-series anomaly detection by adapting the randomized smoothing paradigm. We develop this certificate by bridging the $\ell_p$-norm to DTW distance through a lower-bound transformation. Extensive experiments across various datasets and models validate the effectiveness and practicality of our theoretical approach. Results demonstrate significantly improved performance, e.g., up to 18.7\% in F1-score under DTW-based adversarial attacks compared to traditional certified models.

paragraphs: Time-series anomaly detectors can be manipulated by changes to their inputs. A complication is that a small shift in timing can look large under ordinary point-by-point distance measures. Dynamic Time Warping, or DTW, instead compares sequences while accounting for temporal alignment, making it a relevant measure for this kind of robustness.

The paper develops a certified defense for anomaly detection under DTW. It adapts randomized smoothing and builds a mathematical connection from norm-based distances to DTW through a lower-bound transformation. This connection allows the authors to establish a robustness certificate in a metric that reflects temporal variation, extending beyond defenses justified only under conventional norm constraints.

Under DTW-based adversarial attacks, the authors report F1-score improvements of up to 18.7% over traditional certified models. The stated contribution combines a theoretical guarantee with empirical evidence: certification addresses robustness within the DTW framework, while the experiments show how the proposed defense performs under the evaluated attacks.
summary.tldr: The paper adapts randomized smoothing to certify time-series anomaly detection robustness using Dynamic Time Warping distance.

title: Fortifying Time Series: DTW-Certified Robust Anomaly Detection

abstract: State Space Models (SSMs) have emerged as promising alternatives to attention mechanisms, with the Mamba architecture demonstrating impressive performance and linear complexity for processing long sequences. However, the fundamental differences between Mamba and Transformer architectures remain incompletely understood. In this work, we use carefully designed synthetic tasks to reveal Mamba's inherent limitations. Through experiments, we identify that Mamba's nonlinear convolution introduces an asymmetry bias that significantly impairs its ability to recognize symmetrical patterns and relationships. Using composite function and inverse sequence matching tasks, we demonstrate that Mamba strongly favors compositional solutions over symmetrical ones and struggles with tasks requiring the matching of reversed sequences. We show these limitations stem not from the SSM module itself but from the nonlinear convolution preceding it, which fuses token information asymmetrically. These insights provide a new understanding of Mamba's constraints and suggest concrete architectural improvements for future sequence models.

However, the fundamental differences between Mamba and Transformer architectures remain incompletely understood. In this work, we use carefully designed synthetic tasks to reveal Mamba's inherent limitations. Through experiments, we identify that Mamba's nonlinear convolution introduces an asymmetry bias that significantly impairs its ability to recognize symmetrical patterns and relationships. paragraphs: Mamba offers linear-complexity processing of long sequences, making it a promising alternative to attention-based architectures. This paper uses deliberately constructed synthetic tasks to investigate a more specific question: which kinds of relationships does its architecture find difficult to recognize? The emphasis is on understanding architectural behavior through controlled tasks.

The experiments examine composite functions and matching sequences presented in reverse order. The authors find that Mamba strongly favors compositional solutions and has difficulty with symmetrical relationships, including reversed-sequence matching. They attribute this asymmetry bias to the nonlinear convolution that combines token information before it reaches the state-space module.

That attribution is the central finding: the reported difficulty comes from how information is fused before state-space processing, rather than from the state-space module itself. It identifies a concrete component to reconsider when designing sequence models that must handle symmetry. Because the evidence comes from carefully designed synthetic tasks, the findings describe specific architectural difficulties rather than establishing a universal performance ranking between Mamba and Transformers.
summary.tldr: Synthetic tasks identify Mamba’s preceding nonlinear convolution as a source of difficulty with symmetry and reversed-sequence matching.

title: Achilles' Heel of Mamba: Essential difficulties of the Mamba architecture demonstrated by synthetic data

abstract: Low rank matrix recovery is a fundamental task in many real-world applications. The performance of existing methods, however, deteriorates significantly when applied to ill-conditioned or large-scale matrices. In this paper, we therefore propose an efficient method, called Riemannian Pursuit (RP), that aims to address these two problems simultaneously. Our method consists of a sequence of fixed-rank optimization problems. Each subproblem, solved by a nonlinear Riemannian conjugate gradient method, aims to correct the solution in the most important subspace of increasing size. Theoretically, RP converges linearly under mild conditions and experimental results show that it substantially outperforms existing methods when applied to large-scale and ill-conditioned matrices.

paragraphs: Recovering a low-rank matrix is useful across many applications, but existing methods can deteriorate when matrices are large or ill-conditioned. This paper proposes Riemannian Pursuit to address both difficulties together. The approach organizes recovery as a sequence of optimization problems with progressively increasing rank.

Each stage fixes the rank and uses a nonlinear Riemannian conjugate gradient method to improve the current solution. The correction focuses on an important subspace whose size increases over the sequence. This makes recovery a process of refining a constrained representation and then expanding the space in which further improvements can be made.

The authors prove linear convergence under conditions they describe as mild. They also report substantial experimental improvements over existing methods on large-scale and ill-conditioned matrices. The theoretical result concerns the rate of progress under its conditions, while the experiments demonstrate the method’s practical behavior on the difficult matrix settings that motivated it. Together, they support combining fixed-rank refinement with progressive subspace expansion.
summary.tldr: Riemannian Pursuit progressively expands fixed-rank optimization subproblems to recover large and ill-conditioned matrices efficiently.

title: Riemannian Pursuit for Big Matrix Recovery

abstract: We consider an online optimization problem on a subset S of R^n (not necessarily convex), in which a decision maker chooses, at each iteration t, a probability distribution x^(t) over S, and seeks to minimize a cumulative expected loss, where each loss is a Lipschitz function revealed at the end of iteration t. Building on previous work, we propose a generalized Hedge algorithm and show a O(\sqrtt \log t) bound on the regret when the losses are uniformly Lipschitz and S is uniformly fat (a weaker condition than convexity). Finally, we propose a generalization to the dual averaging method on the set of Lebesgue-continuous distributions over S.

paragraphs: This paper studies online decisions over a continuous set of possible choices. At each iteration, the decision maker selects a probability distribution over a subset of Euclidean space, then learns the loss function afterward. The aim is to control cumulative expected loss despite having to choose before seeing that iteration’s loss.

The authors generalize Hedge to this setting and prove a regret bound of O(√t log t). The guarantee requires uniformly Lipschitz losses and a uniformly fat decision set. Uniform fatness is weaker than convexity, so the result applies to some nonconvex sets as well. It does not require convexity, but it still depends on a stated geometric condition.

The sublinear growth of the bound means the corresponding regret per iteration decreases as the number of iterations grows under those assumptions. The paper also generalizes dual averaging to Lebesgue-continuous distributions over the decision set. Together, the contributions extend distribution-based online optimization to continuous domains while making explicit the regularity conditions supporting the regret guarantee.
summary.tldr: A continuous-domain Hedge algorithm achieves O(√t log t) regret under uniform Lipschitz and geometric fatness assumptions.

title: The Hedge Algorithm on a Continuum

abstract: How does coarsening affect the spectrum of a general graph? We provide conditions such that the principal eigenvalues and eigenspaces of a coarsened and original graph Laplacian matrices are close. The achieved approximation is shown to depend on standard graph-theoretic properties, such as the degree and eigenvalue distributions, as well as on the ratio between the coarsened and actual graph sizes. Our results carry implications for learning methods that utilize coarsening. For the particular case of spectral clustering, they imply that coarse eigenvectors can be used to derive good quality assignments even without refinement{—}this phenomenon was previously observed, but lacked formal justification.

paragraphs: Graph coarsening replaces a large graph with a smaller representation, making it important to understand which mathematical properties survive that reduction. This paper focuses on the graph Laplacian’s spectrum. It provides conditions under which principal eigenvalues and eigenspaces of the smaller graph remain close to those of the original graph.

The quality of the approximation depends on recognizable graph properties, including degree distributions and eigenvalue distributions. It also depends on the size of the coarsened graph relative to the original. These dependencies connect the reliability of the smaller representation to both the graph’s structure and the amount of reduction, rather than treating all coarsening choices as equivalent.

For spectral clustering, the results imply that eigenvectors computed on the coarse graph can yield good cluster assignments without an additional refinement stage under the relevant conditions. This gives formal support to a phenomenon previously observed in practice. The contribution helps explain when learning methods can use a smaller graph while retaining the spectral information that their outputs depend on.
summary.tldr: The paper gives conditions for graph coarsening to preserve key spectral information and support good clustering assignments without refinement.

title: Spectrally Approximating Large Graphs with Smaller Graphs

abstract: Patients in the intensive care unit (ICU) require constant and close supervision. To assist clinical staff in this task, hospitals use monitoring systems that trigger audiovisual alarms if their algorithms indicate that a patient’s condition may be worsening. However, current monitoring systems are extremely sensitive to movement artefacts and technical errors. As a result, they typically trigger hundreds to thousands of false alarms per patient per day - drowning the important alarms in noise and adding to the exhaustion of clinical staff. In this setting, data is abundantly available, but obtaining trustworthy annotations by experts is laborious and expensive. We frame the problem of false alarm reduction from multivariate time series as a machine-learning task and address it with a novel multitask network architecture that utilises distant supervision through multiple related auxiliary tasks in order to reduce the number of expensive labels required for training. We show that our approach leads to significant improvements over several state-of-the-art baselines on real-world ICU data and provide new insights on the importance of task selection and architectural choices in distantly supervised multitask learning.

paragraphs: ICU monitoring systems can mistake movement artifacts and technical errors for signs of deterioration, producing large numbers of false alarms. These alarms can obscure important warnings and exhaust clinical staff. This paper treats false-alarm reduction as a learning problem over multivariate time series, where data are plentiful but reliable expert annotations are expensive.

The proposed multitask network draws on distant supervision from several related auxiliary tasks. Its purpose is to reduce dependence on costly labels for the main alarm-reduction task. This makes the relationship between tasks central to training: auxiliary supervision supplies additional learning signals when direct expert annotation is difficult to obtain.

On real ICU data, the authors report significant improvements over several state-of-the-art baselines. They also examine the importance of auxiliary-task selection and network architecture in distantly supervised multitask learning. The contribution therefore includes both an alarm-reduction approach and evidence about how to design learning systems that use related tasks to make better use of limited expert labels.
summary.tldr: A distantly supervised multitask network improves ICU false-alarm reduction while reducing reliance on expensive expert labels.

title: Not to Cry Wolf: Distantly Supervised Multitask Learning in Critical Care

abstract: Modeling and generating graphs is fundamental for studying networks in biology, engineering, and social sciences. However, modeling complex distributions over graphs and then efficiently sampling from these distributions is challenging due to the non-unique, high-dimensional nature of graphs and the complex, non-local dependencies that exist between edges in a given graph. Here we propose GraphRNN, a deep autoregressive model that addresses the above challenges and approximates any distribution of graphs with minimal assumptions about their structure. GraphRNN learns to generate graphs by training on a representative set of graphs and decomposes the graph generation process into a sequence of node and edge formations, conditioned on the graph structure generated so far. In order to quantitatively evaluate the performance of GraphRNN, we introduce a benchmark suite of datasets, baselines and novel evaluation metrics based on Maximum Mean Discrepancy, which measure distances between sets of graphs. Our experiments show that GraphRNN significantly outperforms all baselines, learning to generate diverse graphs that match the structural characteristics of a target set, while also scaling to graphs 50 times larger than previous deep models.

Here we propose GraphRNN, a deep autoregressive model that addresses the above challenges and approximates any distribution of graphs with minimal assumptions about their structure. GraphRNN learns to generate graphs by training on a representative set of graphs and decomposes the graph generation process into a sequence of node and edge formations, conditioned on the graph structure generated so far. In order to quantitatively evaluate the performance of GraphRNN, we introduce a benchmark suite of datasets, baselines and novel evaluation metrics based on Maximum Mean Discrepancy, which measure distances between sets of graphs. Our experiments show that GraphRNN significantly outperforms all baselines, learning to generate diverse graphs that match the structural characteristics of a target set, while also scaling to graphs 50 times larger than previous deep models.

paragraphs: Generating graphs is difficult because graphs have nonunique representations, many possible connections, and dependencies between edges that can extend across the structure. GraphRNN addresses this by learning from a representative collection of graphs. The authors present it as a model capable of approximating any graph distribution with minimal structural assumptions.

GraphRNN generates a graph through a sequence of node and edge additions. Each step depends on the structure already produced, allowing earlier choices to inform later connections. This autoregressive formulation turns generation into a series of conditional decisions while retaining information about the growing graph.

The paper also introduces a benchmark suite and evaluation measures based on Maximum Mean Discrepancy to compare sets of graphs. In the reported experiments, GraphRNN significantly outperforms all included baselines and generates diverse graphs matching the target collection’s structural characteristics. It also scales to graphs fifty times larger than previous deep models. These results address both the quality of generated structures and the size of graphs the approach can handle.
summary.tldr: GraphRNN generates graphs through conditional node and edge additions, producing diverse structures and scaling beyond earlier deep models in reported experiments.

title: GraphRNN: Generating Realistic Graphs with Deep Auto-regressive Models

abstract: Q-learning methods are a common class of algorithms used in reinforcement learning (RL). However, their behavior with function approximation, especially with neural networks, is poorly understood theoretically and empirically. In this work, we aim to experimentally investigate potential issues in Q-learning, by means of a "unit testing" framework where we can utilize oracles to disentangle sources of error. Specifically, we investigate questions related to function approximation, sampling error and nonstationarity, and where available, verify if trends found in oracle settings hold true with deep RL methods. We find that large neural network architectures have many benefits with regards to learning stability; offer several practical compensations for overfitting; and develop a novel sampling method based on explicitly compensating for function approximation error that yields fair improvement on high-dimensional continuous control domains.

paragraphs: Q-learning becomes difficult to diagnose when a neural network approximates the values used to choose actions. Errors can arise from the approximation itself, from limited samples, or from changes in the quantities being learned. This paper investigates those potential bottlenecks experimentally, aiming to separate effects that normally occur together.

The authors organize the investigation as a unit-testing framework using oracles. These controlled sources of information let them disentangle particular causes of error and study their effects individually. Where possible, they then check whether trends observed in the oracle settings also appear in deep reinforcement learning methods, linking controlled diagnosis to practical algorithms.

The experiments find several benefits of larger neural networks for learning stability. The paper also offers practical ways to compensate for overfitting and develops a sampling method that explicitly accounts for function-approximation error. That method yields a reported improvement on high-dimensional continuous-control tasks. The contribution combines evidence about failure mechanisms with changes intended to address the issues identified through that evidence.
summary.tldr: Oracle-based experiments separate Q-learning error sources and motivate practical stability measures and an approximation-aware sampling method.

title: Diagnosing Bottlenecks in Deep Q-learning Algorithms

abstract: We present a Bayesian view of counterfactual risk minimization (CRM) for offline learning from logged bandit feedback. Using PAC-Bayesian analysis, we derive a new generalization bound for the truncated inverse propensity score estimator. We apply the bound to a class of Bayesian policies, which motivates a novel, potentially data-dependent, regularization technique for CRM. Experimental results indicate that this technique outperforms standard $L_2$ regularization, and that it is competitive with variance regularization while being both simpler to implement and more computationally efficient.

Experimental results indicate that this technique outperforms standard $L_2$ regularization, and that it is competitive with variance regularization while being both simpler to implement and more computationally efficient.

paragraphs: Offline learning from logged bandit feedback uses records of past decisions and their observed outcomes to learn a policy. This paper develops a Bayesian view of that learning problem and uses it to motivate a different form of regularization.

The theoretical starting point is a new PAC-Bayesian generalization bound for a truncated inverse propensity score estimator. Such an estimator adjusts feedback according to action-selection probabilities, with truncation limiting the resulting weights. Applying the bound to a class of Bayesian policies yields a regularization technique that can potentially depend on the data.

Experiments indicate that the resulting regularization performs better than standard L2 regularization. It is also competitive with variance regularization while being simpler to implement and more computationally efficient. These findings connect a theoretical generalization argument to a practical training choice: the bound supplies a reason for the regularizer, and the experiments assess its usefulness relative to established alternatives.
summary.tldr: A PAC-Bayesian bound motivates a CRM regularizer that experimentally improves on L2 and competes with variance regularization at lower computational cost.

title: Bayesian Counterfactual Risk Minimization

abstract: We give a formal and complete characterization of the explicit regularizer induced by dropout in deep linear networks with squared loss. We show that (a) the explicit regularizer is composed of an $\ell_2$-path regularizer and other terms that are also re-scaling invariant, (b) the convex envelope of the induced regularizer is the squared nuclear norm of the network map, and (c) for a sufficiently large dropout rate, we characterize the global optima of the dropout objective. We validate our theoretical findings with empirical results.
originalAbstract: We give a formal and complete characterization of the explicit regularizer induced by dropout in deep linear networks with squared loss. We show that (a) the explicit regularizer is composed of an $\ell_2$-path regularizer and other terms that are also re-scaling invariant, (b) the convex envelope of the induced regularizer is the squared nuclear norm of the network map, and (c) for a sufficiently large dropout rate, we characterize the global optima of the dropout objective. We validate our theoretical findings with empirical results.

paragraphs: This paper gives a complete mathematical characterization of the explicit regularization induced by dropout in deep linear networks trained with squared loss. The setting is specific: the results concern networks whose layers are linear and an objective based on squared prediction errors. Within that setting, the analysis identifies exactly how dropout modifies the optimization problem.

The induced penalty contains an l2 path regularizer together with additional terms that are invariant to rescaling. The authors also show that its convex envelope is the squared nuclear norm of the network’s overall map. A convex envelope is the largest convex function lying below the original penalty, so this result establishes a precise connection between dropout’s penalty and a matrix-level regularizer.

For a sufficiently large dropout rate, the paper further characterizes the global optima of the dropout objective. The authors support their theoretical findings with empirical results. Together, these contributions clarify both the form of the regularization and the solutions it produces under the stated dropout-rate condition.
summary.tldr: For deep linear networks with squared loss, the paper characterizes dropout’s regularizer, its squared-nuclear-norm convex envelope, and global optima at sufficiently large dropout rates.

title: On Dropout and Nuclear Norm Regularization

abstract: Given a graphical model (GM), computing its partition function is the most essential inference task, but it is computationally intractable in general. To address the issue, iterative approximation algorithms exploring certain local structure/consistency of GM have been investigated as popular choices in practice. However, due to their local/iterative nature, they often output poor approximations or even do not converge, e.g., in low-temperature regimes (hard instances of large parameters). To overcome the limitation, we propose a novel approach utilizing the global spectral feature of GM. Our contribution is two-fold: (a) we first propose a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme (FPTAS) for approximating the partition function of GM associating with a low-rank coupling matrix; (b) for general high-rank GMs, we design a spectral mean-field scheme utilizing (a) as a subroutine, where it approximates a high-rank GM into a product of rank-1 GMs for an efficient approximation of the partition function. The proposed algorithm is more robust in its running time and accuracy than prior methods, i.e., neither suffers from the convergence issue nor depends on hard local structures, as demonstrated in our experiments.

paragraphs: Computing a graphical model's partition function is generally intractable. Common approximations use local structure and iterative consistency updates, but these can be inaccurate or fail to converge on difficult instances. This paper instead uses global spectral information to organize the approximation.

The first contribution is a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme for graphical models associated with a low-rank coupling matrix. The second extends the approach to general high-rank models through a spectral mean-field scheme. It approximates a high-rank model using a product of rank-one graphical models and uses the low-rank procedure as a subroutine.

The distinction between these contributions matters: the formal approximation scheme applies to the low-rank setting, while the general setting uses an additional approximation. Experiments demonstrate greater robustness in running time and accuracy than prior methods, without the convergence issues or dependence on difficult local structures described in the abstract. The overall approach makes global matrix structure a computational resource for approximate inference.
summary.tldr: Spectral approximate inference uses low-rank structure to approximate partition functions, with a formal low-rank scheme and a spectral mean-field extension.

title: Spectral Approximate Inference

abstract: Building accurate language models that capture meaningful long-term dependencies is a core challenge in natural language processing. Towards this end, we present a calibration-based approach to measure long-term discrepancies between a generative sequence model and the true distribution, and use these discrepancies to improve the model. Empirically, we show that state-of-the-art language models, including LSTMs and Transformers, are miscalibrated: the entropy rates of their generations drift dramatically upward over time. We then provide provable methods to mitigate this phenomenon. Furthermore, we show how this calibration-based approach can also be used to measure the amount of memory that language models use for prediction.

paragraphs: A language model needs to capture dependencies that persist across a sequence, so evaluating its behavior over long stretches matters. This paper develops a calibration-based approach for measuring discrepancies between a generative sequence model and the true distribution. The goal is to use those measurements both to diagnose problems and to improve the model.

The empirical finding is that the tested language models, including LSTMs and Transformers, are miscalibrated over time. The entropy rates of their generated sequences rise dramatically as generation continues. Entropy rate describes uncertainty per step, so this drift identifies a changing statistical property of the model's own output. The finding concerns behavior across a sequence, beyond an isolated prediction.

The authors provide methods with theoretical guarantees for mitigating this phenomenon. They also show that the calibration framework can measure how much memory a model uses when making predictions. This gives the approach two related purposes: detecting long-term distributional mismatch and examining the extent to which predictions use past information. Both bear directly on the challenge of modeling meaningful long-term dependencies.
summary.tldr: A calibration framework detects and mitigates entropy-rate drift in language models and measures their use of memory.

title: Calibration, Entropy Rates, and Memory in Language Models

abstract: We show that on-policy policy gradient (PG) and its variance reduction variants can be derived by taking finite-difference of function evaluations supplied by estimators from the importance sampling (IS) family for off-policy evaluation (OPE). Starting from the doubly robust (DR) estimator (Jiang & Li, 2016), we provide a simple derivation of a very general and flexible form of PG, which subsumes the state-of-the-art variance reduction technique (Cheng et al., 2019) as its special case and immediately hints at further variance reduction opportunities overlooked by existing literature. We analyze the variance of the new DR-PG estimator, compare it to existing methods as well as the Cramer-Rao lower bound of policy gradient, and empirically show its effectiveness.

We analyze the variance of the new DR-PG estimator, compare it to existing methods as well as the Cramer-Rao lower bound of policy gradient, and empirically show its effectiveness.

paragraphs: Policy-gradient methods improve a policy using estimates of how its performance changes with its parameters. Off-policy evaluation addresses the related task of estimating policy performance from data. This paper connects the two by showing how policy-gradient estimators can be derived from importance-sampling-based estimators of policy value.

The construction takes finite differences of the value estimates. Through this perspective, the authors recover on-policy policy gradients and existing variance-reduction variants. Starting specifically from a doubly robust value estimator produces a flexible policy-gradient form that includes a leading variance-reduction technique as a special case and points toward additional opportunities to reduce variance.

The authors analyze the new estimator’s variance and compare it with existing methods and the Cramer-Rao lower bound for policy gradients. They also provide empirical evidence of effectiveness. The significance is a shared derivation that connects evaluation and optimization: improvements in how policy values are estimated can suggest improvements in how learning directions are estimated, within the framework developed in the paper.
summary.tldr: Deriving policy gradients from off-policy value estimators yields a flexible doubly robust estimator and new variance-reduction opportunities.

title: From Importance Sampling to Doubly Robust Policy Gradient

abstract: We investigate the ability of popular flow models to capture tail-properties of a target density by studying the increasing triangular maps used in these flow methods acting on a tractable source density. We show that the density quantile functions of the source and target density provide a precise characterization of the slope of transformation required to capture tails in a target density. We further show that any Lipschitz-continuous transport map acting on a source density will result in a density with similar tail properties as the source, highlighting the trade-off between the importance of choosing a complex source density and a sufficiently expressive transformation to capture desirable properties of a target density. Subsequently, we illustrate that flow models like Real-NVP, MAF, and Glow as implemented lack the ability to capture a distribution with non-Gaussian tails. We circumvent this problem by proposing tail-adaptive flows consisting of a source distribution that can be learned simultaneously with the triangular map to capture tail-properties of a target density. We perform several synthetic and real-world experiments to complement our theoretical findings.

paragraphs: A generative model must represent not only typical observations but also the tails of a distribution, where extreme values occur. This paper studies how triangular transformations in normalizing flows change tail behavior. It connects the slope needed in the transformation to density quantile functions of the source and target distributions.

The authors show that a Lipschitz-continuous transport map preserves similar tail properties to those of its source distribution. This creates a tradeoff: achieving the desired target tails depends on both the source distribution and the transformation’s expressiveness. They illustrate that Real-NVP, MAF, and Glow, as implemented in the examined setting, cannot capture distributions with non-Gaussian tails.

To address this, the paper proposes tail-adaptive flows that learn the source distribution alongside the triangular map. The starting distribution can therefore adjust its tail behavior instead of leaving all adaptation to the transformation. Synthetic and real-world experiments complement the theory. The architectural limitation is stated for the implementations examined, rather than for every possible modification of those flow families.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes tail restrictions in Lipschitz flows and proposes learning the source distribution to better capture target tails.

title: Tails of Lipschitz Triangular Flows

abstract: Contrastive divergence is a popular method of training energy-based models, but is known to have difficulties with training stability. We propose an adaptation to improve contrastive divergence training by scrutinizing a gradient term that is difficult to calculate and is often left out for convenience. We show that this gradient term is numerically significant and in practice is important to avoid training instabilities, while being tractable to estimate. We further highlight how data augmentation and multi-scale processing can be used to improve model robustness and generation quality. Finally, we empirically evaluate stability of model architectures and show improved performance on a host of benchmarks and use cases, such as image generation, OOD detection, and compositional generation.
