We show that this gradient term is numerically significant and in practice is important to avoid training instabilities, while being tractable to estimate. We further highlight how data augmentation and multi-scale processing can be used to improve model robustness and generation quality. Finally, we empirically evaluate stability of model architectures and show improved performance on a host of benchmarks and use cases, such as image generation, OOD detection, and compositional generation.

paragraphs: Contrastive divergence is widely used to train energy-based models, but unstable training can limit its usefulness. This paper revisits a gradient term that is often omitted because it is difficult to calculate. The authors investigate whether that convenience discards information that materially affects the learning process and propose a training adaptation based on their findings.

They show that the term has a numerically significant contribution, can be estimated tractably, and matters in practice for avoiding instability. This gives a concrete reason to retain it in training rather than treating it as negligible. The paper also examines data augmentation and processing at multiple scales as ways to improve model robustness and generated outputs.

Empirical evaluation considers the stability of different model architectures and reports improved performance across image generation, out-of-distribution detection, and compositional generation. These results support the practical value of the revised training approach across several uses of energy-based models. The contribution combines a closer examination of the training gradient with complementary choices that improve robustness and generation quality.
summary.tldr: Estimating an often-omitted gradient term improves contrastive divergence training stability, with empirical gains across several energy-based modeling tasks.

title: Improved Contrastive Divergence Training of Energy-Based Models

abstract: Alternating minimization (AM) procedures are practically efficient in many applications for solving convex and non-convex optimization problems. On the other hand, Nesterov’s accelerated gradient is theoretically optimal first-order method for convex optimization. In this paper we combine AM and Nesterov’s acceleration to propose an accelerated alternating minimization algorithm. We prove $1/k^2$ convergence rate in terms of the objective for convex problems and $1/k$ in terms of the squared gradient norm for non-convex problems, where $k$ is the iteration counter. Our method does not require any knowledge of neither convexity of the problem nor function parameters such as Lipschitz constant of the gradient, i.e. it is adaptive to convexity and smoothness and is uniformly optimal for smooth convex and non-convex problems. Further, we develop its primal-dual modification for strongly convex problems with linear constraints and prove the same $1/k^2$ for the primal objective residual and constraints feasibility.

paragraphs: Alternating minimization is useful in practice for convex and nonconvex optimization, while Nesterov acceleration offers strong theoretical performance for convex problems. This paper combines them in an accelerated alternating minimization algorithm. The aim is to retain the practical structure of alternating updates while obtaining fast convergence guarantees.

For convex problems, the authors prove that the objective error decreases at a rate proportional to 1/k². For nonconvex problems, they establish a 1/k rate for the squared gradient norm, where k counts iterations. These measures describe different achievements: objective accuracy in the convex case and progress toward stationarity in the nonconvex case. The algorithm requires neither prior knowledge of convexity nor smoothness parameters such as a gradient Lipschitz constant.

The authors characterize the method as uniformly optimal for smooth convex and nonconvex problems. They also develop a primal-dual version for strongly convex problems with linear constraints. That extension achieves 1/k² rates for both the primal objective residual and constraint feasibility, addressing solution quality and satisfaction of the constraints together.
summary.tldr: Accelerated alternating minimization achieves convex and nonconvex convergence guarantees without requiring prior knowledge of convexity or smoothness parameters.

title: On a Combination of Alternating Minimization and Nesterov’s Momentum

abstract: Several recent applications of optimal transport (OT) theory to machine learning have relied on regularization, notably entropy and the Sinkhorn algorithm. Because matrix-vector products are pervasive in the Sinkhorn algorithm, several works have proposed to \textit{approximate} kernel matrices appearing in its iterations using low-rank factors. Another route lies instead in imposing low-nonnegative rank constraints on the feasible set of couplings considered in OT problems, with no approximations on cost nor kernel matrices. This route was first explored by \citet{forrow2018statistical}, who proposed an algorithm tailored for the squared Euclidean ground cost, using a proxy objective that can be solved through the machinery of regularized 2-Wasserstein barycenters. Building on this, we introduce in this work a generic approach that aims at solving, in full generality, the OT problem under low-nonnegative rank constraints with arbitrary costs. Our algorithm relies on an explicit factorization of low-rank couplings as a product of \textit{sub-coupling} factors linked by a common marginal; similar to an NMF approach, we alternatively updates these factors. We prove the non-asymptotic stationary convergence of this algorithm and illustrate its efficiency on benchmark experiments.

paragraphs: Optimal transport represents how mass moves between distributions through a coupling. Many computational approaches use entropy regularization and the Sinkhorn algorithm, whose repeated matrix operations can be costly. This paper studies an alternative way to impose low-rank structure: constraining the coupling itself to have low nonnegative rank.

That choice leaves the cost and kernel matrices unapproximated while restricting the transport plans considered. The authors develop a generic approach for arbitrary costs, extending beyond an earlier method tailored to squared Euclidean cost. Their construction explicitly factors a coupling into smaller sub-couplings connected by a shared marginal. The algorithm alternates between updating these factors, in a manner related to nonnegative matrix factorization.

The paper proves non-asymptotic convergence to stationarity and illustrates computational efficiency in benchmark experiments. Stationary convergence is the stated guarantee; it does not assert a globally optimal solution. The contribution provides a general computational framework for low-nonnegative-rank transport, with structure imposed directly on the object that describes the movement of mass.
summary.tldr: The paper factors transport couplings directly to solve low-nonnegative-rank optimal transport with arbitrary costs and stationary-convergence guarantees.

title: Low-Rank Sinkhorn Factorization

abstract: Multivariate Hawkes processes (MHPs) are widely used in a variety of fields to model the occurrence of causally related discrete events in continuous time. Most state-of-the-art approaches address the problem of learning MHPs from perfect traces without noise. In practice, the process through which events are collected might introduce noise in the timestamps. In this work, we address the problem of learning the causal structure of MHPs when the observed timestamps of events are subject to random and unknown shifts, also known as random translations. We prove that the cumulants of MHPs are invariant to random translations, and therefore can be used to learn their underlying causal structure. Furthermore, we empirically characterize the effect of random translations on state-of-the-art learning methods. We show that maximum likelihood-based estimators are brittle, while cumulant-based estimators remain stable even in the presence of significant time shifts.

In this work, we address the problem of learning the causal structure of MHPs when the observed timestamps of events are subject to random and unknown shifts, also known as random translations. paragraphs: Multivariate Hawkes processes model streams of discrete events whose occurrences are causally related over continuous time. Learning those relationships often assumes accurately recorded event times. This paper studies a more difficult observation setting: timestamps are displaced by random, unknown shifts introduced during event collection.

The authors prove that cumulants of these processes remain unchanged under random translations. Cumulants are statistical summaries, and their invariance provides information that survives this particular form of timing noise. Consequently, they can be used to learn the underlying causal structure even when the observed timestamps have been shifted. The result connects a mathematical property of the summaries directly to the structure-learning problem.

The paper also investigates how existing learning methods respond to random timestamp shifts. In the reported experiments, maximum likelihood estimators are brittle, whereas cumulant-based estimators remain stable even with substantial shifts. The theoretical and empirical findings therefore identify cumulants as a robust basis for learning under the specific timestamp corruption studied.
summary.tldr: Cumulants preserve information about Hawkes-process causal structure under random timestamp shifts, and cumulant-based estimators show empirical stability.

title: Cumulants of Hawkes Processes are Robust to Observation Noise

abstract: Double machine learning is a statistical method for leveraging complex black-box models to construct approximately unbiased treatment effect estimates given observational data with high-dimensional covariates, under the assumption of a partially linear model. The idea is to first fit on a subset of the samples two non-linear predictive models, one for the continuous outcome of interest and one for the observed treatment, and then to estimate a linear coefficient for the treatment using the remaining samples through a simple orthogonalized regression. While this methodology is flexible and can accommodate arbitrary predictive models, typically trained independently of one another, this paper argues that a carefully coordinated learning algorithm for deep neural networks may reduce the estimation bias. The improved empirical performance of the proposed method is demonstrated through numerical experiments on both simulated and real data.

The idea is to first fit on a subset of the samples two non-linear predictive models, one for the continuous outcome of interest and one for the observed treatment, and then to estimate a linear coefficient for the treatment using the remaining samples through a simple orthogonalized regression. While this methodology is flexible and can accommodate arbitrary predictive models, typically trained independently of one another, this paper argues that a carefully coordinated learning algorithm for deep neural networks may reduce the estimation bias. The improved empirical performance of the proposed method is demonstrated through numerical experiments on both simulated and real data.

paragraphs: Double machine learning uses flexible prediction models to help estimate treatment effects from observational data with many covariates. Under a partially linear model assumption, it aims for approximately unbiased estimates. Its usual procedure first learns two predictive relationships on part of the data: one for the continuous outcome and one for the observed treatment.

The remaining samples are then used in an orthogonalized regression to estimate the treatment’s linear coefficient. Although the two predictive models contribute to the same final estimate, they are commonly trained independently. This paper investigates whether coordinating their learning can improve the treatment-effect estimate.

The proposed approach coordinates deep neural networks within this procedure. The authors argue that carefully linking their training may reduce estimation bias, and experiments on simulated and real data demonstrate improved empirical performance. The significance is that prediction models serving a shared statistical estimator may benefit from being learned together. The claim remains tied to the partially linear setting and to the reported evidence, rather than guaranteeing that coordination always reduces bias.
summary.tldr: Coordinating the neural predictors used in double machine learning may reduce treatment-effect estimation bias, with improvements demonstrated empirically.

title: Coordinated Double Machine Learning

abstract: In this paper, we investigate the problem of stochastic multi-level compositional optimization, where the objective function is a composition of multiple smooth but possibly non-convex functions. Existing methods for solving this problem either suffer from sub-optimal sample complexities or need a huge batch size. To address this limitation, we propose a Stochastic Multi-level Variance Reduction method (SMVR), which achieves the optimal sample complexity of $\mathcal{O}\left(1 / \epsilon^{3}\right)$ to find an $\epsilon$-stationary point for non-convex objectives. Furthermore, when the objective function satisfies the convexity or Polyak-{Ł}ojasiewicz (PL) condition, we propose a stage-wise variant of SMVR and improve the sample complexity to $\mathcal{O}\left(1 / \epsilon^{2}\right)$ for convex functions or $\mathcal{O}\left(1 /(\mu\epsilon)\right)$ for non-convex functions satisfying the $\mu$-PL condition. The latter result implies the same complexity for $\mu$-strongly convex functions. To make use of adaptive learning rates, we also develop Adaptive SMVR, which achieves the same optimal complexities but converges faster in practice. All our complexities match the lower bounds not only in terms of $\epsilon$ but also in terms of $\mu$ (for PL or strongly convex functions), without using a large batch size in each iteration.

Existing approaches either require more samples than the best possible rate or depend on very large batches at each iteration.

The proposed Stochastic Multi-level Variance Reduction method, SMVR, reaches an epsilon-stationary point for nonconvex objectives using O(1/epsilon³) samples. A stationary-point guarantee concerns reaching a point with a small gradient. The latter guarantee also applies to mu-strongly convex functions. These complexities match lower bounds in their dependence on accuracy and, where relevant, mu, without requiring large batches per iteration. An adaptive-learning-rate version retains the same optimal complexity guarantees and converges faster in the reported practical results. The contribution thus pairs improved sample efficiency with variants tailored to stronger objective structure and adaptive updates.
summary.tldr: SMVR achieves optimal sample complexities for nested stochastic optimization without large batches, with stronger guarantees under additional objective conditions.

title: Optimal Algorithms for Stochastic Multi-Level Compositional Optimization

abstract: Inferring the abstract relational and causal structure of the world is a major challenge for reinforcement-learning (RL) agents. For humans, language{—}particularly in the form of explanations{—}plays a considerable role in overcoming this challenge. Here, we show that language can play a similar role for deep RL agents in complex environments. While agents typically struggle to acquire relational and causal knowledge, augmenting their experience by training them to predict language descriptions and explanations can overcome these limitations. We show that language can help agents learn challenging relational tasks, and examine which aspects of language contribute to its benefits. We then show that explanations can help agents to infer not only relational but also causal structure. Language can shape the way that agents to generalize out-of-distribution from ambiguous, causally-confounded training, and explanations even allow agents to learn to perform experimental interventions to identify causal relationships. Our results suggest that language description and explanation may be powerful tools for improving agent learning and generalization.

The authors show that language supports learning on challenging relational tasks and investigate which aspects of language contribute to that benefit. They then extend the analysis to causal structure. Explanations can influence how agents generalize beyond training conditions when the original experience is ambiguous and contains causal confounding.

The experiments also show that explanations can help agents learn to perform interventions to identify causal relationships. This goes beyond recognizing a relationship in observed experience: the agent learns to take actions that help resolve causal questions. Together, the results suggest that language descriptions and explanations may improve learning and generalization by shaping the relational and causal knowledge agents acquire in the studied environments.
summary.tldr: Training agents to predict descriptions and explanations supports relational learning, causal generalization, and experimental interventions in the studied environments.

title: Tell me why! Explanations support learning relational and causal structure

abstract: Optimization of atomic structures presents a challenging problem, due to their highly rough and non-convex energy landscape, with wide applications in the fields of drug design, materials discovery, and mechanics. Here, we present a graph reinforcement learning approach, StriderNet, that learns a policy to displace the atoms towards low energy configurations. We evaluate the performance of StriderNet on three complex atomic systems, namely, binary Lennard-Jones particles, calcium silicate hydrates gel, and disordered silicon. We show that StriderNet outperforms all classical optimization algorithms and enables the discovery of a lower energy minimum. In addition, StriderNet exhibits a higher rate of reaching minima with energies, as confirmed by the average over multiple realizations. Finally, we show that StriderNet exhibits inductivity to unseen system sizes that are an order of magnitude different from the training system. All the codes and datasets are available at https://github.com/M3RG-IITD/StriderNET.

paragraphs: Finding low-energy atomic arrangements is difficult because the energy landscape is rough and nonconvex. Many different configurations can form local minima, making optimization challenging in applications such as materials discovery and drug design. StriderNet approaches this problem with graph reinforcement learning, learning a policy that moves atoms toward lower-energy configurations.

The authors evaluate the approach on three atomic systems: binary Lennard-Jones particles, calcium silicate hydrates gel, and disordered silicon. In those evaluations, StriderNet outperforms all classical optimization algorithms considered and finds a lower-energy minimum. Results averaged over multiple realizations also support its reported advantage in reaching minima, providing evidence across repeated optimization runs.

The paper further demonstrates transfer to unseen system sizes that differ from the training system by an order of magnitude. This result matters because it shows the learned policy being applied beyond the size used during training. Taken together, the experiments support graph reinforcement learning as an approach to atomic optimization, with reported benefits in the quality of discovered configurations and applicability across different system sizes.
summary.tldr: StriderNet learns atomic displacements through graph reinforcement learning, finding lower-energy configurations and transferring to substantially different system sizes in the reported tests.

title: StriderNet: A Graph Reinforcement Learning Approach to Optimize Atomic Structures on Rough Energy Landscapes

abstract: We present two new classes of algorithms for efficient field integration on graphs encoding point cloud data. The first class, $\mathrm{SeparatorFactorization}$ (SF), leverages the bounded genus of point cloud mesh graphs, while the second class, $\mathrm{RFDiffusion}$ (RFD), uses popular $\epsilon$-nearest-neighbor graph representations for point clouds. Both can be viewed as providing the functionality of Fast Multipole Methods (FMMs), which have had a tremendous impact on efficient integration, but for non-Euclidean spaces. We focus on geometries induced by distributions of walk lengths between points (e.g. shortest-path distance). We provide an extensive theoretical analysis of our algorithms, obtaining new results in structural graph theory as a byproduct. We also perform exhaustive empirical evaluation, including on-surface interpolation for rigid and deformable objects (in particular for mesh-dynamics modeling) as well as Wasserstein distance computations for point clouds, including the Gromov-Wasserstein variant.

paragraphs: Point clouds can be represented as graphs whose connections describe the geometry of a shape. This paper develops efficient algorithms for integrating fields on those graphs, focusing on geometries determined by walk lengths between points, including shortest-path distance. The aim is to provide functionality analogous to Fast Multipole Methods for these non-Euclidean settings.

RFDiffusion works with epsilon-nearest-neighbor graph representations. These choices connect the computational approach to how the point cloud is encoded, giving separate routes for handling mesh-based and neighborhood-based geometry.

The paper provides theoretical analysis, with additional structural graph theory results emerging from the work. Its empirical evaluation covers interpolation on rigid and deformable surfaces, including applications to mesh dynamics. It also examines Wasserstein and Gromov–Wasserstein distance computations for point clouds. These applications demonstrate the range of geometric computations the integrators target, linking the underlying graph algorithms to surface modeling and comparisons between shapes.
summary.tldr: Two graph integration algorithm families exploit mesh or neighborhood structure to support efficient geometric computations on point clouds.

title: Efficient Graph Field Integrators Meet Point Clouds

abstract: We consider the problem of learning a target function corresponding to a deep, extensive-width, non-linear neural network with random Gaussian weights. We consider the asymptotic limit where the number of samples, the input dimension and the network width are proportionally large and propose a closed-form expression for the Bayes-optimal test error, for regression and classification tasks. We further compute closed-form expressions for the test errors of ridge regression, kernel and random features regression. We find, in particular, that optimally regularized ridge regression, as well as kernel regression, achieve Bayes-optimal performances, while the logistic loss yields a near-optimal test error for classification. We further show numerically that when the number of samples grows faster than the dimension, ridge and kernel methods become suboptimal, while neural networks achieve test error close to zero from quadratically many samples.

paragraphs: The paper asks how accurately one can learn a target function generated by a deep nonlinear neural network with random Gaussian weights. Its main setting is an asymptotic regime in which the sample count, input dimension, and network width all become large in proportion. Within this setting, the authors propose a closed-form expression for Bayes-optimal test error for regression and classification.

They also compute test-error expressions for ridge regression, kernel regression, and random features regression. These comparisons show that optimally regularized ridge regression and kernel regression achieve Bayes-optimal performance in the proportional regime. For classification, the logistic loss gives nearly optimal test error. Thus, a target generated by a deep network does not by itself establish an advantage for learning with a neural network in this regime.

The numerical findings change when the sample count grows faster than the input dimension. Ridge and kernel methods then become suboptimal, while neural networks attain test error close to zero with quadratically many samples. This distinguishes the proportional-limit results from a richer-data regime where the experiments show a neural-network advantage.
summary.tldr: For deep random-network targets, simple regression methods attain Bayes-optimal performance in a proportional asymptotic regime, while numerical results favor neural networks with more samples.

title: Bayes-optimal Learning of Deep Random Networks of Extensive-width

abstract: This paper presents fast first-order methods for solving linear programs (LPs) approximately. We adapt online linear programming algorithms to offline LPs and obtain algorithms that avoid any matrix multiplication. We also introduce a variable-duplication technique that copies each variable $K$ times and reduces the optimality gap and constraint violation by a factor of $\sqrt{K}$. Furthermore, we show how online algorithms can be effectively integrated into sifting, a column generation scheme for large-scale LPs. Numerical experiments demonstrate that our methods can serve as either an approximate direct solver, or an initialization subroutine for exact LP solving.

paragraphs: Linear programming seeks the best value of a linear objective subject to linear constraints. This paper develops fast first-order methods for obtaining approximate solutions. Its starting point is to adapt algorithms designed for online linear programming to the offline setting, where the linear program is treated as a fixed problem.

The resulting algorithms avoid matrix multiplication. The authors also introduce variable duplication: each variable is copied K times, and the method reduces both the optimality gap and constraint violation by a factor of the square root of K. These two quantities capture different aspects of an approximate solution: how far its objective is from optimal and how much it fails to satisfy the constraints.

The paper further integrates online algorithms into sifting, a column-generation scheme for large linear programs. Numerical experiments support two uses: serving directly as an approximate solver or supplying an initialization for exact solving. This gives the approach a role both when an approximate answer is useful and when it is an intermediate step toward an exact solution.
summary.tldr: Adapted online algorithms solve linear programs approximately without matrix multiplication and can initialize exact solvers.

title: Solving Linear Programs with Fast Online Learning Algorithms

abstract: Retrosynthesis, which aims to find a route to synthesize a target molecule from commercially available starting materials, is a critical task in drug discovery and materials design. Recently, the combination of ML-based single-step reaction predictors with multi-step planners has led to promising results. However, the single-step predictors are mostly trained offline to optimize the single-step accuracy, without considering complete routes. Here, we leverage reinforcement learning (RL) to improve the single-step predictor, by using a tree-shaped MDP to optimize complete routes. Specifically, we propose a novel online training algorithm, called Planning with Dual Value Networks (PDVN), which alternates between the planning phase and updating phase. In PDVN, we construct two separate value networks to predict the synthesizability and cost of molecules, respectively. To maintain the single-step accuracy, we design a two-branch network structure for the single-step predictor. On the widely-used USPTO dataset, our PDVN algorithm improves the search success rate of existing multi-step planners (e.g., increasing the success rate from 85.79% to 98.95% for Retro$^{\ast}$, and reducing the number of model calls by half while solving 99.47% molecules for RetroGraph). Additionally, PDVN helps find shorter synthesis routes (e.g., reducing the average route length from 5.76 to 4.83 for Retro$^{\ast}$, and from 5.63 to 4.78 for RetroGraph).

summary.tldr: PDVN trains reaction prediction around complete synthesis routes, improving planner success, efficiency, and route length on USPTO.

title: Retrosynthetic Planning with Dual Value Networks

abstract: Contrastive Language-Image Pretraining (CLIP) has demonstrated impressive zero-shot learning abilities for image understanding, yet limited effort has been made to investigate CLIP for zero-shot video recognition. We introduce Open-VCLIP, a simple yet effective approach that transforms CLIP into a strong zero-shot video classifier that can recognize unseen actions and events at test time. Our framework extends CLIP with minimal modifications to model spatial-temporal relationships in videos, making it a specialized video classifier, while striving for generalization. We formally show that training an Open-VCLIP is equivalent to continual learning with zero historical data. To address this problem, we propose Interpolated Weight Optimization, which utilizes the benefit of weight interpolation in both training and test time. We evaluate our method on three popular and challenging action recognition datasets following various zero-shot evaluation protocols and we demonstrate our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods by clear margins. In particular, we achieve 87.9%, 58.3%, 81.1% zero-shot accuracy on UCF, HMDB and Kinetics-600 respectively, outperforming state-of-the-art methods by 8.3%, 7.8% and 12.2%. Code is released at https://github.com/wengzejia1/Open-VCLIP.

summary.tldr: Open-VCLIP combines minimal video-modeling changes with weight interpolation to adapt CLIP for strong reported zero-shot action recognition.

title: Open-VCLIP: Transforming CLIP to an Open-vocabulary Video Model via Interpolated Weight Optimization

abstract: Conformal prediction is a statistical framework that generates prediction sets containing ground-truth labels with a desired coverage guarantee. The predicted probabilities produced by machine learning models are generally miscalibrated, leading to large prediction sets in conformal prediction. To address this issue, we propose a novel algorithm named $\textit{Sorted Adaptive Prediction Sets}$ (SAPS), which discards all the probability values except for the maximum softmax probability. The key idea behind SAPS is to minimize the dependence of the non-conformity score on the probability values while retaining the uncertainty information. In this manner, SAPS can produce compact prediction sets and communicate instance-wise uncertainty. Extensive experiments validate that SAPS not only lessens the prediction sets but also broadly enhances the conditional coverage rate of prediction sets.

paragraphs: Conformal prediction expresses uncertainty by returning a set of possible labels with a desired coverage guarantee. For deep classifiers, inaccurate probability estimates can make these sets unnecessarily large. A large set may still contain the correct answer, but it gives the user less precise information about which label applies.

The paper introduces Sorted Adaptive Prediction Sets, or SAPS, to reduce reliance on those probability values. It retains the maximum softmax probability and discards the other probability magnitudes, using label ranking in constructing prediction sets. The aim is to preserve information about an example’s uncertainty while making the non-conformity score less dependent on potentially miscalibrated numerical probabilities.

Experiments show that SAPS produces smaller prediction sets and broadly improves conditional coverage rates. The latter is an empirical finding about coverage beyond an overall aggregate, rather than a stated universal conditional-coverage guarantee. The approach matters because it suggests that retaining every probability value is not required for useful uncertainty estimates: ranking information and a limited confidence signal can support compact, informative sets.
summary.tldr: SAPS relies on label ranking and the maximum predicted probability to produce smaller conformal prediction sets with improved empirical conditional coverage.

title: Conformal Prediction for Deep Classifier via Label Ranking

abstract: We study low-rank matrix trace regression and the related problem of low-rank matrix bandits. Assuming access to the distribution of the covariates, we propose a novel low-rank matrix estimation method called LowPopArt and provide its recovery guarantee that depends on a novel quantity denoted by $B(Q)$ that characterizes the hardness of the problem, where $Q$ is the covariance matrix of the measurement distribution. We show that our method can provide tighter recovery guarantees than classical nuclear norm penalized least squares (Koltchinskii et al., 2011) in several problems. To perform an efficient estimation with a limited number of measurements from an arbitrarily given measurement set $\mathcal{A}$, we also propose a novel experimental design criterion that minimizes $B(Q)$ with computational efficiency. We leverage our novel estimator and design of experiments to derive two low-rank linear bandit algorithms for general arm sets that enjoy improved regret upper bounds. This improves over previous works on low-rank bandits, which make somewhat restrictive assumptions that the arm set is the unit ball or that an efficient exploration distribution is given. To our knowledge, our experimental design criterion is the first one tailored to low-rank matrix estimation beyond the naive reduction to linear regression, which can be of independent interest.

paragraphs: This paper connects estimating a low-rank matrix with choosing informative measurements and making sequential decisions. Its estimator, LowPopArt, assumes access to the distribution of measurement covariates. The recovery guarantee depends on a new quantity, B(Q), which describes problem difficulty using the covariance matrix Q of that measurement distribution.

summary.tldr: LowPopArt and a new measurement-design criterion improve low-rank recovery guarantees in several settings and yield stronger bandit regret bounds for general arm sets.

title: Efficient Low-Rank Matrix Estimation, Experimental Design, and Arm-Set-Dependent Low-Rank Bandits

abstract: Cross-modal transformers have demonstrated superiority in various vision tasks by effectively integrating different modalities. This paper first critiques prior token exchange methods which replace less informative tokens with inter-modal features, and demonstrate exchange based methods underperform cross-attention mechanisms, while the computational demand of the latter inevitably restricts its use with longer sequences. To surmount the computational challenges, we propose GeminiFusion, a pixel-wise fusion approach that capitalizes on aligned cross-modal representations. GeminiFusion elegantly combines intra-modal and inter-modal attentions, dynamically integrating complementary information across modalities. We employ a layer-adaptive noise to adaptively control their interplay on a per-layer basis, thereby achieving a harmonized fusion process. Notably, GeminiFusion maintains linear complexity with respect to the number of input tokens, ensuring this multimodal framework operates with efficiency comparable to unimodal networks. Comprehensive evaluations across multimodal image-to-image translation, $3$D object detection and arbitrary-modal semantic segmentation tasks, including RGB, depth, LiDAR, event data, etc. demonstrate the superior performance of our GeminiFusion against leading-edge techniques. The PyTorch code is available here.

Comprehensive evaluations across multimodal image-to-image translation, $3$D object detection and arbitrary-modal semantic segmentation tasks, including RGB, depth, LiDAR, event data, etc. demonstrate the superior performance of our GeminiFusion against leading-edge techniques. The PyTorch code is available here.

paragraphs: Combining visual modalities can provide complementary information, but the way a model combines them affects both accuracy and cost. The authors find that replacing less informative tokens with features from another modality underperforms cross-attention. Cross-attention, however, becomes computationally demanding when the input contains many tokens.

GeminiFusion exploits aligned representations to combine modalities at the pixel level. It brings together attention within a modality and attention between modalities, allowing complementary information to influence the result dynamically. Layer-adaptive noise controls how these two forms of attention interact at different layers of the network.

The method’s computational complexity grows linearly with the number of input tokens, supporting efficiency comparable to networks that use a single modality. Evaluations cover image-to-image translation, three-dimensional object detection, and semantic segmentation with modalities including RGB, depth, LiDAR, and event data. The reported improvements over leading methods support the value of using alignment to make multimodal interaction efficient while preserving useful exchanges between information sources.
summary.tldr: GeminiFusion combines aligned modalities through pixel-level attention with linear token complexity and reports improvements across several vision tasks.

title: GeminiFusion: Efficient Pixel-wise Multimodal Fusion for Vision Transformer

abstract: In this paper, we prove the universal consistency of wide and deep ReLU neural network classifiers. We also give sufficient conditions for a class of probability measures for which classifiers based on neural networks achieve minimax optimal rates of convergence. The result applies to a wide range of known function classes. In particular, while most previous works impose explicit smoothness assumptions on the regression function, our framework encompasses more general settings. The proposed neural networks are either the minimizers of the $0$-$1$ loss that exhibit a benign overfitting behavior.

paragraphs: This paper studies whether wide and deep ReLU neural network classifiers approach the best achievable prediction accuracy as more data becomes available. It proves universal consistency for the classifiers under study. Consistency concerns their eventual statistical behavior, while the separate question of convergence rates asks how quickly improvement occurs with increasing data.

The authors also provide sufficient conditions on classes of probability measures under which neural network classifiers attain minimax-optimal convergence rates. Such rates describe the best achievable worst-case behavior for a specified class. The conditions are sufficient: the result establishes optimal rates when they hold, without claiming that those conditions are necessary.

The framework applies to a broad range of known function classes and extends beyond settings that impose explicit smoothness assumptions on the regression function. The abstract also identifies classifiers minimizing zero-one loss and exhibiting benign overfitting. Together, these results connect expressive ReLU architectures with statistical guarantees, including settings where fitting the training data closely can coexist with good generalization.
summary.tldr: The paper proves consistency for wide and deep ReLU classifiers and gives sufficient conditions for minimax-optimal convergence rates.

title: Universal Consistency of Wide and Deep ReLU Neural Networks and Minimax Optimal Convergence Rates for Kolmogorov-Donoho Optimal Function Classes

abstract: In the rapidly evolving field of online test-time adaptation (OTTA), effectively managing distribution shifts is a pivotal concern. State-of-the-art OTTA methodologies often face limitations such as an inadequate target domain information integration, leading to significant issues like catastrophic forgetting and a lack of adaptability in dynamically changing environments. In this paper, we introduce a stationary latent weight inference (SLWI) framework, a novel approach to overcome these challenges. The proposed SLWI uniquely incorporates Bayesian filtering to continually track and update the target model weights along with the source model weight in online settings, thereby ensuring that the adapted model remains responsive to ongoing changes in the target domain. The proposed framework has the peculiar property to identify and backtrack nonlinear weights that exhibit local non-stationarity, thereby mitigating error propagation, a common pitfall of previous approaches. By integrating and refining information from both source and target domains, SLWI presents a robust solution to the persistent issue of domain adaptation in OTTA, significantly improving existing methodologies. The efficacy of SLWI is demonstrated through various experimental setups, showcasing its superior performance in diverse distribution shift scenarios.

paragraphs: Online test-time adaptation updates a model as it encounters data whose distribution may differ from its training data. In changing environments, poor integration of new information can contribute to catastrophic forgetting and weak adaptability. This paper introduces stationary latent weight inference, or SLWI, to improve how the model manages that continuing stream of evidence.

SLWI uses Bayesian filtering to track and update target-model weights together with source-model weights in an online setting. This combines information from the original domain with information arriving from the current domain. A distinctive part of the framework identifies and backtracks nonlinear weights exhibiting local non-stationarity, aiming to prevent unreliable adaptation from propagating further errors.

The authors report superior performance across several experimental settings with diverse distribution shifts. These findings support the framework's combination of source information, ongoing target updates, and backtracking of locally unstable weights. Its contribution is an adaptation procedure that remains responsive to change while explicitly addressing the accumulation of errors that can arise during repeated model updates.
summary.tldr: SLWI combines Bayesian weight tracking with backtracking of locally non-stationary weights to improve online adaptation under distribution shifts.

title: Stationary Latent Weight Inference for Unreliable Observations from Online Test-Time Adaptation

abstract: Diffusion models have shown remarkable performance in generation problems over various domains including images, videos, text, and audio. A practical bottleneck of diffusion models is their sampling speed, due to the repeated evaluation of score estimation networks during the inference. In this work, we propose a novel framework capable of adaptively allocating compute required for the score estimation, thereby reducing the overall sampling time of diffusion models. We observe that the amount of computation required for the score estimation may vary along the time step for which the score is estimated. Based on this observation, we propose an early-exiting scheme, where we skip the subset of parameters in the score estimation network during the inference, based on a time-dependent exit schedule. Using the diffusion models for image synthesis, we show that our method could significantly improve the sampling throughput of the diffusion models without compromising image quality. Furthermore, we also demonstrate that our method seamlessly integrates with various types of solvers for faster sampling, capitalizing on their compatibility to enhance overall efficiency.

paragraphs: Diffusion models generate outputs through a sequence of steps that repeatedly evaluate a score estimation network. These repeated evaluations create a practical speed bottleneck. The paper asks whether every step needs the same amount of computation, observing that the work required to estimate the score may change depending on the time step.

Its proposed framework uses early exits to allocate computation according to a time-dependent schedule. At selected stages, inference skips a subset of the score network’s parameters. This makes the computational effort within a network evaluation adjustable, allowing the sampling process to spend less work where the schedule permits it.

Experiments on image synthesis show that the approach can substantially increase sampling throughput without reducing image quality. The authors also demonstrate compatibility with several types of sampling solvers, so early exiting can be combined with methods that accelerate the sampling procedure itself. The stated result is an experimentally supported way to make diffusion generation more efficient by adapting how much of the network is evaluated over time.
summary.tldr: Time-dependent early exits reduce computation inside diffusion networks and improve image sampling throughput without compromising quality in the reported experiments.

title: A Simple Early Exiting Framework for Accelerated Sampling in Diffusion Models

abstract: Spiking neural network (SNN) is studied in multidisciplinary domains to (i) enable order-of-magnitudes energy-efficient AI inference, and (ii) computationally simulate neuroscientific mechanisms. The lack of discrete theory obstructs the practical application of SNN by limiting its performance and nonlinearity support. We present a new optimization-theoretic perspective of the discrete dynamics of spiking neuron. We prove that a discrete dynamical system of simple integrate-and-fire models approximates the subgradient method over unconstrained optimization problems. We practically extend our theory to introduce a novel sign gradient descent (signGD)-based neuronal dynamics that can (i) approximate diverse nonlinearities beyond ReLU, and (ii) advance ANN-to-SNN conversion performance in low time-steps. Experiments on large-scale datasets show that our technique achieve (i) state-of-the-art performance in ANN-to-SNN conversion, and (ii) is first to convert new DNN architectures, e.g., ConvNext, MLP-Mixer, and ResMLP. We publicly share our source code at www.github.com/snuhcs/snn_signgd .

paragraphs: This paper develops an optimization-based account of how spiking neurons evolve in discrete time. Spiking neural networks are studied for energy-efficient inference and for simulating neural mechanisms, but limited discrete theory constrains their practical performance and support for nonlinear functions. The authors address that gap by relating neuron dynamics to familiar optimization procedures.

They prove that the discrete dynamics of simple integrate-and-fire models approximate the subgradient method for unconstrained optimization problems. Building on that result, they introduce neuronal dynamics based on sign gradient descent. The new formulation can approximate a range of nonlinearities beyond ReLU and improves conversion from conventional neural networks to spiking networks using few time steps.

Experiments on large-scale datasets report state-of-the-art conversion performance. The authors also report the first conversions of architectures including ConvNext, MLP-Mixer, and ResMLP. These findings connect the theoretical interpretation to practical architectural coverage: a broader model of neuronal dynamics supports conversion of networks whose nonlinear behavior extends beyond the previously emphasized ReLU setting.
summary.tldr: An optimization-based model of spiking dynamics enables broader nonlinearities and improves low-time-step conversion from conventional to spiking neural networks.

title: Sign Gradient Descent-based Neuronal Dynamics: ANN-to-SNN Conversion Beyond ReLU Network

abstract: In recent years many methods have been developed to understand the internal workings of neural networks, often by describing the function of individual neurons in the model. However, these methods typically only focus on explaining the very highest activations of a neuron. In this paper we show this is not sufficient, and that the highest activation range is only responsible for a very small percentage of the neuron’s causal effect. In addition, inputs causing lower activations are often very different and can’t be reliably predicted by only looking at high activations. We propose that neurons should instead be understood as a linear combination of concepts, and develop an efficient method for producing these linear explanations. In addition, we show how to automatically evaluate description quality using simulation, i.e. predicting neuron activations on unseen inputs in vision setting.

paragraphs: Many neuron-interpretation methods explain a neuron by examining inputs that produce its strongest activations. This paper argues that such examples provide an incomplete account. The authors find that the highest activation range contributes only a small share of the neuron’s causal effect, making it an insufficient basis for understanding the neuron’s overall role.

They also show that inputs producing lower activations can be very different from the strongest examples. Those responses cannot reliably be predicted just by inspecting high activations. To capture a broader range of behavior, the paper proposes describing a neuron as a linear combination of concepts and introduces an efficient method for generating such explanations.

The authors additionally develop an automatic evaluation approach in vision: use the explanation to predict a neuron’s activations on previously unseen inputs. This treats explanation quality as something that can be checked through simulation. The contribution connects a richer description of neuronal behavior with a test of whether that description actually predicts responses beyond the examples used to form it.
summary.tldr: Describing neurons as linear combinations of concepts captures behavior missed by explanations based only on their strongest activations.

title: Linear Explanations for Individual Neurons

abstract: Feature selection is a crucial tool in machine learning and is widely applied across various scientific disciplines. Traditional supervised methods generally identify a universal set of informative features for the entire population. However, feature relevance often varies with context, while the context itself may not directly affect the outcome variable. Here, we propose a novel architecture for contextual feature selection where the subset of selected features is conditioned on the value of context variables. Our new approach, Conditional Stochastic Gates (c-STG), models the importance of features using conditional Bernoulli variables whose parameters are predicted based on contextual variables. We introduce a hypernetwork that maps context variables to feature selection parameters to learn the context-dependent gates along with a prediction model. We further present a theoretical analysis of our model, indicating that it can improve performance and flexibility over population-level methods in complex feature selection settings. Finally, we conduct an extensive benchmark using simulated and real-world datasets across multiple domains demonstrating that c-STG can lead to improved feature selection capabilities while enhancing prediction accuracy and interpretability.

paragraphs: A feature can be useful in one context and uninformative in another. Selecting one shared feature set for an entire population can overlook this variation. The paper addresses the additional subtlety that context may change which features matter even when the context variable does not directly affect the outcome being predicted.

Conditional Stochastic Gates, or c-STG, selects features using gates whose probabilities depend on context. Each gate is modeled with a conditional Bernoulli variable, representing a probabilistic decision to include a feature. A hypernetwork maps context variables to the parameters controlling these gates. The gates and the prediction model are learned together, allowing feature selection to adapt to the circumstances of a prediction.

The theoretical analysis indicates that this architecture can offer greater flexibility and better performance than population-level selection in complex settings. Benchmarks on simulated and real datasets across multiple domains also show potential improvements in selection, prediction accuracy, and interpretability. The explanation becomes contextual: it concerns which inputs matter under particular conditions, rather than only which inputs matter overall.
summary.tldr: c-STG learns context-dependent feature-selection probabilities, enabling more flexible prediction and interpretation than a single shared feature set.

title: Contextual Feature Selection with Conditional Stochastic Gates

abstract: Bayesian flow networks (BFNs) iteratively refine the parameters, instead of the samples in diffusion models (DMs), of distributions at various noise levels through Bayesian inference. Owing to its differentiable nature, BFNs are promising in modeling both continuous and discrete data, while simultaneously maintaining fast sampling capabilities. This paper aims to understand and enhance BFNs by connecting them with DMs through stochastic differential equations (SDEs). We identify the linear SDEs corresponding to the noise-addition processes in BFNs, demonstrate that BFN’s regression losses are aligned with denoise score matching, and validate the sampler in BFN as a first-order solver for the respective reverse-time SDE. Based on these findings and existing recipes of fast sampling in DMs, we propose specialized solvers for BFNs that markedly surpass the original BFN sampler in terms of sample quality with a limited number of function evaluations (e.g., 10) on both image and text datasets. Notably, our best sampler achieves an increase in speed of $5\sim20$ times for free.

paragraphs: Bayesian flow networks generate data by repeatedly refining distribution parameters through Bayesian inference. Diffusion models instead refine samples. This paper connects the two approaches using stochastic differential equations, with the goal of explaining Bayesian flow networks and improving their sampling procedures for continuous and discrete data.

The authors identify linear stochastic differential equations corresponding to the noise-addition processes in Bayesian flow networks. They show that the training regression losses align with denoising score matching and interpret the original sampler as a first-order solver for the associated reverse-time equation. These connections make established diffusion sampling techniques relevant to Bayesian flow networks.

Using that connection, the authors design specialized solvers that produce better samples than the original sampler when the number of function evaluations is limited, including a ten-evaluation setting. Experiments cover image and text datasets, and the best sampler reports a five- to twenty-fold speed increase. The contribution is both a mathematical unification and a practical improvement obtained by changing how the generative process is solved.
summary.tldr: An SDE connection between Bayesian flow networks and diffusion models enables improved samplers with reported speedups of five to twenty times.

title: Unifying Bayesian Flow Networks and Diffusion Models through Stochastic Differential Equations

abstract: We explore ensembles of axis-aligned decision stumps, which can be viewed as a generalized additive model (GAM). In this model, stumps utilizing the same feature are grouped to form a shape function for that feature. Instead of relying on boosting or bagging, we employ alternating optimization to learn a fixed-size stump forest. We optimize the parameters of each stump exactly through enumeration, given the other stumps are fixed. For fixed stump splits, the leaf values are optimized jointly by solving a convex problem. To address the overfitting issue inherent in naive optimization of stump forests, we propose effective regularization techniques. Our regularized stump forests achieve accuracy comparable to state-of-the-art GAM methods while using fewer parameters. This work is the first to successfully learn stump forests without employing traditional ensembling techniques like bagging or boosting.

paragraphs: This paper builds generalized additive models from ensembles of axis-aligned decision stumps. Stumps that use the same input feature are grouped into that feature's shape function. This organization expresses the overall prediction through separate feature contributions, while allowing each contribution to be assembled from multiple simple decision rules.

The authors learn a fixed-size forest through alternating optimization instead of boosting or bagging. With the other stumps held fixed, they optimize each stump exactly by enumerating possibilities. Once the split choices are fixed, they optimize all leaf values together by solving a convex problem. These are exact solutions to particular subproblems within the alternating procedure, rather than a stated global guarantee for the whole training problem.

Naively optimizing stump forests can overfit, so the paper introduces regularization techniques to control that behavior. The resulting models achieve accuracy comparable to leading generalized additive models while using fewer parameters. The findings show that direct, regularized optimization can successfully train these forests, offering a different route from the traditional ensemble-building procedures.
summary.tldr: Directly optimizing regularized stump forests produces generalized additive models with competitive accuracy and fewer parameters.

title: Generalized additive models via direct optimization of regularized decision stump forests

abstract: Training deep neural networks (DNNs) on memory-limited GPUs is challenging, as storing intermediate activations often exceeds available memory. Re-materialization, a technique that preserves exact computations, addresses this by selectively recomputing activations instead of storing them. However, existing methods either fail to scale, lack generality, or introduce excessive execution overhead. We introduce ${\mbox{HiRemate}}$ a ${\textit hierarchical}$ re-materialization framework that recursively partitions large computation graphs, applies optimized solvers at multiple levels, and merges solutions into a global efficient training schedule. This enables scalability to significantly larger graphs than prior ILP-based methods while keeping runtime overhead low. Designed for single-GPU models and activation re-materialization, HiRemate extends the feasibility of training networks with thousands of graph nodes, surpassing prior methods in both efficiency and scalability. Experiments on various types of networks yield up to 50-70% memory reduction with only 10-15% overhead, closely matching optimal solutions while significantly reducing solver time. Seamlessly integrating with PyTorch Autograd, HiRemate requires almost no code change to use, enabling broad adoption in memory-constrained deep learning.

paragraphs: Training can exhaust GPU memory because intermediate activations must be available for later computation. Re-materialization reduces storage by recomputing selected activations when needed, while preserving the exact computation. The challenge is to choose a schedule that saves substantial memory without excessive execution overhead or an impractically expensive scheduling process.

HiRemate handles this planning problem hierarchically. It recursively divides a large computation graph, applies optimized solvers at several levels, and combines their solutions into a global training schedule. This structure allows it to handle substantially larger graphs than earlier integer-linear-programming methods while keeping runtime overhead low.

The framework targets activation re-materialization for single-GPU models and supports networks with thousands of graph nodes. Across the tested networks, the paper reports memory reductions reaching 50%–70% with 10%–15% overhead, while closely approaching optimal solutions and reducing solver time. Integration with PyTorch Autograd requires almost no code changes. Together, these results address both the quality of the memory-saving schedule and the practicality of producing and using it.
summary.tldr: HiRemate hierarchically schedules activation recomputation to reduce single-GPU training memory with modest reported execution overhead.

title: HiRemate: Hierarchical Approach for Efficient Re-materialization of Neural Networks

abstract: The ability to organically reason over and with both text and images is a pillar of human intelligence, yet the ability of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to perform such multimodal reasoning remains under-explored. Existing benchmarks often emphasize text-dominant reasoning or rely on shallow visual cues, failing to adequately assess integrated visual and textual reasoning. We introduce EMMA (Enhanced MultiModal reAsoning), a benchmark targeting organic multimodal reasoning across mathematics, physics, chemistry, and coding. EMMA tasks demand advanced cross-modal reasoning that cannot be addressed by reasoning independently in each modality, offering an enhanced test suite for MLLMs’ reasoning capabilities. Our evaluation of state-of-the-art MLLMs on EMMA reveals significant limitations in handling complex multimodal and multi-step reasoning tasks, even with advanced techniques like Chain-of-Thought prompting and test-time compute scaling underperforming. These findings underscore the need for improved multimodal architectures and training paradigms to close the gap between human and model reasoning in multimodality.

paragraphs: A model can accept both images and text without reasoning effectively across them. This paper argues that existing evaluations often obscure that distinction: some mainly test textual reasoning, while others can be solved using superficial visual information. EMMA is designed to assess problems where understanding depends on combining the two modalities throughout the reasoning process.

The benchmark covers mathematics, physics, chemistry, and coding. Its defining requirement is that tasks cannot be solved by reasoning independently about the image and the text. This makes the relationship between visual and textual information central to the assessment, providing a more demanding test of integrated reasoning than simply including an image alongside a question.

Evaluations of leading multimodal language models reveal substantial difficulty with complex, multistep problems on EMMA. Chain-of-Thought prompting and additional test-time computation also underperform in the reported evaluation. The findings identify a gap that these techniques do not adequately close on this benchmark and motivate improvements to multimodal architectures and training methods.
summary.tldr: EMMA tests reasoning that must integrate images and text, exposing substantial weaknesses in evaluated multimodal language models.

title: Can MLLMs Reason in Multimodality? EMMA: An Enhanced MultiModal ReAsoning Benchmark

abstract: Inspired by the well-known coreset in clustering algorithms, we introduce the definition of the core kernel for multiple kernel clustering (MKC) algorithms. The core kernel refers to running MKC algorithms on smaller-scale base kernel matrices to obtain kernel weights similar to those obtained from the original full-scale kernel matrices. Specifically, the core kernel refers to a set of kernel matrices of size $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(1/\varepsilon^2)$ that perform MKC algorithms on them can achieve a $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximation for the kernel weights. Subsequently, we can leverage approximated kernel weights to obtain a theoretically guaranteed large-scale extension of MKC algorithms. In this paper, we propose a core kernel construction method based on singular value decomposition and prove that it satisfies the definition of the core kernel for three mainstream MKC algorithms. Finally, we conduct experiments on several benchmark datasets to verify the correctness of theoretical results and the efficiency of the proposed method.

paragraphs: Multiple kernel clustering combines several kernel matrices, with weights determining their contributions. Computing those weights from full-scale matrices can be expensive. This paper introduces a core kernel: a smaller collection of kernel matrices on which clustering can estimate weights close to those obtained using the original matrices.

The definition makes that approximation precise. Core matrices of size roughly proportional to the inverse square of an accuracy parameter, with logarithmic factors suppressed, support a one-plus-that-parameter approximation for kernel weights. The authors construct these matrices using singular value decomposition and prove that their construction meets the definition for three mainstream multiple kernel clustering algorithms.

The approximate weights can then support large-scale extensions of those algorithms with theoretical guarantees. Experiments on benchmark datasets provide evidence consistent with the analysis and demonstrate the method’s efficiency. The important distinction is what gets compressed: the matrices used to learn kernel weights. The paper connects this smaller estimation problem to a guaranteed extension of the original clustering procedures.
summary.tldr: COKE uses smaller kernel matrices to approximate multiple-kernel clustering weights with guarantees for three established algorithms.

title: COKE: Core Kernel for More Efficient Approximation of Kernel Weights in Multiple Kernel Clustering

abstract: Data imbalance remains a fundamental challenge in real-world machine learning. However, most existing work has focused on classification, leaving imbalanced regression underexplored despite its importance in many applications. To address this gap, we propose PRIME, a framework that leverages learnable proxies to construct a balanced and well-ordered feature space for imbalanced regression. At its core, PRIME arranges proxies to be uniformly distributed in the feature space while preserving the ordinal structure of regression targets, and then aligns each sample feature to its corresponding proxy. By using proxies as reference points, PRIME induces the desired structure of learned representations, promoting better generalization, especially in underrepresented target regions. Moreover, since proxy-based alignment resembles classification, PRIME enables the seamless application of class imbalance techniques to regression, facilitating more balanced feature learning. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness and broad applicability of PRIME, achieving state-of-the-art performance on four real-world regression benchmark datasets across diverse target domains.

paragraphs: PRIME addresses regression problems in which some target values have many training examples while others have few. The paper focuses on how this imbalance shapes learned representations. Its goal is a feature space that gives underrepresented target regions better support while retaining the ordering inherent in the values being predicted.

The method introduces learnable proxies that serve as reference points for sample features. It arranges these proxies uniformly in feature space while preserving the ordinal structure of the regression targets, then aligns each sample’s representation with its corresponding proxy. This combines balanced organization with the requirement that regression values have a meaningful order.

Because alignment to proxies resembles classification, the framework also allows techniques developed for class imbalance to be used in regression. Experiments across four real-world regression benchmarks in diverse target domains report state-of-the-art performance. The results support the use of an explicitly balanced, ordered representation as a means of improving generalization, particularly for less frequently observed target regions.
summary.tldr: PRIME aligns regression features with balanced, ordered learnable proxies to improve learning across unevenly represented target values.

title: PRIME: Deep Imbalanced Regression with Proxies

abstract: Anti-viral therapies are typically designed to target only the current strains of a virus, a myopic response. However, therapy-induced selective pressures drive the emergence of new viral strains, against which the original myopic therapies are no longer effective. This evolutionary response presents an opportunity: our therapies could both defend against and actively influence viral evolution. This motivates our method ADIOS: Antibody Development vIa Opponent Shaping. ADIOS is a meta-learning framework where the process of antibody therapy design, the outer loop, accounts for the virus’s adaptive response, the inner loop. With ADIOS, antibodies are not only robust against potential future variants, they also influence, i.e. shape, which future variants emerge. In line with the opponent shaping literature, we refer to our optimised antibodies as shapers. To demonstrate the value of ADIOS, we build a viral evolution simulator using the Absolut! framework, in which shapers successfully target both current and future viral variants, outperforming myopic antibodies. Furthermore, we show that shapers modify the distribution over viral evolutionary trajectories to result in weaker variants. We believe that our ADIOS paradigm will facilitate the discovery of long-lived vaccines and antibody therapies while also generalising to other domains. Specifically, domains such as antimicrobial resistance, cancer treatment, and others with evolutionarily adaptive opponents. Our code is available at https://github.com/olakalisz/adios.

paragraphs: An antibody designed against today’s virus may become less effective as the virus adapts under treatment pressure. ADIOS treats that adaptation as part of the design problem. Its aim is to develop antibodies that work against current and possible future variants while also influencing which variants emerge.

The method uses meta-learning with two interacting loops. The outer loop designs antibody therapies, while the inner loop represents the virus’s adaptive response. This lets antibody design account for how treatment changes subsequent evolution. The resulting antibodies, called shapers, are therefore optimized with the opponent’s response in view, rather than only its current form.

In that simulator, shapers outperform myopic antibodies against current and future variants and change evolutionary trajectories toward weaker variants. These are simulation findings. The proposed implications for longer-lived vaccines, antibody therapies, antimicrobial resistance, and cancer treatment are prospective extensions of the paradigm, rather than demonstrated therapeutic outcomes.
summary.tldr: ADIOS designs antibodies around simulated viral adaptation, improving variant targeting while steering evolution toward weaker variants.

title: ADIOS: Antibody Development via Opponent Shaping

abstract: Diffusion models have achieved remarkable progress on image-to-video (I2V) generation, while their noise-to-data generation process is inherently mismatched with this task, which may lead to suboptimal synthesis quality. In this work, we present FrameBridge. By modeling the frame-to-frames generation process with a bridge model based data-to-data generative process, we are able to fully exploit the information contained in the given image and improve the consistency between the generation process and I2V task. Moreover, we propose two novel techniques toward the two popular settings of training I2V models, respectively. Firstly, we propose SNR-Aligned Fine-tuning (SAF), making the first attempt to fine-tune a diffusion model to a bridge model and, therefore, allowing us to utilize the pre-trained diffusion-based text-to-video (T2V) models. Secondly, we propose neural prior, further improving the synthesis quality of FrameBridge when training from scratch. Experiments conducted on WebVid-2M and UCF-101 demonstrate the superior quality of FrameBridge in comparison with the diffusion counterpart (zero-shot FVD 95 vs. 192 on MSR-VTT and non-zero-shot FVD 122 vs. 171 on UCF-101), and the advantages of our proposed SAF and neural prior for bridge-based I2V models. The project page: https://framebridge-icml.github.io/

paragraphs: Image-to-video generation begins with an image that already contains useful visual information. The paper argues that a diffusion process organized around transforming noise into data is inherently mismatched with this starting point and may produce suboptimal results. FrameBridge instead models a transition from the supplied frame to a sequence of frames using a bridge-based, data-to-data generation process.

The authors develop separate techniques for two training situations. SNR-Aligned Fine-tuning adapts a pretrained diffusion model into a bridge model, allowing FrameBridge to benefit from existing text-to-video models. When training from scratch, a proposed neural prior further improves synthesis quality. These components support using the bridge formulation with either inherited model knowledge or new training.

The reported FVD values are 95 versus 192 in zero-shot evaluation on MSR-VTT and 122 versus 171 in non-zero-shot evaluation on UCF-101. The experiments also support the benefits of the fine-tuning technique and neural prior within bridge-based generation.
summary.tldr: FrameBridge models image-to-video generation as a frame-to-frames bridge process and reports better synthesis quality than its diffusion counterpart.

title: FrameBridge: Improving Image-to-Video Generation with Bridge Models

abstract: Inspired by the recent success of LLMs, the field of human motion understanding has increasingly shifted toward developing large motion models. Despite some progress, current efforts remain far from achieving truly generalist models, primarily due to the lack of massive high-quality data. To address this gap, we present MotionLib, the first million-level dataset for motion generation, which is at least 15$\times$ larger than existing counterparts and enriched with hierarchical text descriptions. Using MotionLib, we train a large motion model named Being-M0, demonstrating robust performance across a wide range of human activities, including unseen ones. Through systematic investigation, for the first time, we highlight the importance of scaling both data and model size for advancing motion generation, along with key insights to achieve this goal. To better integrate the motion modality, we propose Motionbook, an innovative motion encoding approach including (1) a compact yet lossless feature to represent motions; (2) a novel 2D lookup-free motion tokenizer that preserves fine-grained motion details while expanding codebook capacity, significantly enhancing the representational power of motion tokens. We believe this work lays the groundwork for developing more versatile and powerful motion generation models in the future. For further details, visit https://beingbeyond.github.io/Being-M0/.

paragraphs: This paper addresses the shortage of large, high-quality datasets for general-purpose human motion generation. It introduces MotionLib, a million-level collection at least fifteen times larger than the existing counterparts described by the authors. Hierarchical text descriptions accompany the motions, providing language information for learning across a broad range of activities.

The scaling investigation highlights the importance of increasing both data and model size for advancing motion generation. Together, the dataset, representation method, and trained model provide evidence toward more versatile motion systems, while the authors frame truly generalist motion generation as a broader goal.
summary.tldr: MotionLib, Being-M0, and Motionbook combine larger-scale data, models, and richer motion encoding to advance human motion generation.

title: Scaling Large Motion Models with Million-Level Human Motions

abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents have recently demonstrated impressive capabilities in various domains like open-ended conversation and multi-step decision-making. However, it remains challenging for these agents to solve strategic language games, such as Werewolf, which demand both strategic decision-making and free-form language interactions. Existing LLM agents often suffer from intrinsic bias in their action distributions and limited exploration of the unbounded text action space, resulting in suboptimal performance. To address these challenges, we propose Latent Space Policy Optimization (LSPO), an iterative framework that combines game-theoretic methods with LLM fine-tuning to build strategic language agents. LSPO leverages the observation that while the language space is combinatorially large, the underlying strategy space is relatively compact. We first map free-form utterances into a finite latent strategy space, yielding an abstracted extensive-form game. Then we apply game-theoretic methods like Counterfactual Regret Minimization (CFR) to optimize the policy in the latent space. Finally, we fine-tune the LLM via Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) to align with the learned policy. By iteratively alternating between these steps, our LSPO agents progressively enhance both strategic reasoning and language communication. Experiment on the Werewolf game shows that our agents iteratively expand the strategy space with improving performance and outperform existing Werewolf agents, underscoring their effectiveness in free-form language games with strategic interactions.
