paragraphs: Werewolf challenges language agents to make strategic decisions through free-form conversation. The possible utterances are enormously varied, making exploration difficult, and language models can have biases in which actions they favor. Latent Space Policy Optimization addresses these problems by working with a compact representation of the strategies underlying spoken actions.

The framework first maps utterances into a finite set of latent strategies, producing an abstract game representation. It then applies game-theoretic methods such as Counterfactual Regret Minimization to optimize decisions in that space. Finally, Direct Preference Optimization fine-tunes the language model to follow the learned policy, connecting strategic optimization back to natural-language behavior.

These stages repeat, allowing strategy learning and language generation to develop together. In Werewolf experiments, the agents expand their strategy space over successive iterations, improve performance, and outperform existing Werewolf agents. The findings support using a manageable strategy representation to guide learning in a much larger language-action space, while progressively enriching that representation through iteration.
summary.tldr: LSPO improves Werewolf agents by alternating compact strategy-space optimization with language-model fine-tuning.

title: Learning Strategic Language Agents in the Werewolf Game with Iterative Latent Space Policy Optimization

abstract: Dynamic data selection aims to accelerate training with lossless performances. However, reducing training data inherently limits data diversity, potentially hindering generalization. While data augmentation is widely used to enhance diversity, it is typically not optimized in conjunction with selection. As a result, directly combining these techniques fails to fully exploit their synergies. To tackle the challenge, we propose a novel online data training framework that, for the first time, unifies dynamic data selection and augmentation, achieving both training efficiency and enhanced performance. Our method estimates each sample’s joint distribution of local density and multimodal semantic consistency, allowing for the targeted selection of augmentation-suitable samples while suppressing the inclusion of noisy or ambiguous data. This enables a more significant reduction in dataset size without sacrificing model generalization. Experimental results demonstrate that our method outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches on various benchmark datasets and architectures, e.g., reducing 50% training costs on ImageNet-1k with lossless performance. Furthermore, our approach enhances noise resistance and improves model robustness, reinforcing its practical utility in real-world scenarios.

paragraphs: Dynamic data selection speeds training by using fewer examples, but the resulting loss of diversity can harm generalization. Data augmentation can increase diversity, yet selecting samples and augmenting them independently may miss useful interactions. This paper introduces an online training framework that makes these decisions together.

For each sample, the method estimates a joint distribution involving local density and multimodal semantic consistency. It uses this information to select examples suited to augmentation while limiting noisy or ambiguous data. Selection is therefore guided partly by how useful the retained examples will be when augmented, enabling a greater reduction in dataset size without sacrificing generalization in the reported evaluations.

Experiments across benchmark datasets and architectures show improvements over existing state-of-the-art approaches. One reported result reduces ImageNet-1k training costs by 50% without performance loss. The method also improves noise resistance and model robustness. These findings support coordinating selection with augmentation as a practical route to faster training, with the gains arising from the quality and diversity of the chosen training data.
summary.tldr: Jointly choosing training samples and their suitability for augmentation reduces training costs while preserving performance and improving robustness in the reported experiments.

title: When Dynamic Data Selection Meets Data Augmentation: Achieving Enhanced Training Acceleration

abstract: Long-context LLMs are increasingly in demand for applications such as retrieval-augmented generation. To defray the cost of pretraining LLMs over long contexts, recent work takes an approach of synthetic context extension: fine-tuning LLMs with synthetically-generated long-context data. However, it remains unclear how and why this synthetic context extension imparts abilities for downstream long-context tasks. In this paper, we investigate fine-tuning on synthetic data for three long-context tasks that require retrieval and reasoning. We vary the realism of "needle” concepts to be retrieved and diversity of the surrounding "haystack” context, from using LLMs to construct synthetic documents to using templated relations and creating symbolic datasets. Although models trained on synthetic data underperform models trained on the real data, the impacts of both training settings can be understood via a shared feature of the attention computation, retrieval heads (Wu et al., 2024). The retrieval heads learned from synthetic data have high overlap with retrieval heads learned on real data. Furthermore, there is a strong correlation between the recall of heads learned and the downstream performance of a model, allowing us to interpret and predict the performance of models trained in different settings. Our results shed light on how to interpret synthetic data fine-tuning performance and how to approach creating better data for learning real-world LLM capabilities over long contexts.

This paper investigates how that training supports later retrieval and reasoning. It studies three tasks while varying both the realism of the information to retrieve and the diversity of its surrounding context.

This connects a measurable internal feature to the effectiveness of context-extension data and offers a basis for investigating how synthetic training examples might better support real-world long-context capabilities.
summary.tldr: Synthetic and real long-context training develop overlapping retrieval heads, whose recall strongly correlates with downstream performance.

title: Understanding Synthetic Context Extension via Retrieval Heads

abstract: We study machine unlearning in large generative models by framing the task as density ratio estimation to a target distribution rather than supervised fine-tuning. While classifier guidance is a standard approach for approximating this ratio and can succeed in general, we show it can fail to faithfully unlearn with finite samples when the forget set represents a sharp, concentrated data distribution. To address this, we introduce Temper-Then-Tilt Unlearning (T3-Unlearning), which freezes the base model and applies a two-step inference procedure: (i) tempering the base distribution to flatten high-confidence spikes, and (ii) tilting the tempered distribution using a lightweight classifier trained to distinguish retain from forget samples. Our theoretical analysis provides finite-sample guarantees linking the surrogate classifier’s risk to unlearning quality, proving that tempering is necessary to successfully unlearn for concentrated distributions. Empirical evaluations on the TOFU benchmark demonstrate that T3-Unlearning improves forget quality and generative utility over existing baselines, while training only a fraction of the parameters with a minimal runtime.

To address this, we introduce Temper-Then-Tilt Unlearning (T3-Unlearning), which freezes the base model and applies a two-step inference procedure: (i) tempering the base distribution to flatten high-confidence spikes, and (ii) tilting the tempered distribution using a lightweight classifier trained to distinguish retain from forget samples. paragraphs: This paper frames generative-model unlearning as estimating a density ratio toward a desired target distribution. Classifier guidance can approximate that ratio, but the authors show a finite-sample failure case: it may not faithfully forget data whose distribution is sharply concentrated. The difficulty is tied to that concentration rather than a general impossibility of classifier-guided unlearning.

Temper-Then-Tilt Unlearning keeps the base model frozen and changes inference in two steps. Tempering first flattens high-confidence peaks in the base distribution. Tilting then uses a lightweight classifier trained to distinguish retained samples from forgotten samples to reshape the tempered distribution. The ordering is central because the classifier operates after those peaks have been softened.

The analysis gives finite-sample guarantees connecting classifier risk with unlearning quality and proves the necessity of tempering for concentrated distributions in the studied setting. On TOFU, experiments report improved forgetting and generative utility over existing baselines while training only a fraction of the parameters with minimal runtime. The results connect a specific distributional failure mode to a targeted inference procedure.
summary.tldr: T3-Unlearning flattens a frozen model’s concentrated probability peaks before applying classifier guidance, improving forgetting and utility on TOFU.

title: Temper-Then-Tilt: Principled Unlearning for Generative Models through Tempering and Classifier Guidance

abstract: We present algorithms for diffusion model sampling which obtain $\delta$-error in $\mathrm{polylog}(1/\delta)$ steps, given access to $\widetilde O(\delta)$-accurate score estimates in $L^2$. This is an exponential improvement over all previous results. Specifically, under minimal data assumptions, the complexity is $\widetilde O(d\mathrm{polylog}(1/\delta))$ where $d$ is the dimension of the data; under a non-uniform $L$-Lipschitz condition, the complexity is $\widetilde O(\sqrt{dL}\mathrm{polylog}(1/\delta))$; and if the data distribution has intrinsic dimension $d_\star$, then the complexity reduces to $\widetilde O(d_\star\mathrm{polylog}(1/\delta))$. Our approach also yields the first $\mathrm{polylog}(1/\delta)$ complexity sampler for general log-concave distributions using only gradient evaluations.

This is an exponential improvement over all previous results. Specifically, under minimal data assumptions, the complexity is $\widetilde O(d\mathrm{polylog}(1/\delta))$ where $d$ is the dimension of the data; under a non-uniform $L$-Lipschitz condition, the complexity is $\widetilde O(\sqrt{dL}\mathrm{polylog}(1/\delta))$; and if the data distribution has intrinsic dimension $d_\star$, then the complexity reduces to $\widetilde O(d_\star\mathrm{polylog}(1/\delta))$. paragraphs: The paper develops sampling algorithms whose step requirements grow slowly as the requested error becomes smaller. For diffusion models, it achieves error δ using a number of steps polynomial in the logarithm of 1/δ. The abstract describes this accuracy dependence as an exponential improvement over previous results.

That guarantee requires access to score estimates with L² error approximately proportional to δ, up to the stated asymptotic factors. Under minimal data assumptions, the reported complexity scales with data dimension d times the polylogarithmic accuracy term. Under a non-uniform L-Lipschitz condition, the dimensional factor becomes the square root of dL. When the distribution has intrinsic dimension d-star, the bound instead depends on that intrinsic dimension.

These results distinguish the cost of demanding higher accuracy from the cost associated with dimensionality and regularity. Their assumptions matter: the sampling improvement is conditional on sufficiently accurate score estimates. The approach also yields a sampler for general log-concave distributions with polylogarithmic dependence on inverse error using only gradient evaluations, which the authors identify as a first.
summary.tldr: New samplers achieve polylogarithmic dependence on inverse error, with diffusion guarantees conditional on sufficiently accurate score estimates.

title: High-Accuracy Sampling for Diffusion Models and Log-Concave Distributions

abstract: Text-to-image (T2I) diffusion models are widely adopted for their strong generative capabilities, yet remain vulnerable to backdoor attacks. Existing attacks typically rely on fixed textual triggers and single-entity backdoor targets, making them highly susceptible to enumeration-based input defenses and attention-consistency detection. In this work, we propose Semantic-level Backdoor Attack (SemBD), which introduces representation-level triggers based on continuous semantic regions rather than discrete textual patterns. SemBD implants such semantic backdoors by distillation-based editing of the key and value projection matrices in cross-attention layers, enabling semantically equivalent but textually diverse prompts to activate the backdoor. To further enhance stealthiness, SemBD incorporates a semantic regularization to prevent unintended activation under incomplete semantics, as well as multi-entity backdoor targets that avoid highly consistent cross-attention patterns. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SemBD achieves a 100% attack success rate while maintaining strong robustness against state-of-the-art input-level defenses. Our code is available at https://github.com/DPAS-Lab/SemBD/.

paragraphs: SemBD investigates backdoors in text-to-image diffusion models that respond to meaning rather than a fixed textual trigger. Existing attacks often rely on specific strings and a single target entity, giving defenses recurring input or attention patterns to detect. Semantic triggers expand activation to differently worded prompts that express equivalent content.

The method introduces these triggers through distillation-based edits to key and value projection matrices in cross-attention layers. It also uses semantic regularization to reduce unintended activation when the triggering meaning is incomplete. Targets containing multiple entities further reduce the highly consistent cross-attention patterns associated with single-entity attacks.

Experiments report a 100% attack success rate and strong robustness against state-of-the-art input-level defenses in the evaluated settings. The finding highlights a distinction between recognizing suspicious wording and detecting malicious behavior tied to a broader semantic region. It also shows why attacks that vary both their wording and attention patterns can challenge defenses designed around fixed, repeatable signatures.
summary.tldr: SemBD creates meaning-based backdoors that activate across differently worded prompts and resist evaluated input-level defenses.

title: Semantic-level Backdoor Attack against Text-to-Image Diffusion Models

abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models rely on balanced expert utilization to fully realize their scalability. However, existing load-balancing methods are largely heuristic and operate on noisy mini-batch assignment statistics, introducing bias relative to population-level objectives. We propose $\phi$-balancing, a principled framework that directly targets population-level expert balance by minimizing a strictly convex, symmetric, and differentiable potential of the expected routing distribution. Using convex duality, we derive an equivalent min-max formulation and obtain a simple online algorithm via mirror descent, yielding an efficient EMA-based routing adjustment with negligible overhead. Across large-scale pretraining and downstream fine-tuning, $\phi$-balancing consistently outperforms prior Switch-style and loss-free baselines, demonstrating more stable and effective expert utilization.

The central contribution connects a population-level balancing objective to a lightweight training procedure, reducing reliance on heuristic responses to noisy batch statistics.
summary.tldr: φ-balancing derives a lightweight routing adjustment from a population-level objective to improve expert utilization during MoE training.

title: $φ$-Balancing for Mixture-of-Experts Training

abstract: While benchmarks measure the accuracy of LLM-powered agents, they mostly assume full automation, failing to represent the collaborative nature of real-world use cases. In this paper, we make two major steps towards the rigorous assessment of human-agent interactions. First, we propose PULSE, a framework for more efficient human-centric evaluation of agent designs, which comprises collecting user feedback, training an ML model to predict user satisfaction, and computing results by combining human satisfaction ratings with model-generated pseudo-labels. Second, we deploy PULSE n software engineering—one of the highest-impact, real-world domains for LLM agents—via a large-scale web platform built around the open-source agent OpenHands. Across 15k users, we evaluate how three agent design decisions impact developer satisfaction rates. We also show how PULSE can lead to more robust conclusions about agent design, reducing confidence intervals by 40% compared to a standard A/B test. Finally, we find substantial discrepancies between in-the-wild results with benchmark performance (e.g., the anti-correlation between claude-sonnet-4 and gpt-5, underscoring the limitations of benchmark-driven evaluation. Our framework PULSE provides guidance for future evaluations, and our findings identify opportunities for better software agent designs.

The authors introduce PULSE to make evaluations centered on human experience more efficient.

Across 15,000 users, they examine how three agent-design decisions affect developer satisfaction, providing an evaluation grounded in real interactions.

The study also finds substantial differences between benchmark performance and results in actual use, including an anti-correlation involving the compared models. The findings show why satisfaction measurements can add information that automation-focused benchmarks do not capture.
summary.tldr: PULSE combines user ratings with predicted satisfaction to evaluate collaborative agents more precisely in real-world use.

title: How can we assess human-agent interactions? Case studies in software agent design

abstract: Representations on the Symmetric Positive Definite (SPD) manifold have garnered significant attention across different applications. In contrast, the manifold of full-rank correlation matrices, a normalized alternative to SPD matrices, remains largely underexplored. This paper introduces Riemannian networks over the correlation manifold, leveraging five recently developed correlation geometries. We systematically extend basic layers, including Multinomial Logistic Regression (MLR), Fully Connected (FC), and convolutional layers, to these geometries. Besides, we present methods for accurate backpropagation for two correlation geometries. Experiments comparing our approach against existing SPD and Grassmannian networks demonstrate its effectiveness.

paragraphs: This paper develops neural networks for full-rank correlation matrices. These matrices form a normalized alternative to symmetric positive definite matrices, whose use as learned representations has already received considerable attention. The authors focus on the comparatively underexplored geometry of correlation matrices and how to build network operations around that structure.

The approach uses five recently developed correlation geometries. For each, the work extends basic network layers, including multinomial logistic regression, fully connected layers, and convolutional layers. The contribution therefore covers several building blocks needed to construct networks over correlation representations. It also provides methods for accurate backpropagation in two of the geometries, addressing how those networks can be trained.

Experiments compare the resulting approach with existing networks based on symmetric positive definite and Grassmannian representations and demonstrate its effectiveness. The findings support correlation geometry as a useful basis for neural-network design. The paper’s main contribution is the systematic development of geometry-aware layers and training methods for this normalized matrix representation.
summary.tldr: The paper builds geometry-aware neural-network layers for correlation matrices and demonstrates their effectiveness against other geometric networks.

title: Riemannian Networks over Full-Rank Correlation Matrices

abstract: Accurate mechanical properties (or materials) Young’s modulus ($E$), Poisson’s ratio ($\nu$) and density ($\rho$) are essential for reliable physics simulation of digital worlds, but most 3D assets lack this information. We propose AdaVoMP, a method for predicting accurate dense spatially-varying $(E, \nu, \rho)$ for input 3D objects across representations, improving the resolution, accuracy, and memory efficiency over the state-of-the-art. The foundation of our technique is a sparse and adaptive voxel structure SAV that efficiently represents both the input 3D shape and the material field output. We replace the fixed-voxel model of the most accurate prior method, VoMP, with a novel sparse transformer encoder-decoder model that learns to generate a unique SAV autoregressively for every input shape to represent its materials, achieving a resolution $16^3\times$ higher than prior art. Experiments show that AdaVoMP estimates more accurate volumetric properties, even with lesser test-time compute than all prior art. This allows us to convert high-resolution complex 3D objects into simulation-ready assets, resulting in realistic deformable simulations.

paragraphs: A detailed 3D shape is not enough to simulate how an object deforms. A simulator also needs material properties throughout its volume, including stiffness, Poisson’s ratio, and density. AdaVoMP predicts these spatially varying properties for input 3D objects, turning geometric assets into objects that can participate in physical simulations.

Their experiments also show these improvements with less test-time computation than the previous methods considered. The practical outcome is the conversion of complex, high-resolution objects into simulation-ready assets that produce realistic deformable behavior.
summary.tldr: AdaVoMP uses adaptive sparse voxels to predict detailed material properties for 3D objects with improved accuracy and computational efficiency.

title: Adaptive Volumetric Mechanical Property Fields Invariant to Resolution

abstract: Deep neural networks have recently advanced infrared and visible image fusion (IVIF), but most existing methods rely on sophisticated yet redundant designs, which hinder real-time deployment on mobile devices with limited compute and memory. In this paper, we present MobileFusion, an extremely lightweight and effective convolutional framework that achieves high-quality fusion under strict resource constraints. MobileFusion leverages a novel re-parameterizable multi-branch convolution module to promote cross-modal interactions during training while collapsing into a single-path operator for fast inference. It further incorporates a lightweight attention module to enhance context awareness, together with a re-parameterized feed-forward network to improve feature expressiveness. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MobileFusion delivers a favorable trade-off between fusion quality and computational efficiency, enabling real-time and high-quality IVIF on resource-constrained platforms. The source code is available at https://github.com/sucessfullys/MobileFusion.

paragraphs: Combining infrared and visible images can produce a fused image that draws information from both modalities. However, sophisticated fusion networks can demand too much computation and memory for mobile deployment. MobileFusion develops a lightweight convolutional framework aimed at maintaining fusion quality within these strict resource constraints.

Its central module has multiple convolutional branches during training to promote interaction between the two modalities. Through structural re-parameterization, those branches collapse into a single-path operator for inference. This gives training a richer structure while simplifying the computation needed when the model is deployed. A lightweight attention module adds context awareness, and a re-parameterized feed-forward network improves feature expressiveness.

Extensive experiments report a favorable balance between fusion quality and computational efficiency, enabling real-time, high-quality fusion on resource-constrained platforms. The significance lies in the coordinated design: cross-modal learning, contextual processing, and expressive features are retained within an architecture built for inexpensive inference. The reported outcome supports structural re-parameterization as a practical tool for mobile image fusion.
summary.tldr: MobileFusion collapses a rich training architecture into efficient inference operators for real-time infrared and visible image fusion.

title: MobileFusion: Mobile-Friendly Infrared and Visible Image Fusion via Structural Re-parameterization

abstract: Generation-time text watermarking embeds statistical signals into text for traceability of AI-generated content. We explore post-hoc watermarking where an LLM rewrites existing text while applying generation-time watermarking, to protect copyrighted documents, or detect their use in training or RAG via watermark radioactivity. Unlike generation-time approaches which are constrained by how LLMs are served, this setting offers additional degrees of freedom for both generation and detection. We thus investigate how allocating compute (through larger rephrasing models, beam search, multi-candidate generation, or entropy filtering at detection) affects the quality-detectability trade-off. Among our findings, the simple Gumbel-max scheme surprisingly outperforms more recent alternatives under nucleus sampling, and achieves strong detectability and semantic fidelity on open-ended text such as books. Moreover, most methods benefit significantly from beam search, and we counterintuitively find that smaller models outperform larger ones. However, our solutions struggles when watermarking verifiable text such as code. This study reveals both the potential and limitations of post-hoc watermarking, laying groundwork for practical applications and future research.

paragraphs: Post-hoc text watermarking rewrites an existing document while inserting a statistical signal that can later be detected. This paper investigates that approach for copyright protection and for detecting document use in training or retrieval-augmented generation. Because rewriting happens after the original text exists, the system has additional choices about how to generate candidates and detect their watermarks.

The study examines how computation affects the balance between preserving text quality and making the watermark detectable. It considers larger rewriting models, beam search, multiple candidate generations, and entropy filtering during detection. Under nucleus sampling, the simple Gumbel-max watermark performs better than more recent alternatives and provides strong detectability while preserving meaning in open-ended material such as books.

Most evaluated methods benefit substantially from beam search, while smaller models unexpectedly outperform larger ones in the study. The approach struggles with verifiable text such as code. The findings therefore support post-hoc watermarking for some kinds of text while showing that model size and rewriting flexibility do not automatically produce better results.
summary.tldr: Rephrasing-based watermarking shows strong results on open-ended text, but struggles with code and does not consistently benefit from larger models.

title: How Good is Post-Hoc Watermarking With Language Model Rephrasing?

abstract: Discrete flow matching (DFM) provides a principled framework for generative modeling on discrete state spaces via continuous-time Markov chain dynamics. In practice, sampling for DFM commonly employs discretizations such as $\tau$-leaping, yet efficient sampling methods under a limited number of function evaluations (NFE) remain less studied. To address this gap, we propose the Time-Reparameterized Cumulative Intensity Extrapolation (TR-CIE) sampler, which aims to improve sampling quality when function evaluations are restricted. TR-CIE consists of two components. First, a schedule-based time reparameterization rescales the time grid according to the noise schedule. Under standard factorized DFM rate parameterizations, this transformation of variables absorbs the schedule-dependent growth term and mitigates stiffness near the terminal sampling stage. Second, we introduce a cumulative-intensity extrapolation updating rule. By reusing cached model outputs from the previous step as a history term, this improves the approximation of stepwise cumulative intensities on the resulting non-uniform time grid. We provide a theoretical analysis that bounds the local approximation error of cumulative intensities and establishes convergence results. The resulting sampler requires one NFE per step and introduces no additional model evaluations compared to the standard $\tau$-leaping sampler. Extensive experiments on synthetic tasks, text generation, and text-to-image benchmarks demonstrate that our method improves sampling quality under limited NFE.

paragraphs: Discrete flow matching generates discrete outputs through a process of changes over continuous time. Running that process requires numerical sampling, and quality can suffer when only a small number of model evaluations is affordable. TR-CIE changes how the sampler advances through time and estimates the accumulated intensity of transitions within each step.

The contribution is therefore a way to extract more sampling accuracy from the same evaluation budget.
summary.tldr: TR-CIE improves discrete flow sampling under limited model evaluations by reshaping sampling time and reusing previous model outputs.

title: A Time-Reparameterized Cumulative Intensity Extrapolation Sampler for Discrete Flow Matching

abstract: Recent advances have empowered large language models (LLMs) with remarkable fine-grained instruction-following capabilities in text generation tasks. However, embedding methods typically rely solely on the hidden state of the input’s last token, limiting their ability to capture complete semantic signals distributed across the full output tokens. Moreover, existing discrete-to-continuous re-encoding approaches introduce semantic discontinuity. To address these limitations, we propose $\textbf{InstEmb}$, a novel instruction following embedding framework. InstEmb jointly optimizes two key aspects: (1) Input-Intrinsic semantic information, achieved by employing contrastive learning focused on the representation of the last input token, and (2) Output-Aware semantic information, captured through representation self-distillation leveraging learnable look-ahead tokens without introducing additional decoding latency. Additionally, we introduce $\textbf{Dual-Anchor Alignment Pooling (DAAP)}$, explicitly aligned with our dual training objectives. Extensive experiments demonstrate that InstEmb achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple instruction following benchmarks without benchmark-specific supervised data.

paragraphs: Language models can follow detailed instructions when generating text, but embedding methods often summarize an input using only its final token’s hidden representation. The paper argues that this misses semantic information distributed across the output the model would produce. Generating discrete text and then encoding it again also introduces a discontinuity in the representation process.

InstEmb combines two training objectives. Contrastive learning strengthens information intrinsic to the input through its last-token representation. Representation self-distillation adds output-aware information using learnable look-ahead tokens, without introducing additional decoding latency. These tokens provide a way to incorporate information associated with future output into an embedding rather than requiring ordinary output decoding.

The method also introduces Dual-Anchor Alignment Pooling, designed to match the two complementary training objectives when forming the final representation. Experiments report state-of-the-art performance across multiple instruction-following benchmarks without benchmark-specific supervised data. The result supports jointly training embeddings to capture what the input contains and what an instruction-following model would express in response.
summary.tldr: InstEmb improves instruction-following embeddings by combining input representations with output-aware information from learnable look-ahead tokens.

title: InstEmb: Instruction-Following Embeddings through Glimpses of the Future

abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable success in dyadic (one-on-one) instruction, they face significant challenges in One-to-Many alignment, such as clinical ward rounds, where an instructor must simultaneously guide a diverse group of trainees. Current models often suffer from context dilution and goal misalignment, failing to balance individual scaffolding with collective learning progress. To address this, we introduce ClinEdu, a multi-agent pedagogical simulator that model the complexity of group dynamics. Leveraging this platform, we construct ClinTeach, a large-scale dataset of Socratic teaching dialogues, and propose ClinTutor-R1, the first multimodal agent explicitly architected to achieve one-to-many alignment in clinical education, employing an explicit internal thinking mechanism to model both individual belief states and group consensus. We validate our framework through a comprehensive protocol covering both standard static benchmarks and rigorous in-situ interactive evaluation within ClinEdu. Experimental results demonstrate that ClinTutor-R1 outperforms base models by over 20% and achieves parity with proprietary reasoning models , while exhibiting exceptional scalability in maintaining instructional quality across expanding student cohorts.

paragraphs: Teaching a group requires tracking individual understanding while keeping everyone moving toward a shared learning goal. The paper studies this challenge in clinical Socratic education, including settings resembling ward rounds. Models designed for one-on-one instruction can lose relevant context or pursue mismatched goals when several trainees need different kinds of guidance.

title: ClinTutor-R1: Advancing Scalable and Robust One-to-Many Alignment in Clinical Socratic Education

abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models often suffer from performance degradation under distribution shifts, as they struggle to learn generalized behavior representations across varying environments. While existing approaches attempt to construct behavior representations through action-centric latent variables, they are often limited by short-horizon temporal fragmentation and static execution-alignment, leading to inconsistent behaviors in complex scenarios. To address these limitations, we propose BehaviorVLA, a framework that facilitates robust manipulation through the learning of a temporally coherent behavioral representations. Our approach features two symmetric components: (1) the Visuomotor Behavior Encoder (VBE), which utilizes a causal Mamba-based architecture to aggregate long-horizon trajectory information into a unified behavior representation; and (2) the Phase-conditioned Behavior Decoder (PBD), which decodes this representation into precise actions by dynamically aligning task-level priors with real-time execution progress. Experiments on RoboTwin 2.0, LIBERO, and CALVIN demonstrate state-of-the-art success rates of 58%, 98%, and 4.36 (Avg.Len), respectively. Notably, in real-world sim-to-real transfer, BehaviorVLA matches the performance of OpenVLA-OFT using only 50% of the demonstration data, showcasing its superior data efficiency and generalization.

BehaviorVLA addresses representations that fragment behavior into short intervals or align execution too rigidly. It aims to capture a coherent behavior over longer trajectories and adapt its realization to the task’s current progress.

The encoder uses a causal Mamba-based architecture to combine long-horizon trajectory information into a unified representation. summary.tldr: BehaviorVLA combines long-horizon behavior encoding with progress-aware action decoding to improve robotic manipulation and demonstration efficiency.

title: From Abstraction to Instantiation: Learning Behavioral Representation for Vision-Language-Action Model

abstract: Privacy protection has become a critical requirement in the era of ubiquitous visual data sharing, imposing higher demands on efficient and robust privacy detection algorithms. However, current robust detection models are severely hindered by the lack of comprehensive datasets. Existing privacy-oriented datasets often suffer from limited scale, coarse-grained annotations, and narrow domain coverage, failing to capture the intricate details of sensitive information in real-world environments. To bridge this gap, we present a large-scale, fine-grained Visual Privacy Dataset (VPD-100K), designed to facilitate generalized privacy detection. We establish a holistic taxonomy comprising four primary domains: Human Presence, On-Screen Personally Identifiable Information (PII), Physical Identifiers, and Location Indicators, containing 100,000 images annotated with 33 fine-grained classes and over 190,000 object instances. Statistical analysis reveals that our dataset features long-tailed distributions, small object scales, and high visual complexity. These characteristics make the dataset particularly valuable for demanding, unconstrained applications such as live streaming, where actors frequently face unintentional, real-time information leakage. Furthermore, we design an effective frequency-enhance lightweight module consisting of frequency-domain attention fusion and adaptive spectral gating mechanism that breaks the limitations of spatial pixel intensity to better capture the subtle details of sensitive information. Extensive experiments conducted on both diverse image and streaming videos benchmarks consistently demonstrate the effectiveness of our VPD-100K dataset and the well-curated frequency mechanism.
originalAbstract: Privacy protection has become a critical requirement in the era of ubiquitous visual data sharing, imposing higher demands on efficient and robust privacy detection algorithms. However, current robust detection models are severely hindered by the lack of comprehensive datasets. Existing privacy-oriented datasets often suffer from limited scale, coarse-grained annotations, and narrow domain coverage, failing to capture the intricate details of sensitive information in real-world environments. To bridge this gap, we present a large-scale, fine-grained Visual Privacy Dataset (VPD-100K), designed to facilitate generalized privacy detection. We establish a holistic taxonomy comprising four primary domains: Human Presence, On-Screen Personally Identifiable Information (PII), Physical Identifiers, and Location Indicators, containing 100,000 images annotated with 33 fine-grained classes and over 190,000 object instances. Statistical analysis reveals that our dataset features long-tailed distributions, small object scales, and high visual complexity. These characteristics make the dataset particularly valuable for demanding, unconstrained applications such as live streaming, where actors frequently face unintentional, real-time information leakage. Furthermore, we design an effective frequency-enhance lightweight module consisting of frequency-domain attention fusion and adaptive spectral gating mechanism that breaks the limitations of spatial pixel intensity to better capture the subtle details of sensitive information. Extensive experiments conducted on both diverse image and streaming videos benchmarks consistently demonstrate the effectiveness of our VPD-100K dataset and the well-curated frequency mechanism.

paragraphs: Detecting privacy-sensitive information in images requires recognizing many different kinds of small or visually complex details. Existing privacy datasets can be too limited in size, annotation detail, or domain coverage to support that goal. VPD-100K addresses this data problem with 100,000 images, 33 fine-grained classes, and more than 190,000 annotated object instances.

Its taxonomy covers human presence, personally identifiable information on screens, physical identifiers, and location indicators. The dataset contains uneven class frequencies, small objects, and complex scenes. Those characteristics make it relevant to unconstrained settings such as livestreaming, where sensitive information can appear unintentionally during ongoing activity.

The paper also introduces a lightweight frequency-enhancement module combining frequency-domain attention fusion with adaptive spectral gating. It aims to capture subtle sensitive details beyond what spatial pixel intensities alone provide. Experiments on image and streaming-video benchmarks report consistent effectiveness for both the dataset and the frequency mechanism. The combined contribution addresses what detectors can learn from and how they represent difficult visual evidence when identifying potential privacy exposure.
summary.tldr: VPD-100K supplies detailed visual privacy annotations and a lightweight frequency-based module to improve detection of sensitive information in images and streams.

title: VPD-100K: Towards Generalizable and Fine-grained Visual Privacy Protection

abstract: Evaluating LLM reliability via scalar probabilities often fails to capture the structural dynamics of reasoning. We introduce TRACED, a framework that assesses reasoning quality through theoretically grounded geometric kinematics. By decomposing reasoning traces into Progress (displacement) and Stability (curvature), we reveal a distinct topological divergence: correct reasoning manifests as high-progress, stable trajectories, whereas hallucinations are characterized by low-progress, unstable patterns (stalled displacement with high curvature fluctuations). Leveraging these signatures, our probabilistic framework achieves competitive performance and superior robustness across diverse benchmarks. Crucially, TRACED bridges geometry and cognition by mapping high curvature to "Hesitation Loops” and displacement to ”Certainty Accumulation”, offering a physical lens to decode the internal dynamics of machine thought.

paragraphs: TRACED evaluates language-model reasoning by examining the geometry of a reasoning trace. A single probability score can miss how reasoning develops along the way. The paper instead asks whether the trace makes sustained progress and whether its path remains stable, treating these as complementary signals of reasoning quality.

The framework measures progress through displacement and stability through curvature. The authors identify a separation in which correct reasoning follows trajectories with substantial progress and relatively stable movement, while hallucinations show stalled progress and fluctuating curvature. They interpret high curvature as hesitation loops and displacement as accumulating certainty, connecting the geometric measurements to recognizable reasoning behaviors.

These signals feed into a probabilistic framework that reports competitive performance and superior robustness across diverse benchmarks. The contribution is both evaluative and interpretive: the geometry helps assess reliability while describing how a trace proceeds or gets stuck. The reported patterns support this approach to understanding reasoning dynamics without reducing the entire process to one confidence value.
summary.tldr: TRACED uses geometric progress and stability in reasoning traces to assess reliability and interpret patterns associated with correct reasoning and hallucinations.

title: Beyond Scalars: Evaluating and Understanding LLM Reasoning via Geometric Progress and Stability

abstract: The proliferation of Large Language Models (LLMs) has shifted serving systems from processing isolated requests to orchestrating high-concurrency, multi-tenant agentic workflows. However, existing solutions typically prioritize intra-workflow optimization, largely neglecting the significant potential for inter-workflow optimization. In this paper, we propose HeraSys, an LLM serving system designed to optimize the end-to-end performance of concurrent workflows. Through fine-grained orchestration, HeraSys eliminates cross-workflow computational redundancy via structural node merging and reuse. Furthermore, HeraSys introduces a load-aware joint scheduling policy that dynamically manages execution order by evaluating both inter- and intra-query priorities. By integrating a resource skewing mechanism with adaptive batching and pipeline decomposition, HeraSys effectively mitigates tail latency while maintaining low average latency, thereby substantially improving system throughput. Extensive experiments demonstrate that HeraSys reduces P99 latency by up to 2.17$\times$ and increases serving throughput by up to 1.85$\times$ under strict latency guarantees.

paragraphs: HeraSys targets serving environments where many users run agentic language-model workflows concurrently. Each workflow contains multiple computational steps, and optimizing those steps within one workflow can miss shared work across workflows. The system treats concurrent execution as an opportunity for both reuse and coordinated scheduling.

It merges and reuses structurally matching workflow nodes to remove redundant computation. A load-aware scheduler considers priorities both within and across queries when deciding execution order. Resource skewing, adaptive batching, and pipeline decomposition then work together to manage execution. These mechanisms aim to keep average response times low while also reducing unusually slow completions.

The experiments report P99 latency reductions by a factor of up to 2.17 and throughput increases of up to 1.85 times under strict latency guarantees. P99 latency describes the slow end of the response-time distribution, so that improvement concerns requests poorly represented by the average alone. The results support optimizing whole concurrent workflows together, with shared computation and scheduling contributing to end-to-end serving performance.
summary.tldr: HeraSys combines cross-workflow computation reuse and coordinated scheduling to improve LLM serving throughput and tail latency.

title: HeraSys: Collaborative Serving of Multiple LLM Workflows via Fine-Grained End-to-End Optimization

abstract: Recent text-to-video diffusion models can synthesize visually compelling clips from natural language prompts. However, practical applications increasingly demand long-form videos with evolving narratives and persistent identity. A common solution is autoregressive generation, where the video is produced clip by clip over long horizons, yet coherence often degrades as errors compound. In this work, we study long-video generation under an autoregressive setting, where videos are synthesized clip by clip over long horizons. Despite strong short-clip quality, existing approaches often suffer from semantic drift, motion decay, and appearance instability as the sequence grows. We present DynaMem, a unified framework that improves long-horizon coherence via three components: Semantic-Adaptive Hierarchical Memory for long-range semantic preservation, Motion-Prioritized Optimization for motion-coherent learning, and Reference-Anchored Perceptual Alignment for stabilizing appearance. Extensive experiments show that DynaMem produces more consistent semantics, stronger temporal dynamics, and more stable appearance on long videos compared to competitive baselines.

paragraphs: Generating a convincing short video does not ensure that a sequence will remain coherent as it grows. In clip-by-clip generation, mistakes can accumulate: the content can drift away from its intended meaning, motion can weaken, and appearances can change. DynaMem targets these interconnected problems in autoregressive long-video generation.

The framework combines three components with distinct roles. Semantic-adaptive hierarchical memory preserves information needed over long spans. Motion-prioritized optimization emphasizes learning coherent movement. Reference-anchored perceptual alignment stabilizes appearance by relating generated content to a reference. This combination addresses continuity in meaning, movement, and visual identity within one generation framework.

Experiments report more consistent semantics, stronger temporal dynamics, and more stable appearance than competitive baselines on long videos. The significance is that maintaining a long sequence requires more than producing individually attractive clips. The reported improvements indicate that explicit mechanisms for remembering content, sustaining motion, and anchoring appearance can work together to reduce the degradation associated with repeated generation.
summary.tldr: DynaMem combines hierarchical memory, motion-focused learning, and reference-based alignment to improve coherence in videos generated clip by clip.

title: DynaMem: Consistent Long Video Generation via Hierarchical Memory and Motion Priors

abstract: Generative AI is reshaping healthcare, yet most existing advances rely on hospital-grade devices, which limits their accessibility and potential for health management outside clinical settings. With the proliferation of portable devices and telemedicine, healthcare is shifting toward home-based Diagnosis-It-Yourself (DIY) care. Despite this promise, several distinctive challenges remain: (i) home-collected data are heterogeneous, exacerbated by the absence of standardized large-scale datasets; (ii) models require adaptation to variable task demands and evolving individual conditions; (iii) the broad spectrum of home care tasks lacks a unified benchmark for systematic evaluation. In this paper, we present DIYHealth Suite, a comprehensive framework designed to address these challenges through a tailored dataset, model, and benchmark. We first curate DIYHealth-900K, a large-scale multimodal dataset capturing diverse real-world home care scenarios. Building on this, we propose DIYHealthGPT, an adaptive foundation model for home-based health management, powered by the novel Hybrid Hyper Low-Rank Adaptation technique. Finally, we establish DIYHealthBench, the first benchmark to evaluate foundation models on home care tasks. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DIYHealthGPT delivers state-of-the-art performance over both general-purpose and medical-specific baselines on 11 home care tasks in both open-QA and closed-QA settings, laying the groundwork for the next generation of personalized health management at home.

title: DIYHealth Suite: Dataset, Model, and Benchmark for Health Management at Home

abstract: Implicit Neural Representations (INRs) based on vanilla Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs) are widely believed to be incapable of representing high-frequency content. This has directed research efforts towards architectural interventions, such as coordinate embeddings or specialized activation functions, to represent high-frequency signals. In this paper, we challenge the notion that the low-frequency bias of vanilla MLPs is an intrinsic, architectural limitation to learn high-frequency content, but instead a symptom of stable rank degradation during training. We empirically demonstrate that regulating the network’s rank during training substantially improves the fidelity of the learned signal, rendering even simple MLP architectures expressive. Extensive experiments show that using optimizers like Muon, with high-rank, near-orthogonal updates, consistently enhances INR architectures even beyond simple ReLU MLPs. These substantial improvements hold across a diverse range of domains, including natural and medical images and novel view synthesis, with up to +9 dB PSNR over the samearchitecture. Code is available here.

paragraphs: Implicit neural representations use networks to represent signals, and plain multilayer perceptrons are widely viewed as poor at learning high-frequency detail. That view has encouraged changes such as coordinate embeddings and specialized activations. This paper challenges the architectural explanation, arguing that degradation of stable rank during training helps explain the observed preference for low frequencies.

The authors empirically show that regulating network rank improves the fidelity of learned signals, including those represented by simple MLPs. Their experiments examine optimizers such as Muon, whose updates have high rank and are nearly orthogonal. This shifts attention toward the geometry of parameter updates as a way to improve what an existing architecture learns.

summary.tldr: Rank-preserving optimization improves implicit neural representations, supporting the view that training dynamics contribute to plain MLPs’ difficulty with high-frequency detail.

title: Optimizing Rank for High-Fidelity Implicit Neural Representations

abstract: Tail-end risk measures such as static conditional value-at-risk (CVaR) are used in safety-critical applications to prevent rare, yet catastrophic events. Unlike risk-neutral objectives, the static CVaR of the return depends on entire trajectories without admitting a recursive Bellman decomposition in the underlying Markov decision process. A classical resolution relies on state augmentation with a continuous variable. However, unless restricted to a specialized class of admissible value functions, this formulation induces sparse rewards and degenerate fixed points. In this work, we propose a novel formulation of the static CVaR objective based on augmentation. Our alternative approach leads to a Bellman operator with: (1) dense per-step rewards; (2) contracting properties on the full space of bounded value functions. Building on this theoretical foundation, we develop risk-averse value iteration and model-free Q-learning algorithms that rely on discretized augmented states. We further provide convergence guarantees and approximation error bounds due to discretization. Empirical results demonstrate that our algorithms successfully learn CVaR-sensitive policies and achieve effective performance-safety trade-offs.

paragraphs: Static conditional value-at-risk evaluates the unfavorable tail of returns, making it useful when rare catastrophic outcomes matter. Its dependence on complete trajectories creates a challenge for reinforcement learning: the objective does not decompose through the ordinary Bellman recursion on the original state space. Classical approaches add a continuous state variable to restore a workable formulation.

The paper proposes a different augmented-state formulation that redistributes rewards across steps. Its Bellman operator provides dense per-step rewards and contraction properties across the full space of bounded value functions. This addresses sparse rewards and degenerate fixed points that arise in the classical formulation unless value functions are restricted to a specialized admissible class.

The authors build risk-averse value iteration and model-free Q-learning on this foundation, using discretized augmented states. They provide convergence guarantees and bounds on the approximation error introduced by discretization. Empirical results show learning of CVaR-sensitive policies with effective performance-safety trade-offs, linking the theoretical reformulation to algorithms that account for unfavorable trajectory outcomes.
summary.tldr: A new augmented-state CVaR formulation supplies dense rewards and contraction properties for convergent risk-averse learning algorithms.

title: Reward Redistribution for CVaR MDPs using a Bellman Operator on L-infinity

abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have achieved remarkable success in general perception, yet complex multi-step visual reasoning remains a persistent challenge. Although recent agentic approaches incorporate tool use, they often neglect critical execution feedback. Consequently, they suffer from the imagination-action-observer (IAO) bias, a misalignment between prior imagination and observer feedback that undermines reasoning stability and optimality. To bridge this gap, we introduce V-ABS, an action-observer driven beam search framework that enables deliberate reasoning through thinker-actor-observer iterations. We also propose an entropy-based adaptive weighting algorithm to mitigate the IAO bias by dynamically balancing the confidence scores between the policy priors and the observational feedback. Moreover, we construct a large-scale supervised fine-tuning (SFT) dataset comprising over 80k samples to guide the model to assign higher prior confidence to correct action paths. Extensive experiments across eight diverse benchmarks show that V-ABS achieves state-of-the-art performance, delivering an average improvement of 19.7% on the Qwen3-VL-8B baseline and consistent gains across both open-source and proprietary models.

paragraphs: Multi-step visual reasoning requires a model to connect its planned actions with what actually happens after execution. The paper identifies a mismatch between prior expectations and observed feedback, termed imagination-action-observer bias. Agents that overlook execution feedback can continue reasoning from expectations that no longer fit their observations.

V-ABS addresses this through beam search organized around thinker, actor, and observer iterations. An entropy-based adaptive weighting method balances confidence from the model’s prior policy with confidence from observational feedback. The authors also construct more than 80,000 supervised fine-tuning samples to teach the model to assign greater prior confidence to correct action paths.

It also yields consistent gains with both open-source and proprietary models. These findings support combining search, execution feedback, and learned action confidence to improve visual reasoning. The framework makes observation an active influence on which reasoning paths receive support as the task unfolds.
summary.tldr: V-ABS improves multi-step visual reasoning by balancing planned-action confidence with execution feedback during beam search.

title: V-ABS: Action-Observer Driven Beam Search for Dynamic Visual Reasoning

abstract: Score-based generative models have recently achieved remarkable success. While they are usually parameterized by the score, an alternative way is to use a series of time-dependent energy-based models (EBMs), where the score is obtained from the negative input-gradient of the energy. Crucially, EBMs can be leveraged not only for generation, but also for tasks such as compositional sampling or building Boltzmann Generators via Monte Carlo methods. However, training EBMs remains challenging. Direct maximum likelihood is computationally prohibitive due to the need for nested sampling, while score matching, though efficient, suffers from mode blindness. To address these issues, we introduce the Diffusive Classification (DiffCLF) objective, a simple method that avoids blindness while remaining computationally efficient. DiffCLF reframes EBM learning as a supervised classification problem across noise levels, and can be seamlessly combined with standard score-based objectives. We validate the effectiveness of DiffCLF by comparing the estimated energies against ground truth in analytical Gaussian mixture cases, and by applying the trained models to tasks such as model composition and Boltzmann Generator sampling. Our results show that DiffCLF enables EBMs with higher fidelity and broader applicability than existing approaches. Our code is available at h2o64/diffclf.

paragraphs: Energy-based generative models describe data through an energy function, with its negative input gradient supplying the score used for generation. This representation also supports model composition and Monte Carlo sampling applications. Training it is difficult: direct maximum likelihood requires expensive nested sampling, while efficient score matching can suffer from mode blindness, failing to adequately capture distinct parts of a distribution.

The paper introduces Diffusive Classification, or DiffCLF, which turns energy learning into supervised classification across noise levels. They report higher-fidelity energy models and broader applicability than existing approaches. The contribution therefore concerns both generating samples and learning energies that remain useful when subsequent tasks depend on the distribution those energies describe.
summary.tldr: DiffCLF trains energy-based generative models through classification across noise levels, improving energy fidelity while avoiding mode blindness efficiently.

title: A Diffusive Classification Loss for Learning Energy-based Generative Models

abstract: Typical reinforcement learning (RL) methods for LLM reasoning waste compute on hard problems, where correct on-policy traces are rare and policy gradients vanish. To bootstrap more efficient RL, we consider reusing old sampling FLOPs (from prior inference or RL training) in the form of off-policy traces. We introduce PrefixRL, where we condition on the prefix of successful off-policy traces and run on-policy RL to complete them, side-stepping instabilities from using off-policy data as supervision targets. PrefixRL boosts the learning signal on hard problems by modulating the difficulty of the problem through the off-policy prefix length. We prove that the PrefixRL objective is not only consistent with the standard RL objective but also more sample efficient. Empirically, we discover back-generalization: training only on prefixed problems generalizes to out-of-distribution unprefixed performance, with learned strategies often differing from those in the prefix. In our experiments, we source the off-policy traces by rejection sampling with the base model, creating a self-improvement loop. On hard reasoning problems, PrefixRL reaches the same training reward 2x faster than the strongest baseline (SFT on off-policy data then RL), even after accounting for the compute spent on the initial rejection sampling, and increases the final reward by 3x.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning on difficult reasoning problems can spend substantial computation producing unsuccessful solutions, leaving little useful learning signal. PrefixRL reuses successful traces obtained earlier by providing the beginning of a solution and letting the current model complete it. The supplied prefix makes an otherwise difficult problem more accessible.

The prefix comes from off-policy data, but the continuation is generated and trained with on-policy reinforcement learning. This avoids directly using old traces as supervision targets. Changing prefix length adjusts difficulty and the availability of successful continuations. The authors prove consistency with the standard reinforcement-learning objective and greater sample efficiency for the PrefixRL objective.

Empirically, training on prefixed problems improves performance even when prefixes are removed, and learned strategies often differ from those supplied. The experiments obtain successful traces through rejection sampling with the base model. Including that initial sampling cost, PrefixRL reaches the same training reward twice as fast as the strongest baseline, supervised training on off-policy data followed by RL, and achieves three times the final reward.
summary.tldr: PrefixRL reuses successful solution prefixes to strengthen on-policy learning on hard problems and improves performance even without prefixes at evaluation.

title: Reuse your FLOPs: Scaling RL on Hard Problems by Conditioning on Very Off-Policy Prefixes

abstract: We propose DynVLA, a driving VLA model that introduces a new CoT paradigm termed Dynamics CoT. DynVLA forecasts compact world dynamics before action generation, enabling more informed and physically grounded decision-making. To obtain compact dynamics representations, DynVLA introduces a Dynamics Tokenizer that compresses future evolution into a small set of dynamics tokens. Considering the rich environment dynamics in interaction-intensive driving scenarios, DynVLA decouples ego-centric and environment-centric dynamics, yielding more accurate world dynamics modeling. We then train DynVLA to generate dynamics tokens before actions through SFT and RFT, improving decision quality while maintaining latency-efficient inference. Compared to Textual CoT, which lacks fine-grained spatiotemporal understanding, and Visual CoT, which introduces substantial redundancy due to dense image prediction, Dynamics CoT captures the evolution of the world in a compact, interpretable, and efficient form. Extensive experiments on NAVSIM, Bench2Drive, and a large-scale in-house dataset demonstrate that DynVLA consistently outperforms Textual CoT and Visual CoT methods, validating the effectiveness and practical value of Dynamics CoT.

Compared to Textual CoT, which lacks fine-grained spatiotemporal understanding, and Visual CoT, which introduces substantial redundancy due to dense image prediction, Dynamics CoT captures the evolution of the world in a compact, interpretable, and efficient form. Extensive experiments on NAVSIM, Bench2Drive, and a large-scale in-house dataset demonstrate that DynVLA consistently outperforms Textual CoT and Visual CoT methods, validating the effectiveness and practical value of Dynamics CoT.

paragraphs: A driving model needs to account for how a scene will evolve before choosing an action. DynVLA introduces Dynamics CoT, an intermediate reasoning process that predicts compact representations of world dynamics. The intended benefit is to ground action generation in anticipated physical changes while keeping inference efficient.

A Dynamics Tokenizer compresses future evolution into a small collection of tokens. The model separately represents dynamics centered on the vehicle itself and dynamics centered on the surrounding environment, helping it model interaction-heavy situations. Training then teaches the model to generate these dynamics tokens before producing actions, using supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement fine-tuning.

This representation addresses two shortcomings identified in other reasoning formats: textual reasoning can miss detailed spatial and temporal information, while dense image prediction can introduce substantial redundancy. Experiments on NAVSIM, Bench2Drive, and a large in-house dataset find that DynVLA consistently outperforms the textual and visual reasoning methods evaluated. The findings support compact dynamics prediction as a useful intermediate step for driving decisions.
summary.tldr: DynVLA predicts compact world-dynamics tokens before driving actions, improving decisions while preserving efficient inference.

title: DynVLA: Learning World Dynamics for Action Reasoning in Autonomous Driving

abstract: The advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs) into higher-level reasoning domains has rendered traditional heuristic evaluators insufficient for long-form open-ended responses, precipitating the widespread adoption of rubric-based benchmarks. While these frameworks utilize expert-curated criteria and LLM-as-a-judge to assess open-ended generation, the intrinsic robustness of these evaluation harnesses to fundamental validity assessments remains critically under-investigated. To bridge this gap, we introduce RubricRobustness, a systematic sensitivity analysis framework that subjects these benchmarks to three common sense perturbations: semantic negation, stochastic deletion and irrelevant addition. We investigate the extent to which manipulating the semantic veracity of a model’s response impacts its resulting score by applying the robustness framework to two of the most popular rubrics-based benchmarks: HealthBench and WildBench. Our findings reveal systematic vulnerabilities: while both benchmarks respond sharply to semantic negation (e.g., degradation slopes of approximately $-0.38$ on HealthBench and $-0.55$ on WildBench), they are substantially less responsive to irrelevant addition, often requiring over 35% of sentences to be perturbed before inducing even a 25% score drop. We argue that perturbation-based sensitivity analyses of this form are a necessary prerequisite for validating rubric coverage, ensuring that automated evaluation frameworks reliably penalize basic semantic failures. We will release our framework as an open-source tool for building more resilient benchmarks.

paragraphs: Rubric-based benchmarks use expert criteria and a language-model judge to score open-ended responses. Their usefulness depends on whether scores respond appropriately when answers become worse. RubricRobustness tests that sensitivity through three simple changes: reversing meaning, randomly deleting content, and inserting irrelevant material.

The authors apply these tests to HealthBench and WildBench. Both react strongly to semantic negation, with reported degradation slopes of approximately −0.38 and −0.55 respectively. This exposes different sensitivities within the same evaluation systems.

The findings matter because a benchmark’s detailed rubric does not by itself establish that its scores penalize basic response failures consistently. The authors argue that perturbation-based sensitivity analysis should be a prerequisite for validating rubric coverage. They also plan to release the framework as an open-source tool, allowing benchmark builders to examine how particular degradations change scores before relying on those scores for comparisons.
summary.tldr: RubricRobustness finds that HealthBench and WildBench penalize reversed meaning much more strongly than irrelevant additions.

title: RubricRobustness: Evaluating the Sensitivity of Rubrics-Based Benchmarks to Simple Perturbations

abstract: Editing complex, long-form knowledge in Large Language Models remains a significant challenge due to the difficulty of maintaining generation coherence. Existing autoregressive methods like AnyEdit alleviate length constraints but rely on Fixed-window Chunking, which disregards logical structure and compromises consistency. To address this, we present AnyEdit++, a structure-aware framework incorporating Bayes-Chunk, an adaptive segmentation mechanism that dynamically identifies semantic boundaries based on Bayesian Surprise. We underpin this approach with a theoretical framework establishing two key principles: (1) Structural Independence: we prove that cross-segment interference is minimized when anchor keys are geometrically orthogonal (a condition naturally satisfied by our surprisal-based boundaries but violated by fixed windows), and (2) Causal Locality: we demonstrate that updates injected at these semantic peaks yield strictly superior control compared to arbitrary split points. Extensive experiments across mathematical reasoning, code generation, and narrative tasks demonstrate that AnyEdit++ achieves superior performance and robustness compared to state-of-the-art baselines, validating that structural awareness is critical for effective long-form knowledge editing.

paragraphs: Changing long passages of knowledge inside a language model requires keeping the resulting generation coherent. Earlier autoregressive editing methods can handle length more effectively, but their fixed-size chunks may cut across logical structure. AnyEdit++ addresses this issue by choosing editing segments according to the content, so that the boundaries reflect semantic changes within the material.

Its Bayes-Chunk mechanism uses Bayesian Surprise to identify those boundaries dynamically. The accompanying theory connects segmentation to two properties. First, cross-segment interference is minimized when anchor keys are geometrically orthogonal; the authors state that their surprise-based boundaries naturally satisfy this condition. The results connect a practical editing choice to a structural explanation: where a passage is divided affects how independently and effectively its parts can be updated. The theoretical interference claim specifically rests on the stated geometric condition.
summary.tldr: AnyEdit++ uses Bayesian Surprise to choose semantic editing boundaries, improving long-form knowledge editing in the reported tasks.

title: AnyEdit++: Adaptive Long-Form Knowledge Editing via Bayesian Surprise

abstract: Text-to-image diffusion models achieve impressive generation quality but inherit and amplify training-data biases, skewing coverage of semantic attributes. Prior work addresses this in two ways. Closed-set approaches mitigate biases in predefined fairness categories (e.g., gender, race), assuming socially salient minority attributes are known a priori. Open-set approaches frame the task as bias identification, highlighting majority attributes that dominate outputs. Both overlook a complementary task: uncovering rare or minority features underrepresented in the data distribution (social, cultural, or stylistic) yet still encoded in model representations. We introduce RAIGen, the first framework, to our knowledge, for label-free rare-attribute discovery in diffusion models, requiring no predefined minority categories. RAIGen leverages Matryoshka Sparse Autoencoders and a novel minority metric combining neuron activation frequency with semantic distinctiveness to identify interpretable neurons whose top-activating images reveal underrepresented attributes. Experiments show RAIGen discovers attributes beyond fixed fairness categories in Stable Diffusion, scales to larger models such as SDXL, supports systematic auditing across architectures, and enables targeted amplification of rare attributes during generation. The project page is available at https://vssilpa.github.io/RAIGen_webpage/.

paragraphs: Text-to-image models can encode attributes that appear only rarely in their outputs. Audits built around predefined fairness categories may miss these features, while analyses of dominant attributes emphasize what the model produces most often. RAIGen targets the complementary problem of discovering underrepresented social, cultural, or stylistic attributes without predefined minority labels.

The framework uses Matryoshka Sparse Autoencoders to identify interpretable neurons in model representations. A minority metric combines how frequently a neuron activates with how semantically distinctive it is. Images that activate selected neurons most strongly then reveal the associated rare attributes. Combining frequency and distinctiveness connects rarity to interpretable content rather than treating infrequent activation alone as the discovery.

Experiments show that RAIGen finds attributes beyond fixed fairness categories in Stable Diffusion and scales to larger models such as SDXL. It supports systematic auditing across architectures and targeted amplification of rare attributes during generation. The contribution is a discovery framework for underrepresented features already encoded in the model, allowing auditing and generation control to extend beyond categories chosen in advance.
summary.tldr: RAIGen discovers and helps amplify rare attributes encoded in diffusion models without requiring predefined minority categories.

title: RAIGen: Rare Attribute Identification in Text-to-Image Generative Models

abstract: Fair graph clustering has emerged as a critical research area for addressing algorithmic bias in machine learning. The objective is to ensure that the proportion of each protected group within a cluster is consistent with its representation in the entire dataset. However, most existing spectral solutions rely on computationally expensive eigendecompositions of the graph Laplacian, limiting their scalability. In this paper, we propose Riemannian Fair Spectral Clustering (R-FairSC), a novel method that formulates fair spectral clustering as a constrained optimization problem on a Riemannian manifold. We develop a Riemannian alternating direction method of multipliers employing a variable-splitting strategy to efficiently solve the associated subproblems. Numerical experiments on large synthetic and real-world graphs demonstrate that R-FairSC significantly improves computational efficiency over state-of-the-art methods while maintaining high clustering quality and fairness.

paragraphs: Fair graph clustering aims to make each cluster’s protected-group proportions consistent with those of the full dataset. This adds a representation requirement to the task of finding useful groups in a graph. Existing spectral approaches often rely on expensive eigendecompositions of the graph Laplacian, creating a computational obstacle for large graphs.

R-FairSC reformulates fair spectral clustering as constrained optimization on a Riemannian manifold, a geometric space used to express the constrained problem. The authors develop a Riemannian version of the alternating direction method of multipliers. A variable-splitting strategy divides the computation into subproblems that can be solved efficiently, providing an alternative optimization route for the clustering objective.

Numerical experiments on large synthetic and real-world graphs show substantially improved computational efficiency over state-of-the-art methods while preserving high clustering quality and fairness. The result matters because the method addresses the cost of enforcing the stated group-representation objective at scale. Its contribution is a new optimization formulation and solver with empirical support for achieving that balance efficiently.
summary.tldr: R-FairSC uses constrained Riemannian optimization to make fair spectral clustering more computationally efficient while maintaining high quality and fairness in experiments.

title: Riemannian Optimization for Fair Spectral Clustering

abstract: Parameter sharing is a key model compression technique, yet existing methods overlook the geometric properties of the loss landscape, often causing severe accuracy degradation under high compression ratios. Inspired by second-order optimization, we propose Curvature-aware Graph Coloring (CGC), a cross-layer parameter sharing framework that treats each network layer as a graph node, with each node assigned to a shared low-rank basis. CGC leverages Hessian eigenspace information to group layers with similar curvature profiles, aligning the perturbations introduced by parameter sharing with the low-curvature (flat) directions of the loss ellipsoid. This effectively mitigates performance loss while enabling flexible, global cross-layer sharing. Experiments on LLaMA-7B and Swin Transformer show that CGC achieves 28%–50% parameter compression with Top-1 accuracy loss no more than 0.01% on Swin—or even accuracy gains on LLaMA—while delivering over 60% higher inference throughput, significantly outperforming SVD-based and heuristic-based methods. This work demonstrates that curvature-guided, geometry-aware sharing is essential for efficient, stable, and high-ratio model compression.
