paragraphs: Parameter sharing compresses a model by letting multiple parts reuse parameters, but aggressive sharing can damage accuracy. Curvature-aware Graph Coloring chooses which layers should share by considering the geometry of the loss landscape. The aim is to make compression-induced changes occur along directions where the loss is comparatively insensitive.

The framework represents each layer as a graph node and assigns nodes to shared low-rank bases. It uses Hessian eigenspace information to group layers with similar curvature profiles. This guides sharing across the whole network while aligning the resulting perturbations with flatter directions of the loss geometry, reducing the performance cost of compression.

Experiments on LLaMA-7B and Swin Transformer report 28%–50% parameter compression and more than 60% higher inference throughput. Swin’s Top-1 accuracy loss is no more than 0.01%, while LLaMA shows accuracy gains. The method significantly outperforms SVD-based and heuristic alternatives in these experiments. The findings support using curvature information to identify compatible layers when pursuing substantial compression with stable predictive performance.
summary.tldr: Curvature-aware Graph Coloring compresses networks by sharing low-rank parameters across layers with compatible loss geometry.

title: Rethinking Parameter Sharing as Graph Coloring for Structured Compression

abstract: Despite rapid advances in autonomous AI scientists powered by language models, generating publication-ready illustrations remains a labor-intensive bottleneck in the research workflow. To lift this burden, we introduce PaperBanana, an agentic framework for automated generation of publication-ready academic illustrations. Powered by state-of-the-art VLMs and image generation models, PaperBanana orchestrates specialized agents to retrieve references, plan content and style, render images, and iteratively refine via self-critique. To rigorously evaluate our framework, we introduce PaperBananaBench, comprising 292 test cases for methodology diagrams curated from NeurIPS 2025 publications, covering diverse research domains and illustration styles. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that PaperBanana consistently outperforms leading baselines in faithfulness, conciseness, readability, and aesthetics. We further show that our method effectively extends to the generation of high-quality statistical plots. Collectively, PaperBanana paves the way for the automated generation of publication-ready illustrations.

paragraphs: Research illustrations must communicate scientific content clearly while remaining visually readable. Producing them is still labor-intensive even as other parts of research become more automated. PaperBanana addresses this step with a framework that coordinates specialized agents powered by vision-language and image-generation models.

The workflow includes retrieving references, planning content and visual style, rendering an image, and refining it through self-critique. Separating these activities gives the system explicit stages for deciding what a figure should communicate and how it should look. Iterative review then provides a mechanism for revising the rendered result rather than stopping after the first image.

The authors introduce PaperBananaBench, containing 292 methodology-diagram test cases curated from NeurIPS 2025 publications across varied research areas and styles. Experiments report consistent improvements over leading baselines in faithfulness, conciseness, readability, and aesthetics. They also demonstrate extension to statistical plots. These findings support coordinated planning and revision as a useful approach to academic illustration, with evaluation covering both communication quality and visual presentation.
summary.tldr: PaperBanana coordinates reference retrieval, planning, rendering, and self-critique to automate academic diagrams and statistical plots.

title: PaperBanana: Automating Academic Illustration for AI Scientists

abstract: In this paper we argue that influential critiques dismissing Large Language Models (LLMs) as a dead end for AGI misidentify the bottleneck: they confuse the ocean with the net. Pattern repositories are the necessary System-1 substrate; the missing component is a System-2 coordination layer that recruits relevant patterns, verifies their use, preserves state, and governs convergence. We separate two uses of control that are often conflated. Semantic anchoring, formalized by UCCT (Unified Contextual Control Theory), binds labels and task intent to learned pattern regions through a phase transition governed by effective support ($\rho_d$), representational mismatch ($d_r$), and an adaptive anchoring budget ($\gamma \log k$). Trace–answer verification, implemented by Recursive Causal Audit (RCA), tests whether a final causal judgment is warranted by its own reasoning trace under pressure. We translate these ideas into MACI, a multi-agent coordination stack that integrates diversity and control via baiting (PID-modulated debate), filtering (Socratic and causal audit), and persistence (transactional memory). Empirical validation on causal judgment and the sycophancy–paranoia trade-off demonstrates that static prompting fails where adaptive control succeeds. By reframing common objections as testable coordination failures, we argue that the path to AGI runs through LLMs, not around.

paragraphs: This paper argues that the main obstacle to AGI is how learned patterns are coordinated. The authors regard language models as a necessary store of patterns and propose a deliberative layer that selects relevant patterns, checks their use, maintains state, and controls how reasoning reaches a conclusion. This reframes criticisms of LLMs as potentially testable coordination problems.

Semantic anchoring connects task intent and labels to learned representations; its proposed theory describes a transition governed by effective support, representational mismatch, and an adaptive anchoring budget. Their empirical evaluation examines causal judgment and the balance between excessive agreement and excessive suspicion. They report settings where adaptive control succeeds and static prompting fails. These results support their coordination argument, while the claim about the route to AGI remains the paper’s broader position.
summary.tldr: The authors argue that progress toward AGI requires adaptive coordination that selects, checks, and preserves the use of patterns learned by LLMs.

title: Position: AGI Requires a Coordination Layer on Top of Pattern Repositories

abstract: Time series (TS) modeling has come a long way from early statistical, mainly linear, approaches to the current trend in TS foundation models. With a lot of hype and industrial demand in this field, it is not always clear how much progress there really is. To advance TS forecasting and analysis to the next level, here we argue that the field needs a dynamical systems (DS) perspective. TS of observations from natural or engineered systems almost always originate from some underlying DS, and arguably access to its governing equations would yield theoretically optimal forecasts. This is the promise of DS reconstruction (DSR), a class of ML/AI approaches that aim to infer surrogate models of the underlying DS from data. But models based on DS principles offer other profound advantages: Beyond short-term forecasts, they enable to predict the long-term statistics of an observed system, which in many practical scenarios may be the more relevant quantities. DS theory furthermore provides domain-independent theoretical insight into mechanisms underlying TS generation, and thereby will inform us, e.g., about upper bounds on performance of any TS model, generalization into unseen regimes as in tipping points, or potential control strategies. After reviewing some of the central concepts, methods, measures, and models in DS theory and DSR, we will discuss how insights from this field can advance TS modeling in crucial ways, enabling better forecasting with much lower computational and memory footprints. We conclude with a number of specific suggestions for translating insights from DSR into TS modeling.

Measurements from natural and engineered processes almost always reflect underlying dynamics. The authors advocate reconstructing those dynamics from data, using learned surrogate models that approximate how the observed system evolves.

The appeal extends beyond predicting the next few observations. A model grounded in dynamical systems can also describe long-term statistical behavior, which may matter more in some applications. The paper reviews concepts, methods, measures, and models from dynamical systems theory and reconstruction to explain how this perspective can support forecasting and analysis.

They argue that these insights could enable better forecasts with substantially smaller computational and memory demands. Their contribution is a research direction and concrete suggestions for connecting reconstruction methods with time series modeling.
summary.tldr: The authors argue that reconstructing underlying dynamics can advance time series forecasting, long-term analysis, and computational efficiency.

abstract: We present an extension of Isomap nonlinear dimension reduction (Tenenbaum etal. 2000) for data with both spatial and temporal relationships. Our method,ST-Isomap, augments the existing Isomap framework to consider temporalrelationships in local neighborhoods that can be propagated globally via ashortest-path mechanism. Two instantiations of ST-Isomap are presented forsequentially continuous and segmented data. Results from applying ST-Isomapto real-world data collected from human motion performance and humanoid robotteleoperation are also presented.

paragraphs: This paper extends Isomap to data whose observations have both spatial and temporal relationships. Its method, ST-Isomap, brings those two kinds of information into the dimensionality reduction process. This is relevant when observations belong to an unfolding sequence, so their relationships include how they follow one another as well as how they are arranged in the input space.

ST-Isomap incorporates temporal relationships into local neighborhoods within the existing Isomap framework. A shortest-path mechanism then propagates this local information globally. The resulting construction allows temporal relationships to contribute to the overall embedding through the same neighborhood-to-global pathway used to organize the data.

The paper presents two versions, addressing sequentially continuous data and segmented data. It also reports applications to real-world observations from human motion performance and humanoid robot teleoperation. These applications demonstrate the proposed extension in settings involving movement over time, while the two versions accommodate different forms of temporal organization.
summary.tldr: ST-Isomap incorporates temporal relationships into local neighborhoods and propagates them globally to embed spatial and temporal data.

title: A spatio-temporal extension to Isomap nonlinear dimension reduction
Clustering graphs by weighted substructure mining

abstract: Structural alignments are the most widely used tools for comparing proteins with low sequence similarity. The main contribution of this paper is to derive various kernels on proteins from structural alignments, which do not use sequence information. Central to the kernels is a novel alignment algorithm which matches substructures of fixed size using spectral graph matching techniques. We derive positive semi-definite kernels which capture the notion of similarity between substructures. Using these as base more sophisticated kernels on protein structures are proposed. To empirically evaluate the kernels we used a 40% sequence non-redundant structures from 15 different SCOP superfamilies. The kernels when used with SVMs show competitive performance with CE, a state of the art structure comparison program.

paragraphs: Comparing protein structures is useful when proteins have low sequence similarity. This paper develops kernels that compare proteins through structural alignments without using sequence information. The goal is to turn structural resemblance into a similarity representation that can be used for protein structure classification.

At the center of the method is an alignment algorithm that matches substructures of fixed size using spectral graph matching. The authors derive positive semidefinite kernels representing similarity between these substructures, then use them as building blocks for more sophisticated kernels over protein structures. The construction connects local structural matches with a representation suitable for kernel-based classifiers.

The evaluation uses a 40% sequence-nonredundant collection of structures from 15 SCOP superfamilies. When combined with support vector machines, the kernels achieve performance competitive with CE, a state-of-the-art structure comparison program. The finding supports the use of alignment-derived structural similarities for classification in the evaluated collection. The contribution includes both the substructure alignment method and the kernels built from its comparisons.
summary.tldr: Structural alignment kernels classify proteins without sequence information and perform competitively with CE when used with SVMs.

title: Structural alignment based kernels for protein structure classification

abstract: For large-scale classification problems, the training samples can be clustered beforehand as a downsampling pre-process, and then only the obtained clusters are used for training. Motivated by such assumption, we proposed a classification algorithm, Support Cluster Machine (SCM), within the learning framework introduced by Vapnik. For the SCM, a compatible kernel is adopted such that a similarity measure can be handled not only between clusters in the training phase but also between a cluster and a vector in the testing phase. We also proved that the SCM is a general extension of the SVM with the RBF kernel. The experimental results confirm that the SCM is very effective for largescale classification problems due to significantly reduced computational costs for both training and testing and comparable classification accuracies. As a by-product, it provides a promising approach to dealing with privacy-preserving data mining problems.

paragraphs: Large classification datasets can be reduced by clustering examples before training. The Support Cluster Machine develops a classifier around that setup, using the resulting clusters as its training inputs. Its purpose is to reduce computational cost while still allowing predictions for individual examples at test time.

The key ingredient is a compatible kernel that measures similarity both between two clusters and between a cluster and an individual vector. These two capabilities connect cluster-based training with ordinary example-based prediction. The paper also proves that the method is a general extension of the support vector machine with a radial basis function kernel.

Experiments report substantially lower computational costs for both training and testing, with comparable classification accuracy. This supports the cluster representation as an effective way to handle the evaluated large-scale problems. The authors additionally describe the approach as promising for privacy-preserving data mining. That is a potential application of working with clusters, rather than a stated guarantee that clustering alone establishes privacy.
summary.tldr: The Support Cluster Machine trains on clusters through a compatible kernel, substantially reducing training and testing costs while retaining comparable accuracy in experiments.

title: Support cluster machine

abstract: We investigate a family of poisoning attacks against Support Vector Machines (SVM). Such attacks amount to injecting specially crafted training data so as to increase the test error of the trained SVM. Central to the motivation for these attacks is the fact that most learning algorithms assume that their training data comes from a natural or well-behaved distribution. However, this iassumption does not generally hold in security-sensitive settings. As we demonstrate in this contribution, an intelligent adversary can to some extent predict the change of the SVM decision function in response to malicious input and use this ability to construct malicious data points. The proposed attack uses a gradient ascent strategy in which the gradient is computed based on properties of the SVM's optimal solution. The gradient ascent method can be easily kernelized and enables the attack to be constructed in the input space even for non-linear kernels. We experimentally demonstrate that our gradient ascent procedure reliably identifies good local maxima of the non-convex validation error surface and inflicts a significant damage on the test error of the trained classifier.

paragraphs: The paper studies poisoning attacks that introduce deliberately constructed examples into an SVM’s training data to increase its later test error. The motivation is that learning methods commonly assume naturally generated or well-behaved training data. In security-sensitive settings, an adversary may instead shape part of that data to influence the learned classifier.

The authors show that an attacker can predict, to some extent, how malicious inputs change the SVM decision function. Their method uses gradient ascent, deriving the gradient from properties of the SVM’s optimal solution. The approach also supports kernels, allowing malicious points to be constructed in the original input space even when the classifier uses a nonlinear kernel.

Experiments show that the procedure reliably finds good local maxima of the non-convex validation-error surface and substantially worsens the trained classifier’s test error. The local nature of these maxima is part of the reported result. The work demonstrates how sensitivity of a fitted model to training data can become a practical attack mechanism when that data can be manipulated.
summary.tldr: Gradient-based poisoning exploits how SVM solutions respond to training data, producing attacks that substantially increase test error in experiments.

title: Poisoning Attacks against Support Vector Machines
